situations: Day 2 opens with eight players alive, the trailseer and speculator dead from night 1, and no vote or accusation yet on record. As the lone killer who is unseen by the town, I must decide whether to speak early or stay quiet while the village builds its first read. Information landscape: Information-starved: only two night deaths and their revealed roles, with no claims, no checks, no watches, and no vote record. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win and no single result able to end the game; a mistaken early public move costs more than a quiet one because the village has no information to correct it yet. Consensus: No clear consensus yet; the village has had no vote and the day discussion has no recorded accusations, so alignment is not formed. My position: Not driving the forming view; I am with no majority because none has formed, and I am holding out from any accusation. Heat: Low: no accusations are recorded against me in the day discussion, and I have no public action on record beyond being alive on day 2. Forward exposure: Any visible claim or accusation I make would commit me to a public read that cannot be walked back once the village records it; staying silent keeps my options open but lets the discussion set the frame without me. Target landscape: Eight living players with no public role claims yet and no vote history; the only hard information is the two night deaths, so every living player is an unknown with no evidence either way. Public vs private: As the serial killer I privately know my own kills and that no one has a verified read on me; publicly I am an ordinary unclaimed player while the village discusses the two dead players, one a revealed trailseer and one a revealed speculator, with no accusations yet on record.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

situations: Day 2 opens with the village holding no claims and no accusations after a night-1 wolf kill of a trailseer and a serial killer kill of a speculator, while you, a wolf illusionist with two body-concealing uses and an unrevealed partner, must decide whether to speak early or stay silent. Information landscape: Information-starved: only the two night-1 deaths and their revealed roles are public; no investigator, sentinel, or trailseer results have been announced, and no claims exist to test. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win; the next result cannot end the game, so early visible missteps are recoverable but a lost wolf pair would compound with every later vote. Consensus: No clear village consensus has formed; day 2 discussion has not yet begun and no accusations are on record. My position: Holding out, with no public stance, in line with the quiet approach of staying unexposed until a concealment would protect a real trace. Heat: Low: no accusations were recorded in the day discussion and no one has named you, so suspicion on you is at baseline. Forward exposure: Any visible move now (a claim, a defense, a push on a target) commits you publicly before any night information exists; concealing a body is only valuable when a trace would otherwise be seen, so spending a use on a quiet night wastes it and reversibility is low once a claim is made. Target landscape: Eight living players with no public role claims and no vote history yet; the only public facts are the two night-1 deaths, so every candidate rests on behavior alone with no evidence basis. Public vs private: Privately, as the illusionist and a wolf, you know your pack partner is alive and unrevealed, and you hold two body-concealing uses; publicly, the village sees only that a trailseer and a speculator died on night 1 with roles revealed, and has no read on you.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

situations: Day two opens with eight players alive, no claims and no accusations after a day-one kill of a trailseer, and you, a wolf, must decide how visible to be before the first vote while your partner's identity is still hidden from the village. Information landscape: Information-starved: only the day-one kill and the absence of any Town result to share; no investigator, sentinel or sigilist claims have surfaced, and the block you placed last night is private. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote ends the game, but a sequence of wrong or wolf-protecting votes would close that gap steadily; the coming votes carry real cost. Consensus: No consensus has formed; the room has not yet produced any accusation or claim on the record. My position: With no forming consensus, you are neither driving nor opposing; you are holding out on any commitment. Heat: Low: no accusations recorded and the day-one wolf-channel vote on the trailseer was private; your visible footprint is a single quiet opening. Forward exposure: Any visible push or early accusation would tie your name to a specific read and is hard to walk back once the village records it; staying quiet keeps the same public footprint as every other silent player. Target landscape: Eight players alive with no public claims and no accusations on record; the day-one kill was a trailseer and the day-one block fell on a player who was not reported as roleblocked publicly, so there is no evidence-based target yet, only behavioral openings. Public vs private: As the chanteuse, you privately know you are a wolf and hold the pack's kill history, while the public sees only an unremarked day-two table with no accusations yet; your wolf partner is not revealed, so you carry the concealed identity alone at the table.

A roleblocked town player from night one may now be publicly reporting a blocked result, which would tie your night action to a visible identity claim before the first vote. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public facts are two night deaths and no claims; any roleblock report would be a player's own claim, not an announcement. Stakes: Eight alive and four eliminations from a wolf win, meaning the first vote is not decisive but each misdirected elimination moves the board toward the wolves; a single wrong vote is recoverable but costly. Consensus: The village has no shared consensus yet; the opening round has produced no accusations. My position: Holding out: you are with no faction because none has formed. Heat: Low publicly, but the wolf-channel record shows you already voted in a private day-one tally, so any late shift in your stance could look inconsistent to a careful reader. Forward exposure: Raising a claim about the night block or a specific reading would commit you to a checkable story; a later Town claim that contradicts it would expose you, and this cannot be withdrawn once spoken. Target landscape: Players with no public role status; any target chosen now would rest on behavior alone since the only public role evidence is the dead trailseer's pre-death record, which is not available. Public vs private: You privately know the trailseer died on night one and that your block on a player was placed, but the public has no record of which player was blocked or any Town result, so an accusation built on night information would rest on your private knowledge alone.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator has outed your wolf partner with a suspicious check, or a true investigator is dueling the partner's counterclaim. The room is forming an elimination consensus while you are unsuspected. Information landscape: Moderately to highly informative. There are role claims, a check report, and possibly sentinel or healer-save evidence that backs the investigator, so the town has concrete leads. Stakes: The partner is likely lost, so the wolf side's survival now depends on you staying unsuspected. Staying uncorrelated with the partner is worth more than a failed rescue that could expose you next. Consensus: The village is converging quickly on eliminating the accused partner. Its basis is the investigator's report and supporting mechanical logic from other town roles, and the room is largely ignoring pleas to slow down. My position: holding out Heat: Low to none. You are not named, but speaking up for the accused partner would put you in the spotlight. Forward exposure: Any defense of the partner is permanent on the record and becomes an associative link once the partner flips wolf, and it cannot be undone. Silence or neutral talk commits you to nothing and leaves later options open. Target landscape: The candidates are the accused wolf partner and the claimed investigator, possibly with a counterclaimer. The room is deciding on the strength of check reports and mechanical deductions, such as a healer save or ruling out other roles, rather than on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you know the accused partner is a wolf and the accusing investigator is accurate or at least credible. Publicly the room is still debating the check, and you have no suspicion on you.
lessons.action: When a credible investigator accusation or counterclaim is pulling the room against your wolf partner, stay out of the partner's defense: do not urge caution, vouch for them, or advocate for them. Keep your day talk short and about other players, or stay silent, so nothing visibly ties you to the partner and the room's attention stays on the duel. If you must speak, give only neutral points that would still stand if the partner flipped wolf.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

verdicts.why: No hard leads and the room is leaning abstain; a lone vote adds exposure without benefit.
Information-starved day; matching the majority abstain avoids a visible wolf-linked push.
No claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me; I am not the primary target.

situations: Day 2 after a night-1 kill of a trailseer: a player publicly says they had an active night role that was blocked but refuses to name it, and several players demand a name before any vote, while no one has a checkable result yet. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigator or sentinel results have been claimed, the trailseer who could have cross-checked follows is dead, and the only public evidence is the blocked claim itself. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so a wrong vote today is recoverable but would still shift the balance toward a wolf-led endgame; no single elimination ends the game. Consensus: The village is not aligned; the room is split between pressing the blocked claimant to name their role and treating the lack of any result as insufficient to vote on. My position: Holding out from any accusation, with the village focused on player_5's unverified blocked-role claim. Heat: Low to moderate: player_10 has said they would vote player_5 at low confidence, and player_9 and player_6 are pressing player_5 to name a role, so the pressure is on player_5 rather than on me. Forward exposure: Any claim of a night result or role now would be unverifiable and would commit me to a story that the block on player_5 and the night-1 kill can be tested against; retracting it later is not possible, so staying quiet keeps the option open. Target landscape: Eight alive; player_5 is the only player publicly claiming a blocked night role, with no name and no result, so the claim rests on the blocked state alone; other players have made no claims, so no one has public role evidence against them. Public vs private: Privately, as the Chanteuse, I know my pack killed a trailseer on night 1 and that I blocked player_5 that night; publicly I have claimed nothing and hold no night result, and player_5 is publicly claiming a blocked active role without naming it.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No one has claimed a tracker or exposed my visit; I am not under scrutiny.
Room leans toward abstaining with no hard leads and no accusation against me; blending with the majority is safest.
My wolf partner player_9 is not under a consensus accusation today.

situations: Day 2 after a night in which a speculator was killed by the serial killer and a trailseer died to the wolves, with a blocked player_5 refusing to name their role while several players press for a vote on that basis. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified night results, no revealed Town wills beyond role reveals, and only claims about blocks and unnamed roles. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a wrong vote is recoverable but costly, and no single vote or kill can end the game this day. Consensus: The room is unsettled and fragmented, with no shared read; discussion is centered on demanding that player_5 name a role, and no coalition has formed. My position: Holding out from any forming consensus, since none exists yet; I am engaging with checkable points to avoid being the passive default vote. Heat: Low to moderate: player_5 has drawn several pointed demands and a light low-confidence vote lean from player_10, but I have not been named by anyone with a result. Forward exposure: Any visible claim about my night or any push against another player commits me to a checkable account; a Sentinel or Trailseer naming me would turn the visit into a public test, and a denial would be hard to reverse. Target landscape: Eight alive, all unclaimed on the public record except player_5 who says a night role was blocked without naming it; the accusations so far rest on behavior and unverified blocked-role claims rather than any result. Public vs private: As the serial killer, I privately know I killed player_2 on night 1, while the public record shows only that a speculator was stabbed by the serial killer; the village now knows the killer is alive and unnamed, and I have publicly said nothing about my own night, which is the gap I must keep hidden.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

verdicts.why: No one has accused me or claimed a result that places me at the victim's door, so this situation does not hold yet.

situations: As the illusionist, I am deciding tonight's pack kill and whether to conceal its victim after the day-2 lynch removed a revealed healer (player_5, who had claimed nothing and was roleblocked night 1) and the town is now debating whose blocked role claim is real. The night-1 victim was a trailseer whose role became public, so a concealed victim would hide a role the town might otherwise use to test claims. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified checks, watches, or follows are public; the only hard facts are the revealed roles of the two dead town players and the healer's night-1 roleblock, with the vote record showing which players accused the healer. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the wolves can win, so no single kill or vote ends the game this turn; a concealed victim keeps a claimable role hidden from the town for the rest of the game, but spending one of two conceals now leaves only one for a later, more valuable kill. Forward exposure: Conceal the pack's victim would hide the victim's revealed role and will from the town, and the carrier's visit to the victim would leave no trace for a watcher or follower; using a conceal now spends one of the two remaining and is irreversible. Target landscape: Tonight's pack target is not yet named; as the illusionist and carrier this night, I hold the choice. Surviving players are player_8, player_3, player_4, player_6, player_7, player_10; the earlier victim was a trailseer (revealed) and the day-2 lynch was a healer (revealed), so the town has lost two info-role players while the remaining info claimants are unverified.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

verdicts.why: Night 2 with the pack at three players; no conceal is currently in play to spend on a victim.
Chanteuse is still alive and I am not the lone wolf yet.
This is night 2, not night 1, so the early-conceal logic does not apply directly; I will hold my charges.
Victim player_1 was a trailseer with no public claim; no concealment decision is needed while the carrier is the only wolf acting and the kill is unclaimed.
Two wolves are alive, so this lone-wolf endgame does not apply.
Night 1 situation is past; I hold both conceals and the pack should keep them since the victim's role and will are already public.
Victim player_1 was a trailseer with no conceal in use this night; the carrier is me and I am not concealing tonight's kill.
Chanteuse is still alive and I am not the lone wolf.
Night 1 concealment was already decided; tonight I hold both charges to keep my visit less exposed while still a quiet unread target.

situations: Day 3 is approaching with the village just having lynched a Town healer on thin evidence after a blocked role claim that was never named. As the investigator with two checks, I hold the only unspent information tool among the living, and I must decide whether to spend a check on a player the village is currently divided over, or hold both checks until a stronger accusation forms. The concern is that the wolves and serial killer are still active and the village has no reliable reads. Information landscape: Information-starved. No confirmed roles beyond the public deaths of the trailseer and speculator and the revealed healer. No claimed results have been tested against a night death. My own two checks are the only private information source on the board, and no other living player has a verified result. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win. A wrong lynch is recoverable but costly, and each further mis-elimination moves the wolves and the serial killer closer to parity, so my two checks are a scarce resource that should resolve the most uncertainty before a vote. Target landscape: Seven players alive: player_3, player_6, player_7, player_8, player_9, player_10, and me. Public roles: player_5 was just eliminated and revealed as the healer, a Town role, so the village is down its protector. The three day-2 accusers of player_5 and the abstainers differ in basis. Player_10 pressed the vote and accused player_5 on the basis of a blocked role claim with no result, and player_5 had accused player_10 in return. No candidate has a verified role; all are unknown and judged from behavior and vote history.

lessons.situation: After the Day 2 vote and a Day 1 or 2 reveal, the voting record shows a few players splitting from the room: defending an eliminated wolf, or pushing to eliminate the Investigator without evidence. One wolf (or the pack's remainder) is likely hiding among them, and the Investigator has one check left. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed wolf or sentinel death is on the record, plus public vote tallies showing clear outliers. No private proof yet, so the final check converts behavioral suspicion into a result. Stakes: The pack is already thinned and one check remains, so the last check is the Investigator's final chance to confirm a wolf. A correct hit can lead to eliminating the remaining wolves and winning, while a wasted check leaves Town without direction. Target landscape: Seven or so living players, with roles of the dead revealed. The best candidates are outlier voters on Day 2: a sole counter-voter defending a revealed wolf, or two voters who coordinated against you while the rest abstained. The basis is public vote behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With your last check, check the player whose Day 2 vote record most clearly diverges from the room: the lone defender of a revealed wolf, or a voter who pushed against you without evidence. Voting records are public and permanent, so these outliers are the likeliest wolf partners, and a Suspicious result gives you a concrete lead to act on.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a discussion-only Day 1. The Investigator holds both checks and must choose between holding them and probing an unread player blind. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no claims, no votes, no night results. Stakes: Early board with no pressure, so no single check is decisive. But the Investigator may die before a banked check is ever used, and any early read, whether it finds a wolf or clears an ally, compounds into later votes. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, flips or behavioral tells. Pick a quiet, non-prominent player at random, since nothing separates them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no leads, spend one check on a quiet, unclaimed player instead of banking both. An early Suspicious finds a wolf, and a Not suspicious gives you a baseline read. Treat a clean result as clearing only wolves: the Serial Killer and neutrals also read Not suspicious, and a Necromancer reads that way on any night it does not attack.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended in an abstain after multiple night deaths, with two killing factions active and only soft, unverified role claims on the table; the Investigator still has both checks. Information landscape: Information-starved: the claims are unverifiable and no alignments are confirmed, so any read has to come from behavior. Stakes: With two killing factions active and no hard leads, the village needs at least one verified collaborator; an early check on a central voice yields a lasting anchor even if the investigator dies. Target landscape: Unverified claimants, quiet players, and an analytical non-claimant who is actively evaluating claims; no one has confirmed alignment, and behavior is the only basis for choosing.
lessons.action: If the night has no hard lead, use a check on an active, influential player who has not claimed a role and is shaping the vote, to build a verified anchor among the central voices. A Not suspicious read clears a wolf or town member but does not clear a lone killer, so treat the anchor as likely town rather than certain.

situations: Day 2 ends a lynch on a player who had stonewalled about a blocked night role; the revealed healer's roleblock is now public. The table is split between those who pushed the lynch and two abstainers, and no night result has been claimed publicly yet, so the next day's vote rests on behavior alone. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified investigation, sentinel, or trailseer results have been made public; the only hard fact is the revealed healer role and its night-one roleblock. Evidence is behavioral (voting patterns, abstentions, defenses of the lynched player). Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single elimination can end the game; a wrong vote is recoverable but each mis-elimination moves the evil side closer to parity. Forward exposure: Any visible move now, such as a named accusation or a claimed night result, commits the speaker to a public role or result that can later be checked against deaths; a vote is permanent on the record, so a wrong vote cannot be withdrawn. Target landscape: Six surviving candidates: player_3, player_4, player_7, player_8, player_9, player_10 (the speaker is one of seven living). No living player has a revealed role. Player_5 was just lynched and revealed as healer, so its earlier roleblock is now public fact. Remaining candidates are judged only on behavior: who piled onto the lynch, who abstained, and who spoke on the blocked role.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

verdicts.why: Night 1 is over and the board now has two deaths and a lynch, so the blind opening-kill advice no longer applies.
No claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect or cleared me, so this situation does not hold.
No healer save has been announced on a claimed investigator, and the healer is dead after the lynch.

situations: As the sigilist with two sigils, you face a night where the pack or the serial killer will likely attack one of the six remaining players, and a sigil placed on whoever attacks will strike that attacker. The village lynched a healer who claimed a blocked role without naming it, so no one is publicly verified as a night actor; the question is whether a sigil spent on a behaviorally suspicious player would catch a wolf or a serial killer attacking. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigator or sentinel result has been announced, the only verified fact is the night-one block on the lynched healer, and day-two accusations rest on behavior and claims rather than results. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single wrong sigil or lynch is recoverable but each sigil spent without a strike removes one of only two remaining traps, and a wrong target would leave the wolves or serial killer free to act at no cost. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil on a player is a visible visit-commitment that spends one of two sigils permanently; it only reveals itself as a trap if the target attacks, and a sigil on a non-attacker returns only 'no effect', which would narrow suspicion without spending the other sigil's worth of information. Target landscape: Seven alive: the surviving players are player_3, player_4, player_6, player_8, player_9, player_10 and you. No one has a public role claim tied to tonight's kill. Public role status: player_1 (trailseer) and player_2 (speculator) dead by night, player_5 (healer) lynched and revealed. The remaining players' roles are unknown; the only evidence is behavioral: player_10 pressed the lynch on player_5, player_8 and player_9 abstained, and player_5 claimed a blocked role without naming it.

A night attack is likely from the wolves or the serial killer, but a sigil only strikes an attacker who is not night-immune, and the chanteuse can block a visiting player before the sigil resolves. The sigilist is deciding whether to hold both sigils through another night rather than spend one on a player whose behavior is the only read available. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public result is a night-one block on the lynched healer; the village has no investigator or sentinel check to test anyone against, so any sigil placement would rest on the sigilist's own read. Stakes: Seven alive and three eliminations from an evil win, so the village can absorb a few more non-decisive nights, but each night of holding sigils without a strike lets the pack or serial killer kill again at the cost of one player per night, which the village cannot afford indefinitely. Forward exposure: Keeping both sigils commits to no visible move tonight; the cost is that an attack lands unpunished, and any later sigil placement reveals the sigilist's trust in a specific player to the table. Target landscape: Six surviving players other than yourself, none publicly confirmed as an active night role. The serial killer is unrevealed and cannot be killed at night, so an attack on it would fail silently, which means a sigil placed on it would not register. The wolves' carrier rotates through the living wolves, and the chanteuse is still active and blocks a player each night.

lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten players alive, day one was discussion only with no vote or deaths. The sigilist must decide between placing a sigil on a blind guess and keeping the charges. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no role claims, no voting records, no visit histories to separate likely attackers from passive roles. Stakes: Early board with a large margin before any faction can win. Nothing is forcing a spend, and each of the two charges is worth more on a night with a real lead than on a coin-flip target. Forward exposure: Holding reveals nothing and commits nothing, and the charge stays available. Placing is irreversible, spends one of two charges, and is a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unvetted: no claims, no votes, no night results. Any target is a pure guess, and most players, including investigative, protective and passive roles, will not attack.
lessons.action: On night one, when there are no deaths, claims, votes or visit data, keep both sigils and place none. A sigil only does anything if its target attacks that night, and a blind pick usually lands on a non-attacker (several observations show it striking nothing and spending a charge). Hold the charges until a night when a specific suspect is likely to attack.

verdicts.why: No wolf attack or carrier evidence yet; no night deaths on day 2 night to target.
Day two ended with a clear lynch of player_5, not an abstain or split vote.
No night attack or save has happened since day 1 deaths on the current board.
Still no attack evidence or visit data on any living player, so holding both sigils is the sound choice.

situations: Day 2 has just ended with player_5, a revealed healer, lynched by a 5-vote majority after refusing to name the role it claimed was blocked; the village now has no confirmed information source on the night dead, and the sentinel holds two unspent watches while a night's deaths are still unknown. Player_1 (trailseer) and player_2 (speculator) died on night 1, and the wolf pack and serial killer remain hidden. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has published a verified night result, the only checkable public events are the day-2 vote record and the night-1 deaths, and the sentinel's own watch results are private. The deciding evidence would come from a watch on a likely night victim or a suspect, and both watches are unspent. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single wrong night result or lynch is recoverable but each further mis-elimination moves the wolves and serial killer closer to parity; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so the two watches can be held for a higher-value night without immediate loss. Target landscape: Seven players alive: player_4, player_6, player_7, player_8, player_9, player_10, and the sentinel's own seat. Public role status: no living player has claimed a role; player_5 (healer) was eliminated and revealed, and player_5 had refused to name the role they claimed was blocked. Evidence is behavioral only: player_5 pushed a blocked-active-role claim, player_10 voted to eliminate player_5, and player_8 and player_9 abstained on the vote.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. The Night 1 kill, a possible roleblock and the lone killer's attack can all land the same night, so the result may be lost, show nothing, or catch a key visitor. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no night results, no claims and no voting record. Only opening-round chatter exists. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive, so one blind watch is a cheap bet. Results across the cluster varied: zero visitors, a visit from the healer or trailseer, a multi-visitor cluster, and the serial killer caught at the door. The cost is that the Sentinel itself may be killed or blocked that night and the result lost, so only one of the two charges should be committed. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes or role flips. Every door is equally unknown, so choose a quiet, unpressured player on pure behavior, since there is no evidence to separate them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, deaths or reads, spend one of the two watches on a quiet, unclaimed player and keep the second for later. A watch can catch the killer's visit or reveal who is acting at night, and the visitor list is the only hard evidence a Sentinel can gather before Day 2. Pick a target the pack or the lone killer might plausibly hit, not a loud player who is likely to draw heat.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night after an abstain or tied vote. Conflicting role claims are on the board and you hold one watch left. You must decide whose door to watch, knowing results come only from visitors to that player. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, vote records and some prior night results, but nothing is verified. Alignments of the candidates are unconfirmed, and visit data exists only for whoever you watch. Stakes: Town can still afford a mistake, but this is the last watch, so a wasted use leaves no visitor-tracking for the rest of the game. A watch that exposes a visit pattern or kill trace can settle a claim fight before wolves reach parity. Target landscape: The choice is between a contested claimant (e.g. counter-claimed investigator or sigilist) under heavy suspicion, the obvious wolf-priority targets (claimed investigator, healer, trailseer), a quiet player from a tied vote, or an investigator-cleared player. The claim conflicts are public, but none of the candidates is verified. Only the contested claimant or the likely kill target is likely to draw visits.
lessons.action: With your last watch, pick the player most likely to receive a visit tonight. That means a contested or heavily accused claimant whose claim other roles can verify or attack, or the likely wolf kill target. A watch on a quiet suspect or an already-cleared player usually returns "no visitors", because attackers visit their victims, not themselves.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, with the first watch already spent and one watch left. The Sentinel is deciding whether to use it on a personal adversary or hold it for a higher-value door.
