Every watch is a visit, and the Sentinel is not told of its own visit. Information landscape: Still thin: the Night 1 result is the main hard fact, plus a few public claims and one vote record. There are no confirmed wolf identities, so targeting rests on likely attack paths and not on proof. Stakes: The last watch is the Sentinel's final hard evidence, and once it is spent the role has nothing left to do at night. Spending it on a low-traffic door gave nothing in the cluster, so a likely-attack target improves the chance of a usable visitor list. Target landscape: A handful of living players: a prominent claimed or confirmed Town role, a player who has accused you, and quiet unverified players. Favor the one most likely to be attacked or visited, based on public claims or revealed roles, over one picked because they are hostile to you.
lessons.action: Save the last watch for a night when you can name a door that is likely to be attacked or visited, such as a prominent claimed role or a player the wolves or killer plausibly want dead. A watch on a vocal accuser or a quiet bystander tends to return a zero-visitor result, and a watch is spent whether or not it shows anything.

verdicts.why: This is Night 2, not Night 1, and the board now has a lynch and a healer reveal.
No tied or abstain vote produced this night; the day ended with a lynch of player_5.
I have not spent my first watch yet, so this point's premise does not hold.

situations: Day 2 after a day-one lynch of a claimed-but-unnamed blocked role player who turned out to be the healer. The village has no sentinel or investigator result to test against deaths, and one player is pressing a single target while two players abstained. The vigilante holds shots without any verified information about who the wolves or the serial killer are. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigator or sentinel result has been publicly claimed, the trailseer died night one, and the only public facts are the day-two vote record and the healer's roleblock record read out after elimination. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong shot or vote is recoverable but each bullet is one of only two, so a shot spent on an untested read cuts the vigilante's remaining reach to a single kill. Forward exposure: Firing a shot is a public visit that reveals the vigilante role to the village at night's result and spends one of two bullets irreversibly; holding fire keeps the role hidden and leaves both bullets available. Target landscape: Seven players alive: the vigilante's own suspects are the remaining six others. No candidate has a public role claim; the only accusation so far was against the healer, who was just eliminated by vote and revealed as healer with a night-one roleblock record. Evidence is almost entirely behavioral: a blocked role was claimed but never named, and votes split between an abstain pair and an accusing majority.

The day-two vote closed with an accusing majority against the just-revealed healer and two abstentions. One player is repeatedly pushing a single accusation and asking others to name roles, while the eliminated player had refused to name a blocked role. The vigilante is deciding how much of their private suspicion to surface before any night result exists. Information landscape: Information-starved: only voting record and speech patterns are public; no role claims are confirmed and no night results are testable yet. Stakes: Seven alive and three eliminations from the leading evil faction's win means a wrong day vote costs one of the few reachable eliminations; the village has room for one or two mistakes before a wolf-favoring count emerges, so public reads should stay tied to testable outcomes. Forward exposure: Stating a suspicion of a player in the open day discussion commits the vigilante's read publicly and can be tested against the next night's deaths; it does not spend a bullet but makes the vigilante a visible target if the read proves wrong. Target landscape: Among the seven alive, the player pushing a single-target accusation (who voted with the majority to eliminate the healer) and the two abstainers are the candidates; none has a claimed role, so all reads rest on voting pattern and speech behavior alone.

lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.
lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

verdicts.why: No role is confirmed and no result singles out a wolf, so I hold fire again and keep both bullets.
The healer lynch was a Town loss, but no revealed role or contradiction points to a specific living wolf.

situations: Day 2 follows a lynch of a player who refused to name a blocked night role after being roleblocked on night 1. Several players pressed for the role claim and voted him out, while others abstained. The next night's pack kill and any town role's night action (protect, watch, check, follow, shot, sigil) must be chosen among the surviving town players and the pack partner. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results are public beyond the night 1 kill and the healer's block. Claims are unverified, and the only checkable thread is which claimed results match the coming night's deaths. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single wrong lynch or kill is recoverable but each error shortens the margin; the game cannot end within one more elimination. Forward exposure: Any visible night-target or vote choice commits me to a position in a public record; a revealed block or claim cannot be retracted, and the wolf pack's kill on the public record is already fixed by its own night choices. Target landscape: Seven players alive: the remaining town-aligned roles, the pack partner, and unknown others. No live player has a confirmed role; the healer was lynched on day 2 and the trailseer and speculator died earlier. Candidates are judged by behavior, not evidence.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

verdicts.why: No confirmed vigilante has revealed itself and the trailseer died night 1 without a wolf-partner kill context; the lethal-role threat is unconfirmed.
No Day 2 public role claims exist yet, so the investigator or tracker block logic cannot be applied on this board.
Opening-night blind block was already spent on player_5, who was lynched; remaining choice is a fresh block target among unrevealed town players.
No confirmed vigilante has revealed itself; the lethal-role kill-and-block pattern does not apply yet.
No public information role has claimed and no Day 2 night result exists for a block decision on the investigator or trailseer.
Opening-night blind block logic is outdated; the pack already has a planned quiet kill on player_7 and my block should stay off that target.

situations: As a wolf illusionist with two conceals left, you face the night after the town lynched a claimed-blocked healer on day 2 and the pack has settled on a quiet kill. The open question is whether the chosen victim's revealed role and record would give the town useful information, which would make a conceal worth spending, or whether a plain kill is cleaner. A player who was roleblocked and never named their role is still pushing the town toward a second accusation, and the wolf channel shows the pack agreeing to follow the carrier's call. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living claimed result, only the public death of the trailseer and the lynched healer's blocked night; the only checkable evidence is future night deaths. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single kill or vote ends the game; the wolves have room to spend a conceal, but each spent conceal removes one of only two hidden-trace protections for later nights, and a wrong or revealing kill costs more because the remaining pool is small. Forward exposure: Choosing tonight's pack kill and whether to conceal the victim commits the illusionist's carrier visit and a conceal use; a conceal is irreversible and spends one of two remaining uses, while a plain kill leaves the victim's role public to the town. Target landscape: Seven players alive; the pack is weighing quiet unclaimed candidates such as the quiet player_7, who has pushed no read. No living player has publicly claimed a night role with a verified result, so every candidate is information-starved; the healer and trailseer are already dead.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

verdicts.why: No investigator or sentinel has claimed a result, and the chanteuse is alive, so the lone-illusionist scenario does not hold.
I hold both conceals and no victim role is publicly claimed, so there is no conceal decision to make tonight.
Night 1 is past; the pack already killed, so the quiet unread-kill logic applies only as a general preference.

situations: Night 2 for a chanteuse who blocked the healer on night 1 and whose pack has agreed on a quiet town player as the kill. The healer was lynched on day 2 after being blocked on night 1 and refusing to name their role, and the village is still waiting for a claimed sentinel or investigator result to test against tonight's deaths. The carrier rotates to a partner wolf, who has set the kill, so this night's block must be chosen to avoid the pack's victim while removing the most dangerous town night action. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public result has been announced except the day 1 kill and the day 2 lynch. The only private information is the chanteuse's own block record and the pack's kill. No town claim has been checked against a death, so every candidate block target is unverified. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the next single elimination does not end the game, so a misdirected block or kill is recoverable but each wasted night brings the wolves closer to parity. Forward exposure: Any visible move tonight (a claim, a block declared, or a vote) would commit the chanteuse's standing in a village where the healer was just lynched and no claim has yet been tested; a public block cannot be retracted once the blocked player reports it. Target landscape: Town players alive: the quiet player the pack has settled on as the kill (no public role claim, no pushed read), the player who has been pressing for claimed results, and the player who has been voting with the majority. None of these has a verified public role; all judgments rest on behavior and vote pattern, not evidence.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles such as the healer and necromancer are confirmed, and the investigator and trailseer have public claims and results on record. Stakes: Town has lost its healer protection but still has information roles; removing the investigator while blinding the tracker for a night shifts the information balance toward the wolves before parity pressure builds. Forward exposure: Blocking shows the village only that some blocker exists, if the blocked player speaks of it; nothing ties the block to you, and you can switch block targets nightly. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.
lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

verdicts.why: No Town information role has claimed or produced a result yet, so the claimed-investigator threat does not hold.
This is no longer the opening night, and the board has public deaths and a day vote.
The healer died by lynch, not claims and results on record, so this situation does not hold.

situations: Day 3 opens with five alive after two prior eliminations (a lynched healer and two night deaths of a speculator and a vigilante plus a concealed-role death). You, the serial killer, must decide whether to speak aggressively and push a vote, or to stay low, while the village lacks any verified role information beyond one concealed body. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a verified role claim; the only public data are the revealed records of the dead (the trailseer, speculator, healer, vigilante) and one concealed death whose role is hidden by an illusionist. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from the leading evil faction's parity point, meaning a single wrong lynch or night kill can put the game within reach of an evil win; a wrong vote is costly and hard to undo. Consensus: The room is unsettled after the day-2 lynch of a healer; no clear consensus has formed on a target for today, and the discussion has not yet begun. My position: Holding out: you have no public stance and are not yet part of any forming majority. Heat: Low to moderate: no public accusation names you, but the day-2 lynch of the healer was driven by a bloc of pushers, and you are a living unrevealed player in a room where the village is hunting roles. Forward exposure: Any visible accusation or vote you push would tie you to a side and draw scrutiny toward the most vocal pusher; a public lynch push is hard to reverse once votes are recorded on the permanent public record. Target landscape: Five living players: three unrevealed players whose roles are unknown to the village, and two others with no public role claims; the choice is among vocal pushers versus quiet players, based on behavior rather than evidence, since no role claims or verified results exist today. Public vs private: As the serial killer you privately know you killed the speculator on night 1 and the vigilante on night 2; publicly the village only knows that a speculator and a vigilante died and that a concealed player's role is unknown. Your private knowledge is complete on your own kills, while the village reads the deaths as wolf or unknown-killer activity.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

verdicts.why: No Sentinel has claimed on me and no visit report exists, so the Day 2 duel is not in play.
I am not under a role-result accusation and have no concrete case to build yet.
No role claimant has named me as passive, so I do not need to answer that pressure today.

situations: Day 3 opens with five players alive and no claimed information roles; the village has no checkable results to test, and you, a wolf, hold a concealed-body record that the village cannot see while your partner's identity remains unknown. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation, sentinel, or trailseer result has been publicly claimed, and the only public facts are the day-2 vote record and the concealed death of a player whose role is hidden. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a wolf-side win at worst; a single wrong lynch or kill could let the evil side reach parity, so every vote carries near-decisive cost, and the concealed-body record gives the wolves an information edge that the village cannot counter. Consensus: The room is quiet and has not formed a clear consensus on a target; prior agreement was to follow whoever holds a checkable result, and no such result has been claimed. My position: With the majority by default, not driving any read, holding a quiet position. Heat: Low: you have made no claims and pushed no reads, and your votes followed the room, but the wolf partner's identity is unknown to the village and the record of day-2 votes is public. Forward exposure: Any visible push now would tie your name to a read the village can test against the still-living roles; the one remaining conceal use cannot be undone once spent on a victim, and drawing attention now raises heat before the next kill. Target landscape: Five living players: player_3, player_4, player_6, player_8 and one other; none publicly claimed a role this day, and the only public basis is voting history and earlier pushes (player_5 lynched on a majority, player_10 argued for it), with no hard evidence on any remaining player. Public vs private: Privately, as the illusionist, you know the body of player_7 was concealed and that they were a sigilist, while the public only sees a death with a hidden role; you also know the pack's kill history, which the village does not.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

verdicts.why: Nobody has put a tracking report or shared vote on me, so I am not under that pressure.
Early day with no claims to answer; keeping quiet and low-profile fits this board.
Five players are alive, not four, and no late-game consensus has formed against me.

situations: Day 3 with five alive and no claims: the village has lost a healer and a vigilante and wants an investigator or sentinel to speak, while I, the wolf Chanteuse, hold a block history and an unrevealed partner that a public read could expose. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has claimed a role, the day-2 lynch was based on behavior, and the only night results are private to their holders. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a possible wolf-side parity at worst for the town; a wrong day vote or one more kill could end the game, so every visible move carries weight. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned behind the day-2 lynch outcome and wants a checkable information role to surface, with no shared target for today. My position: With the room's quiet-majority posture, holding out from any public accusation. Heat: Low to moderate: I have voted only once and abstained on day 2 with the room, and no one has named me, but I am one of the quiet voices the table notices. Forward exposure: Any visible push on the day-3 vote or any claim about night results would tie my name to the pack's line; a claim is hard to retract and would expose the block history and the pack's kill pattern. Target landscape: Five living players: two quiet non-claimers who have not pushed reads, and one analytical voice who could be an information role; none has a public role claim, so every candidate rests on behavior alone, not evidence. Public vs private: Privately, as the Chanteuse, I know my wolf partner is alive and unrevealed, and I know which player my block hit last night did not take; publicly the village sees only a quiet day-3 table with no claims and a day-2 lynch that went to a majority.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

verdicts.why: My wolf partner is alive, so this partner-loss situation does not hold.
Five players are alive, not three, so the final-day situation does not apply.
My partner has not been eliminated, so this situation does not hold.

situations: A claimed investigator announced a Suspicious read on me and asked for a vote today, while another player pressed me to explain my day 2 abstention, creating a pressure point where my silence reads as evasion. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified investigator claim with a single Suspicious result, no confirmed eliminations of claimants, and the concealed body's role unknown to the town. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a wolf-side win at worst for the town (a concealed body's side is unknown, so this is the closest it could be); a wrong lynch of the one wolf-side player among these five would leave the pack needing only one more kill to reach parity, so this vote is decisive. Consensus: The room is forming toward voting player_9 today, based on the investigator's Suspicious claim and the day 2 abstention, with no independent confirmation. My position: Holding out against the forming consensus on my own case while needing to avoid visibly resisting it. Heat: Moderate and rising: a claimed investigator named me as Suspicious, and another player asked me to explain my day 2 abstention, so suspicion sits on me from the claim alone. Forward exposure: Any visible move now, such as defending or attacking the investigator claimant or revealing my concealment history, would commit me publicly; I have only said I have no claim, so staying silent or voting with the room keeps the option open. Target landscape: Two live options in the public read: the investigator claimant's Suspicious check on player_9 (a claim with no confirmation yet, no elimination has tested it) versus player_9 themself, who abstained on day 2 without reasons; the wolf-side identity of player_9 is my own private fact, not public. Public vs private: Privately, as the illusionist (a wolf), I know my own role and that player_7 was a sigilist whose body I concealed; publicly the role is hidden and the room reads the concealed death as an unknown role, so my cover is unclaimed while the room treats the investigator claim as the only hard information.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been revealed and killed. You are pressured over a lone vote against a dead Town player, while a Town player's result (a non-triggering sigil) is available as a defense. Information landscape: Moderate: public voting records and a privately held Town result that can be used to clear you, but no hard role confirmations on the quiet alternative suspect. Stakes: Each vote now decides whether the last wolf survives. Moving even a couple of swing voters off you keeps the wolf team alive into the final few players. Consensus: The village is split. Some players press you over the vote record, while players holding a clearing result and neutral voters are open to another suspect. My position: holding out Heat: High. Players cite your isolated vote against a now-dead player as the basis for suspicion. Forward exposure: Citing a Town player's result ties you to a non-attacking story that you cannot take back, and later tracking evidence could break it. The alternative-suspect push can be adjusted as new information arrives. Target landscape: Candidates are you, under pressure from the vote record, and a quiet player with no confirmed role who was targeted by the dead wolf. Suspicion of the quiet player is behavioral, while the case against you is the vote record. Public vs private: Privately you are an active wolf, but the partner carried the kill that night, so a Town result such as an un-triggered sigil looks exculpatory. The room reads that result as evidence you are not the killer.
lessons.action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Use only what the rules show: the sigil not triggering means only that you did not attack on that night, and it does not clear you of being a wolf. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

decision.message: I abstained on day 2 because the lynch on player_5 rested on a blocked-role argument with no result behind it, not because I'm hiding something. player_4, you're the only one with a check on me, so what did you check on night 1, and what did you get? If you have nothing else, that's a single unverified result to vote on.

verdicts.why: My partner is still alive, so no wolf partner has been revealed dead and I have no lone vote to defend.
No tracking report or shared vote with a dead wolf points at me on the public record.
The room is comparing claims, but I was directly addressed, so I must answer rather than stay low-content.

decision.message: player_4, one Suspicious result is all you've given, and you still hold a check from night 1 you didn't use. If you're the real investigator, check player_3 tonight and we'll have a second data point before a lynch. My abstain was about a lynch resting on a blocked-role argument, not hiding anything.

verdicts.why: No sigil or lone vote on my record; I'm not being pressed over a shared kill vote.
No tracking report or dead-wolf vote overlap points at me; the pressure is one Suspicious check.
Investigative roles are not comparing notes; player_4 has made a direct accusation I must answer.

decision.message: Yes, I'm town, and I'm not claiming a role or sharing night details. As I said earlier, I abstained because the day-2 lynch rested on no result. player_4, you have one check left, so use it on player_3 and we get a second data point before anyone gets voted.

verdicts.why: My wolf partner player_8 is still alive, and no one has pressed a vote against me alone.
No tracking report or shared vote with a dead wolf points at me; the pressure is only player_4's single Suspicious read.
Town investigative roles are arguing over a live accusation, not comparing night logs, so this early-silence advice doesn't fit.

decision.message: player_4, you have given one Suspicious result, and you refuse to use your last check on player_3 to test it. player_3 is pushing this vote hard on that single read, so I'd rather see the test run before anyone is lynched. I abstained on day 2 because that lynch rested on a blocked-role argument with no result, and I'm not hiding anything.

verdicts.why: I have no sigil or check result to show, so I won't cite one; I'll rely on the abstain reason and a concrete test.
Nobody has a tracking report or shared dead-wolf vote on record against me, so this point doesn't match the board.
Day 3 has an accusation and a lynch vote, not an early quiet-claims phase, so this point doesn't fit.

situations: A claimed investigator announced a Suspicious read on a player and pushed for a vote today; the accused demanded a second data point, noting the claimant still holds an unused check, and the claimant refused to spend it on the accuser. The village must decide whether one unverified result justifies an elimination. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious result, no second check, no confirmed role claims beyond the investigator claim, and two prior deaths whose roles are public but give no information about the living. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination until the leading evil faction can win at worst for the town, so a wrong lynch today could bring the game within one more elimination of a loss; the next result can end it, making each vote consequential and a mis-elimination hard to recover from. Consensus: The village is split: one side is building toward a lynch of the accused on the basis of a single Suspicious check, the other side is asking for a second result before voting; no clear consensus has formed. My position: Holding out from the forming lynch push, neither driving the accusation nor defending the accused. Heat: Low on the agent: no public accusations name the serial killer, and the agent has spoken little and only with new information, though the village's attention is on the investigator dispute. Forward exposure: Any visible push to eliminate a player or any accusation you make would tie your reads to the village's record; staying quiet keeps you unexposed, and a lynch is reversible only by the village's next vote, so visible moves commit you to a position others can later check. Target landscape: Five living players: one claimed investigator with a single Suspicious read on a player, the accused who abstained on day 2 and is demanding a second data point, the claimant's accuser who pushes for a second check, and two quieter players with no claims; the only hard information is one unverified Suspicious result. Public vs private: As the serial killer, you privately know you killed two players (a speculator on night 1 and a vigilante on night 2), while the public only sees two stabbings with roles revealed; you know the wolves' kill and your own are separate, and the village reads the day-3 investigator dispute with no knowledge of your role.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

decision.message: player_3, you're pushing a vote on player_9 off one Suspicious result from player_4. Is there anything you've checked yourself, or is it only that claim? Before anyone is lynched, a second data point from the night would be a fairer test than a single read.

verdicts.why: No Sentinel has named me as a visitor, so there is no Day 2-style visit accusation.
I am not the main target today; the lynch debate centres on player_9.
No claimed role has labelled me passive, and I have not been singled out.

situations: A claimed investigator announced a Suspicious read on the abstaining player_9 and demanded an immediate vote, while player_9 and others demand a second check before any lynch; the claimant still holds one unused check and a wolf-side accuser has pressed for it. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious result from a claimed investigator, no sentinel or trailseer results, and two wolf-side-adjacent accusations with no corroboration. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a wolf-side win at worst for the town, so the next result can end the game; a wrong lynch on day 3 is nearly fatal and cannot be recovered from easily. Consensus: The room is split: one faction presses a vote on player_9 off the single Suspicious read, while others want a second data point before any lynch. My position: Holding out, with no public stance; I am neither driving the vote on player_9 nor defending them. Heat: Low to moderate on me: I have made no public claims and kept a quiet profile, but my day-1 and day-2 wolf-channel discussion is private, so my public record is thin and unexamined. Forward exposure: Any public stance on the day-3 vote commits me visibly; pushing or defending either side would be hard to reverse and would tie my visible record to the wolf-side or town-side read. Target landscape: A claimed investigator (player_4) reads player_9 Suspicious on a single check; player_9 abstained on day 2 and denies the claim's basis; player_6 and others ask for a second data point. Role status of all five living players is unrevealed; the only hard information is one unverified Suspicious read. Public vs private: Privately I am the chanteuse, a wolf, and know my pack partner (the illusionist) is still hidden; publicly I am an unclaimed quiet player while the village debates a player's Suspicious read against an abstaining accuser-target.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out.
