Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

decision.message: Agreed that one Suspicious result is thin, but player_4's check on player_9 is still the only hard data we have. Before anyone is voted, player_4, what did your check on player_9 tell you about their night, and is there any other town claim we can line it up against? A lynch on one read is a risk if we're wrong.

verdicts.why: Five players are alive, not three, so no final-day vote is in play yet.
My wolf partner has not died, so there is no partner loss to react to.
No wolf partner has been eliminated, and no town claimant has stumbled on their night action.

situations: A claimed investigator announced a Suspicious read on a player and demanded an immediate vote, while the accused abstained previously and defends by demanding the claimant test another player with their last check; the claimant refuses, and the village has five alive with one wolf-side read and no second result. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious result, the day-2 vote record, and a concealed-role death on night 2; no confirmed role except revealed dead town-side records. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a leading evil win at worst for the town, so the game can end within one more elimination; a wrong lynch on a single unverified read could hand the wolves a path to parity, making the next vote consequential and the village's evidence thin. Consensus: The village is split between backing the single Suspicious read on player_9 and demanding a second test before any lynch; no clear consensus has formed. My position: Holding out from the forming push on player_9, leaning toward requesting a second data point rather than joining the vote. Heat: Moderate and indirect: you have been asked by player_3 to state what you checked, and player_4 pointed at players who have not given night details, so no direct accusation is aimed at you yet. Forward exposure: Any visible push to lynch or claim now would tie your name to the vote and draw scrutiny; staying silent or abstaining on new information keeps you low-profile, and a claimed result cannot be retracted once given. Target landscape: Player_4 claims investigator with one Suspicious read on player_9 and refuses to use the last check on player_3, a claim with no corroboration yet. Player_9 abstained on day 2 and is defending itself. Player_3 and player_8 are pressing for a second data point; player_6 is you, unclaimed. Public vs private: As the serial killer, you privately know you stabbed the two players who died on nights 1 and 2 and that the wolves killed a third whose role is hidden, yet publicly you are an unclaimed player with no role and no visible results, while the village debates an investigator's Suspicious read on player_9.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

verdicts.why: No Sentinel or Trailseer has reported a visit to me; the only claim is player_4's Suspicious check on player_9.

situations: A claimed investigator announced a Suspicious read on me and demanded an immediate vote, while I, as an unclaimed wolf, defend my abstain by insisting the lynch rested on no result and push the claimant to use their last check on another player. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious result from a claimed investigator, no second check, no sentinel or trailseer results shared, and only public day-discussion claims. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a wolf-side parity win (worst case for town, since the concealed body's side is unknown); a wrong lynch on a single read would be decisive, so the next vote carries direct end-of-game weight. Consensus: The room is split: player_3 and player_4 are pressing a vote on player_9 from a single Suspicious result, while player_6 and player_8 call for a second data point before any lynch, so no consensus has formed yet. My position: Holding out against the forming vote on me, while aligned with the cautious group asking for a second data point. Heat: Moderate and rising: player_4 has publicly named me as Suspicious, and player_3 is pushing a vote on that read; my abstain on day 2 is already questioned by two players. Forward exposure: Pressing player_4 to spend their last check on player_3 would produce a second data point; I have already committed publicly to abstaining on day 2 and voting player_7 as the kill, and that line is hard to reverse without exposing the wolf side. Target landscape: Two candidates are in play: player_9 (me, unclaimed, publicly abstained with no night detail) and player_3 (pushing a vote on a single Suspicious read from player_4). Both are alive and unrevealed; the only hard public item is player_4's Suspicious result on player_9, which is a single unverified claim. Public vs private: Privately, as the illusionist, I know my wolf partner (the chanteuse) is still hidden and that I concealed player_7's sigilist body; publicly I am reading as an unclaimed town-aligned abstainer, and the village does not know that the concealed body was a sigilist.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

verdicts.why: No information-role claimant is being pushed by the wolves tonight; the live question is a vote on me from player_4's claimed check.
The room is not abstaining on an information-starved day; a concrete Suspicious claim already names me.
A claimed investigator has hard evidence against me as primary target and the room is consolidating, so I cast my vote on that accuser, player_4.

situations: A claimed investigator announced a Suspicious read on a quiet player and pressed for an immediate vote; the accused, citing the single unverified result and the claimant's refusal to test it, asked for a second check before any lynch, while the claimant refused to use a remaining check on a third player. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious read, one unused investigator check claimed to remain, and no sentinel or trailseer results shared; the one hard fact is the day-2 lynch and the night kill record. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a point where the evil faction can win, and the game can end on the next elimination at worst for the town; a wrong lynch of a town player would leave the wolves needing only one more kill, so the vote on a single unverified read is high-cost. Consensus: The room is split. One faction (player_3, with player_4's claim) wants to lynch the accused player on one Suspicious read; another faction (player_6, player_8, and the accused) calls for a second data point before any lynch. No consensus has formed yet. My position: Holding out, sitting with the call for a second data point rather than the driving vote on the accused. Heat: Moderate and indirect: you have not been named, but the village is building a pattern around quiet players and the earlier blocked-role lynch argument, and you were among those who pressed a blocked-role test on day 2. Forward exposure: Any visible push for the day-3 vote on the investigator's accused player would commit you to a stance on a single Suspicious read; claiming or defending a night result would tie you to block and kill records you hold privately, and a reversal after the vote is hard to walk back. Target landscape: Five alive. The investigator's accused player (player_9) has a single Suspicious read from player_4 with no second data point; player_3 is pushing the vote on that read; player_4 refuses to test it further. Other living players have no public role claims, and their evidence is only behavioral. Public vs private: Privately, as the chanteuse, you know your pack killed a trailseer on night 1 and a concealed-role player on night 2, and that you blocked a healer who was later lynched; publicly you are an unclaimed player who has said nothing about nights and has only voted on the quiet kill target.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No claimed trailseer has exposed my visit on this board, so the retaliation-avoidance situation does not hold.
Day 3 has only one accuser and one soft claim, so staying off a lone or paired vote and keeping cover fits the board.
The accusation on player_9 rests on one Suspicious result and is not yet overwhelming, so I abstain instead of joining the push.

situations: A claimed investigator (player_4) has read a player Suspicious and is pressing a lynch, while the accused (player_9) and another player (player_3) are locked in a tie vote that eliminated no one, leaving the board with three unverified town-facing voices and an open kill decision for the pack tonight. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious result from a claimed investigator, no second check, no sentinel or trailseer results public, and the Serial Killer and an illusionist-hidden body still unexplained. Stakes: Five alive with a distance to parity of 1, and the game can end within one more elimination: a wrong kill or a wrong lynch at this point could hand the wolves parity or the Serial Killer the last-standing win, so each remaining elimination is decisive. Forward exposure: Any visible move tonight (a block, a kill, or a stated night result) would expose a wolf-side agent to the town's accusations; a block is only private and reversible in its effect, but the kill is public the next morning and cannot be undone. Target landscape: Surviving town-side candidates for tonight's cancelled action are player_3 and player_6, both unclaimed and with no role claims on the board, plus player_4 who claims Investigator with one Suspicious result on player_9. Player_9 is the accused and has given no night claim.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles such as the healer and necromancer are confirmed, and the investigator and trailseer have public claims and results on record. Stakes: Town has lost its healer protection but still has information roles; removing the investigator while blinding the tracker for a night shifts the information balance toward the wolves before parity pressure builds. Forward exposure: Blocking shows the village only that some blocker exists, if the blocked player speaks of it; nothing ties the block to you, and you can switch block targets nightly. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.
lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

verdicts.why: The confirmed vigilante is already dead, so no lethal Town role is alive to target.

Blocking the claimed investigator is attractive, but player_4's claim may be false and blocking the investigator would be a visible tell tonight; the kill target and block must differ, and I should keep quiet.
The healer is dead and the claimed investigator is unprotected, so pressing on the investigator's check claims is the main threat to the pack.
The vigilante is already dead and no wolf has been killed, so the lethal-Town-threat scenario does not hold.
The investigator claim (player_4) is the live threat, but the pack should keep the block off the kill target and decide the kill, which is a wolf-side decision to make in chat.
The healer is dead, but no trailseer is claimed alive and the investigator's status is contested, so this exact setup does not hold.

situations: A claimed investigator announced a Suspicious read on a player and pressed an immediate vote, while the accused refused to back down and demanded a second check from the claimant's unused night. The day-3 vote tied between the claimant and the accused, so no one was eliminated, and the village is split between them. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious result from a self-claimed investigator, no second check, no other town result to cross-reference, and no confirmed role for either side of the dispute. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a point where the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town since a concealed body's side is unknown; the next result, a lynch or a kill, can end the game, so a wrong vote on this tie is very costly and hard to recover from. Forward exposure: Any vote or accusation I make now is visible and public; voting against the investigator-claimant or against their accuser commits me to a side in a tie that has no resolution yet, and a public lean is hard to take back once votes are on record. Target landscape: Two live candidates remain tied on the last vote: the player claiming Investigator with one Suspicious read on the other candidate, and that accused player who denies the read and asks for a second check. Neither has public confirmation; the claim rests on a single unverified result and the denial rests on a demand for corroboration.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

verdicts.why: Player_4 has not cleared me; they only reported a Suspicious check on player_9, so the clearance condition does not hold.
This is night 3 with prior deaths and a vote, not an opening night.
No healer save or confirmed investigator exists on my board; the healer was already lynched on day 2.

situations: Day 3 ended in a tie between a self-claimed Investigator and the player it accused, with neither lynched. The accuser is refusing to spend its last check on the other accuser to test its single Suspicious read, while the accused argues the lynch rests on a single unverified result. You, a Sentinel holding one watch, must decide whether to spend it tonight on a contested player to test the claims. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious result from a self-claimed Investigator, one private Sentinel watch showing a visit to the accused, a day-2 vote record, and an earlier healer lynch resting on a blocked-role argument. No night result is publicly confirmed beyond deaths. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from a point where the leading evil side can win, at worst for the town (a concealed body's side is unknown, so this is the closest it could be); the next result can end the game, so a wrong lynch or a wasted watch is very costly and the single remaining watch is the only confirmed-value test left. Target landscape: Living candidates are player_4 (self-claimed Investigator with one Suspicious result on player_9, publicly pushing the lynch) and player_9 (accused by player_4 and player_3, denies being a wolf, abstained day 2). Both are unrevealed; the claim is unverified and the accused's stance rests on behavior, with player_9 having refused to answer the claimant's test request. Your sentinel watch on player_9 showed player_4 visiting them, which fits the claim but does not prove it.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night after an abstain or tied vote. Conflicting role claims are on the board and you hold one watch left. You must decide whose door to watch, knowing results come only from visitors to that player. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, vote records and some prior night results, but nothing is verified. Alignments of the candidates are unconfirmed, and visit data exists only for whoever you watch. Stakes: Town can still afford a mistake, but this is the last watch, so a wasted use leaves no visitor-tracking for the rest of the game. A watch that exposes a visit pattern or kill trace can settle a claim fight before wolves reach parity. Target landscape: The choice is between a contested claimant (e.g. counter-claimed investigator or sigilist) under heavy suspicion, the obvious wolf-priority targets (claimed investigator, healer, trailseer), a quiet player from a tied vote, or an investigator-cleared player. The claim conflicts are public, but none of the candidates is verified. Only the contested claimant or the likely kill target is likely to draw visits.
lessons.action: With your last watch, pick the player most likely to receive a visit tonight. That means a contested or heavily accused claimant whose claim other roles can verify or attack, or the likely wolf kill target. A watch on a quiet suspect or an already-cleared player usually returns "no visitors", because attackers visit their victims, not themselves.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. The Night 1 kill, a possible roleblock and the lone killer's attack can all land the same night, so the result may be lost, show nothing, or catch a key visitor. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no night results, no claims and no voting record. Only opening-round chatter exists. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive, so one blind watch is a cheap bet. Results across the cluster varied: zero visitors, a visit from the healer or trailseer, a multi-visitor cluster, and the serial killer caught at the door. The cost is that the Sentinel itself may be killed or blocked that night and the result lost, so only one of the two charges should be committed. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes or role flips. Every door is equally unknown, so choose a quiet, unpressured player on pure behavior, since there is no evidence to separate them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, deaths or reads, spend one of the two watches on a quiet, unclaimed player and keep the second for later. A watch can catch the killer's visit or reveal who is acting at night, and the visitor list is the only hard evidence a Sentinel can gather before Day 2. Pick a target the pack or the lone killer might plausibly hit, not a loud player who is likely to draw heat.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, with the first watch already spent and one watch left. The Sentinel is deciding whether to use it on a personal adversary or hold it for a higher-value door. Every watch is a visit, and the Sentinel is not told of its own visit. Information landscape: Still thin: the Night 1 result is the main hard fact, plus a few public claims and one vote record. There are no confirmed wolf identities, so targeting rests on likely attack paths and not on proof. Stakes: The last watch is the Sentinel's final hard evidence, and once it is spent the role has nothing left to do at night. Spending it on a low-traffic door gave nothing in the cluster, so a likely-attack target improves the chance of a usable visitor list. Target landscape: A handful of living players: a prominent claimed or confirmed Town role, a player who has accused you, and quiet unverified players. Favor the one most likely to be attacked or visited, based on public claims or revealed roles, over one picked because they are hostile to you.
lessons.action: Save the last watch for a night when you can name a door that is likely to be attacked or visited, such as a prominent claimed role or a player the wolves or killer plausibly want dead. A watch on a vocal accuser or a quiet bystander tends to return a zero-visitor result, and a watch is spent whether or not it shows anything.

verdicts.why: Tied vote and a contested investigator claim make player_4 the likely visit target, so the last watch goes there.
This is night 3 with deaths and claims on the board, not the blind Night 1 situation.
The last watch should go to a likely-attacked claimant rather than a personal adversary such as player_9.

situations: As the claimed-and-self-known investigator with one check left, I face a tied day-3 vote between me-as-accuser and player_9, who has been pressing me to spend my last check on player_3 to get a second data point. Player_9 abstained on day 2 and then voted against me; player_3 and player_6 are voting against player_9 on my single read, while player_8 abstained. Night 2 had a kill on a concealed-role player (illusionist hid the body) and a serial killer kill, so the wolf pack is still active. Information landscape: Information-starved: one private Suspicious result (on player_9, night 2) is the only hard data; no other investigator-type or sentinel/trailseer results are public; the day-2 lynch rested on a blocked-role argument with no result; the wolves' identity and the illusionist's two concealments are unknown to the village. Stakes: Five alive with one more elimination possible: at worst for town, the next elimination could bring the wolves to parity and a wolf win, because a concealed body's side is unknown and the serial killer also counts as a threat; a wrong lynch on the tied vote is nearly unrecoverable, so the single check is the main remaining way to resolve the uncertainty. Target landscape: Four surviving candidates for tonight's check: player_3 (accuser of player_9 and player_4, no revealed role), player_6 (pressing for a second data point, no revealed role), player_8 (abstained, asking for lined-up town claims, no revealed role), and player_9 (my Suspicious-read target, tied in a day-3 vote, claims town without a role). Public role status: no one has a confirmed role except the dead; evidence is my single Suspicious read on player_9 versus player_9's abstain and defense.

lessons.situation: After the Day 2 vote and a Day 1 or 2 reveal, the voting record shows a few players splitting from the room: defending an eliminated wolf, or pushing to eliminate the Investigator without evidence. One wolf (or the pack's remainder) is likely hiding among them, and the Investigator has one check left. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed wolf or sentinel death is on the record, plus public vote tallies showing clear outliers. No private proof yet, so the final check converts behavioral suspicion into a result. Stakes: The pack is already thinned and one check remains, so the last check is the Investigator's final chance to confirm a wolf. A correct hit can lead to eliminating the remaining wolves and winning, while a wasted check leaves Town without direction. Target landscape: Seven or so living players, with roles of the dead revealed. The best candidates are outlier voters on Day 2: a sole counter-voter defending a revealed wolf, or two voters who coordinated against you while the rest abstained. The basis is public vote behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With your last check, check the player whose Day 2 vote record most clearly diverges from the room: the lone defender of a revealed wolf, or a voter who pushed against you without evidence. Voting records are public and permanent, so these outliers are the likeliest wolf partners, and a Suspicious result gives you a concrete lead to act on.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a discussion-only Day 1. The Investigator holds both checks and must choose between holding them and probing an unread player blind. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no claims, no votes, no night results. Stakes: Early board with no pressure, so no single check is decisive. But the Investigator may die before a banked check is ever used, and any early read, whether it finds a wolf or clears an ally, compounds into later votes. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, flips or behavioral tells. Pick a quiet, non-prominent player at random, since nothing separates them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no leads, spend one check on a quiet, unclaimed player instead of banking both. An early Suspicious finds a wolf, and a Not suspicious gives you a baseline read. Treat a clean result as clearing only wolves: the Serial Killer and neutrals also read Not suspicious, and a Necromancer reads that way on any night it does not attack.

lessons.situation: The investigator has publicly claimed, survived a counter-claim or a wolf elimination, and is now a primary target for a night kill or roleblock, with one check left. Information landscape: Information-rich: vote records separate those who backed the investigator from those who backed the counter-claimant, and a role contradiction is public. Stakes: The investigator is likely to be killed or blocked tonight, so the final check should go to the highest-value unverified suspect where a result, or a tracker seeing the visit, can still help the village. Target landscape: Players who voted against the true investigator or pushed an aggressive line versus the majority voters and a counter-claimant already confirmed as a liar; the basis is voting record and public behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: After a counter-claim or an elimination that exposes you, put your remaining check on a player whose daytime behavior links them to the exposed wolf, such as someone who voted against you or backed the counter-claimant, rather than on a player already confirmed or about to be removed. This produces a read that can be traced and carried forward even if you die.

situations: Day 3 ended in a tie between a claimed investigator and the accused player, with no lynch. A town claimant's single Suspicious read on the illusionist is being pressed for a second data point, and the illusionist is the accused under pressure while the carrier is quiet. The pack must decide tonight's kill and whether to spend its last conceal on the victim. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious claim from a self-declared investigator, one revealed-by-death record of a healer (blocked on night 1) and a vigilante who held fire, and a concealed body whose role the town cannot read; no confirmed results from any living claimant. Stakes: Five alive with the pack's count at two wolves and one lone killer: at worst for the town, one more elimination lets the wolves equal everyone else, so the next kill or lynch can end the game; a concealed victim's role would stay unknown to the town, so the last conceal is only worth using if the victim's record would otherwise point the town at the pack. Forward exposure: Concealing tonight's victim would hide the pack's kill trace from a Sentinel or Trailseer and reveal to the town nothing directly, but it spends the last conceal and the victim's role would stay hidden until game end; a visible vote or kill pattern would tie the illusionist to the pack's choice. Target landscape: Surviving candidates are player_8 (the carrier, publicly quiet and unclaimed), player_3, player_4 (claimed investigator with one Suspicious read on the illusionist's own seat), and player_6; the remaining Town information roles (sentinel, trailseer) are unrevealed and their identities are unknown to the town, so kill choice rests on behavioral read and on the wolf channel's prior agreement.

A concealment decision: the victim tonight would be a surviving player whose role, if revealed by death, would give the town a record to test against the claimed investigator's Suspicious read; the illusionist must decide whether the body's role and any night trace are worth hiding. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town, but the illusionist privately knows the concealed role of the previous victim (a sigilist) and that the claimed investigator has one check left. Stakes: At worst for the town, one elimination (one of the four surviving non-wolf-side players or the carrier's victim) lets the wolves reach parity with everyone else, so a concealed body whose side is unknown is the closest it could be; the conceal is the illusionist's last use, so spending it now leaves no further hiding for the rest of the game. Forward exposure: Using the last conceal on a victim whose record matters would make the attacking trace invisible to a watcher or follower, and the illusionist would learn the victim's role privately; not using it leaves the victim's revealed role and will public to the town. Target landscape: Revealed-role Town candidates are none alive; surviving players have no public role confirmation, so the town's information roles that remain unrevealed are the likely high-value targets for a sentinel or trailseer, but the illusionist cannot confirm which surviving player holds them.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack picks a quiet, unread first victim and you are the wolf who carries the kill. The risk is that the Trailseer or Sentinel catches your visit and gives Town a day-2 accusation against you. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day-1 vote, no claims, no confirmed roles, no night history. Only private wolf talk exists. Stakes: Early game with plenty of time. The main risk is losing a wolf early to a traced visit, which would cost the pack the endgame. A clean first night matters more than saving a charge. Forward exposure: Announces that an illusionist exists and spends one of two conceals if the victim dies. Your own visit leaves no trace, and the spent charge cannot be undone. If the victim survives, nothing is announced and the use is kept. Target landscape: Eight or nine unclaimed, unread players with no roles revealed. The target is picked from quiet behavior, not evidence, and could be a watcher, a tracker, or the night-immune lone killer.
lessons.action: When the carrier rotation makes you the carrier on night 1, carry the kill and use a conceal on the victim. A conceal on a victim you carried yourself leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer, and if the target turns out immune the use is kept.

situations: A claimed investigator's single Suspicious read on a player has produced a tied day vote, with the accused and the claimant each pushing the other to be tested. The pack must choose tonight's kill and whether to block a town player whose night action could expose them, while its own partner sits in the accused's position in the public argument. Information landscape: Information-starved. The only hard-looking result is one unverified Suspicious read from a claimed investigator; no other town result is public, and the only dead revealed roles are a trailseer, a healer, and a vigilante, with one concealed role among the dead. Behavioral signals dominate. Stakes: Five alive with one elimination from the leading evil faction winning, at worst for the town since a concealed body's side is unknown; a single wrong kill or lynch can end the game, so this night's choice of victim is decisive rather than recoverable. Forward exposure: Tonight's kill or block is hidden, but the victim's death reveals the attack and an announced role; a block that is reported as a roleblock or a kill on a claimed investigator would make the pack's choice visible to the village by deduction. Choosing a target now commits the pack to a line before the next vote, and the choice cannot be undone once the morning report is read. Target landscape: Four living players besides the acting wolf. The claimed investigator (player_4) has a single Suspicious read on the chanteuse's wolf-side partner and is publicly pressing the vote; the accused player_9 abstained and is publicly defending. The other two, player_3 and player_6, are unclaimed and have pressed for evidence without claiming roles. Evidence basis: the investigator's claim rests on one unverified Suspicious result; the rest is behavioral.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.
