situations: A dead-of-night kill removed a claimed investigator's accuser-adjacent player, leaving a four-person village where a claimed investigator's single Suspicious read on player_9 drives a pending vote, and the serial killer must avoid drawing attention while the wolves are still alive. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified claimed Suspicious result, a tied prior vote, no confirmed roles among the living, and a concealed body whose role is unknown to the town. Stakes: Four alive with a distance to parity of 0 means the next elimination can end the game, so a single wrong vote or kill could hand the wolves or the lone killer the win; the room is small enough that one mislynch is decisive. Consensus: No consensus; the room is divided over whether player_9 or the claimed investigator is the wolf-side read, resting on one unverified Suspicious claim. My position: Holding out from the forming push against player_9, with the vote split and no majority. Heat: Low on you personally; no one has accused you and your kills are unattributed, though the village is drawn into a dispute about a claimed investigator. Forward exposure: Any visible accusation or push to vote would reveal interest in the claimant pair and commit you to a side; staying quiet keeps the public read unchanged and is easy to reverse. Target landscape: Four living players: the claimed investigator (unverified, one Suspicious read on player_9), player_9 (denying, abstained day 2), and player_3 who is pushing the vote on player_9 with no checks shown; the sole hard datum is the single claimed Suspicious result. Public vs private: As the serial killer, you privately know you killed three players and that the wolves remain alive; publicly the village reads a split between a claimed investigator and a denier, with no knowledge of your kills.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

verdicts.why: No one has a mechanical result against me and I am not the main target today.
I have not been labeled passive by a claimed role, so the opening does not need a speech from me.
No Sentinel or Trailseer has named me as a visitor to any victim.

situations: Four players remain after a tie vote on day 3 left no lynch; a claimed investigator's single Suspicious read on another player is untested, and the village must decide whether to lynch on it while the two wolves are still alive and hidden. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified investigator claim with one Suspicious result, no second data point, and no confirmed role reveal since the last lynch; the concealed bodies hide roles from the village. Stakes: Four alive with the wolves holding two hidden seats; one more elimination can end the game, at worst for the town, so a wrong lynch or a successful kill here is nearly decisive and the town has no margin for another tie. Consensus: The village has no settled consensus; the day-3 vote tied and the room is split on whether the single Suspicious read is enough to act on, with no hard evidence either way. My position: Holding out, with no public read; you are neither driving nor aligned with a forming majority. Heat: Low to moderate: you have not pushed a read in public, but the village has been asking who checked whom, and a quiet player may be seen as a low-information target. Forward exposure: Any visible vote or claim you make now ties your name to the day's lynch outcome; your partner the chanteuse is still unrevealed, so a public move that draws suspicion cannot be undone and will be read against your concealments. Target landscape: Four players alive: three remaining Town-aligned or unknown-role players and the chanteuse wolf partner. The public record ties the claimed investigator's Suspicious read to one player, but the claim has no independent confirmation; the day-3 tie left no lynch and the vote on the claimed investigator is now the open question. Public vs private: Privately you are the illusionist, a wolf, and you concealed the body of the player killed on night 3, whose role stays hidden from the village; publicly the village only knows that a player was attacked and their role was hidden by an illusionist, and it does not know who the hidden-role players were.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been revealed and killed. You are pressured over a lone vote against a dead Town player, while a Town player's result (a non-triggering sigil) is available as a defense. Information landscape: Moderate: public voting records and a privately held Town result that can be used to clear you, but no hard role confirmations on the quiet alternative suspect. Stakes: Each vote now decides whether the last wolf survives. Moving even a couple of swing voters off you keeps the wolf team alive into the final few players. Consensus: The village is split. Some players press you over the vote record, while players holding a clearing result and neutral voters are open to another suspect. My position: holding out Heat: High. Players cite your isolated vote against a now-dead player as the basis for suspicion. Forward exposure: Citing a Town player's result ties you to a non-attacking story that you cannot take back, and later tracking evidence could break it. The alternative-suspect push can be adjusted as new information arrives. Target landscape: Candidates are you, under pressure from the vote record, and a quiet player with no confirmed role who was targeted by the dead wolf. Suspicion of the quiet player is behavioral, while the case against you is the vote record. Public vs private: Privately you are an active wolf, but the partner carried the kill that night, so a Town result such as an un-triggered sigil looks exculpatory. The room reads that result as evidence you are not the killer.
lessons.action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Use only what the rules show: the sigil not triggering means only that you did not attack on that night, and it does not clear you of being a wolf. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.

verdicts.why: No one has pressed a tracking or shared-vote record against me yet, so the defense isn't needed this round.
Four are alive, but the table isn't converging on me in the opening round.
No Town result clears me and I have no lone-vote defense to make right now.

situations: After a claimed investigator was killed in the night with their role concealed by an illusionist, the village is split over a tie between a player who accused another of wolf-side on a single Suspicious result and the accused, who argues the result is untested. As a wolf whose pack's kill took the claimant, you are a quiet voice who has abstained twice and must avoid drawing a read. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious claim, no second data point, and no confirmed roles among the living; the concealed body means the claimed investigator's role remains unconfirmed. Stakes: Four alive with the wolves holding one seat and the serial killer still alive; zero eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and the next result can end it, so a wrong lynch or a successful kill each carries an immediate decisive cost. Consensus: The village has no consensus; the day-3 tie left player_4 and player_9 unresolved and the room is divided between those who trust the single Suspicious read and those who want a second data point. My position: Holding out from any strong read, currently with the abstaining minority and not pushing a lynch. Heat: Moderate and mostly indirect: the room has not pointed at you, but a quiet abstainer on the day-2 and day-3 votes is a pattern others may notice. Forward exposure: Any visible push for or against player_9, player_3, or player_6 would commit you to a side in a tie-vote dispute with no verifiable evidence; the vote record is permanent, so a vote now cannot be withdrawn. Target landscape: Four alive: player_3, player_6, player_8 (self), player_9. The dead player_4 was a claimed investigator, unconfirmed, and its role was concealed by an illusionist so its side is unknown to town. Evidence is a single claimed Suspicious read on player_9 versus behavioral pressure from player_3 and player_6. Public vs private: Privately, as a wolf (chanteuse) you know the pack killed player_4 last night and your own blocks on player_6 did not take; publicly, the village read player_4 as a claimed investigator whose Suspicious result on player_9 is the only hard information, and the tie-vote record is split.

A player who has been asking pointed questions about another's checks is the most active town-looking voice, while the accuser pressing a lynch on one Suspicious read is the other live pole; the carrier's kill and block choices have been made around these two voices without public signal. Information landscape: Information-starved: behavioral questioning only, one unverified claimed Suspicious, and no living confirmed roles. Stakes: Four alive, zero eliminations from the leading evil faction winning, and the game can end on one more elimination, so a single mis-lynch or kill decides the outcome. Consensus: No clear consensus; discussion is split between player_3's push to lynch player_9 and player_6's call for more evidence. My position: Holding out, with the room divided and no faction forming a majority. Heat: Low to moderate: player_6 has directed questions at player_3 but not at you, so your own suspicion is not elevated yet. Forward exposure: Pushing the room to scrutinize player_6 or relying on player_6's questions would make a visible alignment that could later expose your block pattern; reversing that stance later would be visible in the record. Target landscape: Living candidates: player_3 and player_6 are the active accusers, player_9 is the accused under a single Suspicious read. None has a confirmed role; all evidence is behavioral and claimed. Public vs private: Privately you know the blocks you placed on player_6 on nights 2 and 3 did not take, which the village cannot see; publicly player_6 is simply a questioner who has been pressing player_3 about checks and is a town-looking voice.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.situation: The endgame has 3-4 players left, you are the last wolf, and an unconfirmed player is pushing a case built on your voting record. A claimed Town role's result could clear the swing player and make them an ally. Information landscape: Information-rich: full public voting records, a claimed trailseer result, and a dead player's final vote are all available. These details can be used to rebut the accuser. Stakes: One vote or one night kill decides the game: winning this vote brings the wolves to parity at the next kill, while losing it eliminates the last wolf. Consensus: The room is split with no majority. Everyone is working from public vote history and one or two claimed results, and one swing player is deciding whom to believe. My position: Driving a counter-narrative to form a defensive voting coalition with the swing player. Heat: High: the accuser has laid out your voting record and tied you to a dead wolf on a key mis-elimination. Forward exposure: Answering the accuser head-on commits you to a specific story about your old vote and to a coalition with one other player. If the swing player sides with the accuser, you are voted out right away and cannot undo it. If the swing player sides with you, you can win the vote or at least split the room. Target landscape: A field of three or four: the vocal accuser citing voting records, a claimed Town role whose claim has some support (such as a cleared visit report), and possibly another claimed role. The case against you rests on past votes, evidence rather than behavior; the case against the accuser rests on behavior and on the dead players' positions. Public vs private: Privately you are the last wolf who drove the earlier kills and mis-eliminations, while publicly you pose as an innocent Town player who made an honest deduction alongside the room.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf in a tiny endgame (3-4 alive) and are accused with hard evidence like voting records, answer the accusation directly. Reframe your past vote as a reasonable reaction to the situation, then cite a result or vote from a still-living or already-dead Town player that undercuts the accuser. Aim to win over the swing Town player; if they are not yet persuaded, shift your pitch to the accuser's inconsistencies and to the accuser as the likelier wolf.

verdicts.why: My wolf partner is still alive and no wolf has been exposed, so this scenario does not hold.
Three players are not alive and this is day 4, not a final three-way vote.
No wolf partner has been eliminated, and no Town claimant has stumbled on their night action.
The field is larger than three or four and no one has built a case on my voting record.

situations: Day 4 with four alive. A claimed sentinel announced that its last watch on the night-3 victim showed two visitors and pointed at a claimed investigator's visit history, while the claimed investigator's single Suspicious read is being used by others to push a vote on the accused; I, the serial killer, must avoid being drawn into either claim. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious read, one sentinel claim with a single watch result, and a concealed-role death whose role is unknown to the village; no public confirmations. Stakes: Four alive with the distance to parity at 0: the next elimination can end the game, so a single wrong vote or a kill at this point is decisive and cannot be recovered from. Consensus: The village is split; the accusing faction is pressing a vote on one player based on a single Suspicious read, while others want a second data point before voting. My position: Holding out, outside the forming pressure on the accused; I am not defending the claimant and not driving the vote. Heat: Low to moderate: I have not spoken much and have not been named in accusations, though the sentinel's claim places visitors near the dead player and the village is focused on the investigator-versus-accused split. Forward exposure: Speaking up or claiming a role would make me a visible target for a daytime vote and would commit me to a story I cannot verify; staying silent keeps my position unrevealed but lets the accusation narrative run without me. Target landscape: Four living players: a claimed sentinel whose watch named two visitors on the last night, a claimed investigator whose Suspicious read on another player is unconfirmed, and the player who was accused and is now being pushed by both, with no hard evidence either way. Public vs private: As the serial killer I privately know I killed the speculator, vigilante, and a concealed-role player, while publicly the village only sees a sentinel claim naming player_4's visitors and a contested Suspicious read; my own kill record is hidden from everyone.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

decision.message: Player_3, you're right that I went to player_4 on night 3, and I won't pretend otherwise. The check worth running is player_4's night 2 Suspicious read on player_9 against player_9's visit from player_4, since that's the only hard result left on the table.

verdicts.why: Player_3's sentinel claim is directly about my night 3 visit, so a flat denial would clash with a real watch; I should answer briefly without spending my cover.
Four players are alive and the room is not yet unified against me.
I should keep engaging with specific checkable points rather than going quiet while someone names me.

decision.message: player_9, I went to player_4 on night 3 and I'm not claiming a role, so I won't say what I was doing there. Nothing from that visit is public, and player_4 died that night, so you're right that their Suspicious read on you is only their word. player_8, you've abstained twice with no reason given; what made you hold back on player_5 and player_4?

verdicts.why: Same visit-trace situation, but I already admitted the visit, so I answer directly without a denial or a unique role claim.
Only about four players are alive and no one has pressed a vote-record case against me yet.
I have been quiet, so I should give a specific read tied to the public record.

situations: Day 4 of a 10-player game after a tie vote on day 3: a claimed investigator's Suspicious read on one player is being contested by a sentinel-claimant whose watch recorded that accused player visiting the claimant's target, while the accused asks for the read to be tested against that visit. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified Suspicious read, one sentinel claim with a visit record, and a visit-based counter-argument; no confirmed results, two dead players with concealed roles, and no eliminated role reveals since day 2. Stakes: Four alive with the game able to end within one more elimination at worst for the town; a wrong lynch or a kill on the wrong player hands the pack a parity win, so the next elimination is decisive and a mistaken vote is not recoverable. Consensus: The village is split on a tie with no hard evidence settled; the room is arguing over one Suspicious read versus a visit record, not converging on a lynch. My position: Holding out from any driving push, not with a forming majority. Heat: Moderate and indirect: my own day-3 vote went to the investigator-claimant, and I have been silent on reads, which is consistent with cover but not a public accusation against me. Forward exposure: Any visible push now on the tie between the claimed investigator and the village voice would commit me to a side on a read I cannot verify; a public vote or claim is hard to walk back once the room records it. Target landscape: Two living players are in open dispute: a claimed investigator whose single Suspicious read on one player is contested, and the player who was accused in that read. Both are unrevealed; the claim rests on one unconfirmed result and the defender's visit record is publicly disputed, so the evidence is thin and behavior-based. Public vs private: Privately, as the chanteuse, I know my wolf partner (the illusionist, hidden) is alive and that the pack has killed several Town players; publicly I hold only the stated 'no claim, no night result' cover, so the public read treats me as an ordinary unclaimed townsman.

A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

situations: The investigator claim of player_4 is dead with role concealed by the illusionist, leaving a sentinel claim by player_3 that names the illusionist's visit history as evidence against the claimed investigator's Suspicious read, while player_6 admits visiting the claimant on night 3 and the village debates a vote on one Suspicious result. Stakes: Four alive with the wolves needing parity: a single wrong elimination or kill can end the game, so the wolf team's remaining pair is at the edge of winning and a wrong vote is unrecoverable. Consensus: The room is split between a lean toward player_4's claim being credible and skepticism that one Suspicious read is enough to vote on, with no settled majority. My position: Holding out, with no public position taken on the day's accusations. Heat: Moderate: the sentinel claim names you as having been visited by player_4 on night 2, and the investigator's Suspicious read on you is the central accusation, though its source is now dead with a concealed role. Forward exposure: Any visible defense of player_9 or push against the sentinel or player_6 commits you to a public stance on the Suspicious read; the partner chanteuse is unrevealed so a wrong public read would expose both. Target landscape: Four living players: player_3 claiming sentinel with a watch on player_4 showing visits, player_6 who admitted visiting player_4, player_8 the living partner, and yourself; the only evidence is claims and visit records, no confirmed role. Public vs private: Privately you are the illusionist who concealed the investigator's body; publicly the claimed investigator player_4 is dead with role hidden, and the village has only player_4's night 2 Suspicious read on player_9 (you) as its hard information.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been revealed and killed. You are pressured over a lone vote against a dead Town player, while a Town player's result (a non-triggering sigil) is available as a defense. Information landscape: Moderate: public voting records and a privately held Town result that can be used to clear you, but no hard role confirmations on the quiet alternative suspect. Stakes: Each vote now decides whether the last wolf survives. Moving even a couple of swing voters off you keeps the wolf team alive into the final few players. Consensus: The village is split. Some players press you over the vote record, while players holding a clearing result and neutral voters are open to another suspect. My position: holding out Heat: High. Players cite your isolated vote against a now-dead player as the basis for suspicion. Forward exposure: Citing a Town player's result ties you to a non-attacking story that you cannot take back, and later tracking evidence could break it. The alternative-suspect push can be adjusted as new information arrives. Target landscape: Candidates are you, under pressure from the vote record, and a quiet player with no confirmed role who was targeted by the dead wolf. Suspicion of the quiet player is behavioral, while the case against you is the vote record. Public vs private: Privately you are an active wolf, but the partner carried the kill that night, so a Town result such as an un-triggered sigil looks exculpatory. The room reads that result as evidence you are not the killer.
lessons.action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Use only what the rules show: the sigil not triggering means only that you did not attack on that night, and it does not clear you of being a wolf. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

Did you learn anything from that visit, or did it go to nothing? I want a straight answer on what you saw before we pin the night 2 Suspicious on me.

No sigil result or lone vote against me is in play on this board.

situations: Night 3's kill removed the claimed investigator, whose Suspicious read on you is now only their word. A sentinel's watch showed two visits to that player, and the sentinel is pushing a vote on the illusionist-adjacent accused while the other survivors trade accusations over who visited the dead claimant's door and why. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a verified result, the only hard data is a dead claim, and the sentinel's watch shows visits without content. Stakes: Four alive with the game able to end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a wrong lynch or a single kill could hand the wolves parity; a mis-vote is effectively unrecoverable. Consensus: The room is split and no clear consensus has formed; the sentinel is pressing a vote on the Suspicious read while others argue one unverified result is too thin. My position: Holding out against a lynch on the sentinel's current push, aligned with the cautious view that one result is insufficient. Heat: Moderate: you are named in the day discussion as having visited a dead claimed investigator and as the recipient of an unverified Suspicious read, but no one has yet tied you to a concrete contradiction. Forward exposure: Any visible push to lynch the sentinel or investigator would commit you publicly to a read the room can test against the next night's result; the move is hard to reverse once a vote is recorded, and a visible defense of your own visit would invite scrutiny of the concealed night. Target landscape: Four players alive. The claimed investigator (player_4) is dead, so their Suspicious read on you remains unverified. The sentinel (player_3) claims a watch on player_4 showing two visits; player_6 admits that visit and player_9 (you) admits it too. The remaining candidates are the sentinel, player_6 and player_8, with evidence mostly behavioral: player_6 is challenged for an unexplained visit, player_8 for repeated abstaining. Public vs private: Privately you are the illusionist, a wolf, who concealed the bodies of two prior kills; publicly you are an unclaimed player whose night 3 visit to a now-dead player is explained only as a test of that player's claim, while the village reads you as one of four survivors facing a split between a sentinel's watch result and an investigator claim.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

situations: After a claimed investigator died at night with an untested Suspicious read on player_9 still open, the sentinel publicly reported that two players visited the dead claimant on night 3, one of whom is me, and player_9 pressed me to say what I learned from that visit while the village debated whether to vote on player_9. Stakes: Four alive with distance to parity 0 means the next elimination can end the game; a wrong lynch or any kill that leaves the remaining evil faction at parity hands it the win, so a single vote or kill here is decisive. Consensus: The room is split and no consensus has formed: the village is divided over whether player_9 or player_4 is the wolf-side party, with player_3 pushing on player_9, player_8 holding out on any vote without a second data point, and no shared read on the night 3 visit. My position: Holding out from the forming pressure on player_9, while standing in a contested middle position as a player with a visit to the dead player_4 on record. Heat: Moderate and rising: my night 3 visit to player_4 is public through the sentinel's watch, and player_6 and player_9 are both pressing me on what I learned, so I am being asked directly to explain a visit I cannot explain without revealing my role. Forward exposure: Admitting the night 3 visit to player_4 is already in the open room and cannot be retracted; any further specific claim about what I did or learned would commit me to a story that the remaining players can test against later public results, and would be hard to reverse. Only player_4's claim and the sentinel's watch are on record; no role among survivors is confirmed by elimination. Public vs private: As the serial killer I privately know I killed player_2, player_10 and player_4, and that I visited player_4 on night 3; publicly I am one of four survivors whose visit to player_4 is on record through the sentinel's watch, while my role remains unknown to the village.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

verdicts.why: Voting on a rival with competing evidence (player_9's Suspicious read) avoids a lone vote on the sentinel claimant and spreads suspicion away from me.

situations: Four players remain after a night in which a claimed investigator was killed and its role concealed; the village is deadlocked on day 4 between a claimed sentinel whose watch shows visits to the dead player and the one remaining accuser's single Suspicious read, and the agent, as an unclaimed wolf, must avoid visible commitments while a player who visited the dead claimant pressures the agent for a justification. Information landscape: Information-starved: one Suspicious read from a dead claimant that no one can test, one sentinel watch whose contents are only a claim, and a visit record with no revealed roles beyond the night-1 trailseer and day-2 healer. Stakes: Four alive with the leading evil faction needing 0 more eliminations: the next result (a vote or a kill) can end the game, so a wrong lynch of a town player hands the wolves a win at parity; with the concealed body's side unknown, this is the closest it could be. Consensus: The village is split with no consensus: the sentinel-claimant and the accuser of player_9 are pressing for a lynch on one read, while the others are holding and asking for a second data point. My position: Holding out, with the abstain-leaning minority, not driving a lynch. Heat: Moderate and indirect: the agent's two abstains and its vote on player_4 (a night-3 kill target) are on record, and player_6 asked the agent to explain its abstains, but no one has yet named the agent as a wolf. Forward exposure: Any visible push to lynch the sentinel-claimant or the accused player would commit the agent to a side in the tie, and the block record and abstain history are already public, so a sudden shift would draw attention; the vote can be reversed on later days but the public record of votes stays. Target landscape: Four alive: a player claiming sentinel with a watch record that shows two visits to player_4 on night 3, a player who admits visiting player_4 on night 3 and refuses to say why, the wolf partner (hidden), and the agent. The tie on day 3 rests on a single Suspicious read by the now-dead claimed investigator, with no hard evidence on either accused player. Public vs private: As the Chanteuse, the agent privately knows its wolf partner is still alive and hidden, and that it blocked player_6 on night 3 without effect; publicly the agent is an unclaimed player who has only abstained on two votes and pushed no read.

The village is split on day 4 over whether a sentinel-claimant's watch record that two players visited a claimed investigator who died that night can be trusted, while one of those visitors refuses to explain their visit and the accused player is asking for a second check. Information landscape: Information-starved with conflicting claims: a sentinel watch record, a Suspicious read from a dead claimant, and public visit records, none independently confirmed. Stakes: Four alive, zero eliminations until the leading evil faction can win: a single vote or kill can end the game, so a mis-elimination of a town player is near-fatal for the town at this count, and the closest worst case is one result away. Consensus: No consensus on who to lynch; the room is divided into a lynch faction and a hold faction, with the hold faction asking for evidence. My position: With the holding-out group, neither driving nor opposing the lynch on player_9 or the sentinel-claimant. Heat: Low to moderate: the agent's abstains are questioned but the accusations are aimed at others. Forward exposure: Using the pack's kill or the agent's own block results in public discussion would reveal a wolf-side pattern, since the agent's blocks and kills match the public deaths; any claim of a role would be a commitment that cannot be undone within the game. Target landscape: Among the living, the sentinel-claimant's watch is a claim with no independent check, the player who visited the dead claimant has an unexplained visit, and the accuser of player_9 has pressed the same read twice; none has public role confirmation. Public vs private: The agent privately knows the night-2 and night-3 kills and its own blocks, and that the wolf partner remains unrevealed; publicly the village does not know who the wolf-side players are and the tie on day 3 has left the outcome open.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No claimed trailseer has exposed my visit; that situation does not hold on this board.
This is a late four-player endgame with a live sentinel claim, not an early info-poor abstain day.
My wolf partner is not under a consensus-backed check or tracking accusation right now.

situations: Three players remain: a player claiming sentinel with an unverified watch result, a player who admitted visiting the night-3 victim but refuses to name a role, and the chanteuse's own position as a wolf who has lost its pack partner to a day-4 lynch. The chanteuse must decide which of the two living rivals to cancel tonight and whether to keep the block on the same player as before. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only results are one unverified sentinel watch showing two visits, one admitted but unexplained visit to a dead player, and the night-2 Suspicious read on a player now revealed as a wolf that was confirmed by elimination. No role of any living player is confirmed by the system. Stakes: Three alive with the leading evil faction one elimination from parity (distance 1, at worst for the town since a concealed body's side is unknown): the next kill or lynch can end the game, so a wrong elimination now is decisive rather than recoverable. Forward exposure: Any visible move tonight or at the next vote (a block, a kill, or a vote aligned with a faction) would commit the pack's partner and the chanteuse to a visible pattern; a block that does not take is only visible to the blocker, while a vote is public and permanent. Target landscape: Three players are alive: one claimed sentinel whose watch on the last night showed visits from two living players, one player who has admitted visiting the night-3 victim without claiming a role, and the chanteuse's own living wolf partner was already removed by day-4 vote, so the remaining wolf-side question concerns the surviving non-wolf candidates. Public role status is unrevealed for the two living rivals; the only checkable evidence is a sentinel claim and a visit admission, both unverified.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones.
