The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

situations: Four players were alive at the start of this day and a day-4 vote just removed the revealed illusionist, leaving three. Player_3 claims Sentinel and says a watch on player_4 showed player_6 and the since-eliminated illusionist visiting that night. Player_8 has abstained twice and pressed player_6 on the night-3 visit, while player_6 refuses to state what the visit was for. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town: one Sentinel claim with a single watch result, one Suspicious read on a player now dead and revealed, and no independent confirmation. Player_8 has no claim at all. Stakes: Three alive with one remaining evil faction (the lone killer) needing only to reach at most one other living player; at worst for the town, one more elimination ends the game, so the next vote or kill is decisive and a wrong lynch leaves the table with two players. Forward exposure: Any visible vote or claim now commits this serial killer's seat to the lynch and is hard to walk back once the four-player table has seen it; a vote against player_3 or player_8 would reveal the alignment of the hunter's own targeting pattern. Target landscape: Three survivors remain: player_3 (publicly claims Sentinel with a watch on player_4 that showed two visitors, unverified), player_8 (abstained twice, no role claim, pressing player_6 about the night-3 visit), and player_6 (the speaker's own seat, not a candidate). Player_9 was just eliminated and revealed as the illusionist, so the wolf pack is already gone; the only remaining evil faction is the lone killer.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

verdicts.why: The claimed investigator who cleared me is dead, and no living investigator has singled out a suspect.
No healer is alive and no town leader was just saved, so the protection pattern does not apply.
This is night 4 with several deaths and votes on record, not the opening night.

situations: Day 2 opens with the village having lost an Investigator and a Fortune Teller to night-one kills and no accusations yet, while you hold a hidden wolf role and must speak in the opening round without a claim, a block result, or a public basis for any vote. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public facts are the two night-one deaths and their revealed roles; no checks, watches, or claims have surfaced, so every day-2 statement is an unverified opinion. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game now; a wrong mislynch is recoverable but each town loss narrows the margin for the wolves' later push. Consensus: No clear village consensus has formed; the day opens with no accusations and no shared read on any living player. My position: With no consensus, you are neither driving nor opposing the room; you are an unaccused voice at the start of the day. Heat: Low: no one has accused you publicly, and the summary records no accusations in day discussion. Forward exposure: Any visible claim, block disclosure, or early accusation would commit you publicly and is hard to reverse once spoken; staying silent on day 2 keeps your exposure low but leaves the village without a read on who blocked whom. Target landscape: Eight living players with no public accusations on record yet; the only revealed roles are the night-1 dead (Fortune Teller and Investigator), and no living player has a public role claim or evidence basis to separate them. Public vs private: Privately you are the Chanteuse, a wolf, with your pack partner still alive and unrevealed; publicly you are one unverified player among eight survivors, and the village has no role claims yet from anyone and only the night-1 deaths of a Fortune Teller and an Investigator, whose roles were revealed by the morning report.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

verdicts.why: Describes a wolf partner already dead; my partner player_9 is alive and no Town claimant has reported a block on me.
Three players are alive, not three on a final day.
My partner player_9 is still alive, so I am not the surviving wolf.

decision.message: Nobody has claimed a role yet, and player_7 died as an investigator without a public check. If anyone holds a night result, say so now, before we start pointing at anyone.

verdicts.why: Describes a later game state with a dead partner and a blocked claimant; day 2 here has no such board.
Describes a three-player final day; far more players are alive now.
Assumes my partner is already eliminated and a claimant has stumbled; neither is true on this board.

situations: Day 2 opens with eight players alive after a fortune teller and an investigator were killed on night 1, and no one has yet claimed a role or made an accusation. You are a lone killer whose kill is hidden from the public and must blend in without drawing attention while the village starts looking for suspects. Information landscape: Information-starved: two role reveals and no claims, checks, watches, or votes yet exist publicly, so every later accusation will rest on behavior rather than evidence. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single mistaken or wrongly-directed vote is recoverable at this count but would spend one of the four margins that remain. Consensus: No clear consensus yet; the room has not formed a view on who to target because no accusations have been made in discussion. My position: Unanchored; neither driving a vote nor aligned with a forming majority. Heat: Low; no one has accused you and the public record contains no link between you and the night kills. Forward exposure: Any visible move on day 2 (accusing, defending, or voting) commits you to a public stance that later night results may contradict; a vote is public and permanent, so a wrong-direction vote cannot be withdrawn. Target landscape: Eight living players with no claims surfaced yet and no hard evidence against anyone; the only public information is the two revealed deaths, a fortune teller and an investigator, which gives no basis yet to rank candidates. Public vs private: As the serial killer, you privately know you killed player_5 on night 1, the fortune teller, while the public only knows a player was stabbed and revealed as a fortune teller; the village reads the kill as a wolf-or-lone-killer mystery with no suspect yet.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

verdicts.why: No Sentinel has claimed a visit to me, so this situation does not hold yet.
Five players are not alive yet and no role has pointed at me.
No claimed role has named me and no wolf vote has been cast.
No Sentinel or Trailseer has named me, so the claimed-visitor situation does not hold yet.
Only two players are dead and no one is near elimination, so the late-game pressure does not apply.
No claimed role has pointed at me and no wolf has voted for me, so I am not the quiet target yet.
No Sentinel or Trailseer has named me as a visitor, so the claimed-visitor situation does not hold.
It is Day 2 with eight players alive and no claimed role pointing at me, so the late-game case does not apply.
No claimed role has labeled me passive or tied me to a dead wolf's vote.

situations: Day 2 opens with eight players alive and no claims made. Two town-side roles are already gone, and the village must decide whether to build a case on behavior alone while I hold private knowledge of the pack's kill and two remaining conceals. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigations, sentinel watches, or trailseer follows are public, and the only hard facts are the two death announcements and their revealed roles. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong vote is recoverable but leaves the wolves closer to parity, and no single result can end the game this day. Consensus: No clear village consensus yet; the room is still waiting for claims and has no shared read on any player. My position: With no consensus forming, I am neither driving nor opposing the room; I sit with the quiet majority. Heat: Low: I have made no claims and only spoke in agreement with the pack's kill on day 1, so suspicion on me rests on nothing public. Forward exposure: Any visible push now would commit me to a read on the board that the village can later check against the morning report; a conceal used now is spent for good, and a visible accusation cannot be taken back. Target landscape: Eight living players with no public claims yet; the only public role facts are the two deaths. Candidates are judged on behavior alone since no one has an evidence-based role read. Public vs private: Privately I am the illusionist, a wolf, with two conceals left and knowledge of the pack's day-1 kill of a investigator; publicly no one has a claim, the village knows only that two players died (a fortune teller stabbed by the serial killer and an investigator killed by the wolves, whose role was revealed) and my partner is unrevealed.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

verdicts.why: No tracking report or shared vote with a dead wolf exists on the record yet.
Early day with town roles still forming claims; a short low-content opener beats a call-out.
Many players are still alive and no final-stage consensus has formed.

decision.message: No night result from me to share yet. If anyone with a Sentinel or Trailseer read has someone who visited them, say who came or who they went to, so we have something concrete to cross-check.

verdicts.why: No one has tied me to a wolf on the public record yet; this is day 2 with no votes.
Few claims exist, so a short, neutral, on-topic remark keeps me out of the silent bucket without new information.
Four players are not alive and no wills or past votes exist against me.

situations: Day two opens after an unclaimed first-night double death (fortune teller and investigator, neither role's result public); players are asking for anyone with a night read to speak before any accusations, and I hold the only knowledge of who killed the fortune teller. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public checks, watches, follows, claims, or wills; the only public facts are two deaths with roles revealed by the system and no vote has yet occurred. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill can end the game this day; a mis-elimination of a town player is recoverable but reduces the village's information, which benefits the lone killer's hidden position. Consensus: The village has no consensus yet; players are asking for night results and Sentinel or Trailseer reads before pointing at anyone, so the room is informationally starved and unaligned. My position: Holding out from any accusation; I am not part of any forming majority and not driving the discussion. Heat: Currently low; no one has named me and I have made no accusation, though the day-two prompts asking for night results could draw attention to whoever stays quiet. Forward exposure: Any claim of a night result or any visible accusation commits me to a story that other players can cross-check against the night record; retracting it later is not possible, so staying silent and passing keeps exposure lowest for now. Target landscape: Eight living players with no public role claims; no one has offered a Sentinel or Trailseer read yet, so there is no evidence basis to rank any candidate and all targets are only behavioral guesses. Public vs private: As the serial killer, I privately know I stabbed the fortune teller on night 1, while the public sees only that a fortune teller and an investigator died with no checks or results announced; the village is pressing for night results I cannot share without exposing myself.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

situations: Day 2 opens after a night kill of the Investigator with no public check; players are demanding Sentinel or Trailseer results before committing, while you hold a private Chanteuse block and a pack kill from night 1 that remain hidden. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified night results, no public claims, and only the two revealed dead roles; the only concrete data is what players privately say they saw. Stakes: Eight alive and four eliminations until the wolves can win, so a single mistaken day vote is recoverable but would move the pack closer to parity; the game cannot end within one more elimination. Consensus: The room is not yet aligned; players are asking for claims and cross-checks before naming a target, with no clear direction. My position: Holding out from any forming consensus, since none has formed; speaking briefly as an engaged town-looking player. Heat: Low so far: no one has accused you directly, but you are one of several players asking for concrete night results, which is a neutral posture. Forward exposure: Volunteering a claim or night result (such as the block on player_10 or any visit story) would commit you to a checkable account and cannot be undone once the table cross-checks it, so staying unclaimed keeps options open. Target landscape: Eight alive with no claims made; the village has only the two dead players' revealed roles (Fortune Teller and Investigator) and no public evidence against any living player, so every candidate rests on behavior alone. Public vs private: Privately you are the Chanteuse, a wolf, and know your pack killed player_7 and that you blocked player_10 on night 1; publicly no one has claimed any role, the table asks for night results, and a dead Investigator left no public check.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No hard leads and the room leans toward abstaining; an outlier vote would draw attention.
No claimed tracker has exposed my visit; no one has challenged me.
My wolf partner player_9 is not under any accusation today.

situations: Day 2 opens with no claims after two town-role deaths on night 1 (a fortune teller and an investigator, the latter killed by your pack); the village is asking for Sentinel or Trailseer reads to cross-check, and you must stay unexposed while players start to demand concrete information. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified night results, no claims, no votes beyond a day-1 vote that was not held; only self-described absence of results from players. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game; a misdirected or early vote is recoverable but would still spend a town elimination that the wolves need to be spent wisely, and the concealment charges (two) are unspent. Consensus: No consensus yet. Players are asking for night results to be shared before pointing at anyone, with no basis for a shared target. My position: With the room: asking for claims and cross-checks before any vote, not driving any target. Heat: Low. You have said only that you hold no night result, which is neutral; no one has pointed at you. Forward exposure: Any public claim of a night result or any defense of a target would commit you to a story that can be checked later; staying unclaimed keeps the option to speak later and is reversible, while a claim is not. Target landscape: Eight living players with no public claims; no one has claimed a role, the only dead players are the fortune teller and the investigator (concealed by no one), and no accusation or vote beyond player_6's vote on player_7 has produced evidence against anyone. Public vs private: Privately, as the illusionist and a wolf, you know your pack partner player_6 is alive and that player_7 was your pack's night-1 kill; publicly you are an unclaimed town-style player with no night story, and the village has no reason yet to suspect either wolf.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

verdicts.why: Room leans abstain on an information-starved day with no evidence; joining the abstain majority avoids a lone wolf-linked vote beside player_6.
No information-role claimant has been named yet, so there is no claimed trailseer or sentinel to vote against.
No claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me; I am not under a hard-evidence duel.

situations: Day 2 opened with no role claims after two night kills and an unanimous abstain vote; players are pressing each other to state night results, and the Trailseer holds a private follow of one living player whose visit could be cross-checked against tomorrow's morning report. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public claims, no announced checks or watches, no verified night results; only the public death roles and the abstain tally exist. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the next vote or kill cannot end the game, so a mistaken lynch is recoverable but each lost town member narrows the margin, and the unresolved abstain pattern means no information is being produced yet. Target landscape: Seven-to-eight living players with no public role claims; the only confirmed facts are the two night deaths (a fortune teller and an investigator, roles revealed) and an abstain-everywhere day 2 vote. No candidate has a public role status or verified evidence; every suspect is judged on behavior in discussion alone.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

lessons.situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The Trailseer must pick a first follow target blindly, while the wolves and a lone killer may also pick arbitrary opening kills, including the Trailseer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no voting record, no night history, only baseline impressions from Day 1. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and evil far from parity, so no single follow is decisive. The value is in collecting a first concrete visit link before wagons and claims form, and the Trailseer may be killed before reporting it. Target landscape: Nine unrevealed other players with no claims, votes or behavioral deviations; any pick is an exploratory behavioral guess, so choose an unread player who does not stand out.
lessons.action: On the opening night with no claims or reads, follow one unread, low-profile player to get a concrete movement baseline. If the result names a door, keep it as a checkable link to cross-reference against other night results and later claims. If it shows no visits, treat that as weak information, because a wolf carrier whose victim was concealed leaves no trace, and the target may also be a passive role.

lessons.situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

situations: Day 2 opened with two deaths from night 1 (a fortune teller killed by the serial killer and an investigator killed by the wolves, neither with a public check). Players are pressing for night results to be shared, and the village abstained on the day-2 vote, so no one was eliminated and the next night will decide the next kill and protection. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public claims, no checks, no sentinel or trailseer reads have been shared, and the only private knowledge held is the healer's own protection record from night 1 with no attack announced on the protected player. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single elimination can end the game; a mis-elimination is costly but recoverable, though the two abstain-led days leave the village without a confirmed information source. Target landscape: Seven-to-eight living players with no public role claims or checks; no candidate has any public role status beyond being alive, and no accusation has been confirmed. Evidence is limited to day-2 discussion requests for night results and an abstaining vote, so every candidate rests on behavior alone.

lessons.situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The healer must pick a protect target for the pack's first kill with no prior results, and the wolves may kill the healer instead. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, no checks, no votes and no claims, only brief introductory remarks. Stakes: Early game with a full board, so a single night's protection will not decide the game. Losing the healer early removes protection from Night 2 onward, but the blind target cannot be improved with the information available. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public claims, no verified roles and no vote record. The only basis is thin Day 1 behavior, so the pick is speculative.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, protect one engaged, neutral-baseline player rather than stalling over the choice, since there is no evidence to rank candidates and you cannot protect yourself. Treat the night as a free baseline visit: if the morning shows a save or a death, that is the first real data for choosing Night 2 targets.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: Early night (night 2) after a public information-role claim, with the wolves (and possibly a lone killer) choosing their kill and the town's key information source an obvious target. Information landscape: Mostly unverified claims with few or no confirmed flips or wills, sometimes partly confirmed by a correct elimination; the claimant's visibility is the main evidence, and the healer has no hard read on which claim is real. Stakes: Losing the lead information role this early strips the town of checks before any roles are confirmed, while a save wastes the wolves' kill and keeps the town's lead intact; the board is not yet at parity, so one lost key role hurts but is not decisive. Target landscape: Several claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and quiet unclaimed players; the investigator who cleared the healer or whose check was validated is the most prominent unverified-or-confirmed target, versus a sentinel or trailseer with less impact.
lessons.action: On the night after a claimed investigator, sentinel or other information role has become the town's most visible information source, protect that claimant, since the wolves most likely attack the player who is verified or clearing others. If two claimants compete, protect the one whose results are most useful to the town (an investigator who has cleared you, or one whose check was confirmed by an elimination) over a less-pressing claimant.

verdicts.why: Night 2 is not an opening night; two deaths and a day of record already exist.
No public Town power-role claims have been made yet, so there is no claimed role to protect.
No information role has claimed publicly, so there is no claimant to protect.

situations: Day two opened with two information roles already dead and no role claim made by anyone; the village abstained on its first vote, so no one was eliminated, and players are asking anyone holding a night result to speak before pointing at anyone. The vigilante holds two shots and is deciding whether a shot now is justified or whether to keep bullets for a night when a claim can be checked. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified night results are public, the two town info roles that could have produced checks died unrevealed to the table, and the only public facts are the day-one kills and the unanimous abstain vote. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a single wrong shot is recoverable but spends one of only two bullets while wolves and the serial killer remain hidden. Forward exposure: Firing a shot now would reveal to the table that the vigilante role is in play and commit the shot to a target with no checkable evidence; the kill itself is irreversible, and a visible shot would mark the shooter as a potential wolf-slayer target at night. Target landscape: Eight alive players with no public role claims beyond the two dead town info roles (investigator and fortune teller both died without public checks); no candidate carries solid evidence, only discussion pressure to name a night result and a day-two abstain outcome.

lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.
lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

verdicts.why: No role confirmed and no night result or vote singles anyone out; hold fire and keep bullets for a real lead.

situations: Day 2 after two night deaths (a fortune teller killed by a stab on night 1 and an investigator killed by the wolves on night 1) with no public checks or sentinel/trailseer claims. Day 2 vote abstained, so no one was eliminated. Players are pressing for anyone holding a night result to speak before accusations begin, and the village has not yet identified any credible information source. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no public night results, no checks or watches reported; only the two revealed deaths and the abstain record exist as public facts. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and the game cannot end within one more elimination; a single mis-vote is recoverable but each day without a result narrows the margin for error. Forward exposure: Any visible move now, such as naming a night result, claiming a role, or voting a specific player, would commit the speaker publicly; the vote record is permanent and claims cannot be withdrawn, so exposure is effectively irreversible for the day. Target landscape: Eight players alive, none publicly claimed; no night result has been shared. Two roles already dead unrevealed in public terms except the fortune teller and investigator deaths were revealed. Candidates rest on behavior only, with no verified evidence against anyone.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

verdicts.why: Night 1 opening already passed; I already made my first kill on player_5.
No Investigator claim or check singling out a suspect exists on this board; player_7 died without a public check.
No healer save announced and no claimed investigator confirmed by a wolf flip.

situations: As a surviving Sentinel with one watch left and a private night-1 result of no visitors on the player watched, the village is discussing whether anyone holds a night result and is asking for visitor reports, while the day-2 vote abstained and no one was eliminated. The Sentinel must decide whether to spend the last watch tonight on a suspected likely victim or hold it for a stronger lead. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public claims, no public night results, no investigator check, and one private sentinel result (no visitors on the watched player on night 1). Votes are all abstentions, so no voting pattern exists yet. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so the game cannot end within one more elimination; a single watch spent on a weak lead costs the only remaining door-watch the Sentinel has, while holding it keeps a last visitor check for a stronger lead later. Target landscape: Eight players alive with no public role claims and no public night results; the only evidence is the day-2 abstain vote (everyone abstained) and the two deaths so far (a Fortune Teller and an Investigator, both killed at night). Candidates are all unverified; evidence is behavioral only, with no revealed-role confirmation among survivors.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. The Night 1 kill, a possible roleblock and the lone killer's attack can all land the same night, so the result may be lost, show nothing, or catch a key visitor. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no night results, no claims and no voting record. Only opening-round chatter exists.
