Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: player_3 has named me as a visitor to player_4, so I should avoid a lone retaliatory vote against the claimed trailseer.
Abstain is not offered today, so I must name a player and cannot take the abstain move this strategy point recommends.
My wolf partner player_9 is not under a concrete accusation from a claimed role.

situations: Day 3 after two abstain votes: the trailseer has publicly claimed a follow chain placing a player at the dead sentinel's door on night 1, which the sentinel's will contradicts, and the village asks for tests while the vigilante holder has not yet shown a shot. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single unverified trailseer claim, a dead sentinel's will that shows only one watch with no visitors, and no vigilante result; no investigator result exists since the investigator died night 1. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong vote is recoverable but each mis-elimination moves the wolves closer to parity, so the village's pace on tests matters. Consensus: The room is split and quiet: the village has abstained twice, players are asking for tests from the trailseer or vigilante, and no shared target has formed, based on the absence of hard evidence rather than any accusation. My position: Holding out from any push, with the room mostly asking for tests and no consensus to join. Heat: Low: I have not been named by any player in today's discussion, and my only public vote was an abstain on day 2 and a vote for player_4 in the later round, which is the sentinel now dead. Forward exposure: Any visible push for a vote or any night claim would commit me publicly to a position that could be tested against the sentinel's will and the trailseer's chain; a public stance is hard to reverse once the village treats it as a read. Target landscape: The trailseer claim (player_3) names a chain that places a player at the dead sentinel's door on night 1, which the sentinel's will does not confirm; the claimant is a single unverified town-role claim, and the other live players are unclaimed with no hard evidence on any of them. Public vs private: Privately I am the illusionist, a wolf, with two conceal uses left and knowledge of both pack kills; publicly I am an unclaimed town-looking player who has said nothing about any night, so the public read is neutral while my private knowledge is that I was part of the kills of the investigator and the sentinel.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

verdicts.why: Player_3 is a claimed trailseer, so I will not cast a lone vote against them; I vote player_1 instead, which the claimed trailseer already accused.
I am not breaking from the room on a lone elimination; my vote joins the public accusation against player_1.
No investigator or trailseer has hard evidence against me, so I am not in a duel.

situations: Day 3 ended with the healer lynched, and the village is now split between a trailseer claim and players who deny it, with the carrier of the wolves' kill unknown. The sigilist must predict which living player will attack tonight, since a sigil placed on a player who does not attack is wasted, and a sigil on a carrier or on a vigilante who shoots strikes them. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has verified a night result, the sentinel and investigator and fortune teller and healer are dead, and the only public data are the sentinel's will (watched player_9, saw no one) and the healer's will (protected player_4 and player_6, no attacks announced) plus one unverified trailseer chain. Stakes: Six alive with two eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, and the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a single misplaced sigil costs one of two remaining sigils without ending the game but narrowing the margin for error; a wasted sigil leaves the sigilist with one strike for the rest of the game. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a visible-in-outcome act: if it strikes, the struck player is revealed as an attacker, and a sigil with no effect narrows the target to a non-attacker; the sigil itself is spent on placement whether or not it triggers, so the choice is irreversible. Target landscape: Six players alive: the sigilist's own seat plus five others (player_2, player_3, player_6, player_8, player_9). Public roles are unclaimed except a trailseer claim by player_3 with a night chain that has not been verified; the vigilante has not yet revealed. Evidence is behavioral and vote-based, with the trailseer chain the only concrete trail and it places the now-lynched healer, not any living player, at the sentinel.

lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.

situations: A trailseer's follow chain implicated the just-lynched healer, the village voted the healer out, and now the unverified shot-holder and the trailseer's accuser are pressing each other as the next lynch is considered. The trailseer has been voted by two players, and the shot-holder asks for the trailseer's night 3 follow before voting again. Information landscape: Information-starved: the public record has the sentinel's will (one watch on a player, no visitors), the healer's protection record, the vote record, and claimed follow chains with no announced confirmation. Trailseer and shot claims are unverified claims only. Stakes: Six alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a wrong lynch is recoverable but leaves only two safe mistakes before a wolf-side win becomes possible. Target landscape: Six alive: the trailseer (self, honest chain), player_8 (holding an unused shot claim, pushed the lynch on the trailseer), player_9 and player_6 and player_2 (voted with the majority on the healer), player_10. Public role status: the healer was lynched and revealed; the investigator and sentinel and fortune teller are dead and revealed. Evidence versus behavior: the trailseer's night 1 and 2 chains are testable only through the eliminated healer's record, which matches the healer's protections on players 4 and 6; player_8's shot claim is unverified and no shot result has been announced.

lessons.situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

lessons.situation: A wolf was just eliminated by the vote, and the confirmed town investigator is the obvious target for wolf retaliation that night. The trailseer wants to preserve that investigator's last action in case they are killed. Information landscape: Info-rich: a wolf has been caught, the investigator is validated, and earlier night visits and claims are on record. Visit data on the likely victim is more valuable than a blind follow. Stakes: Losing the investigator without recovering their last check would remove a key information source. Seeing the investigator's visit, and getting it reported, can lead directly to the last wolf. Target landscape: The confirmed or strongly vetted info role facing retaliation, versus claimed protectors who were already attacked or saved, versus quiet unread players. The vetted role is the likeliest night victim and a natural way to find their last target.
lessons.action: When the trailseer's own role is likely to draw an attack, follow the player the wolves most want dead, such as the confirmed investigator who just exposed a wolf. If the target dies, the trailseer still learns whom they visited that night. That information can point suspicion at the visited player.

verdicts.why: Five players remain and the lynch voted 2-1-1 against me, so following a live unverified suspect who is holding a shot fits the late-game approach.
This is Night 3, not Night 1, and no blind pick is needed.
No wolf was eliminated by vote and the investigator is already dead on Night 1.

situations: Day 3, after the village lynched a player revealed as the healer on a mostly unanimous vote, the two remaining accusers are the self-described trailseer and a quiet player who has been voting against them, while the vigilante holds two shots and has no verified lead against any living player. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only role-specific evidence is one untested follow chain from a trailseer claim, the sentinel's will (one watch, no visitors), and the healer's protection record; no investigator, sentinel, or healer result is live. Stakes: Six alive with two more eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong elimination would leave the village one step closer to parity, so the vigilante's remaining shots are valuable but a shot on an unverified target would be costly and could not be undone. Forward exposure: Publicly firing a shot would reveal the vigilante role and commit the agent to a target; a shot cannot be taken back, and a miss or a town kill would be irreversible, while holding fire keeps the role hidden. Target landscape: Six living players; the public trailseer claim (player_3) names a night-1 visit to the sentinel that is untested and matches no confirmed record; the sentinel's will shows it watched player_9 and saw no one; no living player has a confirmed role or a verified night result.

lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.
lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

verdicts.why: Healer is now lynched and the board has a concrete trailseer claim, so this is no longer an information-starved night.
The only named lead is player_3's untested trailseer claim, which is not hard evidence, so I hold fire rather than shoot.

situations: The village just lynched a player whose will revealed a Healer record, and a Trailseer claim now names the Chanteuse as a visitor to a dead player, creating pressure to find which Town power to cancel tonight. The Chanteuse must decide which Town player's night action to block while coordinating a kill with the wolf partner, and the lynched Healer's protections suggest the remaining protector may be targeted. Information landscape: Information-starved on the wolf side: no confirmed Investigator or Sentinel alive, only the dead Sentinel's will (watched player_9, saw no one) and an unverified Trailseer chain. Public votes on day 3 are the only hard data; the Chanteuse holds only its own block and kill history. Stakes: Six alive and two eliminations from a wolf win, so one mis-elimination or one successful wolf kill does not end the game but tightens it sharply; a kill tonight leaves five alive and one further elimination to reach parity, making the next block or vote a decisive cost. Forward exposure: Any visible move tonight (a block announced or implied, or a vote tomorrow) is reversible only in the sense that the outcome is public; the carrier's kill and any block become known to the table through morning results, so the pack's choice is already exposed once the night resolves. Target landscape: Six players alive: the Chanteuse's own pack partner, the Fortune Teller (unrevealed, neutral), and Town roles still possibly holding powers including a Trailseer claim whose chain names the Chanteuse as a visitor to a dead Sentinel's victim. The Healer was just lynched and its record shows it protected two players on nights 1 and 2 without any save announced. Remaining claims are unverified, and the Vigilante has not yet revealed a shot.

A Trailseer claimant has publicly named the Chanteuse as a visitor to a dead player and invited testing of the vote pattern, while a silent player has said they are holding a shot. The Chanteuse must choose whether to block the claimed Trailseer, which would stop a follow that could expose the pack, or a silent role whose shot could hit the wolves. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only Town claim is the Trailseer chain, unverified and contradicted by no public fact, while the Vigilante's shot is unrevealed and the Sigilist has not spoken. The most recent vote record shows the village converging on the claimed Healer's lynch, not on the Trailseer. Stakes: Six alive and two eliminations from a wolf win, so a wrong block that leaves the Trailseer able to follow the Chanteuse's visit costs a full night of exposure while the pack still needs two more successful eliminations; the wolves can afford a single misdirected night but not repeated exposure. Forward exposure: Blocking a Town power tonight is visible to the target as a roleblock message and reveals to the table that someone was blocked, so the block itself is a visible act with a hidden source; the pack's kill is visible through the victim's death and role reveal. Target landscape: Surviving Town candidates with active night roles: the Trailseer (claimed, unverified, whose chain names the Chanteuse), the Vigilante (publicly silent, holding a shot), and the Sigilist (unrevealed). The Fortune Teller is neutral. Candidates differ by whether their claimed or silent role could reveal the pack's visits.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: The chanteuse is the pack's carrier this night. A town sigilist is alive and has signaled traps, and the wolves want to kill a tracker or investigator who exposed them. Information landscape: Information-rich: day-2 claims by the trailseer, sentinel and sigilist show active town surveillance. Whether a sigil is already on a given wolf is unknown. Stakes: Dying to a sigil on the kill night loses a wolf and exposes the chanteuse. That leaves a lone illusionist against town, which is close to losing. Forward exposure: The block is a visit but it hides the sigilist's action. If the sigilist is not the one blocked, the sigil still strikes the carrier, kills you, and reveals the chanteuse. You can switch targets each night, but a death by sigil cannot be undone. Target landscape: The claimed or suspected sigilist (2 sigils, possibly already spent), the kill target (a trailseer or sentinel who exposed a wolf visit), and other town info roles. Which player holds the sigil is deduced from public claims.
lessons.action: If you will carry the pack kill and a sigilist has claimed or is likely active, use your block on the sigilist. A blocked sigilist places nothing and makes no visit, so no sigil can strike you when you attack. If you cannot tell who the sigilist is, block the most likely candidate instead of the kill target.

verdicts.why: Opening night is long past; the board now has claims and deaths.
Trailseer player_3 has publicly claimed and can follow me, so blocking the live info role fits; I am a carrier-less blocker tonight, so I should aim at a non-kill target.
No vigilante has been confirmed by a kill on a wolf.
The sigilist has not claimed publicly and no sigil has been shown.
Opening night is past; the board now has deaths and claims.
Trailseer player_3 claims a follow chain that could expose the carrier, so blocking the live info role fits; player_3 is the block target.
No vigilante has been confirmed by a kill on a wolf.
No sigilist has claimed or signaled traps yet.

situations: Day 3 after a healer was lynched; the village is split between a Trailseer claim whose night-1 visit to the dead Sentinel's watch target is unverified and a shot claim that openly challenges it, and two accusers are voting against each other. The agent, a Serial Killer with no public result, must avoid drawing attention while the room coordinates votes against the most accusing players. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public hard facts are the dead players' records (Sentinel watched one player and saw no one; Healer protected two players with no attack announced). All living role claims are unverified claims. Stakes: Six alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a single wrong lynch is recoverable but narrows the margin for the remaining wolves and the Serial Killer. Forward exposure: Any visible move by the agent (naming a player, claiming a result, or voting against a claimed info role) commits it publicly; a vote is permanent on the record and cannot be undone, while a verbal claim can be contradicted later by another claimant. Target landscape: Five living candidates other than the agent: a claimed Trailseer whose chain was partly confirmed by the healer's will (player_3), a player holding an unverified shot claim (player_8), and three quieter players whose roles are unknown. Public role status: the Sentinel, Investigator, Fortune Teller, and Healer are dead and revealed; the Serial Killer is the agent itself. Basis is behavioral and claimed, with no announced confirmation of any living player's role.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

situations: Night 3 with a healer lynched on day 3 by a 5-vote majority against player_1 after a trailseer claim; the trailseer's chain was partially contradicted by the sentinel's will, and the illusionist's pack is choosing its night 3 victim with two conceals still in hand while the claimed trailseer and a shot-holding player remain unresolved. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town: no living claimed investigator or sentinel, only an unverified trailseer claim and an unverified shot claim; the healer's protection record is now public history but the healer is dead. The illusionist privately knows the night 1 and night 2 kills and its own remaining conceal count. Stakes: Six alive with two eliminations needed before the wolves can reach parity; the pack's kill tonight leaves five, so one more kill plus one lynch would bring the wolves to a win, meaning a conceal on a town-revealing victim buys real information denial but each conceal is one of only two remaining and a wrong lynch is recoverable but costly. Forward exposure: Any conceal of tonight's pack victim hides their role and attacker trace from the town and reveals to the illusionist alone; spending a conceal is irreversible and a Sentinel or Trailseer watching the victim would otherwise see the carrier's visit. Target landscape: Living players are the town-looking discussion group (several claimed-free players, one trailseer claimant player_3 whose chain names the healer who was just lynched, and an accuser player_8 pushing a shot-holding narrative); pack target not yet named. Public role status: Sentinel, Investigator, Fortune Teller, Healer are dead; wolf partner player_6 is alive and carries tonight.

Day 3 vote has concluded with the healer lynched; the remaining town is split between an unverified trailseer claim and an accusing player holding a shot, while the illusionist must keep a low-profile cover and avoid lone pushes against claimed information roles. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public evidence is one trailseer chain (partly contradicted by the sentinel's will regarding player_1 visiting the sentinel on night 1) and a sentinel will showing a watch on the illusionist's own position with no visitors; no confirmed investigator results remain alive. Stakes: Six alive, two eliminations from wolf parity; the next day's lynch leaves five, where one more pack kill would bring the wolves to equal footing with the remaining town, so a wrong vote against the trailseer claimant now would be costly and hard to recover from. Forward exposure: Choosing a day vote or a bet-free public accusation commits the illusionist to a visible position; reversing a vote later is possible only through later discussion, not the record, since votes are permanent. Target landscape: Accusable living candidates are the trailseer claimant player_3 (claim unverified, chain partly contradicted), the shot-holding accuser player_8 (claim unverified), and the neutral cover-seeking player_2; the wolf partner is also alive and must not be exposed.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

verdicts.why: Chanteuse is alive and we have two wolves, so the lone-illusionist situation does not hold.
Night 1 already passed and we have no conceals spent; this is night 3 with a different board.

Stakes: Six alive with two eliminations until the wolves can win: the next single elimination does not end the game, but two more wrong lynches or kills would hand the wolf side a win, so a block or kill that misdirects the trailseer's information is costly while the board remains recoverable. Forward exposure: Tonight's visible move is the pack's kill and my own block; a block is a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see, and a kill on a non-wolf reveals nothing directly but is irreversible. Any public claim of the chanteuse role or wolf-side knowledge would be irreversible. Target landscape: Surviving players are six: a live trailseer claim whose chain was tied to a now-lynched healer and cannot be verified, a player pushing a held shot with no named target, an aggressive accuser pair, and one quiet player who has not claimed anything. Public role status: no alive player has a confirmed role; the trailseer and vigilante-style claims rest on claims alone, with the trailseer chain unverifiable since the healer's removal.

lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

situations: As the illusionist with the pack's kill assigned to a quiet unclaimed player, you must decide whether the victim is worth a conceal, since the revealed role and its record would give the town information. Target landscape: Tonight's pack target is one surviving player with no public claim and no public evidence against them; the other living players include a claimed trailseer whose chain cannot be verified, an accuser pushing a shot-holder, and a player currently receiving a lynch vote.

A claimed trailseer and a shot-holding accuser are pushing against each other in the day discussion while the pack still needs a quiet kill tonight. The illusionist must weigh whether the claimed trailseer's public chain, now unverifiable, makes that player a better kill target or a player better left alone. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a confirmed role, one claim is unverifiable, and the vote record shows the town converged on one player by a wide margin. Stakes: Two eliminations remain before the wolves can win with six alive, so this kill is not a swing and does not end the game in one step; a mis-timed kill still leaves the pack two steps from parity, but each wasted conceal reduces the pack's ability to protect its own role reveals later. Forward exposure: Keeping both conceals in reserve preserves options for later nights but does nothing about tonight's victim being revealed; using one now spends it in a night where the victim may not be worth hiding. Target landscape: The living players are the illusionist (self), the pack carrier, the claimed trailseer, a shot-holding accuser, and two other quiet or vocal players; public evidence against any of them is behavioral only.

situations: Four players remain with a split between the claimed vigilante player_8 and the vocal player_2 and player_9, after the day 3 lynch of the healer and the concealed-role death of player_10. The village must choose whether to push the vigilante's shot claim or hold the vote open. Information landscape: Information-starved: only dead players' records (healer, trailseer, sentinel, investigator) and one unverified vigilante claim exist; no living player has a checkable result. Stakes: Four alive, zero eliminations from a wolf-side win at worst for the town (a concealed body's side is unknown, so this is the closest it could be); a single wrong vote or kill can end the game, so each day's move is decisive. Consensus: The village is split between a vigilante claimant and the player pushing back on them, with no hard evidence; no single consensus target has formed among the four survivors. My position: Holding out and following the room, not driving any target. Heat: Low to moderate: I have voted player_10 on day 3 and stayed quiet, so I have not drawn sustained accusation, but my earlier wolf-channel role in the night 1 and 2 kills is private. Forward exposure: Any visible move on day 4, such as a vote or a stated read, commits me publicly and is hard to reverse once the room locks onto a target; staying silent keeps my exposure low but leaves the village deciding without me. Target landscape: Four living players: the active accuser player_8 (claimed vigilante, with a held shot), player_9 (pack-aligned voice, vocal), player_2 (heavily pushed, no confirmed role), and myself. Public role status: no living player has a confirmed role; the only confirmed roles are the dead, including a healer and trailseer. Basis is behavioral and claim-based, not hard evidence. Public vs private: As the Chanteuse, privately known to me as a wolf, I know my pack partner is alive and unrevealed; publicly the village sees only four survivors and an unrevealed concealed body from night 3, while the claimed trailseer player_3 was already dead before this day.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

situations: Day 4 opens with four alive and no vote yet; a claimed vigilante (player_8) is being pressed by player_2 to name the held shot target, while the wolves' partner has not been exposed and one of player_2 or player_8 is the remaining serial killer, creating a public deadlock where any early vote could land on a town player. There are no live checks or watches from alive players. Stakes: Four alive with the wolves at two of them and a possible serial killer among the rest: distance to parity is 0 at worst for the town, so the next elimination can end the game, meaning a wrong lynch hands the wolves a win and must be avoided at all costs. Consensus: The room is split: no consensus on a lynch, with player_2 and player_8 pushing each other and player_6 following the room, so no clear direction has formed yet. My position: Holding out, aligned loosely with player_6 and following the room on the vote rather than driving a target. Forward exposure: Any visible push for or against a claimed role commits you to a side in the player_2 versus player_8 fight and cannot be taken back once it is on the record; a vote is permanent and public, so the move would be irreversible, and your last conceal is spent only at night. Target landscape: Alive are player_2 (no public claim, pushing hard in discussion), player_6 (your partner, unrevealed, voted player_10 on day 3), and player_8 (claimed vigilante, held a shot that has not yet been used). Evidence is mostly behavioral: the player_8 claim is unverified and player_2's accusations rest on talk, not results. Public vs private: Privately you are the illusionist and know your pack partner is alive and unrevealed, and you know the concealed body of player_10 was a sigilist, which the village cannot see. Publicly the village reads a concealed death with no role and a quiet wolf-adjacent player, while player_2 and player_8 argue over a vigilante claim.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.
