Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No trailseer has exposed my visit today; the board is different from this claimant scenario.
Day 4 has no abstain majority to join and the wolves are down to me and player_9; the early-game situation does not hold.
Player_9 is my wolf partner, and the vote is decisive only if I avoid a counter-vote beside them; I will vote with the room.

situations: Four players remain with a claimed vigilante and a serial-killer-aligned player (you) hidden among them; the village argues over a dead trailseer's night chain and a revealed healer's lynch, and the next day's vote will decide whether a claimed vigilante or another player is eliminated. Information landscape: Information-starved for the village: the only hard facts are the revealed roles of dead players and their written records; the trailseer and sentinel chains cannot be cross-checked, and the vigilante claim is unverified. Stakes: Four alive with a concealed-side count at worst for town: the next elimination can end the game, so a single wrong vote or a single kill is decisive and a mislynch of a claimed vigilante would leave the town unable to recover. Consensus: The village is fractured after a day-3 lynch of a revealed healer and the claim-driven fights over the trailseer's chain; no clear consensus on who is wolf-aligned, and the living players have not yet converged. My position: Holding out from any forming consensus, since none has formed; you are not driving the discussion and have no public stance. Heat: Low on you: no one has named you, and your only public record is the day-2 abstention and a day-3 vote for the lynched healer. Suspicion currently sits on no one specific. Forward exposure: Any visible accusation, vote, or defense by you would commit you publicly and is hard to reverse once the village reads it; staying quiet keeps your kill record and hidden identity intact but lets the village's discussion of the day-3 trailseer and healer chains drive the next vote. Target landscape: Four living players: a claimed vigilante (player_8, unverified, with a sharp accusation record against the dead trailseer), a quiet player (player_6), a player (player_9) who pressed the night-1 chain question, and yourself. Basis is behavioral and claim-based; no hard evidence confirms any of them. Public vs private: As the serial killer, you privately know you have killed three players (a fortune teller, a sentinel, a trailseer) and that the wolves and you remain hidden; publicly the village only knows the revealed roles of the dead and a claimed vigilante (player_8) whose claim is unchecked, while the village has no confirmed information about who is wolf-aligned.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

verdicts.why: No living Sentinel or Trailseer report places me at a victim's door; the only trail report named player_1 visiting player_4.

situations: Four players remain alive and the day-4 vote tied between player_9 (the Illusionist) and player_2, with player_6 and player_8 voting them out; the Illusionist holds its last conceal while the pack partner has voted with the room against the non-wolves. Tonight the pack must choose a victim among the remaining non-wolves, and whether the victim's revealed role and record would help the town is the question. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town: no living sentinel, investigator, trailseer or healer remains, only a claimed vigilante (player_8) whose shot has not been used publicly. The Illusionist's private night record shows player_10 was a concealed sigilist and the pack's previous kills were player_7, player_4 and player_10. The Serial Killer's identity and actions are unknown publicly. Stakes: Four alive with the wolves at two and the Serial Killer unknown; distance to parity is 0 at worst for the town, so one more elimination of a non-wolf can let the wolves equal everyone else and win, and a wrong tied or abstained vote keeps the balance razor-thin. Forward exposure: Any conceal used tonight is a permanent, one-shot act: the victim's role stays hidden until game end, and the concealment itself leaves the carrier's kill untraceable only if the illusionist does not carry the kill; carrying and concealing on the same night leaves no trace at that door, but the single remaining conceal cannot be undone. Target landscape: Surviving candidates are player_6 (fellow wolf), player_2 and player_8 (the only living non-wolves, public claimant of vigilante is player_8). Tonight's pack target is not yet named. Public roles of the survivors are unrevealed; the Illusionist's private knowledge is that player_10 was a sigilist, concealed.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack picks a quiet, unread first victim and you are the wolf who carries the kill. The risk is that the Trailseer or Sentinel catches your visit and gives Town a day-2 accusation against you. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day-1 vote, no claims, no confirmed roles, no night history. Only private wolf talk exists. Stakes: Early game with plenty of time. The main risk is losing a wolf early to a traced visit, which would cost the pack the endgame. A clean first night matters more than saving a charge. Forward exposure: Announces that an illusionist exists and spends one of two conceals if the victim dies. Your own visit leaves no trace, and the spent charge cannot be undone. If the victim survives, nothing is announced and the use is kept. Target landscape: Eight or nine unclaimed, unread players with no roles revealed. The target is picked from quiet behavior, not evidence, and could be a watcher, a tracker, or the night-immune lone killer.
lessons.action: When the carrier rotation makes you the carrier on night 1, carry the kill and use a conceal on the victim. A conceal on a victim you carried yourself leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer, and if the target turns out immune the use is kept.

verdicts.why: Chanteuse is alive on this board per the pack, and the investigator is already dead, so this lone-wolf conceal plan does not fit.
This is night 4, not night 1; the early-game quiet-victim plan no longer applies.
Night 1 carrier plan does not apply to the current night 4 board.

situations: After a 2-2 tie on day 4 with three players alive, the serial killer (who knows its own kills) faces a split vote in which the surviving pair have voted each other out and the third living player claimed vigilante; the tie means no one was eliminated and abstaining is no longer offered. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public facts are the dead players' revealed roles and wills (the trailseer's chain and the sentinel's single watch seeing no one); the vigilante claim is unverified and no night results have been shared by the living. Stakes: Four alive with the leading evil faction at distance 0: the next elimination can end the game, so a single vote or kill decides the outcome. The concealed-body side is unknown, so this is the closest it could be, and one wrong lynch of a non-wolf would leave the serial killer and a wolf pair with a path to a two-player finish. Forward exposure: Any visible vote or accusation now would commit the serial killer's public profile to one side of a deadlocked pair; a vote for either tied player is publicly on record and cannot be retracted, though later days can still shift the count. Target landscape: Two tied candidates remain: one player who voted to eliminate the other and was voted back, and the other who cast the opposing vote; no one holds a confirmed role publicly, and the only public claim on the board is an unverified vigilante claim from player_8, who is the third living player.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

verdicts.why: No claimed Investigator is alive; player_7 the investigator died on night 1.
This is day 4 with several deaths and claims on record, not an opening night.
The healer is dead (player_1 was lynched), so no healer save pattern applies.

situations: Day 4 ended in a two-way tie after the two remaining accusers voted against each other, leaving four players alive including the vigilante with two bullets. The vigilante must decide whether to use a shot at night on one of three living players with no night result pointing at a wolf. Information landscape: Information-starved: no role claims among survivors except the vigilante's own, no investigations or watches still active, the only public information is the day vote record and two dead-role wills that do not name anyone alive. Stakes: Four alive with 0 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so the next result (a kill or a lynch) can end the game; at worst for the town a concealed body's side is unknown, so the closest parity is already reached. A wrong shot on a town player would leave a likely wolf or serial killer majority in reach, while holding fire wastes no bullet but leaves the town without a removal. Forward exposure: Firing a shot at a named living player would be a visible attack and a visit that the surviving players would read as a vigilante reveal; the shot spends one of two bullets and cannot be reloaded, so it cannot be undone, while holding fire keeps both bullets and the vigilante claim unverified. Target landscape: Three living candidates: one tied-vote accuser pair (two players who each voted to eliminate the other) and the remaining living player; none has a public role claim, and the vigilante has no night result naming a living player to act on, so basis is behavioral only.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.
lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

verdicts.why: No confirmed role reveal or disproven claim points to a living wolf; the only reveals are dead Town roles.
Still no night result or vote record names a living player as evil, so holding fire keeps both bullets for a real lead.

situations: Day 4 ended in a tie between player_9 and player_2, with player_8 voting player_9 and the chanteuse voting player_2. The claimed vigilante is pressing player_9 and asking whether the shot is held or used, while the wolf partner carries tonight's kill and the pack's target is not yet named. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town: no sentinel, trailseer, investigator, or healer results are alive or public beyond old records; the only public claim with weight is the unverified vigilante claim by player_8. The chanteuse's private night records confirm player_10 and player_3 were removed and player_7 and player_4 were killed earlier. Stakes: Four alive with the leading evil faction at zero eliminations from parity: the next death can end the game, and a concealed-body side is unknown so this is the worst case. A single kill or vote that removes a town-aligned survivor leaves the wolves able to equal the remaining living players, so the decision is decisive rather than recoverable. Forward exposure: Any night block on a town player is a visible-in-hindsight move: if the blocked player is the claimed vigilante or a town role whose result later matters, the block is traced to the chanteuse's side only if the blocked player reports 'You were roleblocked' publicly; a block on the vigilante would also remove a shot the wolves cannot otherwise stop, and that choice is irreversible for the night. Target landscape: Surviving players are player_9 (wolf partner, carrier tonight), player_2 (unrevealed, voted against player_9 on day 4), and player_8 (publicly claimed vigilante, holding a shot, voted against player_9). Two living town-aligned or neutral candidates remain besides the wolves; the serial killer and fortune teller roles are unassigned to any alive player in public knowledge, and the wolf pack's remaining targets are player_2 and player_8. Evidence is behavioral only: the vigilante claim is unverified and the tied vote split is public.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

verdicts.why: The vigilante is only claimed by player_8, not confirmed by a kill, and no wolf partner has died to it.
Block target should be chosen to stop a live info role; player_2 is the only other town-side claim-free player and the investigator is dead.
Opening night rules no longer apply; eight players have died.
No confirmed vigilante has killed a wolf; player_8 is only a claim.
Investigator and trailseer are dead, so the block should target the living threat, player_8's claimed shot, rather than an information role.
It is no longer the opening night.
The vigilante is only claimed by player_8 and not confirmed by a kill on a wolf; no wolf partner has been killed by it.
Player_3 is dead, so the trailseer block is moot; the live info threats are player_2 and player_8, and a block on the kill target is redundant.
This is night 4 with the opening night long past.

situations: A day-4 vote ended in a tie between the illusionist and player_2, with player_8 (claiming vigilante) voting against the illusionist. Tonight the pack must choose among the three remaining non-wolf-known players, and the illusionist holds its last conceal, which would hide the victim's role from the town if the victim is a Town role whose will would otherwise be read out. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town: no living player has a confirmed night result, the sentinel, trailseer, healer and investigator are all dead, and the only public role claim is an unverified vigilante claim. Private information held by the illusionist: last night's concealed victim was a sigilist, and the serial killer's identity is unknown. Stakes: Four alive with zero eliminations until the leading evil faction can win: the next death can end the game, so the next kill or lynch is decisive. A tie-vote on the illusionist and the unaccounted serial killer make a wrong or unhidden result immediately game-ending, while the single remaining conceal is the only way to keep a victim's role off the record. Forward exposure: Conceal on tonight's pack victim would hide the victim's role and the carrier's visit to them, committing the last conceal and revealing nothing publicly; a plain kill reveals the victim's role and will to the town, and that cannot be undone. Target landscape: Three living players other than the illusionist: player_6, player_2, player_8. Player_8 publicly claims vigilante and is voting against the illusionist; player_6 and player_2 are tied in day-4 votes with no public role claims. Public role status is one unverified vigilante claim and two unclaimed players; the evidence is behavioral only.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

verdicts.why: Chanteuse is dead and I am not the lone surviving illusionist with the carrier role alone; the board has two wolves alive.
Night 4 with confirmed deaths and claims already public; this is not an information-starved night 1.
The pack should spend no conceal on a victim here; the choice is between player_2 and player_8, and the trace matters more than the role.

situations: Four players remain alive: the wolf partner (tied on the day 4 vote and under pressure from the claimed vigilante), the claimed vigilante who voted against the wolf partner, one other town-side player who was tied with the wolf partner and voted against the chanteuse's ally, and the chanteuse itself. The day 4 vote tied with two votes each, so no one was eliminated; the claimed vigilante's shot is still an open threat, with its bullets status unstated publicly. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only verified facts are the revealed roles of dead players (trailseer, healer, sentinel, investigator, fortune teller, and one concealed role), and the record of the healer and the trailseer. The claimed vigilante's claim is unverified, and no one has produced a night result that survives scrutiny. Town-side players hold private results that are not shared. Stakes: Four alive with the wolves needing to equal or outnumber everyone else, and the lone serial killer still alive, so the wolves cannot win while it lives; but the distance to parity is 0, meaning the next elimination can end the game for the evil side. One wrong elimination or one unblocked kill of a player who matters could decide the game. Forward exposure: Any visible night action by the chanteuse (block or kill) is only seen in the morning report; a block leaves the blocked player told they were roleblocked, and a kill reveals the pack's choice. Choosing between blocking the claimed vigilante and killing a different player commits the pack to a target publicly once the morning report is out, and that cannot be taken back. Target landscape: Surviving players are the two-player town pair (one claims vigilante with no verification, the other is accused by the wolf partner and is an unclaimed quiet-or-vocal player), plus the serial killer and the fortune teller, who are not visible roles in the public record. The claimed vigilante's claim is unverified; the other town-side player has made no claim in the record.

The claimed vigilante is voting against the wolf partner and has held or used a shot that has not been announced; the wolf partner asks it to name a target or say the shot is held, while the other town-side player continues to push against the room. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results from the surviving town players have been shared, and the vigilante's claim has no confirmation. The only public evidence is the votes on the record. Stakes: Four alive and a distance to parity of 0, so a single kill or a single vote that eliminates a player can end the game for the evil side; a wrong target now is not recoverable. Forward exposure: A block on the claimed vigilante is a visit only if it takes; a block the target does not know about leaves the chanteuse's choice visible only through what the blocked player reports. Naming the vigilante as the block target signals to the remaining town that the pack fears its shot, and that signal cannot be retracted. Target landscape: The claimed vigilante (unverified claim, the player voting against the wolf partner) and the other town-side player (no claim, vocal in the day). The vigilante is the only player in the record whose role is a live lethal threat, though its bullet count is not public.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles such as the healer and necromancer are confirmed, and the investigator and trailseer have public claims and results on record. Stakes: Town has lost its healer protection but still has information roles; removing the investigator while blinding the tracker for a night shifts the information balance toward the wolves before parity pressure builds. Forward exposure: Blocking shows the village only that some blocker exists, if the blocked player speaks of it; nothing ties the block to you, and you can switch block targets nightly. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.
lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

situations: Three players remain alive after a vigilante claim died without firing, and you as the lone killer are one of three; the village has a tied prior vote and no public evidence pointing at any living player. Information landscape: Information-starved: only public death records, two prior will-style records and an unchecked vigilante claim, with no living role claims verified. Stakes: Three alive with the game able to end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a single wrong vote or kill decides the outcome and a misdirected lynch would be fatal to the town's chance. Consensus: No consensus exists yet; the day 4 vote tied with no elimination and the village has only public deaths and claims to work from. My position: Holding out quietly, with no stated position against any forming majority because none has formed yet. Heat: Moderate suspicion on you from the day 4 tie, where two players voted for you, but no hard evidence links you to any death. Forward exposure: Any visible move today, such as defending or attacking a claim, would reveal attention to the living players and commit you to a read; staying quiet keeps the move reversible but leaves the village free to form its own read. Target landscape: Three living players remain: one unknown-role player who has been in a tied vote with you, one player who voted against you, and one player with no public role claim; all three are unverified and their basis is behavioral only. Public vs private: As the serial killer, you privately know you killed the fortune teller, investigator-role-independent victims, sentinel, trailseer and vigilante, while the village reads only public deaths and a claimed vigilante who was killed on night 4 with no shot fired; your private knowledge is complete on your own kills and nothing on the wolves' identities.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

verdicts.why: Room is not yet targeting me, so I stay quiet rather than build a case now.
No sentinel or trailseer has named me as a visitor on day 5.
No claimed role has labeled me passive or tied me to a dead wolf's vote.
Pressure is real, but a fresh accusation now would give the room a checkable target and risk my own cover; I'll stay quiet this turn.
No one has named me as a visitor to a victim today.
I have not been labeled passive by any role claimant today.

decision.message: I voted player_9 on day 4 and player_3 on day 3, both on the record, so I have not just abstained. player_6, you voted me on day 4 and today you only want a clean vote on me. Who do you think is the wolf between player_9 and yourself, and why?

verdicts.why: The room is pressing me with only three alive, so I should give a checkable case against player_9 instead of staying passive.
No Sentinel has named me as a visitor, so there is no visit report to answer.
I have been quiet and voted-against, so I should engage with a specific read based on the public vote record.

decision.message: player_9, the record says you voted to eliminate player_2 on day 4, not player_8. Player_8 voted you that day, and your only read on me is that tied vote plus my abstains. Before a lynch, check your own vote record against what you just said.

verdicts.why: The room is pressing me, so I build a checkable case against player_9 from the public vote record.
No Sentinel or Trailseer has named me as a visitor to a night victim on this board.
I am not passive here; I am answering a specific accusation with a record contradiction, which is more useful than a general read.

decision.message: I have no night result and no claim. Day 3 I voted player_3, who came out as trailseer, and day 4 I voted player_9. player_9, you voted me on day 4 and then named player_8 for it, so the record is your own contradiction. player_6 voted me once and now wants a clean lynch on me, so I'd weigh both votes before lynching.

verdicts.why: The room is against me, so I am turning the vote onto player_9's record contradiction and keeping player_6 in the frame.
No Sentinel or Trailseer has named me as a visitor, so there is no visit report to answer.
I am answering with a specific read tied to the public votes rather than explaining my silence.

decision.message: My day 4 vote went to player_9 and my day 3 vote went to player_3, who came out as trailseer, so the record is not just abstains. player_9 voted me on day 4, then said player_8 did it, and that slip is on the record. player_6 wants a clean lynch on me after one vote, so weigh that against player_9's contradiction before you vote.

verdicts.why: Room is united against me with three alive, so I should split the vote by pressing a concrete contradiction in player_9's record.
No sentinel or trailseer has named me as a visitor to a night victim on this board.
I am being singled out for passivity, so I answer with specific reads tied to the public vote record instead of silence.

situations: With three players alive and a day 5 vote coming, the village has a tied history between two survivors and a just-killed vigilante claimer whose role was revealed; you alone hold the knowledge that the vigilante death was a pack kill, and must decide how visible to be while the other two survivors press each other. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only hard public records are the sentinel's single day 2 watch showing no visitors, the trailseer's two night follows, and the healer's protections that were never announced as saves; no investigator or sentinel result is live. Stakes: Three alive with the distance to parity at -1 means the wolves are already at or past parity on the worst-case count, and the game can end on the next elimination; a wrong lynch is decisive, so a single visible vote carries the full weight of ending the game. Consensus: No clear consensus among the three survivors; the day 4 vote was a tie with no abstain option, and public discussion has centered on demanding claims rather than shared evidence. My position: Holding out from any firm consensus, since none has formed, and avoiding leading a lynch on thin public reads. Heat: Moderate and rising: you voted for the vigilante claimer on day 4, which is public, and the tie on day 4 shows the other survivors have been pressing on each other rather than on you. Forward exposure: Any visible vote or statement that ties you to the pack's last kill or to the lynch of the claimed vigilante would be seen by the two other survivors and cannot be undone once the vote is recorded; your conceal is spent only if used, so holding it keeps that option open. Target landscape: Three living players remain: two other survivors whose roles are not publicly revealed, and yourself; the day 4 tie left both survivors with two votes each, and the only publicly revealed-dead recent claim is the vigilante, so the live choice is between the two survivors on public behavior alone. Public vs private: Privately you are the illusionist, a wolf with one conceal left and knowledge of your pack's kills; publicly the village sees only three living players with no wolf revealed, and the claimed vigilante who was killed night 4 is now a dead claim whose role was publicly revealed.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been revealed and killed. You are pressured over a lone vote against a dead Town player, while a Town player's result (a non-triggering sigil) is available as a defense. Information landscape: Moderate: public voting records and a privately held Town result that can be used to clear you, but no hard role confirmations on the quiet alternative suspect. Stakes: Each vote now decides whether the last wolf survives. Moving even a couple of swing voters off you keeps the wolf team alive into the final few players. Consensus: The village is split. Some players press you over the vote record, while players holding a clearing result and neutral voters are open to another suspect. My position: holding out Heat: High. Players cite your isolated vote against a now-dead player as the basis for suspicion. Forward exposure: Citing a Town player's result ties you to a non-attacking story that you cannot take back, and later tracking evidence could break it. The alternative-suspect push can be adjusted as new information arrives. Target landscape: Candidates are you, under pressure from the vote record, and a quiet player with no confirmed role who was targeted by the dead wolf. Suspicion of the quiet player is behavioral, while the case against you is the vote record. Public vs private: Privately you are an active wolf, but the partner carried the kill that night, so a Town result such as an un-triggered sigil looks exculpatory. The room reads that result as evidence you are not the killer.
lessons.action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Use only what the rules show: the sigil not triggering means only that you did not attack on that night, and it does not clear you of being a wolf. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.

situations: Three players remain after a vigilante claimant was killed at night and a day-4 tie left two players each accused by the other's voters. A night-killed vigilante's shot went unused, and a remaining player is pushing the room hard while another votes with the room, leaving the next elimination as a potential decider. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a confirmed night result, the only claimed roles (vigilante, trailseer, healer, sentinel) are dead or unverifiable, and the village has only vote history and discussion statements to work from. Stakes: Three alive with the evil faction's parity already reached at worst for the town, so the next elimination can end the game; a wrong lynch is not recoverable. Consensus: The room is not aligned: day 4 ended in a tie between player_9 and player_2, and the last vote pattern split across the remaining players with no shared target. My position: Holding out, without a strong public stance, following the room's broad direction rather than leading it. Heat: Moderate: you voted player_2 on day 4 and have been tracking the room without a strong accusation, but a claimed vigilante who was killed leaves the table asking who was pressing that claim. Forward exposure: Any visible move now (accusing, voting, or pushing a claim) commits you to a public position in a 3-player village; a vote on player_9 or player_2 would be visible and hard to reverse once the tie-or-elimination is on the record. Target landscape: Three living players: player_2 (pushing hard against the room on day 3-4, with one tie vote against them), player_9 (voting actively, reading the room), and yourself. Public role status of all three is unrevealed; the evidence is behavioral only, with player_9 having voted on player_8 after player_8's vigilante claim. Public vs private: As the chanteuse, you privately know you are a wolf and your pack killed player_8 last night; the public read is that a vigilante was killed and nothing about wolves is known. lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.
