situations: Three players remain alive. A player voted you out on day 4 and then publicly misstated the day 4 vote target, and a second player is pushing a clean lynch on you after the earlier tie. No claims are verified and no night results are public beyond the death records of the dead players. Stakes: Three alive and the game can end within one more elimination, at worst for the town; a single wrong lynch from a split vote could hand the remaining factions the win, so every vote matters as a board-state event. lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

situations: Day 2 opens with ten players alive, no deaths and no votes yet, after a night in which the pack's kill on player_7 was blocked or saved without anyone dying; the village has no public information and the illusionist must decide how to speak in the opening round without revealing the failed kill or the pack's plans. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations needed before the wolves can equal the others; no single vote or kill can end the game now, so an early misstep is recoverable but the wolves need to keep their concealment intact across many days. Consensus: No consensus exists; the summariser recorded no accusations and day one ended with no vote. My position: No position relative to a forming consensus, since none is forming yet. Heat: Low: no accusations have been recorded and no vote has happened yet, so no suspicion is attached to you by name. Forward exposure: Any claim of a role or night result made now would commit you publicly and could not be undone; staying quiet and passing openers keeps the forward exposure at zero, while spending a conceal would leave a dead role-revealing trace only if the victim were to die. Target landscape: Ten players are alive and all are unrevealed; no one has claimed a role publicly. The only public act so far is the wolf-channel-independent day-one discussion with no accusations recorded, so every candidate rests on no evidence, only on behaviour in the opening round. Public vs private: Privately, you are the Illusionist wolf with two conceals left and a known pack kill on player_7 that failed last night; publicly you are an unclaimed, ordinary-looking player with no role claim and no night result to share, so the public read is simply open suspicion of nobody in particular.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

situations: Day 2 opens with no deaths, no claims, and no votes yet. I am the necromancer, able to kill from night 2 onward through a body or directly, and must stay unnoticed while the town has no information to act on. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results have been announced, no role has been revealed, and the only public material is day-one speech, which carried no claims. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, and the next result cannot end the game; a wrong early vote is recoverable but each mis-elimination of a town player moves the board closer to the wolves' count, so the day's choice matters but is not decisive. Consensus: The village has no established consensus; day 1 produced discussion only and no accusations were recorded, so the room is unaligned. My position: Holding out with no faction; I am neither driving nor following any forming consensus. Heat: Low: no one has accused me on the record and day 1 had no vote, so suspicion on me rests only on my quietness, which I can keep unremarkable. Forward exposure: Any visible move on day 2 (accusing, defending, or pushing a vote) would shape how the village reads my seat; a speech or vote is public and permanent, while a night kill from day 2 onward would be a hidden visit only seen through its outcome. Target landscape: All nine other players are unrevealed with no role claims and no night results yet; no candidate has public evidence against them, so any choice rests on behavior in day-one discussion alone. Public vs private: As the necromancer, I privately know I am the lone killer with no night-one action, while publicly I am just another unrevealed player on day 2 with no claims and no eliminations yet; the public read is that nothing has been established at all.

lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Two town power roles have claimed, their results back each other up, and the necromancer is pushed to state a role or be voted out. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed roles of the dead, public vote history, claimed night results and spent abilities leave very little room to bluff. Stakes: One elimination vote decides the game. If the necromancer is voted out it loses outright, and a failed claim leaves no later day to repair it. Consensus: The few remaining players are converging on a bloc of cross-verifying town claims, with the unclaimed or contradicted player as the obvious elimination. My position: Holding out alone against a forming two-player bloc. Heat: High to critical. Claimed town roles are demanding my claim, or I am the odd player out after their results cleared each other. Forward exposure: A role claim commits me to a night history that the claimed town roles can check against their own results and spent abilities. A claim that fails the check is nearly irreversible, but staying silent is already read as guilt in a small endgame. Target landscape: The claimed power roles (vigilante, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist) and any unclaimed player. Their claims are partly corroborated by revealed deaths and spent abilities, so each can be tested against the record. Public vs private: Privately a lone killer who has been attacking through a dead player's body, while publicly needing to pass as an ordinary town power role under direct claim demands.
lessons.action: When pressed to claim at the final three or four, give a specific role claim instead of stalling. Pick a still-living town role that no revealed death or other claim has already used, and tell a night story that fits every claimed result and the visit rules. For example, a Sentinel is never told of its own watch, and a Trailseer's follow is a visit others can cross-check.

lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or save, the necromancer holds results gathered through a dead town role and wants to redirect suspicion onto the visitors. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: the dead role's death is on record, so the room can tell which living roles could have produced such a result. Stakes: My win needs the room kept off me for many more days, so losing the cover of a hidden identity costs far more than anything the leaked result could gain. Consensus: The village is unsettled after a night attack and save, with no fixed target. The living roles are still working out what the visits mean. My position: Not yet in conflict, but I would be holding out alone if I spoke up with the hidden result. Heat: Zero before sharing. It would jump to universal accusation if I quoted the body-derived result. Forward exposure: Stating a result that only the dead role could have produced points straight at the necromancer, and the room cannot unsee it. A read built on public evidence can be dropped without penalty. Target landscape: The players whose visits I learned about (claimed healer, other claimants) are the targets, but the only support is a hidden source. Public evidence such as claim overlaps is available to use instead. Public vs private: Privately I hold a night result obtained through a dead role, such as who visited a door. Publicly, no living player holds that role, so quoting the result shows I am the necromancer.
lessons.action: If a dead player's ability gave you night information, steer suspicion only through reasons the room can see: public claims, votes, and contradictions between players. Do not quote the body-derived result, such as sentinel visitor names, when no living role could explain how you got it. Only a living claimed role could plausibly share such a result, and you cannot back that claim.

situations: Day 2 opens with no deaths and no prior vote, after a night one with no information. As an unpicked speculator I must decide when to commit a side pick while the village has no accusations yet, weighing the risk of dying before picking against the value of waiting for more evidence. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results shared publicly, no claims, no deaths, no role reveals. Only private speculator state (unpicked) is known to me. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single elimination can end the game; a pick now is far from decisive, but dying unpicked forfeits the win, so the cost of waiting grows with each night survived. Consensus: No consensus formed yet; day 2 discussion has no messages, so the room has no shared target or theory. My position: Holding out as an unpicked speculator, not yet aligned with any forming majority. Heat: Low. As the speculator with no accusations or claims recorded against me, my suspicion comes only from being unrevealed and unpicked. Target landscape: Ten players alive, all unrevealed; no one has died and no vote has occurred yet. Public role status: none confirmed or claimed in the record. Evidence basis: none, only the opening discussion of day 2 with no accusations recorded.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.
lessons.action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.

lessons.situation: The morning after a night attack, with a save or a roleblock reported, a claim conflict erupts between rival investigator or healer claimants, or an unprompted visit report triggers a push on the reporter. The speculator is unpressured and has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced save or death, claimed night results, and rival claims whose contradictions can be tested against announced facts. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. No single vote flips the game yet, so the speculator should stay alive and gather evidence before committing its pick. Consensus: The village is converging on resolving the claim conflict, with attention on the contested claimants and not on quiet players. My position: With the majority, in a grounding, non-leading role. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the speculator, and the room's attention is on the claim conflict. Target landscape: Competing role claims (two investigators or two healers) and an unverified door-traffic or night-result report. Public announcements are the only verified anchor, and the rest is claim versus claim.
lessons.action: While no heat is on you and the room is split over competing claims, anchor your comments on facts the Game Master announced (a save, a death, a revealed role) and on what the rules allow. Stay neutral on the claim dispute, and use the quiet to see which side is gaining ground, since a Speculator that dies before picking loses.

lessons.situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

situations: Day 2 opens with ten players alive and no deaths announced after a quiet first night; the pack's kill on night 1 was unproductive (the target was immune), and I, the Chanteuse, must decide whether to draw attention or stay in the crowd while a living wolf partner remains hidden. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public claims, no checks, no watches, no night results announced; the only hard facts are the absence of deaths and the absence of any vote history. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game; the cost of a misjudged public move is recoverable but compounds over several days of pressure. Consensus: The village has no formed consensus; discussion has just opened with no accusations, and there is no shared basis yet for any target. My position: I am not with any forming majority because none has formed; I am holding out on any accusation until the room shows a direction. Heat: Little suspicion on me so far: day 1 had no vote and no accusations were recorded, so my heat is low and based only on silence. Forward exposure: Any visible move on day 2 (a strong accusation, a defense, or a block pattern the village can see) commits me to a public stance I cannot easily retract, and any evidence of my blocks would be visible through the Sentinel or Trailseer; the move is reversible only in words, not in votes already on record. Target landscape: Ten players alive, none publicly claimed as wolves; village candidates are unrevealed, with no role claims or results yet on the public record, so the choice rests on behavior and the discussion rather than any evidence. Public vs private: As the Chanteuse (a wolf) I privately know my pack's kill and my blocks, and that player_7 was immune on night 1; publicly the village knows only that no one died and no one has spoken of it, so my public read is blank while my private knowledge is that the pack is intact with a living wolf partner who has not been revealed.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.
