situations: Day 2 opens with no accusations and no public information after a quiet first night; as a wolf whose block and pack kill both failed to produce a death, I must decide how much to speak and whether to stay silent in an opening round where every living player speaks once. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public facts are that no one died on night 1 and no one has been voted out; all role information is private, and the village has no checks, watches, or claims yet. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game this day; an early misstep is recoverable but a visible claim now would be a lasting commitment in a game where the village has not yet split. Consensus: No consensus has formed; the village has no shared read and discussion has not started. My position: With no forming consensus, I am neither driving nor holding out; I am at the unaligned baseline. Heat: Low: no accusations have been made in the day discussion, and no one has been publicly linked to the night 1 events, so suspicion on me is at baseline. Forward exposure: Any visible move on Day 2 (pushing a target, defending a player, or claiming a result) would commit me to a public position that cannot be retracted, and a claim about the night's block or the immune target would be checkable against the record only by players who know what the Chanteuse does, so it would expose the block and risk the partner. Target landscape: All nine other living players have no public role status and no evidence against them yet; the only public information is that player_7 and player_8 were involved in night 1 without anyone learning it, so no candidate is currently distinguishable from another on evidence, only on silence and speech pattern. Public vs private: Privately, as the Chanteuse I know I am a wolf and my pack partner is alive and unrevealed; publicly the village has only the bare fact that no one died on night 1 and no accusations exist yet, so my public read is a blank slate while my private knowledge is that my block and the pack's kill both landed on players who survived.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: Room is leaning to abstain with no hard leads; joining the abstain majority avoids a conspicuous lone vote.
No claimant has exposed my visit and no one has accused me today.
My wolf partner player_3 is not under any accusation yet.

situations: Day 2 opens with no deaths and no votes after a no-elimination night 1, and the agent, an unpicked speculator who has learned nothing at night, must choose when to commit a side pick while the village has no information to read. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results shared, no role claims, no vote record, and only the Day 1 no-death announcement exists publicly. Stakes: Six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single elimination can end the game, so a pick made now carries no immediate swing risk but the speculator can die unpicked and lose outright if it waits too long. Consensus: No village consensus has formed; the room has produced no public messages on Day 2 and no accusations were recorded on Day 1, so the basis for any alignment is absent. My position: Holding out from any forming consensus, since none exists; the agent is neutral and unpicked. Heat: No suspicion on the agent so far; the agent is an unpicked speculator with no deaths, votes, or accusations on record. Target landscape: Ten living players with no public role claims, no eliminations, and no votes yet; no candidate has public evidence against them. Day 2 discussion has no messages yet, so the candidate set is the full living roster excluding the agent's own seat.

lessons.situation: The speculator has already picked a side (Town) and sits in a split or deadlocked day vote where its single vote can decide a tie or prevent a bad elimination of a claimed Town role. Both wolves and a lone killer may still be alive. Information landscape: Moderate and muddled: night kills, a hidden role, conflicting role claims and night-result claims, but no confirmed wolf or killer. Mostly unverified claims plus voting records. Stakes: With about six players alive and two killing factions active, one vote can decide an elimination or block a Town loss. A mistaken Town elimination moves evil toward parity and weakens the Town side the speculator picked. Consensus: The village is scattered or split into near-equal camps with no single dominant target; the push is based on muddled claims and behavioral reads. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none; nobody has directed accusations at the speculator, and its speech has been neutral. Target landscape: Several candidates split the room: claimed Town power roles (healer, trailseer, sigilist, vigilante) versus an unconfirmed quiet or counter-accusing player. The evidence is partly claims and conflicting timelines, partly behavior and past votes, with no confirmed wolf.
lessons.action: When you have already picked Town and the day vote is split among several candidates, cast your vote sincerely on the unconfirmed player whose behavior or claims look most evil. Prefer the candidate whose claims conflict with other players' reports over a claimed Town power role. Your vote can swing a split or tie, so use it to stop a Town-aligned elimination and to remove the likeliest killer, which keeps Town the winning side you picked.

lessons.situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.
lessons.action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.
lessons.action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.

verdicts.why: Speculator has not picked a side and there is no split vote yet on day 2 with no information.
Ten players are alive, far from the four-alive match point described.
No claims or wills exist yet to contradict, so the endgame dispute does not apply.

situations: Day 2 opens with ten living players and no deaths or claims. As the necromancer, I am a lone killer who cannot act until the second night, and I must decide whether to stay quiet through the opening round or make a public statement while nobody has yet built a case against anyone. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results have been announced beyond 'no one died', no claims are on record, and no votes have been cast, so every player is reasoning from behavior only. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win means no single vote or kill decides the game now; a wrong early vote is recoverable but each elimination brings the evil side closer to parity. Consensus: The village has no shared read yet: day 1 produced no vote, no accusations, and no claims, so there is no forming consensus. My position: Holding out from any consensus because none exists; I am not driving any accusation. Heat: Little suspicion on me so far because no one has died and I have said nothing; the only basis is that I have stayed quiet on day 1. Forward exposure: Any visible claim or early accusation would commit me to a public position that later night results could contradict; staying silent keeps every option open but makes my silence itself a readable pattern on day 2. Target landscape: Ten living players, no role claims made, no accusations on record; no candidate has public evidence against them, so any target choice rests on behavior alone. Public vs private: As the necromancer I privately know I have no day-1 action and am a hidden lone killer, while publicly I am one of ten unknown players with no claim; the public read is only that nobody has died and no one has been accused yet.

lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

verdicts.why: My board is day 2 with ten alive and no claims or reveals yet, so the endgame cornering does not hold.
No claimant has made a report or accusation yet, so there is no claim-versus-accused split to test.
Nobody has exposed me through a dead body; no one has died and no mechanical contradiction exists.

situations: Day 2 opens with ten players alive and no claims or night results public after a no-death night 1; as the illusionist you hold a private record of a failed pack attack and must speak without revealing it while the village starts to look for information. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no deaths, no wills, and no announced night results; players can only reason from silence, speech order, and the day-1 vote record. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single vote or kill can end the game now, so an early misstep costs reputation rather than the game, but the quiet cover you build now is what will hold later. Consensus: No consensus has formed; the village has no claims, no deaths and no vote on day 2 yet, so the room is unaligned with no clear direction. My position: Not yet committed; you are neither driving nor holding out against any forming majority. Heat: Low: no accusations are recorded in the public discussion so far and your only public act is a day-1 vote, which is not yet contested. Forward exposure: Any public claim about night 1 or any visible accusation would commit you to a night story that must match the wolf channel and the concealed attack; staying silent keeps this fully reversible but leaves no cover if someone pushes a claim. Target landscape: Ten players alive, all unclaimed on day 2 with no revealed roles; the only public trace is the day-1 vote record showing one player receiving votes, and the evidence basis for every candidate is behavioral only. Public vs private: Privately, as the illusionist, you know your wolf partner and the failed night-1 attack on a player who survived as immune; publicly you have said nothing about any night, and the village reads you as an unclaimed quiet player with no public record of suspicion.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

verdicts.why: Day 2 is information-poor with no evidence against anyone; blending with the abstain majority preserves cover and avoids a permanent lone vote.
No information-role claimant has appeared on my board yet, so there is no claimant to protect or avoid voting against.
No claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me; no hard evidence names me.

situations: Day 2 ended with every player abstaining except one vote against player_8, and no deaths have occurred yet; the Sigilist holds two sigils and must decide whether to hold them through tonight, when any attack by the wolves, Necromancer or vigilante would strike the placed target. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night deaths, no claims, no role results, and no discussion content, so only behavioral signals exist. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single misplaced sigil is recoverable but spends one of only two charges while the board is still wide open; a sigil placed on a non-attacker strikes nothing. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil on a player is a visible visit that is irreversible; if it does not trigger, the sigil is spent and the Sigilist learns only that it had no effect, revealing nothing publicly but committing one of two remaining sigils. Target landscape: Nine living candidates with no public role claims and no accusations beyond a single day-1 vote against player_8; no evidence distinguishes attackers, so any sigil placement rests on guessing who will attack tonight.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten players alive, day one was discussion only with no vote or deaths. The sigilist must decide between placing a sigil on a blind guess and keeping the charges. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no role claims, no voting records, no visit histories to separate likely attackers from passive roles. Stakes: Early board with a large margin before any faction can win. Nothing is forcing a spend, and each of the two charges is worth more on a night with a real lead than on a coin-flip target. Forward exposure: Holding reveals nothing and commits nothing, and the charge stays available. Placing is irreversible, spends one of two charges, and is a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unvetted: no claims, no votes, no night results. Any target is a pure guess, and most players, including investigative, protective and passive roles, will not attack.
lessons.action: On night one, when there are no deaths, claims, votes or visit data, keep both sigils and place none. A sigil only does anything if its target attacks that night, and a blind pick usually lands on a non-attacker (several observations show it striking nothing and spending a charge). Hold the charges until a night when a specific suspect is likely to attack.

lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

situations: Day 2 closed with an abstain majority after a lone eliminate vote against one player, and no claims or accusations have been made. As the healer with a private protection record and no shared information, the village must choose protection-relevant threat from silence and voting patterns alone, with no role claim to anchor a read. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no night results shared publicly, no accusations in discussion, and only the public vote record. Private knowledge exists only for the healer's own protection of one player on night 1, which was not attacked. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill can end the game or flip the winning faction this turn. A wrong elimination costs one town player of information but leaves the board far from a wolf win, so the decision is recoverable while the information stays thin. Target landscape: Ten players alive with no public role claims and no accusations beyond one day-2 vote of eliminate on a single player that the village abstained on; all candidates are unknown roles with no public evidence, so every target rests on behavior alone. The only public record is the vote history, where one player voted to eliminate another and the rest abstained.

lessons.situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The healer must pick a protect target for the pack's first kill with no prior results, and the wolves may kill the healer instead. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, no checks, no votes and no claims, only brief introductory remarks. Stakes: Early game with a full board, so a single night's protection will not decide the game. Losing the healer early removes protection from Night 2 onward, but the blind target cannot be improved with the information available. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public claims, no verified roles and no vote record. The only basis is thin Day 1 behavior, so the pick is speculative.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, protect one engaged, neutral-baseline player rather than stalling over the choice, since there is no evidence to rank candidates and you cannot protect yourself. Treat the night as a free baseline visit: if the morning shows a save or a death, that is the first real data for choosing Night 2 targets.

verdicts.why: No Town power role has been validated or claimed yet; no checks or results are public.
No Serial Killer exists in this game and no eliminations or claims have occurred.
Still no information after a quiet day with no deaths or claims, so a neutral protection on an engaged player is the baseline.

situations: Day 2 opened with a lone vote to eliminate one player while the rest of the table abstained, and the town chose to abstain, leaving no elimination. Night 1 produced no deaths, so the table has no information except behavior. As Trailseer, you privately followed one player on night 1 and learned they visited no one; that result is private and cannot be shown without a claim, so the village is reasoning from silence and a single accusation. Information landscape: Information-starved: no announced night results beyond 'no one died', no claims, one public vote, and private Trailseer results held by one player only. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win; a wrong lynch now is recoverable but each mis-elimination moves the board toward the wolves, and with no night information yet the abstain outcome preserves the most players. Target landscape: Nine living players with no public role claims and no deaths; the only public signal is a day-2 vote in which one player alone voted to eliminate another player while the rest abstained, so the accuser and the accused are the only named candidates, with no evidence beyond that single vote and no night results announced yet.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

lessons.situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The Trailseer must pick a first follow target blindly, while the wolves and a lone killer may also pick arbitrary opening kills, including the Trailseer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no voting record, no night history, only baseline impressions from Day 1. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and evil far from parity, so no single follow is decisive. The value is in collecting a first concrete visit link before wagons and claims form, and the Trailseer may be killed before reporting it. Target landscape: Nine unrevealed other players with no claims, votes or behavioral deviations; any pick is an exploratory behavioral guess, so choose an unread player who does not stand out.
lessons.action: On the opening night with no claims or reads, follow one unread, low-profile player to get a concrete movement baseline. If the result names a door, keep it as a checkable link to cross-reference against other night results and later claims. If it shows no visits, treat that as weak information, because a wolf carrier whose victim was concealed leaves no trace, and the target may also be a passive role.

lessons.situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

verdicts.why: Night 1 blind pick is past; now on night 2 with no claims or deaths, the opening-night guidance is only partly relevant.
Still no claims or deaths, so a low-profile unread player is the best baseline visit target.
The game is not yet information-rich; there are no claims, flips or confirmed roles.

situations: After a day-2 vote where the village abstained and only one player cast an eliminate vote against you, you hold two vigilante bullets with no night result from the blocked night 1 and no deaths yet. The discussion has produced no contested claims, so any shot would rest on a thin read. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results beyond a blocked night 1, no deaths, no claims, and only a single public accusatory vote as evidence. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single kill or vote ends the game now; a wrong shot spends one of only two bullets and reveals the vigilante role while the wolf pack is still intact, which is costly but recoverable over several days. Forward exposure: Shooting now would publicly reveal a vigilante role claim or a shot target with no evidence behind it, committing a scarce bullet irreversibly; holding fire keeps both bullets and keeps the role hidden. Target landscape: Day 2 vote: one player (player_8's own vote target was a single eliminate vote against a fellow player, public record) is accused by one voter; no other accusations; all other players abstained. No roles revealed, no claims recorded, evidence is only the day-2 public voting record.

lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.
lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

verdicts.why: No role confirmed and no night result singles anyone out; day 2 vote was all abstains except player_9 voting me, which is thin behavior, not evidence.

situations: As the unpicked Speculator, I face the open question of when to commit to a side. The village abstained on day 2 with one lone accusation (player_9 against player_8) and no claims yet. The board is information-starved, and the day 2 vote suggests the living players are not converging on any target. Dying unpicked would be a loss for me, so the timing of my single pick is the live decision, with the board still too unclear to tell which side is trending. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results have been announced, no deaths, no role claims that are verified, and only one public vote record (an abstain majority with one accusation). Private knowledge is limited to my own speculator status and an unset pick. Stakes: Ten alive and six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill can end the game now; the board is far from any decisive result. The cost of waiting is that a Speculator dying unpicked loses outright, so the pick has to be made before a night kill or lynch removes the option, while still early enough that the board is not yet clear. Target landscape: Day 2 with no eliminations yet; the only public vote so far was an abstain-heavy round in which one player (player_9) voted to eliminate player_8 alone and everyone else abstained. Candidates are all nine other living players, none with a public role claim or public evidence; the sole public signal is player_9's lone accusation of player_8, which rests on no shown evidence. As the Speculator with no pick yet, I have no role-based information to weigh them against.

lessons.situation: Early game, night 1 or 2, with a discussion-only day 1 or an abstained day 2. At most one or two night deaths so far, and neither wolves nor the lone killer have been exposed. The speculator is still unpicked and has not been targeted. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil eliminations, only unverified claims and concealed or ambiguous bodies, and no momentum signal for any faction. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is no immediate pressure to lock in. The only cost of waiting is the risk of dying unpicked, which is low on night 1 and rises as killers act. Holding costs little and keeps the option open for an informed pick later. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self, or keep holding. All ten players are alive with no confirmed roles and no tested claims. Any pick would be a pure guess on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On nights 1-2, while no evil role has been confirmed eliminated and no claim has been tested, keep the one-time pick unspent. Reassess each night, and commit as soon as board evidence clearly favors one side or you suspect you are likely to be killed. Dying unpicked is a loss, but an uninformed early lock-in has no advantage, and the pick cannot be changed once made.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after Town's day vote eliminated a confirmed wolf or lone killer, with healer saves publicly verified. Town holds a large majority, but some killers remain. Past observations show the Town pick won when Town stayed disciplined and lost when Town later mis-eliminated its own power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: system-confirmed evil role reveals, a validated investigator claim, and announced healer saves. The remaining unknown is whether a wolf or killer is still hidden and how well Town will play. Stakes: Town leads, but a few mis-votes or kills could still flip the game, so the pick is only as good as Town's later play. Picking now removes the risk of dying unpicked, but it ties your win to Town's survival and avoiding errors. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self. After a confirmed evil elimination Town looks dominant, with validated investigator or healer claims and a numerical majority. Evil still has a wolf and possibly an unknown lone killer, and Town's later errors can still erase that lead.
lessons.action: Once the day vote has system-confirmed an evil elimination and the surviving power-role claims are validated, make the pick on that night instead of waiting longer. Choose Town only if the lone killer is confirmed gone or Town clearly outnumbers a single remaining wolf; if killers are still active with an uncertain Town lead, keep holding until one side is clearly ahead, unless you are likely to be killed that night.

verdicts.why: Night 2 with no deaths, no confirmed evil eliminations and no tested claims; keeping the pick unspent is still the best option.

situations: Day 2 ended in a forced abstain with no elimination after a single player pushed a lone elimination vote against player_8. As the investigator holding two unrevealed checks, you must decide whether to spend a check on a player tonight, while the lone accuser's motive is unexplained and the rest of the table stayed silent. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed night results, no will read out, and only the vote record exists. The investigator's own private checks are the only hard information in the game. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single check or vote can end the game next turn; the cost of a wasted check is significant because only two remain and the information base is empty, but the board can absorb an early misread. Target landscape: Nine living candidates other than yourself (player_1 through player_8 and player_10); none has a public role claim or confirmed result. The only public signal is the day 2 vote, where everyone abstained except one player who voted to eliminate player_8, a lone accusation with no stated reason on record.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended with an abstain or a failed vote, the Investigator is publicly claimed with one or two checks left, and public reports from the tracking roles point at one or two specific players whose alignment is unresolved. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed tracking, watching, and visit reports plus public voting records give concrete leads, but no alignments are confirmed by the Game Master. Stakes: Mid-game with two evil factions still alive: each check is scarce and the investigator is a likely night target, so a check on a hard-lead player has to produce a verdict the village can use, not a result duplicating what the day will reveal. Target landscape: A few players tied to concrete claimed evidence (tracker or watcher reports, converging visits, vote records) versus quiet, unvetted background players and players already confirmed as liars; the lead is evidence-based, not just behavioral.
lessons.action: Spend a check on the unverified player at the center of a hard lead, such as one a tracker or watcher placed at a night-1 victim's door, or whom several claimed roles' reports converge on, rather than on a player already exposed or about to be removed. If the read is Suspicious, you have a wolf or active killer to drive the vote; if Not suspicious, you have a clearer town anchor. Either way the result is usable by the village.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a discussion-only Day 1. The Investigator holds both checks and must choose between holding them and probing an unread player blind. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no claims, no votes, no night results. Stakes: Early board with no pressure, so no single check is decisive. But the Investigator may die before a banked check is ever used, and any early read, whether it finds a wolf or clears an ally, compounds into later votes. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, flips or behavioral tells. Pick a quiet, non-prominent player at random, since nothing separates them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no leads, spend one check on a quiet, unclaimed player instead of banking both. An early Suspicious finds a wolf, and a Not suspicious gives you a baseline read. Treat a clean result as clearing only wolves: the Serial Killer and neutrals also read Not suspicious, and a Necromancer reads that way on any night it does not attack.

lessons.situation: After the Day 2 vote and a Day 1 or 2 reveal, the voting record shows a few players splitting from the room: defending an eliminated wolf, or pushing to eliminate the Investigator without evidence. One wolf (or the pack's remainder) is likely hiding among them, and the Investigator has one check left. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed wolf or sentinel death is on the record, plus public vote tallies showing clear outliers. No private proof yet, so the final check converts behavioral suspicion into a result. Stakes: The pack is already thinned and one check remains, so the last check is the Investigator's final chance to confirm a wolf. A correct hit can lead to eliminating the remaining wolves and winning, while a wasted check leaves Town without direction. Target landscape: Seven or so living players, with roles of the dead revealed. The best candidates are outlier voters on Day 2: a sole counter-voter defending a revealed wolf, or two voters who coordinated against you while the rest abstained. The basis is public vote behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With your last check, check the player whose Day 2 vote record most clearly diverges from the room: the lone defender of a revealed wolf, or a voter who pushed against you without evidence. Voting records are public and permanent, so these outliers are the likeliest wolf partners, and a Suspicious result gives you a concrete lead to act on.

verdicts.why: No tracking reports or claims exist yet; no hard lead on the board.
Day 2 with no information; probing one quiet player blind is reasonable while keeping one check banked.
No eliminated wolf or revealed roles yet.

situations: Day 2 ended in an abstain: the village voted to abstain with one lone accusation against a single player that nobody joined, and no claims or discussion have been recorded. As the Sentinel, I hold both watches unspent and must decide whether to spend one tonight on a player who is a likely victim or a suspect, knowing that a watch shows who visited that player and never reveals my own visit. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night results, no claims, no recorded discussion. The only public data is the day 2 vote record and the day 1 quiet night. Any watch is the first real evidence on the board. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single night or vote can end the game; the board is far from decisive, which means a watch spent early is recoverable but each of my two watches is a finite resource that cannot be reloaded. Target landscape: Nine living players with no public role claims and no night results yet; the only public action so far is one vote from a player against another on day 2 that drew no support, and the village abstained. Everyone's role status is unverified, so candidates rest on no evidence beyond silence and one lone accusation.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, with the first watch already spent and one watch left. The Sentinel is deciding whether to use it on a personal adversary or hold it for a higher-value door. Every watch is a visit, and the Sentinel is not told of its own visit. Information landscape: Still thin: the Night 1 result is the main hard fact, plus a few public claims and one vote record. There are no confirmed wolf identities, so targeting rests on likely attack paths and not on proof. Stakes: The last watch is the Sentinel's final hard evidence, and once it is spent the role has nothing left to do at night. Spending it on a low-traffic door gave nothing in the cluster, so a likely-attack target improves the chance of a usable visitor list. Target landscape: A handful of living players: a prominent claimed or confirmed Town role, a player who has accused you, and quiet unverified players. Favor the one most likely to be attacked or visited, based on public claims or revealed roles, over one picked because they are hostile to you.
lessons.action: Save the last watch for a night when you can name a door that is likely to be attacked or visited, such as a prominent claimed role or a player the wolves or killer plausibly want dead. A watch on a vocal accuser or a quiet bystander tends to return a zero-visitor result, and a watch is spent whether or not it shows anything.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. The Night 1 kill, a possible roleblock and the lone killer's attack can all land the same night, so the result may be lost, show nothing, or catch a key visitor. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no night results, no claims and no voting record. Only opening-round chatter exists. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive, so one blind watch is a cheap bet. Results across the cluster varied: zero visitors, a visit from the healer or trailseer, a multi-visitor cluster, and the serial killer caught at the door. The cost is that the Sentinel itself may be killed or blocked that night and the result lost, so only one of the two charges should be committed. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes or role flips. Every door is equally unknown, so choose a quiet, unpressured player on pure behavior, since there is no evidence to separate them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, deaths or reads, spend one of the two watches on a quiet, unclaimed player and keep the second for later. A watch can catch the killer's visit or reveal who is acting at night, and the visitor list is the only hard evidence a Sentinel can gather before Day 2. Pick a target the pack or the lone killer might plausibly hit, not a loud player who is likely to draw heat.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night after an abstain or tied vote. Conflicting role claims are on the board and you hold one watch left. You must decide whose door to watch, knowing results come only from visitors to that player. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, vote records and some prior night results, but nothing is verified. Alignments of the candidates are unconfirmed, and visit data exists only for whoever you watch. Stakes: Town can still afford a mistake, but this is the last watch, so a wasted use leaves no visitor-tracking for the rest of the game. A watch that exposes a visit pattern or kill trace can settle a claim fight before wolves reach parity. Target landscape: The choice is between a contested claimant (e.g. counter-claimed investigator or sigilist) under heavy suspicion, the obvious wolf-priority targets (claimed investigator, healer, trailseer), a quiet player from a tied vote, or an investigator-cleared player. The claim conflicts are public, but none of the candidates is verified. Only the contested claimant or the likely kill target is likely to draw visits.
lessons.action: With your last watch, pick the player most likely to receive a visit tonight. That means a contested or heavily accused claimant whose claim other roles can verify or attack, or the likely wolf kill target. A watch on a quiet suspect or an already-cleared player usually returns "no visitors", because attackers visit their victims, not themselves.

verdicts.why: Mid-game with one watch left; we are only on Night 2 with no claims, so this does not apply yet.
Night 2 with no claims or deaths; spend one blind watch on a quiet unclaimed player and keep the second.
No contested claims or tied vote exist yet on this board.

situations: Day 2 closed with a unanimous abstain except one accusation of player_8 by player_9, so no one was eliminated. Night 2 is now the pack's first kill and my first chanteuse block; the pack's last kill (player_7) was unharmed, which points to a protector or immunity on that target that I cannot see, and the wolf partner's prior vote pattern pushes toward a quiet kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public claims, no morning deaths, no revealed will; the only hard fact is that last night's attack on player_7 produced no announcement, meaning the target was immune to night kills rather than saved. Stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single night or vote decides the game yet; a wrong block costs one town action for one night, which is recoverable, but a wasted kill on an immune or protected target loses the pack a night of pressure. Forward exposure: Tonight's night action is private, but whichever town player's action I block becomes a visible absence in their morning report only if they were attacked; a blocked player is told they were roleblocked, so the block itself is known to its target. Blocking a probable protector or checker commits the pack's visible trace to a night the town may later read. Target landscape: Ten players are alive; the town-side roles still acting are Investigator, Sentinel, Trailseer, Vigilante, Sigilist and Healer, with the Speculator and Necromancer also alive and unannounced. No role is publicly claimed or confirmed yet, and no one has died, so every candidate for block or kill rests on behavior and silence rather than evidence.

The pack must pick a second night kill after the first attack on player_7 was blocked by immunity rather than a save. Because the first kill failed silently, the wolves have no confirmed information about which town role protects, and the attacker identity remains public only as a wolf-channel record. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town and partly rich for the pack: the wolves know their own kill attempts and my block on player_8, but the morning gave no public result, so the healer, sentinel and trailseer outcomes remain private to each player. Stakes: With six eliminations still needed before the leading evil faction can win, the pack has room for several failed kills, but each wasted night without a kill narrows the margin the wolves need to convert their later numbers into a majority. Forward exposure: Choosing the pack's victim is shared with the wolf partner, and the kill itself is visible to Sentinels and Trailseers as a visit, so the carrier's choice becomes evidence in the morning report and any watch on the victim. Target landscape: Candidates are the living non-wolf players; the wolf partner has voted with the town majority and pushed player_7 on Day 1, while player_9 is the only player who has openly moved against another. Every candidate's role is unrevealed, and evidence is purely behavioral.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.
