situations: As the illusionist, the pack's Night 1 attack on player_7 failed because player_7 was immune, and the night carrier is now proposing player_9 as tonight's kill, citing their lynch push and information-role tone. The public had no death on Night 1, so no body exists yet to conceal, and the village abstained on day 2 with no claims made. Information landscape: Information-starved: no death, no public claims, no checks or watches announced; the only public record is the day-2 vote, where eight players abstained, one voted to eliminate player_8, and one (player_9) voted to eliminate player_8 as well, leaving the vote pattern thin. Stakes: Nine alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single kill is not decisive; but each conceal is worth more when the town has few other informative results, so spending one on a victim whose revealed role would hand the town a role to build on carries real cost. Forward exposure: Any visible move (a public claim, a conceal announcement, or a vote record) would reveal the illusionist's role to the wolf partner's read and expose the pack's Night 1 failed attack; conceals are spent only on a victim whose body is announced, and the public cannot be told of the failed kill without naming the pack. Target landscape: Ten-player board with nine living: no public role claims yet; the day-2 vote record shows player_9 as the only eliminate vote against player_8; player_9 is being pushed by the pack's carrier as an information-sounding voice, with no verified evidence on any living player.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack picks a quiet, unread first victim and you are the wolf who carries the kill. The risk is that the Trailseer or Sentinel catches your visit and gives Town a day-2 accusation against you. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day-1 vote, no claims, no confirmed roles, no night history. Only private wolf talk exists. Stakes: Early game with plenty of time. The main risk is losing a wolf early to a traced visit, which would cost the pack the endgame. A clean first night matters more than saving a charge. Forward exposure: Announces that an illusionist exists and spends one of two conceals if the victim dies. Your own visit leaves no trace, and the spent charge cannot be undone. If the victim survives, nothing is announced and the use is kept. Target landscape: Eight or nine unclaimed, unread players with no roles revealed. The target is picked from quiet behavior, not evidence, and could be a watcher, a tracker, or the night-immune lone killer.
lessons.action: When the carrier rotation makes you the carrier on night 1, carry the kill and use a conceal on the victim. A conceal on a victim you carried yourself leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer, and if the target turns out immune the use is kept.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

situations: Day 3 opens with nine players alive after the investigator was killed on night 2; no claims have been made and no one has been eliminated, and I, a necromancer who can attack from night two onward, must decide how much to show while the village has no information to act on. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public facts are the day-2 vote record (one eliminate vote against player_8, everyone else abstained) and the night-2 kill of a revealed investigator; no checks, watches, or follows have been shared publicly. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, and the game cannot end on the next elimination; a wrong vote is recoverable at this count, so a quiet, low-exposure day costs little while the village still has time to gather information. Consensus: The village has no clear consensus; day 2 ended in a mass abstain and the discussion board is empty so far today. My position: With the majority by default: I am following the abstain pattern and have no position against the forming view. Heat: Low: my only public record is a quiet day-2 abstain, and no one has accused me or pointed at any evidence against me. Forward exposure: Any visible move (a claim, an accusation, or a conspicuous abstain/vote pattern) would commit me publicly and is hard to reverse, since the village remembers votes and statements permanently; staying silent keeps the option open. Target landscape: Nine players are alive and the village has no confirmed information about any of them; the only public fact is that the investigator was killed on night 2, and no claims or accusations currently exist to weigh against each other. Public vs private: As the necromancer I privately know I have no day-1 action and have made no kills yet, while the public sees only a quiet player with no claim and no visible role; the gap is that my hidden role gives me a lethal night tool the village cannot see.

lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Two town power roles have claimed, their results back each other up, and the necromancer is pushed to state a role or be voted out. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed roles of the dead, public vote history, claimed night results and spent abilities leave very little room to bluff. Stakes: One elimination vote decides the game. If the necromancer is voted out it loses outright, and a failed claim leaves no later day to repair it. Consensus: The few remaining players are converging on a bloc of cross-verifying town claims, with the unclaimed or contradicted player as the obvious elimination. My position: Holding out alone against a forming two-player bloc. Heat: High to critical. Claimed town roles are demanding my claim, or I am the odd player out after their results cleared each other. Forward exposure: A role claim commits me to a night history that the claimed town roles can check against their own results and spent abilities. A claim that fails the check is nearly irreversible, but staying silent is already read as guilt in a small endgame. Target landscape: The claimed power roles (vigilante, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist) and any unclaimed player. Their claims are partly corroborated by revealed deaths and spent abilities, so each can be tested against the record. Public vs private: Privately a lone killer who has been attacking through a dead player's body, while publicly needing to pass as an ordinary town power role under direct claim demands.
lessons.action: When pressed to claim at the final three or four, give a specific role claim instead of stalling. Pick a still-living town role that no revealed death or other claim has already used, and tell a night story that fits every claimed result and the visit rules. For example, a Sentinel is never told of its own watch, and a Trailseer's follow is a visit others can cross-check.

lessons.situation: A claimed information role accuses a player based on a night result, the accused disputes it, and the necromancer is tempted to step in and challenge the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead role with a concealed role, a specific claimed tracking report, and mechanical counter-claims from the accused. All of it is still unverified. Stakes: The board has many living players, so every public commitment matters for the endgame. A defense that turns out wrong leaves a damaging record, while a vote with the majority costs nothing. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on the accused, driven by a concrete claimed report that the claimant has already defended against objections. My position: Holding out, if I contest the lead. Better to move to the majority side. Heat: Low to none. Attention is on the accused player and the claimant, not on me. Forward exposure: Publicly challenging a claimed information lead puts my name on the record against it, and that record cannot be undone if the target flips evil. Joining the consensus costs little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: The accused player denies the charge and argues mechanics. The claimed trailseer, or other power-role claimant, gives a specific sighting. The evidence for the claimant is stronger than the accused's counter-argument. Public vs private: Publicly the room is split between an accused player and a claimed power role with a concrete report. Privately I am the lone killer with no stake in either side's survival, so I can choose the least risky alignment.
lessons.action: When a living claimant's report (for example a trailseer's) already has the room converging on an accused player, go along with that lead and voice a short read that matches it. If you doubt the report, ask a neutral question about it rather than staking your name on a mechanics rebuttal. The accused may flip, and a record of defending them marks you as their ally.

lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

situations: Day 3 opens with no public claims and no accusations after a day-2 vote where only the now-dead investigator pushed an elimination and the rest abstained. The speculator must decide whether to keep holding its pick while the village has no information, and the vote requirement from day 2 onward means each day ends in a vote that can eliminate someone. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no announced night results beyond the investigator's death on night 2, and no vote-based evidence beyond one lone accusation that the dead investigator made. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and the next elimination cannot end the game; a wrong mislynch is recoverable but each one moves the evil faction closer, so the speculator's pick timing matters more as the count falls. Consensus: No alignment: the village abstained on day 2 and no accusations are on record in the discussion. Day 3 has an empty discussion so far, so the room has no shared direction. My position: Holding out: I have not picked a side, and I am not pushing any vote while no evil role is confirmed. Heat: Low suspicion on the speculator (me, player_6) so far; nothing public ties me to any side, and the day-2 record shows no accusation against me. Target landscape: Nine players alive; no one has a public role claim or confirmed role. Only public evidence is the day-2 vote, where the dead investigator alone pushed to eliminate player_8 and everyone else abstained. Candidates are all unverified behavioral reads; no candidate is confirmed evil or confirmed town.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.
lessons.action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.

lessons.situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

lessons.situation: The morning after a night attack, with a save or a roleblock reported, a claim conflict erupts between rival investigator or healer claimants, or an unprompted visit report triggers a push on the reporter. The speculator is unpressured and has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced save or death, claimed night results, and rival claims whose contradictions can be tested against announced facts. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. No single vote flips the game yet, so the speculator should stay alive and gather evidence before committing its pick. Consensus: The village is converging on resolving the claim conflict, with attention on the contested claimants and not on quiet players. My position: With the majority, in a grounding, non-leading role. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the speculator, and the room's attention is on the claim conflict. Target landscape: Competing role claims (two investigators or two healers) and an unverified door-traffic or night-result report. Public announcements are the only verified anchor, and the rest is claim versus claim.
lessons.action: While no heat is on you and the room is split over competing claims, anchor your comments on facts the Game Master announced (a save, a death, a revealed role) and on what the rules allow. Stay neutral on the claim dispute, and use the quiet to see which side is gaining ground, since a Speculator that dies before picking loses.

situations: Day 3 after the wolves killed a self-declared-by-vote investigator-type player on night 2 and the village abstained on day 2; I am an illusionist with two conceal uses and an intact pack, and the body's role is publicly known because I did not conceal it. The dynamic is whether to keep a low profile or spend a conceal to protect the pack from a future role reveal while the village has only a thin public read. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public evidence is the day-2 vote and speeches about player_9's lone lynch push, with no checks, watches, or claims confirmed. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single mis-vote is not decisive but the wolves have a wide margin to absorb losses; the decision is about preserving my hidden status over the next several days rather than an immediate swing. Consensus: The village is not aligned: the day-2 vote abstained, with only one player voting to eliminate, so there is no forming consensus on any target. My position: Holding out, with no public stance and no claim, while staying with the abstaining majority. Heat: Low to moderate: my only public marks are the day-1 silence and the vote record showing I abstained on day 2; no one has accused me directly. Forward exposure: Any visible move now, such as pushing a lynch, spending a conceal on the day-2 Investigator body, or accusing anyone, commits me to a public position that can be checked against night outcomes and is largely irreversible once the village records it. Target landscape: Living candidates are the remaining seven non-wolf-known town players and the unrevealed Chanteuse ally; public role status is unknown for all of them, and the only public basis is votes and speech on day 2 where player_5 pushed for player_9 and the village abstained. Public vs private: Privately I am the illusionist, a wolf with two conceals left, and I know my pack partner the Chanteuse is still hidden; publicly the village sees only an unrevealed player who stayed quiet, while player_9 was killed and revealed as the Investigator and a lone day-2 lynch push on player_8 is on record.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.

situations: After a day-2 vote on an active voice ended in abstention, the village is stalling while a second player presses for a real result before backing any accusation; I must decide whether to keep pressing or to move quietly with the town's caution. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigator result is public after the investigator's death, no sentinel or trailseer result is public, and the only public signals are vote records and speech patterns. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong lynch is recoverable but each mis-elimination pushes the wolves closer to parity, so the stall favors neither side yet. Consensus: The village is split and stalled: repeated abstain votes on day 2 and no clear majority on any target, with the basis being hesitation to lynch without a result. My position: Holding out from a unified push, with my earlier lynch vote on the record and a pull toward a more cautious stance. Heat: Moderate: a player has questioned my support of the day-2 push, and my lynch vote is on public record, but no hard evidence links me to the wolves. Forward exposure: Publicly backing a lynch on the most active voice commits me to that accusation and ties my credibility to its outcome; withdrawing later is reversible but visible as a reversal that draws attention to my earlier push. Target landscape: Nine players alive with no confirmed wolf; the active voice that pushed a day-2 lynch has no public role status, and the quieter players have no public evidence either, so the choice rests on behavioral read only. Public vs private: As the Chanteuse I privately know I am a wolf and my pack killed the investigator on night 2, yet publicly I am a town-aligned voice pushing a lynch of the dead investigator's accuser pattern; my public read is a player with no night result to share, while my private knowledge is that my wolf partner is still unrevealed and alive.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.
lessons.action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.

lessons.situation: The speculator has already picked a side (Town) and sits in a split or deadlocked day vote where its single vote can decide a tie or prevent a bad elimination of a claimed Town role. Both wolves and a lone killer may still be alive. Information landscape: Moderate and muddled: night kills, a hidden role, conflicting role claims and night-result claims, but no confirmed wolf or killer. Mostly unverified claims plus voting records. Stakes: With about six players alive and two killing factions active, one vote can decide an elimination or block a Town loss. A mistaken Town elimination moves evil toward parity and weakens the Town side the speculator picked. Consensus: The village is scattered or split into near-equal camps with no single dominant target; the push is based on muddled claims and behavioral reads. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none; nobody has directed accusations at the speculator, and its speech has been neutral. Target landscape: Several candidates split the room: claimed Town power roles (healer, trailseer, sigilist, vigilante) versus an unconfirmed quiet or counter-accusing player. The evidence is partly claims and conflicting timelines, partly behavior and past votes, with no confirmed wolf.
lessons.action: When you have already picked Town and the day vote is split among several candidates, cast your vote sincerely on the unconfirmed player whose behavior or claims look most evil. Prefer the candidate whose claims conflict with other players' reports over a claimed Town power role. Your vote can swing a split or tie, so use it to stop a Town-aligned elimination and to remove the likeliest killer, which keeps Town the winning side you picked.

lessons.situation: Final-wolf vote at four alive: the village must eliminate the last wolf now or face parity at night, and the Speculator is one of the two unverified players. Information landscape: Information-rich: the dead Investigator's will clears one player, the Sigilist's abilities are logged and spent, and the lone killer is confirmed dead. Stakes: Eliminating the last wolf wins immediately for Town and for a Town pick, while a miss leaves three alive with parity at night. Consensus: Two confirmed Town players treat the vote as a choice between the two unverified players and are open to a clear case. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the cleared players. Heat: Exposed: the remaining suspect openly pushes to eliminate the agent based on a quiet record, and the confirmed Town players see it as a binary choice. Target landscape: Two unverified players, the Speculator and one suspect who survived earlier scrutiny, among four alive. The other two are cleared or confirmed Town, by a dead Investigator's will and spent, logged abilities. The suspect's push on the Speculator is behavioral, while the confirmed Town players are the deciding votes.
lessons.action: When four are alive, one wolf remains, and the Speculator has picked Town, join the cleared Town players in eliminating the one unverified suspect rather than the other. Ignore the suspect's counter-accusation of you when it rests only on a quiet record, because eliminating the last wolf ends the game with a Town win and your pick wins.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

verdicts.why: No claimed information role or contested mechanical accusation exists on this board yet.
Nine players are alive, not three or four, and no town claims have been made.
I have not been exposed by any mechanical contradiction; no one has accused me of acting through a body.

situations: Day 3 discussion: the village has asked everyone who claims a night result to state visit directions, after the night-2 investigator death; a fellow wolf has been pushing the group to name a kill-target from quiet players, and player_8 has been demanding specifics from anyone who had a night 1 result. As the Chanteuse who blocked player_8 on night 1, I am the one holding the visit line the village is asking for. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public night results exist beyond the night 2 death and the day 2 abstain vote; the only claims are denials of having a result, and the investigator's checks died with them. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations needed before the wolves can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game; the cost of a misstep is one step of heat in a long game, but the wolf pack's remaining pool of hidden-role information is what makes a mistaken public read hard to recover from. Consensus: The village is split on method rather than target: no lynch is forming, the day-2 vote abstained, and the room is asking for claims with specific visit directions, with no shared read on any player. My position: Holding out from any forming consensus; I have no alignment with a majority and the public has not yet pinned a direction on me. Heat: Moderate and rising on me specifically: my day-2 vote and push on player_9 is public record, and player_3 is asking pointed questions about who pushed the lone lynch, which keeps my name in the frame. Forward exposure: Claiming any night result or role would tie my visits to a specific public story that the village can check against the next night's reports; an unclaimed stance can be kept, but a denial of having a result, if later contradicted, would be hard to walk back. Target landscape: Nine alive; the only public role-bearing death is the investigator, dead on night 2 and revealed. Remaining candidates have no confirmed roles, and the day-2 lynch push on the dead investigator's behalf came from me and is on record, so the village reads my own vote as an accusation of an info role. Public vs private: Privately I am the Chanteuse, a wolf who blocked player_8 on night 1 and player_6 on night 2 and whose pack killed the investigator; publicly I hold no claim and no result, while the village is pressing for night-visit directions I cannot give without exposing myself.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No claimed trailseer has exposed my visit, so the retaliation-or-abstain scenario does not hold.
Abstain is off the table today, so I must name a player; I will pick the least conspicuous option rather than abstaining.
My partner player_3 is not under a consensus accusation from any claimant.

situations: After the day 3 lynch of the vigilante, the village is split between a player accused by the eliminated player's allies and a group that voted together against the same target, with a cluster of players demanding that anyone claiming a night result name visit directions. The one private Trailseer result (two nights of visit-less targets) cannot yet be shared without exposing the Trailseer to the wolves. Information landscape: Information-starved: no announced night results beyond the deaths and the vigilante's roleblock/held-fire record, no confirmed role claims among survivors, and only the day vote record as public evidence. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single elimination can end the game next; a wrong vote now is recoverable but each mis-elimination shrinks the Town's margin toward that four-step threshold. Target landscape: Seven-to-eight alive candidates for the next vote are not yet settled: player_1 is now the most accused after casting the vote against the eliminated player and being voted against by player_2; no role claim is public for any surviving player except the private Trailseer result held by me. Public role status: player_9 (investigator) and player_8 (vigilante) are dead, player_8's record shows a night 1 roleblock and night 2 held fire. Evidence is almost entirely behavioral (voting patterns, abstain history, demands for visit directions), with no verified night result from any living player.

lessons.situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

lessons.situation: A wolf was just eliminated by the vote, and the confirmed town investigator is the obvious target for wolf retaliation that night. The trailseer wants to preserve that investigator's last action in case they are killed. Information landscape: Info-rich: a wolf has been caught, the investigator is validated, and earlier night visits and claims are on record. Visit data on the likely victim is more valuable than a blind follow. Stakes: Losing the investigator without recovering their last check would remove a key information source. Seeing the investigator's visit, and getting it reported, can lead directly to the last wolf. Target landscape: The confirmed or strongly vetted info role facing retaliation, versus claimed protectors who were already attacked or saved, versus quiet unread players. The vetted role is the likeliest night victim and a natural way to find their last target.
lessons.action: When the trailseer's own role is likely to draw an attack, follow the player the wolves most want dead, such as the confirmed investigator who just exposed a wolf. If the target dies, the trailseer still learns whom they visited that night. That information can point suspicion at the visited player.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

verdicts.why: Late-game claimant pool does not fit; only the vigilante was a claimant and it is now dead.
No wolf was eliminated by vote and no investigator is alive; the investigator was killed by wolves.
This is night 3, not night 1.

situations: The day-3 lynch removed a revealed vigilante after a unanimous-looking pile-on, and the village is now left with no live public information roles. A player who was accused by the lynched vigilante's vote is pressing for visit-direction line-ups, and the night-1 roleblock on the dead vigilante is the only concrete night event on record. The healer must decide how to speak without revealing protections while the village argues over who should be lynched next. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a public result claim, the investigator and vigilante are dead, and the only public facts are the day-2 and day-3 vote records and the vigilante's night record. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single elimination ends the game, so a wrong lynch is recoverable but each mis-elimination moves the wolves closer to parity, and the information vacuum means the village has few tools to correct errors. Target landscape: Surviving players: seven others besides me (the healer). Player_2 voted to eliminate player_1 on day 3 and player_8 voted to eliminate player_1; the lynched player_8 (revealed vigilante, public record: roleblocked night 1, held fire night 2) is dead. Public role status: no surviving player has a public role claim; the investigator is dead (revealed day 2). Evidence basis: only vote records and the dead vigilante's public record; no live role claims.

lessons.situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

verdicts.why: No Town power role has publicly claimed or been corroborated; the investigator died without a validated result.
No publicly claimed information roles are on the record yet, so there is no verified result to protect.
Several wolves and the necromancer remain, so this is not a lone-killer-only endgame.

situations: Day 3 vote eliminated the vigilante after a night-1 roleblock claim, leaving the town without a confirmed investigator or vigilante. The illusionist, with a wolf partner alive, must decide tonight's pack target and whether to conceal the victim's role, while the town is debating which claimed results to trust. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a verified night result; the town has only the day-2 abstain vote and the day-3 lynch record. Player_8's roleblock claim is unverified and now dead. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a concealed kill costs only the town's information and leaves the pack room to keep trading kills, while an exposed kill of a useful role would hand the town a confirmed role to build on. Forward exposure: Spending a conceal on tonight's pack victim would hide the victim's role and the carrier's visit from the Sentinel and Trailseer; the cost is that a hidden body gives the town no role information and the concealment is irreversible for this victim. Target landscape: Surviving candidates for the pack kill are players 5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 10 (player_7 was immune on night 1, a fact the illusionist knows privately). Public roles are mostly unclaimed; the only public role is the dead investigator and the dead vigilante. Evidence is mostly voting behavior: player_5 is the known wolf partner, and player_1 and player_2 traded lynch votes on day 3.

After the lynch of a claimed roleblocked player, the open question is whether the pack should keep killing quiet players or contest the claim-makers still alive, while the illusionist's known wolf partner has been voting in step with the town majority on day 3.
