Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed results, only claims and voting records. The town asks for specific visit directions, but no living player has published one. Stakes: Eight alive, four eliminations from a wolf win, so no single kill or vote ends the game; each wrong lynch or unspent kill is recoverable but the pack's margin shrinks by one with every town elimination. Forward exposure: Carrying the kill and speaking in favor of a target in discussion commits the illusionist's public voice to that target; retracting later is possible only in words, since votes stay on the record. Target landscape: Living players who have spoken in the day-3 discussion, including one claiming a night 1 roleblock who was then lynched; the remaining quiet players have no public role claim. The day-3 vote split between player_1 and player_8, with player_2 voting for player_1.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack picks a quiet, unread first victim and you are the wolf who carries the kill. The risk is that the Trailseer or Sentinel catches your visit and gives Town a day-2 accusation against you. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day-1 vote, no claims, no confirmed roles, no night history. Only private wolf talk exists. Stakes: Early game with plenty of time. The main risk is losing a wolf early to a traced visit, which would cost the pack the endgame. A clean first night matters more than saving a charge. Forward exposure: Announces that an illusionist exists and spends one of two conceals if the victim dies. Your own visit leaves no trace, and the spent charge cannot be undone. If the victim survives, nothing is announced and the use is kept. Target landscape: Eight or nine unclaimed, unread players with no roles revealed. The target is picked from quiet behavior, not evidence, and could be a watcher, a tracker, or the night-immune lone killer.
lessons.action: When the carrier rotation makes you the carrier on night 1, carry the kill and use a conceal on the victim. A conceal on a victim you carried yourself leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer, and if the target turns out immune the use is kept.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

verdicts.why: Chanteuse is alive? No: the chanteuse is not dead, and the lone-illusionist-carry situation does not hold while two wolves and several town roles remain.
Night 1 has passed already; this is night 3.
Night 1 has passed; my conceal decisions now concern a later night.
Chanteuse is alive and the investigator is already dead, so there is no information-bearing claimed role to conceal yet.
This is night 4 with no quiet night-1 kill decision left to make.
Night-1 partner-carry situation no longer applies; both conceals are still held for an information-bearing victim.

situations: Day 3 ended with the town lynching the self-described vigilante player_8 after player_8 had accused player_1 in the vote; no role claims have been made by any living player. Tonight you, a necromancer with no kill yet, hold two usable bodies, the dead vigilante and the dead investigator. Any attack you make through a body reads Suspicious to an investigator that night, and no role result is public yet beyond the day 2 killed investigator. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public facts are the day 2 abstain vote, the day 3 lynch of the vigilante, the night 1 roleblock on player_8 and the night 2 hold-fire, and player_9's death as investigator. No living player has verified a night result, so every visit-direction claim is unverified. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single kill or vote can end the game this night; a wasted attack costs little now, but each lost body or wrongly revealed attack raises the risk that the town identifies the necromancer before the wolf count can reach parity. Forward exposure: Any visible move tonight (a reanimated kill or shot through the dead Investigator-adjacent bodies, or a claim) would reveal to the village that the Necromancer is active, and a kill through a body is announced as 'killed by a reanimated' kind, so the attacker's identity-type becomes public; a kill through the dead Vigilante or Investigator body is irreversible once announced. Target landscape: Seven living candidates besides yourself: player_1, player_2, player_3, player_4, player_5, player_6, player_10. None has a public role claim with confirmation. player_1 and player_2 are on record as the mutual accusers from the day 3 vote (player_2 voted to eliminate player_1), and player_3 has been pressing for visit-direction line-ups. Only dead bodies usable: player_8 (vigilante, shot-capable, a night 2 hold-fire with a night 1 roleblock) and player_9 (investigator, check ability that reads Suspicious on attack nights).

lessons.situation: After a day vote, four players remain, including the Necromancer. The Investigator has no checks left, while the Trailseer still collects visit data each night and can identify who is acting. Information landscape: Mostly info-rich: nearly all town roles are accounted for, the Investigator's exhausted status is public, and the Trailseer's ongoing tracking is the only live source of night evidence against the Necromancer. Stakes: The board is one night from three players. Leaving an active Trailseer alive lets the town confirm who is visiting and vote the Necromancer out the next day. Forward exposure: Any attack through the Vigilante body is announced as a reanimated shot, so the town learns a Necromancer exists, and attacking makes the Necromancer read Suspicious if checked. The kill cannot be undone once placed. Target landscape: Three living candidates: an Investigator publicly out of checks, a claimed Trailseer who follows a player every night, and an unclaimed Sigilist. Choose by remaining information capacity, not by past suspicion.
lessons.action: When choosing a night target with a body's attack in a small endgame, shoot the player who is still gathering information, such as an active Trailseer or Sentinel with uses left, before a player whose checks are spent. An Investigator with no checks left cannot learn anything new, while a Trailseer that follows players each night can narrow down the killer. Killing the active information role denies the town the evidence it needs to vote you out.

lessons.situation: First usable night after an Illusionist has been executed and revealed. The town has several public tracking and protection claims, and the Necromancer must choose between attacking through the wolf body and staying put. Information landscape: Info-rich. There is a system-confirmed dead wolf, public claims from the Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer and Investigator, and possibly earlier save reports. There is no hard evidence on who the Necromancer is. Stakes: Mid-game with many town power roles alive. A kill that lands thins them, while a blocked kill only advertises a Necromancer without reducing town numbers. The Necromancer needs repeated successful kills to reach its win condition. Forward exposure: The morning report will say a reanimated wolf struck, confirming a Necromancer exists. You read Suspicious to any Investigator check that night. An attack on a protected target is announced as a save and gains nothing, and the visit cannot be undone. Target landscape: Usable body is the revealed dead Illusionist, and any earlier concealed victim is unusable. Living targets are the claimed Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer and Investigator, plus unclaimed players. Claims are unverified, and the Healer's likely choices are inferred from public claims and recent save reports.
lessons.action: When a dead Illusionist's body is usable and you are not yet the room's prime suspect, attack through it at a player the Healer is unlikely to be guarding, such as an unclaimed or low-profile player who still matters. Avoid the publicly claimed power roles the Healer is most likely covering. A kill through that body hides the victim's role and denies the town the information and the body.

lessons.situation: The last wolf was voted out and three players remain overnight. One kill brings the count to two, which is the Necromancer's win threshold. Information landscape: Info-rich: eliminated roles are revealed, the Sigilist is confirmed with no sigils left, and the other survivor has no verified protective role. The open question is only which usable body to strike through. Stakes: One kill ends the game in the Necromancer's favor. Failing to attack gives the town another day vote to remove the Necromancer, so the attack must go out this night. Forward exposure: The attack is visible only through the morning report of a reanimated kill, but the game ends at once, so there is no reversibility cost and no later exposure. Target landscape: Two living opponents: a confirmed Town role with spent abilities and an unconfirmed player. A dead Vigilante body with announced role is available for the strike. Choice is by lack of defenses, not by suspicion.
lessons.action: When three players are alive at night and a usable dead attacker body is available (e.g. a Vigilante or Illusionist body), use it to attack one of the two others and finish the game. Attacking leaves two alive, which meets the Necromancer win condition. Pick the target who could not stop the kill, since no later day vote can undo the result.

verdicts.why: Four players remain in that point, but seven are alive here.
No Illusionist has been executed, so that point's conditions do not hold.
Three players are not alive here, so that endgame point does not apply.

situations: As the Sigilist, I have two sigils and must predict whether any living player will attack tonight. Night 2 killed the Investigator with no visible attacker trace, and the Vigilante was lynched on day 3 after claiming a night-1 roleblock. Players are asking for visit-direction claims, and the town has not yet produced a night result that names a visitor, so I cannot tell which living player is the likely carrier. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has publicly announced a night result that names a visitor; the only public facts are the day-2 abstain, the day-3 lynch of the Vigilante, and the Investigator's death. Evidence is mostly the eliminated player's unverified roleblock claim and players' conflicting stances on visit-line questions. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game next turn; a wasted sigil costs one of only two remaining strikes, and with four eliminations of slack the town can afford to wait a night for a visit pattern before committing one. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a visit and spends it whether or not it triggers; a sigil on a player who does not attack that night reveals nothing but wastes a use, while a sigil on a player who attacks strikes them and would be announced as a sigil death if they are the attacker's target. Target landscape: Seven other living players (eight alive including self counted as seven candidates); the vigilante has been eliminated and revealed, so no known shooter remains among town. Evidence is behavioral only: day-3 votes, a roleblock claim by the eliminated player, and deflection about visit lines; no confirmed wolf or Necromancer identity.

Discussion asks anyone with a night result to name visit directions, and the eliminated Vigilante's roleblock claim is the only night-one claim on record. A living player is pressing this line of questioning while I hold a private sigil role, so any public disclosure now would expose me before I know whether a wolf will attack. Information landscape: Information-starved: no public night result that names a visitor, only the eliminated player's unverified roleblock claim and the day-3 vote record. Stakes: Eight alive and four eliminations from a leading-evil win, so the board can absorb a couple of uncertain votes; a premature public role reveal would make the Sigilist a known target for the wolves while the town still lacks any confirmed attacker identity. Forward exposure: Stating a visit-direction or public claim about my own sigil use would reveal my role as the Sigilist and make me a sigil-holding target; staying silent keeps the role hidden but leaves the village without a sigil reading. Target landscape: Seven other living players with no public role claims that a sigil could verify; the strongest public accusation runs against the living player who voted to eliminate the Vigilante, but that is behavioral, not evidentiary.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.

lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

verdicts.why: No night attack or save has happened since night 2, so there is no attacker-or-protector choice to make tonight.
No suspect has attack evidence or a carrier-turn lead, so I have no concrete target for the pack's kill.
Day 2 ended in an abstain, but day 3 produced a lynch and no concrete lead points at a live suspect.

situations: Day 3, after a vigilante was lynched and revealed on the day-3 vote, the village must choose its next elimination with no verified information beyond one night-2 visit line. Sentinel (me) holds one watch left and a visit line on a player that showed two visitors, one of whom was the now-dead investigator. The discussion is centred on who gave night-1 visit directions and which claims are real, while a player who admitted being roleblocked on night 1 is now gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only hard facts are the day-2 and day-3 vote records, the investigator's death and the vigilante's reveal with its record (roleblocked night 1, held fire night 2). The only private night result is my own watch on player_5, which I cannot publish as a verified fact without revealing my role. Other players' night claims are unverified. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so a single wrong lynch is recoverable but narrows the margin; the next vote is not decisive by itself, but the remaining wolves can rely on any mis-elimination of a town role. The last Sentinel watch is worth spending only on a contested claim or a likely attack door, since it is the only night information left. Target landscape: Seven living candidates other than myself are on the board; player_1 is the most accused player after receiving the day-3 votes from several players and the most suspicious visitor on my night-2 watch of player_5 (a visit from player_1 and a visit from the now-dead investigator). Player_1 has no public role claim and no verified result; the evidence against them is a single visit line, and the behavior is pushing others to give specific night-1 visit directions while abstaining.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night after an abstain or tied vote. Conflicting role claims are on the board and you hold one watch left. You must decide whose door to watch, knowing results come only from visitors to that player. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, vote records and some prior night results, but nothing is verified. Alignments of the candidates are unconfirmed, and visit data exists only for whoever you watch. Stakes: Town can still afford a mistake, but this is the last watch, so a wasted use leaves no visitor-tracking for the rest of the game. A watch that exposes a visit pattern or kill trace can settle a claim fight before wolves reach parity. Target landscape: The choice is between a contested claimant (e.g. counter-claimed investigator or sigilist) under heavy suspicion, the obvious wolf-priority targets (claimed investigator, healer, trailseer), a quiet player from a tied vote, or an investigator-cleared player. The claim conflicts are public, but none of the candidates is verified. Only the contested claimant or the likely kill target is likely to draw visits.
lessons.action: With your last watch, pick the player most likely to receive a visit tonight. That means a contested or heavily accused claimant whose claim other roles can verify or attack, or the likely wolf kill target. A watch on a quiet suspect or an already-cleared player usually returns "no visitors", because attackers visit their victims, not themselves.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. The Night 1 kill, a possible roleblock and the lone killer's attack can all land the same night, so the result may be lost, show nothing, or catch a key visitor. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no night results, no claims and no voting record. Only opening-round chatter exists. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive, so one blind watch is a cheap bet. Results across the cluster varied: zero visitors, a visit from the healer or trailseer, a multi-visitor cluster, and the serial killer caught at the door. The cost is that the Sentinel itself may be killed or blocked that night and the result lost, so only one of the two charges should be committed. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes or role flips. Every door is equally unknown, so choose a quiet, unpressured player on pure behavior, since there is no evidence to separate them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, deaths or reads, spend one of the two watches on a quiet, unclaimed player and keep the second for later. A watch can catch the killer's visit or reveal who is acting at night, and the visitor list is the only hard evidence a Sentinel can gather before Day 2. Pick a target the pack or the lone killer might plausibly hit, not a loud player who is likely to draw heat.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, with the first watch already spent and one watch left. The Sentinel is deciding whether to use it on a personal adversary or hold it for a higher-value door. Every watch is a visit, and the Sentinel is not told of its own visit. Information landscape: Still thin: the Night 1 result is the main hard fact, plus a few public claims and one vote record. There are no confirmed wolf identities, so targeting rests on likely attack paths and not on proof. Stakes: The last watch is the Sentinel's final hard evidence, and once it is spent the role has nothing left to do at night. Spending it on a low-traffic door gave nothing in the cluster, so a likely-attack target improves the chance of a usable visitor list. Target landscape: A handful of living players: a prominent claimed or confirmed Town role, a player who has accused you, and quiet unverified players. Favor the one most likely to be attacked or visited, based on public claims or revealed roles, over one picked because they are hostile to you.
lessons.action: Save the last watch for a night when you can name a door that is likely to be attacked or visited, such as a prominent claimed role or a player the wolves or killer plausibly want dead. A watch on a vocal accuser or a quiet bystander tends to return a zero-visitor result, and a watch is spent whether or not it shows anything.

verdicts.why: My last watch should go to a contested suspect with heavy accusation, and player_1 is the one most visibly accused.
Night 1 has passed, so the blind-opening watch decision no longer applies.
This is my final watch, so I should spend it on a likely-visited door rather than a quiet bystander.

situations: As the unpicked speculator, you face the day-3 aftermath: the town just lynched a vigilante, the discussion is now asking who received night results and who visited whom, and the village has no confirmed wolf. Dying without a pick loses, so the open question is whether the board is trending toward Town, the Wolves, or a lone killer strong enough to make a pick worthwhile now. Information landscape: Information-starved. One night-kill record (player_9 investigator, night 2), one lynch record (vigilante, night 1 roleblock, night 2 held fire), public day-2 abstain vote and day-3 vote split, and unverified visit-direction requests with no result claims yet made publicly. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single elimination can end the game, so the pick is not forced this turn, but a speculator that dies unpicked loses outright, so the pick must be made before a death becomes likely. Target landscape: Eight players alive; the decision is whether and when the speculator makes its one irreversible side pick, which must be chosen among Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or itself. Public role status: the day-3 vote eliminated a player revealed as a vigilante (claimed night-1 roleblock, held fire night 2); player_9 was revealed as an investigator killed night 2. Evidence basis: only the vote record and the claims about night 1; no confirmed wolf identity and no confirmed lone killer identity.

lessons.situation: Early game, night 1 or 2, with a discussion-only day 1 or an abstained day 2. At most one or two night deaths so far, and neither wolves nor the lone killer have been exposed. The speculator is still unpicked and has not been targeted. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil eliminations, only unverified claims and concealed or ambiguous bodies, and no momentum signal for any faction. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is no immediate pressure to lock in. The only cost of waiting is the risk of dying unpicked, which is low on night 1 and rises as killers act. Holding costs little and keeps the option open for an informed pick later. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self, or keep holding. All ten players are alive with no confirmed roles and no tested claims. Any pick would be a pure guess on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On nights 1-2, while no evil role has been confirmed eliminated and no claim has been tested, keep the one-time pick unspent. Reassess each night, and commit as soon as board evidence clearly favors one side or you suspect you are likely to be killed. Dying unpicked is a loss, but an uninformed early lock-in has no advantage, and the pick cannot be changed once made.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after Town's day vote eliminated a confirmed wolf or lone killer, with healer saves publicly verified. Town holds a large majority, but some killers remain. Past observations show the Town pick won when Town stayed disciplined and lost when Town later mis-eliminated its own power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: system-confirmed evil role reveals, a validated investigator claim, and announced healer saves. The remaining unknown is whether a wolf or killer is still hidden and how well Town will play. Stakes: Town leads, but a few mis-votes or kills could still flip the game, so the pick is only as good as Town's later play. Picking now removes the risk of dying unpicked, but it ties your win to Town's survival and avoiding errors. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self. After a confirmed evil elimination Town looks dominant, with validated investigator or healer claims and a numerical majority. Evil still has a wolf and possibly an unknown lone killer, and Town's later errors can still erase that lead.
lessons.action: Once the day vote has system-confirmed an evil elimination and the surviving power-role claims are validated, make the pick on that night instead of waiting longer. Choose Town only if the lone killer is confirmed gone or Town clearly outnumbers a single remaining wolf; if killers are still active with an uncertain Town lead, keep holding until one side is clearly ahead, unless you are likely to be killed that night.

verdicts.why: It is night 3, past the night 1-2 window, and the board now has a confirmed Town elimination.
The eliminated player_8 was a vigilante, which is Town, so no evil elimination was confirmed.

situations: Night 3 is approaching with the pack's carrier set to player_3 and the target not yet chosen, while the day-3 vote eliminated the vigilante player_8 after a split that included player_1 and player_2 accusing each other. The living town has no public result to build on; players are pressing each other for night-visit directions, and the wolf channel shows the pack previously chose quiet targets over those pushing lynches. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a public role claim or announced night result. Known facts are the day-2 abstain vote, the day-3 vote record, the vigilante's record (night 1 roleblocked, night 2 held fire), and the night-1 and night-2 deaths or saves. The only private information is the chanteuse's own night records: the night-1 immune attack on player_7 and the night-2 block that did not take on player_6. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong vote or one kill does not end the game, so the board can absorb one mistake, but each further loss of a town voice narrows the margin toward the four-elimination threshold. Forward exposure: Any visible move tonight (a claim, a block revealed in the morning, or a vote) commits the chanteuse's known-block pattern to the open; a block already placed is announced to its target, so the cancelled player learns their night was stopped and can reason from it. Votes stay permanent on the record. Target landscape: Surviving town-aligned players whose night action could stop the pack's kill or check the pack: the seat-order carrier rotation puts player_3 as tonight's carrier, and the pack target is not yet named. Public roles: investigator (player_9) and vigilante (player_8) are dead; no living player has a public role claim. Basis is behavioral only: pressure for visit claims, abstain-versus-eliminate splits on day 2 and day 3, and who voted for the lynch of player_8.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

verdicts.why: No investigator or trailseer claim is public and no living info role has shown itself; the block target question is moot here.
This is night 4-style play with deaths and votes on record, not a blind opening night.
The vigilante was lynched by day, not killed by a wolf, so no confirmed lethal role is alive to target.
No investigator or trailseer is alive on my board to block; the claimed roles are dead or absent, so this block-the-info-role plan does not hold.
Opening night is long past; the board has deaths and a day vote on record.
The vigilante was lynched, not killed by a wolf, and no lethal town shooter is alive.

situations: Your private knowledge as the illusionist: the pack's kill on tonight's night is yours to carry. Two wolves remain (you and your partner player_5), so the pack is one wolf short of a majority margin only if a town member is removed. The town has no confirmed info roles left, and the wolves' kill tonight will be the first since the investigator's death. The day-3 lynch of the vigilante was made by a near-unanimous vote, and the town is now asking which players can produce night results. Your partner has been pushing kills on the quieter players and a previously vocal voice. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town: no living player has a verified result, claims from day 1 and day 2 are absent, and the only public facts are votes and night deaths. Your own private record: night 1 your pack attacked a player who was immune, which means that player is a likely lone killer candidate; night 2 your pack killed the investigator. Stakes: Eight alive and four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single kill or vote can end the game, so a conceal spent now is recoverable but leaves only two conceals for the rest of the game, and each use lowers the number of hidden roles the town can later read. Forward exposure: Placing a conceal on tonight's pack victim would hide that victim's role and the carrier's visit from the Sentinel and Trailseer; it spends one of the two conceals and, once the body is hidden, the victim's role stays unknown to the town until game end. Choosing a victim without a conceal leaves the revealed role and record public, so the town would read the victim's role openly. Target landscape: Seven other living players: player_5 (wolf partner, publicly pushing kills), player_1 and player_2 (in a split over a lynch vote), player_4, player_6, player_7 (immune to night kills on night 1, not confirmed as any role) and player_10. The only confirmed info role left, the investigator, is dead; the vigilante is lynched. No living player has a publicly confirmed role.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

verdicts.why: Investigator is already dead and the pack has no information role to remove; the lone-wolf conceal scenario does not match two living wolves.
Still holding both conceals; no claimed info role is alive to justify spending one tonight.
This is night 3, not night 1.
No information-bearing claimed role is alive; the investigator died night 2 and no sentinel or trailseer has claimed publicly.
Victim player_4 is an unclaimed quiet player, so a conceal could reveal the victim's role and will, which is useful but I have two uses and the town has no info roles to target.
This is night 3, not night 1.

situations: The pack has a carrier who has been choosing quiet non-immune players, and the day 3 lynch of the vigilante leaves the town with one fewer shooter. The town is asking for night-result line-ups, and the most analytical voice is pressing for visit directions, which threatens to expose the chanteuse's block history. Tonight the chanteuse must decide which town player's night action to cancel, and the carrier has already voted to eliminate player_4 today. Information landscape: Information-starved for the town: the only public facts are the investigator's death (role revealed), the vigilante's lynch and will, and the abstain and elimination votes. Private information for the chanteuse: night 1 block on the vigilante, night 2 block on a town player that did not take, and the pack kill history (night 1 on player_7 immune, night 2 on the investigator). Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single elimination ends the game, so a wrong block or kill is recoverable but each lost evil-aligned pair of hands shortens the pack's margin. The pack must still outnumber or equal the remaining non-wolf players, so a block that fails to take on an active town role (sentinel, trailseer, healer, sigilist) costs the pack a visible night action. Forward exposure: Any visible move tonight (a claim, a block announced by the target, or a vote) would reveal the chanteuse's wolf side to the pack's partner or expose the carrier's kill choice; blocks are private, so a block itself stays hidden unless the blocked player reports it, which makes blocking reversible but the target's reaction unpredictable. Target landscape: Seven living players besides the chanteuse's own pack: the carrier (a wolf partner) and the rest of town-aligned or neutral players. Player_7 was immune to a night kill on night 1, marking a possible lone killer or immunity-holder. Player_1 is the most analytical voice, pressing for line-ups; player_2 cast the vote against player_1. Public role status: no one has a confirmed role beyond the dead investigator and vigilante; the vigilante was lynched on day 3 with a roleblock and held-fire record read out.

The town is calling for each player to say who visited them on night 1 and night 2, while a lynch vote on the vigilante has just ended. A player who pushed a lynch on day 3 is being challenged on their vote against another player, and the discussion is forming around whether the pack's next block or kill should land on whoever is driving the line-up. Information landscape: Information-starved publicly: no night results have been announced beyond the investigator kill and the vigilante's record. Privately, the chanteuse knows the pack's kill and block history but has no information about which surviving players hold results. Stakes: Eight alive and four eliminations from the leading evil faction's win, so the next night's block or kill changes the margin but cannot end the game; if the line-up drives toward a real info role that the chanteuse fails to block, the town gains a reliable result source while the pack's numbers stay unchanged. Forward exposure: Any public statement about the night (a claim of a block, an attack, or a result) would tie the chanteuse to a visible role claim and invite a night-result cross-check; staying silent keeps the position reversible but leaves the town without a counter to whatever line-up forms. Target landscape: The town players whose night actions could threaten the pack: any active information or protection role. The public record shows no one has claimed a role. Behavioral signals: one player is pressing the line-up on visit directions, another is accusing a player of a lynch push without a result, and the carrier has voted to eliminate a particular player today. No public evidence distinguishes these candidates.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

verdicts.why: It is Night 3, not the opening night, and the pack has already killed player_9.
No role has publicly claimed yet, so there is no investigator or tracker claim to target, but player_1 is the most analytical voice and a possible info role.
No wolf has been killed by a confirmed vigilante; the vigilante player_8 was lynched by day vote.

situations: Day 4 with six alive and no visible accusation pattern after the day 3 lynch of a vigilante. The village has lost its investigator, illusionist and sigilist, so information sources are thin, and the feud between player_1 and player_2 is the only live conflict in the record. Information landscape: Information-starved: no current checks, watches, or follows are public, no role claims are verified, and the only hard record is the vote history and the night deaths. Stakes: Six alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win means a wrong vote is recoverable but each mis-elimination pulls the margin closer; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so this day's vote is not decisive by itself. Consensus: The village has no open consensus on a target yet; the day 3 vote record shows a unanimous-style lynch of the vigilante and a split between player_1 and player_2 that has not resolved. My position: Holding out from any open accusation while my announced Town pick is on record; I am not yet driving a target. Heat: As the Speculator, I have no public suspicion attached to me; my pick is announced only as Town, not as my identity. Target landscape: Six living players: two remaining Town-side roles unknown, the wolves (two living, unidentified), and the necromancer (unidentified lone killer). Public role status: investigator, vigilante, illusionist, sigilist are dead; the Speculator (me) is unrevealed. Candidates are unrevealed with no public evidence distinguishing them beyond the day 3 vote record, where player_1 and player_2 voted against each other.

lessons.situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.
lessons.action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.

lessons.situation: With four players alive and one wolf left, a claimed vigilante demands the speculator's role while the claimed sentinel and claimed trailseer accuse each other over contradictory logs. Information landscape: Information-rich in confirmed dead roles, but the key conflict is between unverified claims, and a rules-confusion slip is being treated as proof. Stakes: At four alive with one wolf left, a wrong elimination likely hands the wolves the win. Pushing a mis-vote also exposes the speculator to a night shot. Consensus: The room leans toward whoever the credible shooter points at. It is tied up in the conflicting tracking logs and is pressuring the speculator for transparency. My position: Driving: pushing the accusation of one of the conflicting claimants to deflect heat. Heat: High: a credible claimed role singled the speculator out as a suspect for withholding its role all game. Target landscape: Two claimed roles, for example a sentinel and a trailseer, with logs that conflict, plus the speculator, who is being pressed for a role. The vigilante's shot gives it credibility, while the sentinel's and trailseer's results are unverified claims.
lessons.action: When a claimed role demands your role while two others trade accusations over conflicting logs, don't build the case on a rule-confusion or a thin data gap. Test the contradiction against the rules, for example whether a watch counts as a visit and who could have seen what. Back the elimination only if the mechanics actually prove a lie, and otherwise hold your vote for the player whose claim can't be explained.

verdicts.why: Six players are alive, not four, and no speculator-focused accusation is in play yet.
No investigator check is claimed and no contested vote record is under discussion today.
No vigilante is alive to demand my role, and no conflicting sentinel or trailseer logs exist yet.

situations: Day 4 with six players alive and no accusations yet. The night-3 kill I carried through a dead vigilante's body was announced only as a reanimated shot and a wolf kill, so the village has two unexplained deaths and no public leads on who struck. I must keep my solo concealment intact while the discussion opens. Information landscape: Information-starved: only public deaths, one unverified roleblock claim, and the day-3 vote record. No confirmed investigation or sentinel result is public. Stakes: Six alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single vote or kill can end the game next step, so a misstep is recoverable but each public commitment narrows my room to maneuver. Consensus: The village has not yet formed a clear consensus; the discussion is open with no accusations on record and the last vote eliminated a claimed vigilante-type player by majority. My position: With the majority so far, holding no distinct stance. Heat: Low suspicion on me so far; no one has accused me and my votes have followed the visible majority. Forward exposure: Any visible move (claiming a role, acting through a dead body, or voting loudly) would reveal or commit me; a claim is not reversible once the village records it, and a public accusation would tie me to a stance I cannot retract. Target landscape: Six living players are candidates; the publicly revealed dead include an investigator, vigilante, illusionist and sigilist. The only public statement inviting scrutiny is from the player who claimed a roleblock on night 1, which is an unverified claim with no blocker supporting it. Public vs private: As the necromancer I privately know I killed player_3 through player_8's body and that the victim was an Illusionist, while the public only knows a reanimated vigilante shot a player whose role was revealed; the gap is that the town reads the night as an ordinary kill and I hold the reanimation secret alone.

lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Two town power roles have claimed, their results back each other up, and the necromancer is pushed to state a role or be voted out. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed roles of the dead, public vote history, claimed night results and spent abilities leave very little room to bluff. Stakes: One elimination vote decides the game. If the necromancer is voted out it loses outright, and a failed claim leaves no later day to repair it. Consensus: The few remaining players are converging on a bloc of cross-verifying town claims, with the unclaimed or contradicted player as the obvious elimination. My position: Holding out alone against a forming two-player bloc. Heat: High to critical. Claimed town roles are demanding my claim, or I am the odd player out after their results cleared each other. Forward exposure: A role claim commits me to a night history that the claimed town roles can check against their own results and spent abilities. A claim that fails the check is nearly irreversible, but staying silent is already read as guilt in a small endgame. Target landscape: The claimed power roles (vigilante, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist) and any unclaimed player. Their claims are partly corroborated by revealed deaths and spent abilities, so each can be tested against the record. Public vs private: Privately a lone killer who has been attacking through a dead player's body, while publicly needing to pass as an ordinary town power role under direct claim demands.
lessons.action: When pressed to claim at the final three or four, give a specific role claim instead of stalling. Pick a still-living town role that no revealed death or other claim has already used, and tell a night story that fits every claimed result and the visit rules. For example, a Sentinel is never told of its own watch, and a Trailseer's follow is a visit others can cross-check.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or save, the necromancer holds results gathered through a dead town role and wants to redirect suspicion onto the visitors. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: the dead role's death is on record, so the room can tell which living roles could have produced such a result. Stakes: My win needs the room kept off me for many more days, so losing the cover of a hidden identity costs far more than anything the leaked result could gain. Consensus: The village is unsettled after a night attack and save, with no fixed target. The living roles are still working out what the visits mean. My position: Not yet in conflict, but I would be holding out alone if I spoke up with the hidden result. Heat: Zero before sharing. It would jump to universal accusation if I quoted the body-derived result. Forward exposure: Stating a result that only the dead role could have produced points straight at the necromancer, and the room cannot unsee it. A read built on public evidence can be dropped without penalty. Target landscape: The players whose visits I learned about (claimed healer, other claimants) are the targets, but the only support is a hidden source. Public evidence such as claim overlaps is available to use instead. Public vs private: Privately I hold a night result obtained through a dead role, such as who visited a door. Publicly, no living player holds that role, so quoting the result shows I am the necromancer.
lessons.action: If a dead player's ability gave you night information, steer suspicion only through reasons the room can see: public claims, votes, and contradictions between players. Do not quote the body-derived result, such as sentinel visitor names, when no living role could explain how you got it. Only a living claimed role could plausibly share such a result, and you cannot back that claim.

verdicts.why: No sentinel claim or confirmed necromancer exists yet, so this situation does not hold.
Four players are still alive, not three or four, and no role claims have been made.
I hold a body-derived result, so I should not quote it and should steer only with public evidence.

situations: Six players remain after a day-3 lynch and two night kills, with my partner already revealed as an Illusionist and the village still divided over player_1 versus player_2 and the immune player_7; I must decide how much visible engagement to take without exposing my blocking pattern. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a confirmed role, the only public results are the Investigator's and Sentinel's deaths without wills read out, and the day-3 vote record plus each player's stated night results are the only evidence. Stakes: Six alive with four eliminations until the wolves can win; a single mistaken vote is recoverable but each lost night kill or lynch narrows the margin toward a wolf win. Consensus: The village has no clear consensus after day 3; the last lynch removed a vigilante and the room is still sorting out the split between player_1 and player_2 and the immune player_7. My position: Holding out from any firm accusation, with no public alignment with a majority on who to eliminate today. Heat: Moderate suspicion on me is unlikely from public record since I have made no claims, but my repeated pressure toward night kills on quiet players and my aligned votes with the wolf channel are visible patterns to an attentive reader. Forward exposure: Any visible move now, such as a block announced or a day claim, would commit me publicly and is effectively irreversible; staying quiet keeps my wolf identity hidden but leaves my night block pattern open to inference. Target landscape: Six living players remain: player_1 and player_2 as the most analytical town-leaning voices with no revealed roles, player_6 and player_10 as quiet players, player_7 as an immune-on-night-1 player with a possible night ability, and player_5 (me). Evidence is behavioral only; no living player has a public role claim. Public vs private: Privately I am the Chanteuse, a wolf, and my pack partner the Illusionist was already eliminated and revealed on day 3 via a reanimated shot; publicly the village knows only that an Illusionist died and that a Sigilist and an Investigator also died, while I still have no public claim.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

verdicts.why: No Town roleblock claim has been made publicly yet, and I have no partner left to protect.
Four players are still alive, so the three-player final-day situation does not apply yet.
No Town claimant has stumbled on their night action yet, so there is nothing to push.

situations: A claimed Sentinel publicly reported that the only visitor to a player on night 3 was the agent, while that player says they were roleblocked that night and therefore the visitor was the blocker; the accused is asked to explain the visit before a vote. Information landscape: Information-starved on the public side: one unverified Sentinel claim with a single watch result, one roleblock claim, and a vote-pattern history; no announced night results confirm either claim. Stakes: Six alive with four eliminations until the wolves can win; the game cannot end on the next elimination, so a wrong vote is recoverable but each lost wolf-aligned voter shortens the remaining runway. Consensus: The village is forming a lean toward voting the agent through the Sentinel's claim, with the room still open on whether the claim is true. My position: Holding out against the forming lean, with the Sentinel claim as the main pressure point. Heat: Moderate and rising: a visit from the public watch result points at the agent's own block, and player_1 has publicly named the agent's door as the one to explain. Forward exposure: A visible move now (defending or attacking the Sentinel claim, or explaining the visit at player_1's door) would commit the agent to a story that the block on player_1 can be checked against; that story is hard to reverse once the village votes on it. Target landscape: Day 4 candidates: the Sentinel claimant (player_2, unverified claim with a concrete watch result), player_1 (blocked the night of the watch, public read of an analytical voice), and player_7 (immune on night 1, possible necromancer, no direct evidence). Public vs private: Privately I am the chanteuse and my pack partner (the illusionist) is already dead, so I am the only surviving wolf; publicly the village reads a Sentinel claim pointing at player_5 via the visit on player_1 while my private block on player_1 is the actual cause.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific.
