The record is public, so I should keep to it and not raise doubts about claims without evidence.

situations: A claimed sentinel's night-two and night-three watches point at player_1, a claimed trailseer clears player_7 (me) with a follow, and player_1 is blamed for pushing a vote on a now-dead chanteuse while the village debates who was the saved attack's source on night four. Information landscape: Information-starved public record: two unverified role claims, one dead-player record (the vigilante's roleblock and held fire), and private night results only known to each actor. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the next result cannot end the game on its own, but a single wrong lynch would push the wolves and necromancer closer to parity, so each vote is costly and hard to undo. Consensus: The village is split: one faction votes player_1 on player_2's watch, another defends player_1 as a roleblocked innocent, with no hard evidence either way. My position: Holding out from the forming consensus against player_1, with no public stake in that fight. Heat: Moderate: player_2 and player_6 are pointing at player_1 and player_10's trailseer follow is being used to clear player_7, so suspicion on me is low for now but depends on player_10's credibility. Forward exposure: Any visible claim about my night actions or any public stance tied to the attack trail would commit me to a story that can be checked against later nights; staying silent and answering only when addressed keeps this reversible. Target landscape: Surviving players are player_1, player_2 (claims sentinel, unverified), player_6, player_7 (me), and player_10 (claims trailseer, unverified). Player_10's follow claims and player_2's watch claims are each unverified and point at player_1 and player_6 as the likely attacker-or-healer pair. Public vs private: As the necromancer I privately know I attacked player_3 (an illusionist, now dead) and attacked player_2 through a dead illusionist's body last night, and the healer saved them; the public only sees a reanimated attack and a save, not who struck.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

verdicts.why: Two claimants cross-check on player_1, so voting with that majority commits me to little.
With five alive, I should vote on the less-claimed player rather than counter-accuse a claimed town role.
No one has shown my night result to be impossible, so there is no accuser to counter.

situations: Night 4 produced both a save and an attack on the same player, player_2, and the trailseer's follow on player_7 showed no visits. Two players are being pointed at as the possible night 4 visitor: player_1 and player_6. Day 5 has a vote coming, and the claims of the sentinel and trailseer conflict on the one visit that could explain the night 4 result. Information landscape: Information-starved, claim-driven. Only claims exist: a sentinel watch chain (night 2 on player_5 and night 3 on player_1), a trailseer follow chain (player_7 on nights 4 and 5, player_5 on night 3, player_6 on night 1), and the public morning record. The record confirms that player_2 was attacked by a reanimated vigilante and saved by the healer on night 4. No hard result separates the claimants. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and the game can end within one more elimination. A wrong vote now is hard to recover from, because each further mis-elimination moves the board closer to the evil side's win condition. Consensus: The room is split and not aligned. A bloc is forming around the sentinel claim and the trailseer's follow data against player_1; player_1 and player_6 are the names being questioned on the night 4 visit to player_2's door. No single accusation has consensus, and nobody has a confirmed result. My position: Holding out from the forming pressure on player_1: I am not driving the vote and I am not with the majority yet. My private pick is town, so I am tracking which side is ahead while I avoid exposing myself. Heat: Suspicion is on player_1, who is named by player_2 as a visitor to a revealed chanteuse and is being voted by player_2. Player_1 is defending by pointing at the claimed sentinel's watch and at its own roleblock. I (player_6) have only light heat, mostly from player_6-directed questions about night 4 visits. Target landscape: Alive: player_1, player_2, player_6 (the speculator, me), player_7, player_10. Public role status: player_2 claims sentinel with a night 2 and night 3 watch read, unverified; player_10 claims trailseer with follows on players 5, 7 and 1, unverified; player_1 and player_7 make no role claim. Evidence is claims only; the night 4 save and attack both hit player_2, and the morning record confirms that much.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.
lessons.action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.

lessons.situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.
lessons.action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.

lessons.situation: The speculator has already picked a side (Town) and sits in a split or deadlocked day vote where its single vote can decide a tie or prevent a bad elimination of a claimed Town role. Both wolves and a lone killer may still be alive. Information landscape: Moderate and muddled: night kills, a hidden role, conflicting role claims and night-result claims, but no confirmed wolf or killer. Mostly unverified claims plus voting records. Stakes: With about six players alive and two killing factions active, one vote can decide an elimination or block a Town loss. A mistaken Town elimination moves evil toward parity and weakens the Town side the speculator picked. Consensus: The village is scattered or split into near-equal camps with no single dominant target; the push is based on muddled claims and behavioral reads. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none; nobody has directed accusations at the speculator, and its speech has been neutral. Target landscape: Several candidates split the room: claimed Town power roles (healer, trailseer, sigilist, vigilante) versus an unconfirmed quiet or counter-accusing player. The evidence is partly claims and conflicting timelines, partly behavior and past votes, with no confirmed wolf.
lessons.action: When you have already picked Town and the day vote is split among several candidates, cast your vote sincerely on the unconfirmed player whose behavior or claims look most evil. Prefer the candidate whose claims conflict with other players' reports over a claimed Town power role. Your vote can swing a split or tie, so use it to stop a Town-aligned elimination and to remove the likeliest killer, which keeps Town the winning side you picked.

verdicts.why: Five are alive, not four, and the dispute is between claims rather than a settled contradiction.
Evil is one necromancer, not a faction one step from parity with an isolated speculator vote.
I picked Town, the vote is split, and the unconfirmed player whose claims look most evil is the best target.

situations: After a day 5 vote tied between two players, with no elimination, the village has no lynch; a sentinel claim (night 3 watch naming one visitor) conflicts with the accused player's denial, while the trailseer's follow results are private and only partly support the sentinel claim. Night 4 saw a healer save and a reanimated vigilante shot on the sentinel-claimant, and the pair of tied players is being argued over as the likely healer/necromancer pair. Information landscape: Information-starved on roles: no role is confirmed for any living player, the sentinel and trailseer claims are unverified, and the one private check (trailseer follow on night 4 showing player_7 visited no one) clears only one candidate. Town discussion relies on claims and deduction rather than announced results. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the game can end within one more elimination. A wrong lynch on the tied pair would leave three players and make the next night kill a near-decisive event, so the vote is costly to get wrong. Target landscape: Two tied candidates from the day 5 vote: player_6 (claimed nothing publicly; accused of pushing the lynch and of being at player_2's door on night 4 by the trailseer-based reasoning) and player_1 (claimed nothing; was roleblocked night 3 and has a visitor on record from a sentinel claim). Neither has a confirmed role; the Trailseer's own follow results (player_6 visited no one on night 1, player_1 received a visit from player_5 on night 3) are private evidence only. Night 4's attack on the sentinel-claimant came through a dead vigilante, which is a reanimated kill, so the necromancer is the only living threat and the candidates are its possible bodies-of-interest.

lessons.situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

lessons.situation: A wolf was just eliminated by the vote, and the confirmed town investigator is the obvious target for wolf retaliation that night. The trailseer wants to preserve that investigator's last action in case they are killed. Information landscape: Info-rich: a wolf has been caught, the investigator is validated, and earlier night visits and claims are on record. Visit data on the likely victim is more valuable than a blind follow. Stakes: Losing the investigator without recovering their last check would remove a key information source. Seeing the investigator's visit, and getting it reported, can lead directly to the last wolf. Target landscape: The confirmed or strongly vetted info role facing retaliation, versus claimed protectors who were already attacked or saved, versus quiet unread players. The vetted role is the likeliest night victim and a natural way to find their last target.
lessons.action: When the trailseer's own role is likely to draw an attack, follow the player the wolves most want dead, such as the confirmed investigator who just exposed a wolf. If the target dies, the trailseer still learns whom they visited that night. That information can point suspicion at the visited player.

verdicts.why: Remaining threat is the necromancer, a non-wolf lone killer with no claimed night-attacker pattern to test; I follow the most suspicious unverified visitor pair instead of a claimant.
It is night 5, not night 1, so the blind-pick situation does not hold.
No wolf was eliminated by vote and no confirmed investigator is alive.

situations: After a day vote tied between two survivors with no elimination, a trailseer claimant cleared one player with a night follow showing no visits, while a sentinel claimant's night watch named the accused as a visitor, and the accused is pushing back that the watch shows only who came. Players are split on whose night-4 visit reached the sentinel's door, and the tied accusers are trading votes. Information landscape: Information-starved and contested: several role claims (trailseer, sentinel) with no confirmed results; the private healer record is the only verified night outcome known to me; the day-4 save and the reanimated-vigilante attack are public facts; the speculator pick (Town) is public. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, and the necromancer is the only remaining evil threat, so a single wrong elimination is recoverable but still shifts the remaining count; the game can end within one more elimination only if the necromancer is among the final pair, so a wrong vote now leaves the lone killer able to reach the endgame condition sooner. Target landscape: Day 5 tie vote between two surviving players: the healer-side player (self, role known only privately) and a suspected player whose vote-count is tied; public roles: none of the survivors have a confirmed role. Wolves and chanteuse, illusionist are dead; remaining hidden threat is a necromancer (possibly among the survivors) and a speculator whose pick is Town. Evidence basis: a trailseer claim with a follow on the accused, a sentinel claim with watch results, and behavioral accusations.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

lessons.situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.

verdicts.why: Player_2's claimed sentinel result was attacked through the vigilante body, so protecting the claimed power role under pressure fits the board.
Wolves are already gone and the board has no claimed investigator to protect.
Player_2 is the only claimed Town power role the necromancer has tried to remove, so repeat protection is the best use of the save.

situations: Day 5 ended in a tie between two accused survivors after a vote in which the two sides split: one bloc is pushing player_1 while another is pushing player_6, and the day 4 save on a claimed sentinel was attributed by public accusation to the same pair. The necromancer must choose which dead body to act through at night, and any attack reads Suspicious to an investigator, which is a dead role, so only the reanimated kind shows in the morning. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public traces are two conflicting claims (a sentinel watch and a trailseer follow that disagree on who visited whom), a healer save on night 4, and votes. No role among the living is verified; the Speculator has picked Town publicly, so the wolf-side has no living wolves and the lone killer is the only evil threat left. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the necromancer wins at two alive or fewer, so the next elimination brings the board to four alive and any further elimination makes the win close. A wrong lynch on a town player is recoverable but costly, while the necromancer's own survival is what decides the final count. Forward exposure: Any visible night kill or shot is public in the morning and reveals that a body was used; using the Illusionist body is the only route whose role stays hidden, and that route spends a conceal and the Necromancer's presence is still shown as a reanimated attack. Staying put reveals nothing but leaves the pressure on the table. Target landscape: Surviving players are player_1, player_2, player_6, player_10 (and self as necromancer). Player_10 claims trailseer, player_2 claims sentinel, both unverified. Player_1 and player_6 are both tied in today's vote and each has been accused of being the healer or the attacker; neither has a confirmed role. Dead bodies available: investigator, vigilante, Illusionist, sigilist, chanteuse, with the illusionist body carrying two conceals.

lessons.situation: After a day vote, four players remain, including the Necromancer. The Investigator has no checks left, while the Trailseer still collects visit data each night and can identify who is acting. Information landscape: Mostly info-rich: nearly all town roles are accounted for, the Investigator's exhausted status is public, and the Trailseer's ongoing tracking is the only live source of night evidence against the Necromancer. Stakes: The board is one night from three players. Leaving an active Trailseer alive lets the town confirm who is visiting and vote the Necromancer out the next day. Forward exposure: Any attack through the Vigilante body is announced as a reanimated shot, so the town learns a Necromancer exists, and attacking makes the Necromancer read Suspicious if checked. The kill cannot be undone once placed. Target landscape: Three living candidates: an Investigator publicly out of checks, a claimed Trailseer who follows a player every night, and an unclaimed Sigilist. Choose by remaining information capacity, not by past suspicion.
lessons.action: When choosing a night target with a body's attack in a small endgame, shoot the player who is still gathering information, such as an active Trailseer or Sentinel with uses left, before a player whose checks are spent. An Investigator with no checks left cannot learn anything new, while a Trailseer that follows players each night can narrow down the killer. Killing the active information role denies the town the evidence it needs to vote you out.

lessons.situation: The last wolf was voted out and three players remain overnight. One kill brings the count to two, which is the Necromancer's win threshold. Information landscape: Info-rich: eliminated roles are revealed, the Sigilist is confirmed with no sigils left, and the other survivor has no verified protective role. The open question is only which usable body to strike through. Stakes: One kill ends the game in the Necromancer's favor. Failing to attack gives the town another day vote to remove the Necromancer, so the attack must go out this night. Forward exposure: The attack is visible only through the morning report of a reanimated kill, but the game ends at once, so there is no reversibility cost and no later exposure. Target landscape: Two living opponents: a confirmed Town role with spent abilities and an unconfirmed player. A dead Vigilante body with announced role is available for the strike. Choice is by lack of defenses, not by suspicion.
lessons.action: When three players are alive at night and a usable dead attacker body is available (e.g. a Vigilante or Illusionist body), use it to attack one of the two others and finish the game. Attacking leaves two alive, which meets the Necromancer win condition. Pick the target who could not stop the kill, since no later day vote can undo the result.

lessons.situation: First usable night after an Illusionist has been executed and revealed. The town has several public tracking and protection claims, and the Necromancer must choose between attacking through the wolf body and staying put. Information landscape: Info-rich. There is a system-confirmed dead wolf, public claims from the Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer and Investigator, and possibly earlier save reports. There is no hard evidence on who the Necromancer is. Stakes: Mid-game with many town power roles alive. A kill that lands thins them, while a blocked kill only advertises a Necromancer without reducing town numbers. The Necromancer needs repeated successful kills to reach its win condition. Forward exposure: The morning report will say a reanimated wolf struck, confirming a Necromancer exists. You read Suspicious to any Investigator check that night. An attack on a protected target is announced as a save and gains nothing, and the visit cannot be undone. Target landscape: Usable body is the revealed dead Illusionist, and any earlier concealed victim is unusable. Living targets are the claimed Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer and Investigator, plus unclaimed players. Claims are unverified, and the Healer's likely choices are inferred from public claims and recent save reports.
lessons.action: When a dead Illusionist's body is usable and you are not yet the room's prime suspect, attack through it at a player the Healer is unlikely to be guarding, such as an unclaimed or low-profile player who still matters. Avoid the publicly claimed power roles the Healer is most likely covering. A kill through that body hides the victim's role and denies the town the information and the body.

verdicts.why: Four others are alive and player_10 is an active trailseer tracking me nightly, so killing the info role first fits this board.

verdicts.why: The room is not converging on a claimant's report against an accused player; the pressure is on me.
A visit has confirmed a necromancer and I am unclaimed, so I should speak with a specific, checkable point.
Four players are alive, but no one has pressed a claim demand on me yet.

decision.message: I didn't visit anyone on night 4, and player_6's two-visit count is only a claim, not an announcement. Only one of player_1, player_2 and player_6 can be the sentinel, the healer, or the speculator, so the claims should be checked against the record rather than against my denial. Vote whoever's claim the night results actually contradict.

verdicts.why: The claimed sighting is not a trailseer report; the only trailseer is dead, so I should not go along with the lead.
No necromancer has been publicly confirmed by a sentinel report today; the watches were on nights 2 and 3.
Four players remain, but I will defend my position rather than claim a role I cannot support.

situations: Four players remain alive, with a healer claim and a sentinel claim checked against a night 4 save and night 2 to 3 watches; the two-visit dispute on night 4 hinges on an attack through a dead vigilante body, which could indicate a necromancer still alive. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only hard facts are the record of a night 4 save, a night 4 attack through a reanimated vigilante, and a night 5 death via reanimated illusionist; all role claims and visit counts are unverified claims. Stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town; the game can end within one more elimination, so a wrong vote is hard to recover from and a correct vote removes the last unclaimed living player. Consensus: The room is split: the accusers of player_7 are player_2 and player_6, and player_1 and player_7 point at player_6, so no single target has a clear majority behind it. My position: Holding a private speculator pick of town while the agent's accusers are mutually opposed; the agent is voting against player_7 alongside player_6's push. Heat: The agent is accused by player_1 and player_7 over a claimed night 4 two-visit count and the agent's role-less stance; the basis is a count only player_6 has asserted, not confirmed by any announcement. Target landscape: Two living players remain as accused targets: player_7 (claims no role, no night 4 action, accused by two players and has no public role claim) and player_6 (the speculator, which is the agent itself, accused by two players). Among the others, player_1 claims healer and player_2 claims sentinel, both with partial record support. Living candidates for today's vote are player_7 and the other living accusers.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.
lessons.action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.

lessons.situation: Final-wolf vote at four alive: the village must eliminate the last wolf now or face parity at night, and the Speculator is one of the two unverified players. Information landscape: Information-rich: the dead Investigator's will clears one player, the Sigilist's abilities are logged and spent, and the lone killer is confirmed dead. Stakes: Eliminating the last wolf wins immediately for Town and for a Town pick, while a miss leaves three alive with parity at night. Consensus: Two confirmed Town players treat the vote as a choice between the two unverified players and are open to a clear case. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the cleared players. Heat: Exposed: the remaining suspect openly pushes to eliminate the agent based on a quiet record, and the confirmed Town players see it as a binary choice. Target landscape: Two unverified players, the Speculator and one suspect who survived earlier scrutiny, among four alive. The other two are cleared or confirmed Town, by a dead Investigator's will and spent, logged abilities. The suspect's push on the Speculator is behavioral, while the confirmed Town players are the deciding votes.
lessons.action: When four are alive, one wolf remains, and the Speculator has picked Town, join the cleared Town players in eliminating the one unverified suspect rather than the other. Ignore the suspect's counter-accusation of you when it rests only on a quiet record, because eliminating the last wolf ends the game with a Town win and your pick wins.

lessons.situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.
lessons.action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.

verdicts.why: The claims are checked against the record, and the remaining unclaimed suspect is the necromancer threat, so I vote on the record rather than the claim dispute.
Four are alive with one lone killer left, and the unclaimed player_7 is the one unverified suspect to eliminate.
No evil faction is one elimination from parity, since the wolves are dead and only the necromancer remains.

situations: Day 6 with four alive: a claimed healer and a claimed sentinel contest the night 4 record, a third player accuses me of an unexplained visit on night 4, and I am the only unclaimed player facing a vote. A dead vigilante body was used for the night 4 attack, which the town cannot trace to a visitor. Information landscape: Information-starved: the sentinel's two watches are spent on nights 2 and 3, the healer's save is public, visitors are not announced, and the only night 4 visit count is one player's unverified claim. Stakes: Four alive and two eliminations from a leading evil faction win, but the game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town; a wrong lynch now would leave two eliminations between the remaining evil side and victory, so the vote is decisive. Consensus: The room is leaning toward voting me out, driven by the night 4 visit count and the lack of a claimed role, while the healer and sentinel claims split the rest of the table. My position: Holding out against the forming consensus, with a vote on me already public from two players. Heat: High: two living players have named me in the vote and a third accuses me of an unmatched night 4 visit; the basis is the claimed visit count and my refusal to claim a role, not any verified result. Forward exposure: Claiming any role or answering the night 4 visit question in detail would commit me to a checkable statement; a claimed role that is later contradicted would be irreversible, so I have stayed unclaimed and deny only what I did not do. Target landscape: The vote is between me (unclaimed, accused by the sentinel-claimer and the trailseer-style counter) and the other accused on the table. The healer claim and sentinel claim are public but unverifiable now that both sentinel watches are spent; the two-visit count rests only on one player's claim. Public vs private: As the necromancer, I privately know I killed player_3 through player_8's body, attacked player_2 (saved by the healer), and killed player_10 through player_3's body with their role hidden. Publicly I am unclaimed, and the village reads me only as a 'no role' player accused of a night 4 visit.

lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

verdicts.why: Two claimed or accusing town players are pressing me, and the unclaimed player_6 is the other unverified target, so voting them keeps me on the majority side.
No investigator accuser or impossible claimed result is in play on my current board.
This is not a claimant-versus-accused split over a concealed night death; the live question is who pushes the vote on me.

situations: The day 6 vote tied 2-2 between two unclaimed survivors, each accusing the other of a night 4 visit that the public record cannot confirm. The surviving healer protected a different player on night 5 than the one the wolves-equivalent threat would hit, and the healer is questioned about why the night 5 protection went to a player not attacked. Night 4 was an attack through a dead vigilante's body, so a necromancer is the only remaining threat. Information landscape: Information-starved: no night result is verifiable beyond the record of attacks and saves; visitors are not announced, and the only checkable night 4 datum (a follow of player_7 showing no visit) is a single private claim by a claimed trailseer. Stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win at worst for the town, and the game can end within one more elimination; a wrong lynch between the two tied players is one step from a possible necromancer-side win, so each vote carries near-decisive weight. Target landscape: Two surviving players, one claiming no role and one claiming Town-side roles; player_6 (no claimed role, a two-visit count on the night 4 attack door) versus player_7 (no claimed role, denies any night 4 visit). Public role status: both unrevealed. Basis is claims and a night 4 follow result showing no visit, so evidence is thin and mostly behavioral.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

lessons.situation: Early night (night 2) after a public information-role claim, with the wolves (and possibly a lone killer) choosing their kill and the town's key information source an obvious target. Information landscape: Mostly unverified claims with few or no confirmed flips or wills, sometimes partly confirmed by a correct elimination; the claimant's visibility is the main evidence, and the healer has no hard read on which claim is real. Stakes: Losing the lead information role this early strips the town of checks before any roles are confirmed, while a save wastes the wolves' kill and keeps the town's lead intact; the board is not yet at parity, so one lost key role hurts but is not decisive. Target landscape: Several claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and quiet unclaimed players; the investigator who cleared the healer or whose check was validated is the most prominent unverified-or-confirmed target, versus a sentinel or trailseer with less impact.
lessons.action: On the night after a claimed investigator, sentinel or other information role has become the town's most visible information source, protect that claimant, since the wolves most likely attack the player who is verified or clearing others. If two claimants compete, protect the one whose results are most useful to the town (an investigator who has cleared you, or one whose check was confirmed by an elimination) over a less-pressing claimant.

verdicts.why: The Serial Killer is not in this game, and no verified tracker result has exposed a killer here.
Wolves are not all dead here, and the killer is a necromancer acting through bodies, not a serial killer.
Player_2 is the only claimed info role with a living, consistent claim, so I protect them again, though my reason is the necromancer threat rather than the claim-ranking logic of this point.

situations: Day 6 vote tied 2-2 between player_6 and player_7 with no elimination; player_2 and player_6 have each pushed a vote against player_7 over a night 4 visit count, while player_1's healer claim is contested by player_6. Player_7 (the speaker's own seat, the necromancer) must choose whether to act through a body tonight while the town's accusations circulate and the night 4 attack came through a dead vigilante body. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only hard facts are the morning record (night 4 attack on player_2 saved by healer; night 5 kill on player_10 hidden as trailseer) and the night 3 and 4 results the player holds privately. Claims from player_1, player_2, player_10 and player_7 are unverified; player_6's visit count is an unverifiable claim. A spent sentinel watch cannot be re-checked. Stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town since a concealed body's side is unknown; the game can end within one more elimination, so a single kill that takes the count to three alive leaves the town one step from losing. Each kill moves the board toward a Necromancer win at one other survivor, so a wrong or premature kill is near-irreversible. Forward exposure: Using a dead body's ability tonight is a visible attack: a kill through a body is announced by the body's kind as reanimated, and the target's attack reads Suspicious to any investigator, so the act itself reveals a necromancer exists though not who. Staying put reveals nothing and keeps all bodies available; a kill is irreversible. Target landscape: Living candidates are player_1 (publicly claimed healer, which fits a night 4 save), player_2 (publicly claimed sentinel with both watches already spent, nights 2 and 3), and player_6 (no claim, the main accuser, making a two-visit count against player_7). Bodies available: player_3 (illusionist, one conceal left on it), player_8 (vigilante, shots remaining unknown), player_9 (investigator), player_4 (sigilist), player_5 (chanteuse). Player_10 is a dead trailseer whose role was hidden and so has no usable body.

With the day 6 vote deadlocked and no living player's claim confirmed, the necromancer must decide whether a night of no visible action is safer than an attack through a body that would be read Suspicious by any investigator. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed role among the living, one healer claim and one spent sentinel claim, and a two-visit accusation; the necromancer's own night records are the only certain facts. Stakes: Four alive, two eliminations from an evil win at worst for the town, and one more elimination can end the game; staying put preserves the bodies but delays the necromancer's own win, which needs at most one other survivor, so the choice trades tempo for concealment. Forward exposure: Holding fire keeps the illusionist body and its single remaining conceal for later and reveals nothing; a kill or block through a body commits the necromancer to a visible reanimated-kind attack and spends the body's remaining use. Target landscape: Candidates are the same three living players; the choice here is whether to stay put rather than attack one of them, with player_6 as the accuser whose count names player_7 and player_2 as the vote-pusher with no live watch.

lessons.situation: The last wolf was voted out and three players remain overnight. One kill brings the count to two, which is the Necromancer's win threshold. Information landscape: Info-rich: eliminated roles are revealed, the Sigilist is confirmed with no sigils left, and the other survivor has no verified protective role. The open question is only which usable body to strike through. Stakes: One kill ends the game in the Necromancer's favor. Failing to attack gives the town another day vote to remove the Necromancer, so the attack must go out this night. Forward exposure: The attack is visible only through the morning report of a reanimated kill, but the game ends at once, so there is no reversibility cost and no later exposure. Target landscape: Two living opponents: a confirmed Town role with spent abilities and an unconfirmed player. A dead Vigilante body with announced role is available for the strike. Choice is by lack of defenses, not by suspicion.
lessons.action: When three players are alive at night and a usable dead attacker body is available (e.g. a Vigilante or Illusionist body), use it to attack one of the two others and finish the game. Attacking leaves two alive, which meets the Necromancer win condition. Pick the target who could not stop the kill, since no later day vote can undo the result.

lessons.situation: After a day vote, four players remain, including the Necromancer. The Investigator has no checks left, while the Trailseer still collects visit data each night and can identify who is acting. Information landscape: Mostly info-rich: nearly all town roles are accounted for, the Investigator's exhausted status is public, and the Trailseer's ongoing tracking is the only live source of night evidence against the Necromancer. Stakes: The board is one night from three players. Leaving an active Trailseer alive lets the town confirm who is visiting and vote the Necromancer out the next day. Forward exposure: Any attack through the Vigilante body is announced as a reanimated shot, so the town learns a Necromancer exists, and attacking makes the Necromancer read Suspicious if checked. The kill cannot be undone once placed. Target landscape: Three living candidates: an Investigator publicly out of checks, a claimed Trailseer who follows a player every night, and an unclaimed Sigilist. Choose by remaining information capacity, not by past suspicion.
lessons.action: When choosing a night target with a body's attack in a small endgame, shoot the player who is still gathering information, such as an active Trailseer or Sentinel with uses left, before a player whose checks are spent. An Investigator with no checks left cannot learn anything new, while a Trailseer that follows players each night can narrow down the killer. Killing the active information role denies the town the evidence it needs to vote you out.

lessons.situation: The Necromancer attacked a claimed Investigator and the Healer's save was announced. Only a wolf body (the Illusionist) is available, and Town investigative and protective roles are still alive. Information landscape: Moderately informative: deaths and the save are announced, and the Investigator publicly claims results and protection. The Healer's identity is not known and must be guessed from behavior. Stakes: A wasted kill night lets Town's investigative and protective roles live and narrows the suspect pool toward the Necromancer. Each repeated failure brings Town closer to eliminating the lone killer. Forward exposure: Another reanimated attack keeps the town alerted to an active Necromancer and reads Suspicious to an Investigator. A repeated blocked attack wastes the night and leaves nothing to show for the exposure. Choosing a new target keeps the option of a kill and cannot be undone once placed. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed Investigator who was just saved and is probably still guarded, versus quiet or unknown players who may be the Healer or other passive Town roles. The Investigator's protection is confirmed by the morning report, while who the Healer is remains a behavioral guess.
lessons.action: If last night's report showed the Healer saved your target, switch to a different target tonight, or to a different body for your attack, rather than repeating the same target. Aim at the likely protector or at an unshielded power role; if the Healer has protected a player on consecutive nights, choose someone other than that player.

lessons.situation: A Vigilante was just eliminated, giving the Necromancer a fresh announced-role attack body while Town investigative or protective roles are still alive and a wolf is still in play. Information landscape: Information-rich board: roles are confirmed by public night reports and eliminations, and a Healer or Investigator has claimed openly. The Necromancer can see which Town roles are threats and who is publicly shielded. Stakes: The board is small and every kill moves Town closer to parity. Removing the Sentinel or Healer blinds or unshields Town and speeds the Necromancer's path to the last-two win condition. Forward exposure: A body attack is announced as a reanimated kill of that body's kind, so the town learns a Necromancer struck. An attack night also reads Suspicious to an Investigator check. The kill cannot be undone, but it removes an information or protection source. Target landscape: Candidates are the confirmed Sentinel, the claimed Investigator, the confirmed Sigilist with spent sigils, unconfirmed claimants, and a Healer who has publicly declared their protection target. Roles are mostly known from announced deaths or claims. The choice rests on role value and public statements, not on behavior reads.
lessons.action: When a freshly eliminated Vigilante (or other attack-capable body) gives you a new announced-role weapon, use it to strike the key Town power role: a confirmed Sentinel or Investigator whose information threatens you, or a self-declared Healer whose claimed protection target is public. If a Healer has publicly named the player they will protect, hit the Healer rather than that protected target, so the shield goes down and the kill lands.

lessons.situation: The Necromancer holds a dead Chanteuse's body after a wolf elimination. The town is rallying around claimed Investigator and Healer roles, and sentinel watches or vote tallies are already pointing scrutiny at unclear players, including the Necromancer. Information landscape: Info-rich. The dead wolf is confirmed, the Investigator and Healer have made public claims, the Sentinel may have reported visits, and prior vote records are public. Stakes: Late enough that a tied vote or one more exposure can eliminate the Necromancer. A block gives no progress toward the win condition and risks the night being traced to you. Staying hidden keeps you alive for later kills. Forward exposure: Blocking through the dead Chanteuse shows that wolf's name at the door of the target to any watching Sentinel or Trailseer, which tells the town a Necromancer is active. It also kills no one, and it can strip the town's Healer so the surviving wolf's kill goes through, which draws more suspicion onto you. Holding is fully reversible, because you can reanimate on a later night. Target landscape: Only the dead Chanteuse is usable. Candidates are the claimed Investigator, whose checks may be spent, the claimed Healer, the claimed Sigilist, and accusers. They are chosen from public claims and vote history, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: If the only usable body is a dead Chanteuse and the town is already scrutinizing you, hold your action this night. You then make no visit and read Not suspicious to the Investigator. Block with that body only when it serves a concrete purpose, such as stopping one specific role from acting, and not when the target is a high-profile Investigator or Healer.

lessons.situation: A four-player endgame after both wolves and the Sigilist have died. The confirmed Vigilante openly considers spending the last bullet on the lone killer, and the Healer will predictably protect the Vigilante. Information landscape: Info-rich: the Vigilante is publicly confirmed, both wolf bodies are available with announced roles, and the Healer's likely protection target is predictable from public talk. Stakes: The Necromancer needs two kills to win from four players, while one Vigilante bullet or a day vote can end it. A wasted night attack on a protected target costs the game. Forward exposure: An attack through a body is named in the morning as a reanimated kill, revealing a Necromancer exists. A failed or saved attack leaves the Necromancer alive and exposed to the Vigilante's final bullet and the day vote. Target landscape: Dead Illusionist and Chanteuse bodies are usable. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.
