lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

verdicts.why: No claimed information role or accused player exists yet on day 2; only one death and no checks or claims to test.
Nine players alive, not three or four, and no cornering by claimed town players.
I have not been exposed by any claim and no accuser has rallied the room against me.

situations: Day 2 opens after the first night death of a player revealed as the trailseer, leaving no one able to cross-check follows. Players are demanding exact visit directions from any claimant, while the fortune teller privately holds a point from a correct night-one bet and two self-bets for nights when an attack looks likely. Information landscape: Information-starved: one death with its role revealed, no checks, watches, or follows publicly reported, and no votes yet cast because day 2 has not reached its vote. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill can end the game this day. A wrong elimination costs a town player but is recoverable at this distance, so the village has room to gather information before committing. Consensus: The village is aligned on a procedural point: several players want every visit or night-result claim to state its direction and night, so claims can be lined up once they clash. No target has consensus. My position: With the majority on the procedural demand for directional claims, holding out on any target. Heat: Low. As the fortune teller I have made no claim and pushed no target; suspicion on me rests on nothing beyond being a quiet player who has not yet spoken much. Target landscape: Nine living players, all unverified; no role claims or checks have surfaced yet, so no candidate has public role status. The only basis for any future target is behavior in the opening round (players asking for visit directions) and no evidence against anyone.

lessons.situation: The village is about to eliminate a wolf in an information-rich endgame where only one wolf would remain. Town can then win at night through a sigil strike or another kill. The fortune teller has not yet scored its second point. Information landscape: Rich. There is a prior Serial Killer elimination, night-one tracking testimony, and a sigil result, but no certainty about which evil is left. Stakes: Town is close to a win. One more evil removal leaves a lone wolf who can be killed that same night, and the game ends before the fortune teller scores. Your vote helps decide whether the game continues. Consensus: The village is building a majority against the tracked suspect on the strength of testimony and arguments. The agreement is moderately solid. My position: Aligned with the forming majority and reinforcing the case, which makes you a driver of the elimination. Heat: Low overall. The accused player may cast an isolated retaliatory vote at you, but the room is not suspicious of you. Target landscape: A suspected wolf, tracked or accused with an inconclusive sigil test, plus a claimed role under pressure from a quiet player. The suspected wolf is the main case, backed by daytime arguments and a Trailseer's testimony but no hard confirmation.
lessons.action: Before voting, count your points. If you have fewer than two and the leading candidate is a wolf whose removal would leave Town one elimination from winning, abstain if it is offered. If abstaining is not offered, vote for the least-supported candidate who is not a confirmed evil player, so the game runs long enough for your bets to score. A Town win ends the game before you can reach two points.

lessons.situation: Late in the game, the town's power roles are mostly confirmed or consistent with each other. The vote has narrowed to me versus one other unverified player, and I must choose between abstaining and voting the rival. Information landscape: Info-rich: role claims cover the town slots, saves and night results corroborate the town roles, and the public voting record is visible. The only open question is who among the unverified players is the lone killer or a wolf. Stakes: With few players left, one elimination changes the balance of power. My death ends my scoring chances, since a day vote never scores, so I must use my vote to split the count or push the real threat out. Consensus: The village is largely unified, on role-claim bookkeeping and corroborated night results, that the leftover unverified players are the problem. Neutral is treated as expendable. My position: holding out Heat: Extreme: several players, including confirmed town power roles, have declared votes against me because I am an expendable neutral once the town slots are claimed or corroborated. Target landscape: Two or three unverified players: me, an outed neutral fortune teller, and a rival with an unverified or contested claim (e.g. a vigilante or sentinel claimant suspected of being the lone killer). Every other living player holds a role corroborated by night events. The basis is process of elimination, not hard evidence on the rival.
lessons.action: When the room has already stacked elimination votes on you, cast your vote on the other leading suspect, the player with the least verified role or night results. An abstention lowers no one's count and can't force a tie, while a vote on the rival adds to a split or tie that could leave no one eliminated, and it pressures a plausible lone killer or wolf. If the votes against you are already a locked majority, the vote still goes to the rival rather than to nobody.

verdicts.why: Its endgame assumes Town is one elimination from winning, but this board has nine players with several wolves and a lone killer still alive.
Role claims are not yet corroborated and no one is stacking votes against me, so the holdout situation does not hold.

situations: Day 2 opens after a trailseer was killed on night 1 and no checks or watches exist yet; the village is asking every visit claimant to state direction, and I hold private wolf knowledge while my partner remains unrevealed and no one has claimed a role. Information landscape: Information-starved: one death with a revealed role, a trailseer whose records are gone, and no public night results, so any claim will be unverifiable. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, and no single vote or kill can end the game in one step; mistakes now are recoverable but each public commitment narrows future cover. Consensus: The room is aligned on a procedural norm (state visit directions and night-result claims precisely) but has no shared target and no evidence basis for a lynch. My position: With the majority on the procedural norm, not driving any accusation. Heat: Low; I have made only short on-topic remarks and no accusations, so no one has singled me out. Forward exposure: Any explicit visit claim or role claim now would commit me to a checkable direction and could be cross-checked against the night record; staying silent on nights keeps the claim space open and is reversible only by never making one. Target landscape: Nine living players with no checks, watches, or follows yet on record; the day-1 discussion is pure request for visit directions, so every candidate is unevidenced and no one has a public role status beyond the dead trailseer. Public vs private: As the illusionist, I privately know I am a wolf and that the pack killed a trailseer on night 1, and I hold two body-concealing uses; publicly I have no night claim, and the village reads me as an unremarkable player with no visible role.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

verdicts.why: Room leans abstain on an information-starved day; I should not pair with player_5 on a lone elimination vote.
No info-role claimant has accused me or been publicly targeted today; the trailseer is already dead.
No claimed investigator or trailseer has made a hard accusation against me on day 2.

situations: Day 2 opens after a night-1 trailseer kill with no checks or results public; players are demanding that every visit claim state its direction, while I, the unclaimed Chanteuse, sit silent and must avoid drawing attention while keeping my own night block record private. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single death and no public results, so all future evidence will be self-reported night results that must be lined up against each other. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill can end the game this turn; a wrong early lynch is recoverable but costly, and staying unexposed preserves the pack's option to keep blocking town roles. Consensus: The room is aligned on process rather than on a target: several players are insisting that visit claims state their direction and that claimants name the night and watch-or-follow type, with no shared suspect yet. My position: With the majority on process, not yet on any person; I am holding out of the accusation phase. Heat: Low: I have not spoken beyond passing, so no accusation or suspicion attaches to me yet; the only risk is being seen as silent when others are asking for direction-specific claims. Forward exposure: Any visible push now (claiming a result, pressing a visit-direction challenge, or voting hard on a claim) would tie my name to a stance before the village has evidence; it is hard to reverse once made, and the pack's partner remains unrevealed so any misstep could draw attention to the pair. Target landscape: Nine alive with one publicly dead trailseer and no checks, sentinel, or follow results on the table; the only public content is other players asking for visit directions and claims, with no candidate yet carrying role-based evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the Chanteuse and know my pack killed the trailseer on night 1 and that my night 1 block on player_8 did not take; publicly I am an unclaimed town-leaning player who has passed the opening round and says nothing yet, so the village reads me as an uninvolved quiet seat.

With the only trailseer dead and no public checks, the village is trying to create a verification test for visit claims, while I, a silent wolf-aligned Chanteuse whose night-1 block did not take, must decide whether to stay out of that test entirely. Information landscape: Information-starved: one death, no checks, no follows or watches public, so visit claims will be unverifiable and the village's test is procedural rather than evidentiary. Stakes: Nine alive and five eliminations from the leading evil faction's win condition, so the board is far from decisive; the cost of an unforced public commitment now is that it becomes a permanent record the village can cross-check later. Consensus: The village has no shared suspect; agreement exists only on the procedure of stating visit direction and night type for claims. My position: Neither driving nor opposing: I am outside the procedural consensus by staying quiet and have not endorsed the direction-claim demand. Heat: Low and unattached to any basis: I have not been named or pressed, and the village has no night result from me to contest. Forward exposure: Offering a claim of a block or a result would commit me to a checkable statement that a later claimant could contradict, and a false or contradicted night result would be hard to walk back; staying silent avoids commitment but lets others define the frame. Target landscape: No candidate is publicly tied to any role or result; the room is asking whether the first visit claim will come from a Sentinel, Trailseer-type, or Vigilante-type voice, and no one has yet been tested against evidence. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's partner is alive and unrevealed, and I know which night-1 result my block produced; publicly, the village only knows a trailseer died and that visit claims are being asked for in direction terms, so my silence is read as neutral.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No one has exposed my visit or accused me; no tracker has called me out on this board.
Room is leaning toward abstaining with no hard leads and no accusation against me, so I join the abstain majority.
No claimant has exposed my wolf partner, so there is no consensus accusation to respond to.

situations: Day 2 closed with an abstain majority after a split vote, and a trailseer died on night 1 whose role was revealed to the town. As the illusionist and carrier for the pack, you must decide whether tonight's victim's role should be concealed, while the wolf partner has voted against another player and the town has no active checks or watches to cross-check. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a confirmed information result, the only trailseer is dead, and visit claims are unverifiable. Private knowledge is limited to your own conceal count and the pack's kill. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single kill or vote can end the game, so a conceal spent now is recoverable in tempo but permanently removes one of the two hide uses that matter most in later nights. Forward exposure: Spending a conceal now would hide the victim's role from the town and be irreversible; declining keeps both uses but leaves the victim's role public if they die, and any visible vote or claim links the illusionist to the pack's records. Target landscape: Eight living candidates for tonight's pack kill, none publicly claimed as an information role; the revealed-role dead player was a trailseer, and no living player has a public claim, so all candidates rest on behavior only.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

verdicts.why: Chanteuse is alive as a wolf partner here and no investigator or sentinel has claimed results yet, so the lone-illusionist endgame does not hold.
Night 2 with an information-starved board; a quiet unread victim fits, and I should keep both conceals rather than spend one now.
No victim role is public or claimed yet, so there is no claimed role to weigh a conceal against.
No investigator has claimed or been revealed and the chanteuse is alive, so the lone-illusionist endgame does not hold.
Night 1 kill already used; I hold both conceals, and a night-2 conceal is not justified before a clear target emerges.
No claimed victim role or sigil trap exists yet to weigh a conceal against.

situations: Day 2 ended in abstention after one player was accused and another accused back, and the village is now asking every visit claimer to state direction before weighing claims. As an investigator with two checks and no result yet, you are choosing whether to spend a check tonight on the most-accused player or hold both checks until a concrete suspect emerges. Information landscape: Information-starved: one death on night 1 with no revealed information and no checks reported publicly. The only evidence is day-2 vote history and the discussion, which contains no hard results. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single check or vote can end the game. Holding checks costs little immediate time but leaves the village without information, while each check is one of only two remaining Suspicious/Not suspicious reads for the whole game. Target landscape: Nine players alive, none publicly claiming a role or result. Candidates are the players who voted to eliminate others on day 2 and those pressing visit-direction claims. No public role status for anyone; evidence is behavioral only (accusation patterns, a player pushing an accusation at another player with no supporting result).

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended with an abstain or a failed vote, the Investigator is publicly claimed with one or two checks left, and public reports from the tracking roles point at one or two specific players whose alignment is unresolved. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed tracking, watching, and visit reports plus public voting records give concrete leads, but no alignments are confirmed by the Game Master. Stakes: Mid-game with two evil factions still alive: each check is scarce and the investigator is a likely night target, so a check on a hard-lead player has to produce a verdict the village can use, not a result duplicating what the day will reveal. Target landscape: A few players tied to concrete claimed evidence (tracker or watcher reports, converging visits, vote records) versus quiet, unvetted background players and players already confirmed as liars; the lead is evidence-based, not just behavioral.
lessons.action: Spend a check on the unverified player at the center of a hard lead, such as one a tracker or watcher placed at a night-1 victim's door, or whom several claimed roles' reports converge on, rather than on a player already exposed or about to be removed. If the read is Suspicious, you have a wolf or active killer to drive the vote; if Not suspicious, you have a clearer town anchor. Either way the result is usable by the village.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a discussion-only Day 1. The Investigator holds both checks and must choose between holding them and probing an unread player blind. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no claims, no votes, no night results. Stakes: Early board with no pressure, so no single check is decisive. But the Investigator may die before a banked check is ever used, and any early read, whether it finds a wolf or clears an ally, compounds into later votes. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, flips or behavioral tells. Pick a quiet, non-prominent player at random, since nothing separates them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no leads, spend one check on a quiet, unclaimed player instead of banking both. An early Suspicious finds a wolf, and a Not suspicious gives you a baseline read. Treat a clean result as clearing only wolves: the Serial Killer and neutrals also read Not suspicious, and a Necromancer reads that way on any night it does not attack.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended in an abstain after multiple night deaths, with two killing factions active and only soft, unverified role claims on the table; the Investigator still has both checks. Information landscape: Information-starved: the claims are unverifiable and no alignments are confirmed, so any read has to come from behavior. Stakes: With two killing factions active and no hard leads, the village needs at least one verified collaborator; an early check on a central voice yields a lasting anchor even if the investigator dies. Target landscape: Unverified claimants, quiet players, and an analytical non-claimant who is actively evaluating claims; no one has confirmed alignment, and behavior is the only basis for choosing.
lessons.action: If the night has no hard lead, use a check on an active, influential player who has not claimed a role and is shaping the vote, to build a verified anchor among the central voices. A Not suspicious read clears a wolf or town member but does not clear a lone killer, so treat the anchor as likely town rather than certain.

verdicts.why: No public tracking reports or leads exist; the board is only one death and an abstain.
This is night 2, not night 1, and I have no prior results.
Day 2 ended in an abstain after one death with only soft claims, so a check on an active central voice is the best anchor-building move.

situations: Day 2 ended in abstention after a split vote, with no one eliminated; the night ahead is unpredictable because the wolves killed the trailseer on night 1 and the sigilist must decide whether to spend a sigil on a guess about who will attack tonight, knowing that a sigil only strikes a player who attacks and that a vigilante who shoots would also be struck. Information landscape: Information-starved: no morning save or kill pattern beyond the night-1 death of a trailseer, no visit claims that can be cross-checked since the trailseer is dead, and only public voting records and conversational claims about directions of visits. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single sigil spent on a wrong guess costs one of only two charges while the margin before an evil win stays wide; a sigil that lands on an actual attacker would be a rare, high-value strike, but at this distance from parity the game is not decided by one night. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a visible visit and spends one of two sigils on a player who may not attack; it reveals nothing about role outright but commits a scarce charge to a guess, and the spent sigil cannot be recovered if it fails to trigger. Target landscape: Nine-player-scale board with eight living candidates besides the sigilist: no public role claims beyond the dead trailseer, no checks or watches reported yet, all candidates unverified; the only read is behavioral (player_8 voted to eliminate player_1, player_3 voted to eliminate player_10, player_4 voted to eliminate player_5), with no confirmed evidence against any of them.

lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten players alive, day one was discussion only with no vote or deaths. The sigilist must decide between placing a sigil on a blind guess and keeping the charges. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no role claims, no voting records, no visit histories to separate likely attackers from passive roles. Stakes: Early board with a large margin before any faction can win. Nothing is forcing a spend, and each of the two charges is worth more on a night with a real lead than on a coin-flip target. Forward exposure: Holding reveals nothing and commits nothing, and the charge stays available. Placing is irreversible, spends one of two charges, and is a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unvetted: no claims, no votes, no night results. Any target is a pure guess, and most players, including investigative, protective and passive roles, will not attack.
lessons.action: On night one, when there are no deaths, claims, votes or visit data, keep both sigils and place none. A sigil only does anything if its target attacks that night, and a blind pick usually lands on a non-attacker (several observations show it striking nothing and spending a charge). Hold the charges until a night when a specific suspect is likely to attack.

verdicts.why: Concrete lead is absent: the day-two vote split on abstains with no clear accusation carrying evidence, so no suspect plausibly attacks tonight.
No wolf carrier order is identifiable yet and no suspect has attack evidence, so keeping the sigil fits better.
Still no visit data or claims that point to an attacker, so holding both charges is the right call.

situations: Day 2 ended with no elimination after an abstain-heavy vote; one player voted to eliminate the most-discussed accuser and another was targeted by a minority. You privately hold a night-one result showing a visit to the dead trailseer and must decide whether to spend your last watch on the same suspect or hold it for a likelier victim while the village debates direction-of-visit claims. Information landscape: Information-starved: one death with its role revealed, no checks or follows left to cross-check, your private sentinel result from night one, and only verbal claims about visit direction from the living players. Stakes: Five eliminations remain before the leading evil faction can win, so no single night or vote is decisive yet, but the last watch is a fixed resource; spending it on a suspect who may not be the carrier leaves no sentinel information for later nights when the wolves gain numbers. Target landscape: Nine players alive. As the sentinel, your one remaining watch can be placed on any living player; none has a public role claim. Player_5 is the strongest lead from your private result: a player visited the dead trailseer on night 1, but a single visit is not proof of wolf status. Other living players have only discussion behavior, with no hard evidence.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, with the first watch already spent and one watch left. The Sentinel is deciding whether to use it on a personal adversary or hold it for a higher-value door. Every watch is a visit, and the Sentinel is not told of its own visit. Information landscape: Still thin: the Night 1 result is the main hard fact, plus a few public claims and one vote record. There are no confirmed wolf identities, so targeting rests on likely attack paths and not on proof. Stakes: The last watch is the Sentinel's final hard evidence, and once it is spent the role has nothing left to do at night. Spending it on a low-traffic door gave nothing in the cluster, so a likely-attack target improves the chance of a usable visitor list. Target landscape: A handful of living players: a prominent claimed or confirmed Town role, a player who has accused you, and quiet unverified players. Favor the one most likely to be attacked or visited, based on public claims or revealed roles, over one picked because they are hostile to you.
lessons.action: Save the last watch for a night when you can name a door that is likely to be attacked or visited, such as a prominent claimed role or a player the wolves or killer plausibly want dead. A watch on a vocal accuser or a quiet bystander tends to return a zero-visitor result, and a watch is spent whether or not it shows anything.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. The Night 1 kill, a possible roleblock and the lone killer's attack can all land the same night, so the result may be lost, show nothing, or catch a key visitor. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no night results, no claims and no voting record. Only opening-round chatter exists. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive, so one blind watch is a cheap bet. Results across the cluster varied: zero visitors, a visit from the healer or trailseer, a multi-visitor cluster, and the serial killer caught at the door. The cost is that the Sentinel itself may be killed or blocked that night and the result lost, so only one of the two charges should be committed. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes or role flips. Every door is equally unknown, so choose a quiet, unpressured player on pure behavior, since there is no evidence to separate them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, deaths or reads, spend one of the two watches on a quiet, unclaimed player and keep the second for later. A watch can catch the killer's visit or reveal who is acting at night, and the visitor list is the only hard evidence a Sentinel can gather before Day 2. Pick a target the pack or the lone killer might plausibly hit, not a loud player who is likely to draw heat.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night after an abstain or tied vote. Conflicting role claims are on the board and you hold one watch left. You must decide whose door to watch, knowing results come only from visitors to that player. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, vote records and some prior night results, but nothing is verified. Alignments of the candidates are unconfirmed, and visit data exists only for whoever you watch. Stakes: Town can still afford a mistake, but this is the last watch, so a wasted use leaves no visitor-tracking for the rest of the game. A watch that exposes a visit pattern or kill trace can settle a claim fight before wolves reach parity. Target landscape: The choice is between a contested claimant (e.g. counter-claimed investigator or sigilist) under heavy suspicion, the obvious wolf-priority targets (claimed investigator, healer, trailseer), a quiet player from a tied vote, or an investigator-cleared player. The claim conflicts are public, but none of the candidates is verified. Only the contested claimant or the likely kill target is likely to draw visits.
lessons.action: With your last watch, pick the player most likely to receive a visit tonight. That means a contested or heavily accused claimant whose claim other roles can verify or attack, or the likely wolf kill target. A watch on a quiet suspect or an already-cleared player usually returns "no visitors", because attackers visit their victims, not themselves.

verdicts.why: I have a concrete lead in player_5 who visited the dead trailseer, so I am not holding the last watch for a later door.
This is Night 2 with one death already, not the blind Night 1 situation.
With my last watch I target the most active suspect, whose visits are most likely to be informative.

situations: Day 2 ended in an abstain-majority with no elimination after a split vote: one player pushed to eliminate a fellow discussant, the accused abstained along with most of the table, and the discussion centered on demanding exact visit directions from anyone claiming a night result after the only trailseer died on night 1. Information landscape: Information-starved: one night death with a revealed trailseer role, no investigator checks, no sentinel watches, no announced claims; only behavioral signals from the day 2 vote record and the discussion about visit directions. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game; a wrong lynch is recoverable but each mis-elimination pulls the board closer to parity, and an abstain outcome keeps the unresolved accusations open into the next day. Target landscape: Nine alive with no public role claims beyond none; candidates are the accused and vocal players who pressed visit-direction claims. Public role status: all survivors unrevealed. Basis is behavioral only (who abstained, who voted to eliminate whom on day 2), with no checks or watches to weigh.

lessons.situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: Early night (night 2) after a public information-role claim, with the wolves (and possibly a lone killer) choosing their kill and the town's key information source an obvious target. Information landscape: Mostly unverified claims with few or no confirmed flips or wills, sometimes partly confirmed by a correct elimination; the claimant's visibility is the main evidence, and the healer has no hard read on which claim is real. Stakes: Losing the lead information role this early strips the town of checks before any roles are confirmed, while a save wastes the wolves' kill and keeps the town's lead intact; the board is not yet at parity, so one lost key role hurts but is not decisive. Target landscape: Several claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and quiet unclaimed players; the investigator who cleared the healer or whose check was validated is the most prominent unverified-or-confirmed target, versus a sentinel or trailseer with less impact.
lessons.action: On the night after a claimed investigator, sentinel or other information role has become the town's most visible information source, protect that claimant, since the wolves most likely attack the player who is verified or clearing others. If two claimants compete, protect the one whose results are most useful to the town (an investigator who has cleared you, or one whose check was confirmed by an elimination) over a less-pressing claimant.

verdicts.why: No Town power role has been validated or claimed yet; only one death and no checks have been reported.
No Serial Killer was exposed and no public info-role claims have been made on this board.
No information role has publicly claimed yet, so there is no obvious claimant to protect.

situations: Day 2 ended with the town abstaining after a split vote, and the discussion is now centered on whether visit claims must state direction. The fortune teller has a night bet to place on the likeliest victim with no role-revealing evidence, and must decide whether to spend one of two self-bets on a night where an attack on itself may or may not be probable. Information landscape: Information-starved: one night death, no checks, no watches, no follows, no public claims verified by the game master. Only the fortune teller's private point record (1 of 2) and its own bet history are known. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single night or vote ends the game; a wrong bet costs one point's progress toward two, and a self-bet spent without a real threat wastes one of the two remaining uses that protect the scoring path. Target landscape: Nine players alive; the fortune teller's own night bet and self-bet choices range over all living players. Public roles: only player_2 (trailseer) is confirmed dead; no living player has a public role confirmation. Claims are unverified: nobody has announced a checked or watched result, and the day-2 vote split (abstain plurality, two players each accused by one voter) gives no hard evidence on any target.

Night 2 is approaching after a day that ended without elimination; the town has been asking for direction on visit claims, and no one has yet claimed a role. The fortune teller must bet on a victim knowing that a necromancer, if alive, could strike from the second night, and that a night on which the fortune teller is attacked is the only case in which a self-bet changes the outcome. Information landscape: Information-starved and symmetric: no investigator or sentinel results, no role claims with evidence, only vote records and discussion remarks that ask for directional visit claims. Stakes: Five eliminations remain before the leading evil faction can win, so tonight's death is not decisive but each night the wolves kill reduces the Town pool; a fortune teller bet that scores gains one point toward the second point, while a failed self-bet on a real attack leaves its death unscored. Target landscape: Nine living players, with the fortune teller among them; the wolves and lone killer are unrevealed. Vote-based suspicion targets are two accused players (one accused by a voter who wants the other eliminated) plus abstaining players, all with no public evidence behind them.

lessons.situation: After a day elimination or accusation, the remaining killer needs to silence the player who exposed it or holds a deadly tool against it. The Fortune Teller must choose between betting on the accused (who survives) and betting on the exposing claimant (who is attacked). Information landscape: Information-rich: a public claim or result (tracker report, sigil test, investigator checks) points at the killer's side, and several Town roles are out in the open. Stakes: Only one killing source is left, so exactly one death is likely each night and the bet must match it. A miss leaves the Fortune Teller stuck at one point while the game may end that same night. Target landscape: The claimed tracker, sigilist or investigator who exposed or tested the killer's side, versus the accused wolf or suspect, versus bystander claimed roles such as a roleblocked sentinel or unconfirmed healer. The basis is public claims and the day's vote record.
lessons.action: When one killer remains and a claimed power role has just driven the day's outcome (outed a wolf, tested the wolf, or led the vote), bet on that role as the killer's top threat, not on the accused or already-exposed suspect. A killer that is under suspicion usually survives the night, and the threat to it is the likelier victim.

lessons.situation: Early game (night 1 or 2), the Fortune Teller has no points yet and must pick a nightly death bet while wolves and a lone killer are all hunting. Day discussion produced a visible conflict or a prominent claimed power role. Information landscape: Mixed: some claims and night-one movement reports exist, but roles are unverified and votes were mostly abstentions, so the pick rests on behavioral reads. Stakes: No immediate parity pressure. The Fortune Teller needs two points in total, so each night's bet is a cheap, repeatable chance to score, and the self-bets guard against a later attack. Target landscape: Players who publicly claimed or acted as information roles, or who were just singled out by a night result or an open dispute, versus quiet players with no evidence either way. The choice rests on behavioral threat to the killers, not confirmed alignment.
lessons.action: With both self-bets still unspent and no points scored, bet on the player the killers most plausibly want dead tonight: an openly active, publicly claimed information role (such as a trailseer that just exposed someone) or a player the dead Trailseer's last follow pointed to. Name no role, since the death alone scores a point, and keep the self-bets for later nights.

lessons.situation: Last wolf voted out and three players left. A lone killer (the necromancer, who can attack through a reanimated body) wins by killing one more player, so the Fortune Teller is a live kill target and no other player's death is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead, the dead roles are confirmed, and the remaining Town sigilist is confirmed out of sigils. This makes the only remaining attacker and its available bodies clear. Stakes: The lone killer wins if anyone else dies tonight, so a bet that fails to cover your own life can end the game with the Fortune Teller short of two points. A self-bet keeps you alive for another night. Target landscape: The suspected necromancer (alive and holding a usable body, so unlikely to die), a confirmed sigilist with no sigils left (no threat), or a self-bet. Roles are confirmed from the graveyard, and nothing makes the suspect likely to die tonight.
lessons.action: With three alive and a lone killer that can attack, you are one of only two possible victims. If no other victim is predictable, spend a self-bet, because an attack on you fails that night. Don't bet on the suspected killer: a killer that is immune or about to win is unlikely to die, and a wrong bet leaves you open to the attack.

lessons.situation: Late game with the wolves dead or nearly dead and one killer left (serial killer, necromancer or last wolf). The Fortune Teller stands at 0-1 points and needs a death, and the most obvious target is publicly protected, so a bet on them fails to the save or the killer switches targets. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of the dead wolves are confirmed, claims and protection histories are public, and the surviving killer's identity or kill pattern is mostly known. Stakes: Few players remain and the game can end any night. Each night spent without scoring risks being voted out or the game finishing before the second point, so the bet must follow where the killer can actually kill, not just where it wants to. Target landscape: The investigator or leader shielded by a public healer claim, the claimed healer who is exposed, other claimed power roles (sigilist, sentinel, trailseer), and unconfirmed players. Hard evidence of who is protected, not behavior, drives the choice.
lessons.action: When the healer has publicly announced protecting the obvious top target (the confirmed or claimed investigator), place the bet on the next-most-valuable unshielded Town role the surviving killer must remove, such as the claimed healer or another power role. If the killer's last pick is predictable, name that role in the bet for the two-point payoff.

lessons.situation: Three-player endgame tie between a confirmed Town power role, a suspected wolf and the Fortune Teller. The wolves need a kill to close the game, and the Fortune Teller needs points to win. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed by earlier night results and blocked actions, so the wolves' likely victim can be read from the board. Stakes: Each night is nearly decisive. A correct victim-and-role bet gives two points and wins the game for the Fortune Teller, while a miss wastes a night when the kill can end the game. Target landscape: A publicly confirmed Town role (e.g. a claimed vigilante whose shots were blocked), a suspected surviving wolf, or a self-bet. The Town player is the most likely kill target, backed by confirmed evidence from earlier nights and blocks rather than just behavior.
lessons.action: With three alive and a night kill that is predictable (a publicly confirmed Town role whose own actions are blocked or spent, with a wolf free to carry the kill), bet on that player to die and name their confirmed role. A correct victim plus role scores two points and can finish the win.

situations: Day 2 ended in an abstain majority after accusations scattered across several players, and the trailseer was killed on night 1 so no follow information can cross-check any visit claim. The vigilante, holding two bullets and no night information beyond a night-1 hold, must decide whether to act on guesswork or keep the shots until a concrete claim or contradiction surfaces. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigator or sentinel results are public, no claims have been verified, the trailseer's follow history died with them, and the only public material is discussion about visit directions and votes. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, and the game cannot end within one more elimination; this gives room to wait for evidence, but each misdirected shot consumes one of only two bullets and removes a town-side resource that cannot be reloaded. Forward exposure: Taking a shot now would publicly reveal you hold the vigilante role and would commit your remaining bullets to a target chosen with no hard evidence; a shot cannot be taken back, and a miss or a kill on a town player both become public. Target landscape: Eight living candidates other than you, none with a public role claim backed by a verified result; the only accusations are votes on day 2 (one player accused by several, another accused by one player) and a general call for visit directions, so every candidate is public-behavior-only.

Two players pushed opposing accusations on day 2, with the vote splitting the village into a camp that wants a particular player removed and a camp that abstained, and no one has produced a checkable night result. The vigilante has to weigh whether a visible accusation or silence best preserves the two remaining shots for a later concrete target. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only evidence is public vote history and day-two speech, with no investigator, sentinel, or healer results to anchor any accusation and the visit-direction claim test not yet producing any claims. Stakes: With five eliminations still needed before the leading evil faction can win and no single elimination able to end the game, a misjudged accusation costs the village a day rather than the game, but a wasted shot removes one of only two vigilante bullets from the town's remaining pool. Forward exposure: Any public call that names a suspect or a lead to the village would position you as a shooter-aware player; a shot or a strong accusation is visible and binds you to a result that cannot be reversed, while holding silent preserves flexibility. Target landscape: Players who voted to eliminate others on day 2 (one player received two votes against them, another received one) versus players who abstained; no player has a role claim, so the choice rests entirely on voting pattern and speech behavior.

lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

verdicts.why: No role is confirmed and no night result or contradiction singles anyone out, so holding fire keeps my two bullets for a real lead.
No vote has mis-eliminated a Town role and no revealed role contradicts anyone's claim, so there is no hard lead yet.

situations: Day 2 ended in abstention after a split vote, with several players demanding visit claims state their direction. The necromancer holds the dead trailseer's body as its only usable ability and must decide whether to follow a target through it tonight, knowing that a body-based follow is a visit the living trailseer role would otherwise have seen, and that any night attack reads Suspicious to an investigator. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigator checks have been announced, no sentinel or trailseer living, one night death with no will read out, and the day discussion is mostly demands for visit directions with no verified claims. Stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single misjudged night move is recoverable at this distance, but each unrecovered kill or exposed trace pushes the wolves and the necromancer closer to parity while the town remains uninformed.
