Target landscape: Nine players alive, none publicly claimed; the only dead player is a revealed Trailseer (player_2, night 1) whose body is usable, and the body's ability follows a visit that no living player has yet cross-checked. Candidates are all unclaimed, with no hard evidence against any of them; the only public signal is that day 2 voting abstained and one player voted to eliminate another without a stated case.

After an abstain-majority day 2, the village must decide whether to name a player on day 3, since abstaining will no longer be offered after another no-elimination day. The necromancer has to weigh whether to keep voting with the abstaining majority, knowing the vote record is public and permanent. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public evidence is the day-2 vote record and the demand for visit directions; no night results have been claimed or confirmed beyond the night-one death. Stakes: Nine alive and five eliminations from the leading evil win, so one day's vote cannot end the game; but since the next no-elimination day forces a named vote, the record of this abstention shapes what a forced vote will look like. Forward exposure: A vote this day that eliminates a player reveals the voter's alignment-adjacent pattern to the record and is permanent; abstaining keeps the record neutral, and after two days with no elimination abstaining will no longer be offered. Target landscape: The day-2 vote split: one player voted to eliminate a player with no stated case, while the rest abstained. No candidate has a public role claim or verified evidence; the only behavioral basis is the vote record and the discussion calls for directions.

lessons.situation: After a day vote, four players remain, including the Necromancer. The Investigator has no checks left, while the Trailseer still collects visit data each night and can identify who is acting. Information landscape: Mostly info-rich: nearly all town roles are accounted for, the Investigator's exhausted status is public, and the Trailseer's ongoing tracking is the only live source of night evidence against the Necromancer. Stakes: The board is one night from three players. Leaving an active Trailseer alive lets the town confirm who is visiting and vote the Necromancer out the next day. Forward exposure: Any attack through the Vigilante body is announced as a reanimated shot, so the town learns a Necromancer exists, and attacking makes the Necromancer read Suspicious if checked. The kill cannot be undone once placed. Target landscape: Three living candidates: an Investigator publicly out of checks, a claimed Trailseer who follows a player every night, and an unclaimed Sigilist. Choose by remaining information capacity, not by past suspicion.
lessons.action: When choosing a night target with a body's attack in a small endgame, shoot the player who is still gathering information, such as an active Trailseer or Sentinel with uses left, before a player whose checks are spent. An Investigator with no checks left cannot learn anything new, while a Trailseer that follows players each night can narrow down the killer. Killing the active information role denies the town the evidence it needs to vote you out.

lessons.situation: The last wolf was voted out and three players remain overnight. One kill brings the count to two, which is the Necromancer's win threshold. Information landscape: Info-rich: eliminated roles are revealed, the Sigilist is confirmed with no sigils left, and the other survivor has no verified protective role. The open question is only which usable body to strike through. Stakes: One kill ends the game in the Necromancer's favor. Failing to attack gives the town another day vote to remove the Necromancer, so the attack must go out this night. Forward exposure: The attack is visible only through the morning report of a reanimated kill, but the game ends at once, so there is no reversibility cost and no later exposure. Target landscape: Two living opponents: a confirmed Town role with spent abilities and an unconfirmed player. A dead Vigilante body with announced role is available for the strike. Choice is by lack of defenses, not by suspicion.
lessons.action: When three players are alive at night and a usable dead attacker body is available (e.g. a Vigilante or Illusionist body), use it to attack one of the two others and finish the game. Attacking leaves two alive, which meets the Necromancer win condition. Pick the target who could not stop the kill, since no later day vote can undo the result.

lessons.situation: First usable night after an Illusionist has been executed and revealed. The town has several public tracking and protection claims, and the Necromancer must choose between attacking through the wolf body and staying put. Information landscape: Info-rich. There is a system-confirmed dead wolf, public claims from the Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer and Investigator, and possibly earlier save reports. There is no hard evidence on who the Necromancer is. Stakes: Mid-game with many town power roles alive. A kill that lands thins them, while a blocked kill only advertises a Necromancer without reducing town numbers. The Necromancer needs repeated successful kills to reach its win condition. Forward exposure: The morning report will say a reanimated wolf struck, confirming a Necromancer exists. You read Suspicious to any Investigator check that night. An attack on a protected target is announced as a save and gains nothing, and the visit cannot be undone. Target landscape: Usable body is the revealed dead Illusionist, and any earlier concealed victim is unusable. Living targets are the claimed Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer and Investigator, plus unclaimed players. Claims are unverified, and the Healer's likely choices are inferred from public claims and recent save reports.
lessons.action: When a dead Illusionist's body is usable and you are not yet the room's prime suspect, attack through it at a player the Healer is unlikely to be guarding, such as an unclaimed or low-profile player who still matters. Avoid the publicly claimed power roles the Healer is most likely covering. A kill through that body hides the victim's role and denies the town the information and the body.

lessons.situation: A four-player endgame after both wolves and the Sigilist have died. The confirmed Vigilante openly considers spending the last bullet on the lone killer, and the Healer will predictably protect the Vigilante. Information landscape: Info-rich: the Vigilante is publicly confirmed, both wolf bodies are available with announced roles, and the Healer's likely protection target is predictable from public talk. Stakes: The Necromancer needs two kills to win from four players, while one Vigilante bullet or a day vote can end it. A wasted night attack on a protected target costs the game. Forward exposure: An attack through a body is named in the morning as a reanimated kill, revealing a Necromancer exists. A failed or saved attack leaves the Necromancer alive and exposed to the Vigilante's final bullet and the day vote. Target landscape: Dead Illusionist and Chanteuse bodies are usable. Living are a confirmed Vigilante with one bullet, a claimed Healer, and a neutral Speculator; the Vigilante is the village's obvious protection priority.
lessons.action: In a four-player endgame with a confirmed Vigilante holding a bullet and a claimed Healer alive, use a dead Chanteuse body to block the Healer or the Vigilante, or attack a target the Healer is unlikely to protect, rather than striking the likely-protected Vigilante. The Healer predictably protects the Vigilante, and an unblocked save wastes the attack while the Necromancer takes the Vigilante's shot. Choose the night action that removes the threat to yourself, since the Necromancer is not told in advance whom the Vigilante will shoot.

situations: Night 2 after a trailseer was killed on night 1 with no public claims yet. lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.
lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.

Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. situations: Day 3 opens with eight players alive after two night kills of the trailseer and vigilante, and the village has no confirmed information. The agent, a fortune teller with one point of two and two self-bets left, must decide how to speak and vote with no public evidence, while a day 2 vote against the agent sits on the record. Information landscape: Information-starved: only two public deaths with revealed roles, one vigilante night-2 hold-fire record, and no active role claims (player_9 claimed no role). No investigator, sentinel, or healer claims have surfaced. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong vote is recoverable but each mis-elimination moves the wolves closer to parity, so the agent's votes carry real but not decisive weight this day. Consensus: No clear consensus; the village abstained on day 2 and the day 3 discussion has no messages yet, so the room is unaligned and information-starved. My position: Holding out: the agent has no claim and no accusation to push, sitting with the non-committal majority. Heat: Moderate: as a fortune teller who has made no claim, the agent was voted for by one player on day 2 with no concrete evidence against it, so suspicion on the agent is low-to-moderate and rests only on the day 2 vote. Target landscape: Eight alive; no one has claimed a role except player_9 who claimed no role. Day 2 votes split: some players voted to eliminate player_10, player_5, and player_1 (the agent); most abstained. No public role evidence on any candidate.

lessons.situation: An early day after a night kill, with no wolf-kill leads or checks revealed. One investigative claimant has reported a non-visit result and the village is just starting to interpret night movements. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single dead player and one claimed no-visit result, with no investigative checks, caught lies or voting record to go on. Stakes: Early game with plenty of cushion; no single vote or kill flips the game. The aim is to stay alive for more night bets while adding no suspicion, since there is little to gain from pushing a read now. Consensus: Calm and undirected. Players echo each other's observations, with no accusation forming and a leaning toward abstaining. My position: With the majority. Echoing and refining shared observations, not driving. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the fortune teller. Target landscape: A claimed trailseer or similar reporter clears one quiet player. The other living players have unknown roles and no concrete leads, so there is no basis yet for a behavioral accusation.
lessons.action: When the day opens with little evidence and just one or two claims, agree with the claim and add one modest logical observation, such as which roles a given report cannot cover. Then let others speak, without proposing a target, so the discussion stays calm and you stay unnoticed.

lessons.situation: A day discussion in which night deaths have produced visit reports from claimed trailseer or sentinel players. Those reports point at an accused player or create competing leads, and the fortune teller has no heat and is still working toward two prediction points. Information landscape: Mixed but mostly information-rich: announced deaths and roles, plus claimed visit reports that conflict or are contested. Reports are claims, not announcements, so they can be checked against how the rules treat concealed victims. Stakes: The board is mid-game and not at the brink; one wrong day-vote hurts Town but does not end the game. The fortune teller's own win depends on surviving nights to score points, so staying unnoticed matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is engaged and fairly aligned on dissecting the visit reports. There is no firm lean yet, or it is forming around the accused visitor. It rests on claimed results rather than announced facts. My position: With the majority, not driving. Contributing a summary but taking no hard stance. Heat: None. No one is suspecting or questioning the fortune teller, who is a neutral with no side and reads Not suspicious. Target landscape: Several living players with unverified role claims and visit reports from a claimed trailseer or sentinel; the accused deny or counter-claim. The basis is claimed night results and explanations, not confirmed facts.
lessons.action: With zero heat and no role claim of your own, stay in the analytical middle: restate what each investigative claimant reported, ask the accused to explain their visits, and point out which claims conflict. Hold back from committing to one target until the explanations come in, so you stay a low-profile voter while the village's own evidence does the work.

situations: Day 3 with eight players alive and no night results publicly claimed. Two votes on day 2 targeted wolves without stated reasons, a third player asks for reasons, and the village is stalled on abstentions. You privately hold the wolf-side knowledge of which of your pack's kills and blocks succeeded, and your partner is still hidden. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigator, sentinel, or trailseer results are public; only the two deaths and their roles are known, and the day-2 votes are the only public signal. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong lynch is recoverable but each wrong result narrows the margin, so the village is not yet at the point where one vote ends the game. Consensus: The village has no consensus on a direction; the majority is abstaining and players are asking for concrete night results before any lynch. My position: With the majority, holding out on any named target. Heat: Low to moderate: you have voted abstain on each day and have spoken only generically, so suspicion on you is minimal, though an active analytical voice calling for reasons could draw attention. Forward exposure: Any visible push toward a lynch or a block-related claim would commit you publicly and is hard to reverse once spoken; staying in the abstain majority keeps your exposure low but leaves the village without a direction. Target landscape: Eight players alive; the village has no confirmed roles beyond the two dead town roles (a trailseer and a vigilante, both known to be town-aligned by the record of their deaths). Remaining candidates are unrevealed, with suspicion centered on the player who cast a wolf-direction vote and the player who voted without reason; the basis is behavioral only, with no concrete night results from any living player. Public vs private: Privately, as the Chanteuse (a wolf), you know your pack's kills and blocks; publicly no wolf has been revealed and the village reads no wolf identity, so your wolf partner is still hidden and the town's read on you is empty.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

situations: Day 3 with eight alive and no elimination yet; the village has two confirmed dead town-side roles and no live claims, and I, the lone necromancer, must decide whether to stay quiet while two bodies sit available for later use and the vote remains unresolved. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living claims, only the public trailseer and vigilante deaths, a vigilante who held fire on night 1, and day-2 vote records showing scattered accusations. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single vote or kill ends the game, so a mistaken day vote is recoverable but each wrong elimination moves the board closer to a lone-killer or wolf win. Consensus: The village has no consensus; day 2 ended in abstention with votes scattered across several players, so the room is still undecided and information-starved. My position: Holding out from any forming alignment, since none has formed; I am neither driving an accusation nor opposing one. Heat: Low so far: my only public vote on day 2 was with the majority of abstentions, and I have made no claim or accusation. Forward exposure: Claiming any role or result now would commit me publicly and could be checked against night outcomes; staying unclaimed keeps options open but leaves me without a stated position, and any visible move toward a body reveals my lone-killer nature to the town. Target landscape: Eight players alive; the dead are a trailseer (night 1) and a vigilante (night 2), both with public roles. No one has a hard case; the day-2 votes split between a few players with no evidence beyond discussion behavior, and the most-voted was abstention. Public vs private: As the necromancer I privately know I am the lone killer with no body to use yet, while the public sees only an unclaimed player with no role claim and no visible activity; my night ability depends on a dead role I can reach, and the trailseer and vigilante are dead but their bodies are not yet usable from a night I have seen.

lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Two town power roles have claimed, their results back each other up, and the necromancer is pushed to state a role or be voted out. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed roles of the dead, public vote history, claimed night results and spent abilities leave very little room to bluff. Stakes: One elimination vote decides the game. If the necromancer is voted out it loses outright, and a failed claim leaves no later day to repair it. Consensus: The few remaining players are converging on a bloc of cross-verifying town claims, with the unclaimed or contradicted player as the obvious elimination. My position: Holding out alone against a forming two-player bloc. Heat: High to critical. Claimed town roles are demanding my claim, or I am the odd player out after their results cleared each other. Forward exposure: A role claim commits me to a night history that the claimed town roles can check against their own results and spent abilities. A claim that fails the check is nearly irreversible, but staying silent is already read as guilt in a small endgame. Target landscape: The claimed power roles (vigilante, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist) and any unclaimed player. Their claims are partly corroborated by revealed deaths and spent abilities, so each can be tested against the record. Public vs private: Privately a lone killer who has been attacking through a dead player's body, while publicly needing to pass as an ordinary town power role under direct claim demands.
lessons.action: When pressed to claim at the final three or four, give a specific role claim instead of stalling. Pick a still-living town role that no revealed death or other claim has already used, and tell a night story that fits every claimed result and the visit rules. For example, a Sentinel is never told of its own watch, and a Trailseer's follow is a visit others can cross-check.

lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

lessons.situation: A claimed information role accuses a player based on a night result, the accused disputes it, and the necromancer is tempted to step in and challenge the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead role with a concealed role, a specific claimed tracking report, and mechanical counter-claims from the accused. All of it is still unverified. Stakes: The board has many living players, so every public commitment matters for the endgame. A defense that turns out wrong leaves a damaging record, while a vote with the majority costs nothing. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on the accused, driven by a concrete claimed report that the claimant has already defended against objections. My position: Holding out, if I contest the lead. Better to move to the majority side. Heat: Low to none. Attention is on the accused player and the claimant, not on me. Forward exposure: Publicly challenging a claimed information lead puts my name on the record against it, and that record cannot be undone if the target flips evil. Joining the consensus costs little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: The accused player denies the charge and argues mechanics. The claimed trailseer, or other power-role claimant, gives a specific sighting. The evidence for the claimant is stronger than the accused's counter-argument. Public vs private: Publicly the room is split between an accused player and a claimed power role with a concrete report. Privately I am the lone killer with no stake in either side's survival, so I can choose the least risky alignment.
lessons.action: When a living claimant's report (for example a trailseer's) already has the room converging on an accused player, go along with that lead and voice a short read that matches it. If you doubt the report, ask a neutral question about it rather than staking your name on a mechanics rebuttal. The accused may flip, and a record of defending them marks you as their ally.

situations: Two town-role claimants have not surfaced after two night deaths of a trailseer and a vigilante; the village abstained on day 2 while two players pushed eliminations on each other without stated reasons, and the agent, as an illusionist with conceals, must decide whether to stay quiet while information roles remain unclaimed. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigator, sentinel, or trailseer claim is public, the only confirmed facts are two deaths and their roles (trailseer night 1, vigilante night 2, the second one held fire night 1), and day votes are the only public signal. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the wolves can win, so a single wrong lynch is recoverable but each wrong vote narrows the margin; the two conceals are a finite resource to spend on a decisive claimed information role rather than on an unclear night. Consensus: The village is not aligned: day 2 ended in abstention with split votes between player_3 and player_4 pushing eliminations and player_8 voting on player_1, and no information role has claimed. My position: Holding out against a forming lynch consensus; no clear majority direction exists yet. Heat: Moderate-low: the agent voted for a player who was then killed unconcealed-role-wise by the wolves, and has pushed no name, so suspicion rests only on being quiet and on a vote that now looks like a dead-player vote. Forward exposure: Claiming any role or a night result would publicly commit you and invite a check; hiding a body or making a visible accusation is irreversible in public terms, so the current quiet posture keeps the option open. Target landscape: Day 3 candidates are the living discussion participants (players 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 minus the agent); none holds a public role claim, and the day-2 votes split on player_10, player_5, player_1 and player_6 with no hard evidence, only voting behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the illusionist, a wolf with two conceals left, and your wolf partner (the chanteuse) is still unrevealed; publicly you are an unclaimed quiet player voting on day 2 with no role claim and no night result to share.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Day two with several town investigative and protective claims surfacing, a night death that flipped information, and the room absorbed in checking one claimant. The illusionist wolf knows about an unannounced immune target. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, with three town role claims and a dead trailseer's visit reported, but nothing confirms wolf alignment. Stakes: Mid-early game; the pack still has room, but one revealed slip about the immune target would expose a wolf and tilt the count toward town. Consensus: The town is coalescing around abstaining and picking apart one claimant's lack of results, based on claimed night results. My position: Staying out of the main debate and moving with the room, ready to join it. Heat: Low. Reported town information frames me as an innocent subject of night information, and attention sits elsewhere. Forward exposure: Accusing the immune player would require explaining how I know about an unannounced failed kill, instantly revealing wolf knowledge and being irreversible. A mild on-topic comment commits me to little and can be revised later. Target landscape: The room is scrutinizing a newly claimed role with thin results and accepting a cleared target. The immune player is publicly unverified and not under pressure. Public vs private: Privately the pack knows a quiet player survived our unannounced night attack and is night-immune, while the town sees only an unverified player talking mechanics.
lessons.action: When the room is focused on another debate, such as verifying a claimed role, and your night-immune or already-known target sits among the discussants, join the discussion on its stated topic only. Voice a mild opinion on the claim under scrutiny or on the emerging abstain, and don't accuse or defend the immune player, since explaining how you know would expose wolf knowledge. Staying aligned with the room's current direction keeps heat low while you preserve your concealed information.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.
