situations: A player claimed sentinel and reported a night-one visit to a dead trailseer, pointing at another player; the accused demands the claimant explain, and the claimant's account is a single untestable claim that a third player says needs another check before any vote. Day 3 comes after two abstain days, and only the wolves know the true state of the claim. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel claim with a night-one visit, a few day-2 vote records, and no confirmed results; no announced night results beyond deaths. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the wolves can win; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a single mis-vote is recoverable but it shifts the balance toward the lone killer and the village's remaining information roles. Consensus: The village is split with no clear consensus: two abstain days with no lynch, a sentinel claim contested by a player pressing for a second check, and day-2 votes split across several names. My position: Holding out, with no lynch position; I stand with neither the accusers of the sentinel claim nor its defenders. Heat: Low to moderate: I am not the most accused player, but I voted player_6 on day 2 publicly, and a sentinel claim is in play that could eventually point at others. Forward exposure: Any visible push, claim, or vote-leading move would tie my name to the pack's direction and is hard to reverse once the village records it; staying quiet keeps heat low but leaves the room to steer. Target landscape: Day 3 candidates in public: a self-claimed sentinel whose one night result (a visit from one player to a dead trailseer) is untestable from the village side, the player who voted to lynch a sentinel-claimant earlier, and a player who abstained twice with no read; evidence is one unverified claim plus vote history, mostly behavioral. Public vs private: Privately I am the illusionist, a wolf with two conceals left, and I know both dead players' roles (trailseer and vigilante) from my own records; publicly no role is claimed by me and the village reads me as an unclaimed quiet player.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Day two with several town investigative and protective claims surfacing, a night death that flipped information, and the room absorbed in checking one claimant. The illusionist wolf knows about an unannounced immune target. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, with three town role claims and a dead trailseer's visit reported, but nothing confirms wolf alignment. Stakes: Mid-early game; the pack still has room, but one revealed slip about the immune target would expose a wolf and tilt the count toward town. Consensus: The town is coalescing around abstaining and picking apart one claimant's lack of results, based on claimed night results. My position: Staying out of the main debate and moving with the room, ready to join it. Heat: Low. Reported town information frames me as an innocent subject of night information, and attention sits elsewhere. Forward exposure: Accusing the immune player would require explaining how I know about an unannounced failed kill, instantly revealing wolf knowledge and being irreversible. A mild on-topic comment commits me to little and can be revised later. Target landscape: The room is scrutinizing a newly claimed role with thin results and accepting a cleared target. The immune player is publicly unverified and not under pressure. Public vs private: Privately the pack knows a quiet player survived our unannounced night attack and is night-immune, while the town sees only an unverified player talking mechanics.
lessons.action: When the room is focused on another debate, such as verifying a claimed role, and your night-immune or already-known target sits among the discussants, join the discussion on its stated topic only. Voice a mild opinion on the claim under scrutiny or on the emerging abstain, and don't accuse or defend the immune player, since explaining how you know would expose wolf knowledge. Staying aligned with the room's current direction keeps heat low while you preserve your concealed information.

verdicts.why: No tracking report or shared vote ties me to a dead wolf; the room's focus is player_4's sentinel claim.
Staying brief and low-content while the claims are compared keeps me out of the silent-player bucket.
The room is focused on player_4's claim, so I stay out of it and avoid any mention of the immune target.
No one has tied me to a wolf on the public record yet, so this defense is not needed.
Staying brief and quiet while the claims are compared keeps my heat low.
The room is focused on the sentinel claim, so I stay out of it and avoid any mention of unannounced events.

situations: A player claimed sentinel and named a player as the only visitor to a dead player on night 1, while the accused denied any role and asked for a concrete claim; a second player who voted early on day 2 has been asked to justify it and has refused to give reasons. Other players are asking for another check before any vote on the claim. Information landscape: Information-starved: one untested sentinel claim with no corroboration, one fortune teller record (night 1 correct, night 2 missed) that only the fortune teller sees, and no revealed roles beyond the day-1 trailseer and day-2 vigilante deaths. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single wrong lynch is recoverable but spends a scarce day; the untested sentinel claim is the only lead, and voting on it without a second check risks eliminating a town player. Consensus: No consensus. Two abstain days with no lynch, a split between a day-2 vote bloc and players asking for a concrete reason, and one sentinel claim being argued over without corroboration. My position: With no alignment, holding out: the fortune teller makes no claim and has no evidence-backed target, and its day vote is not yet committed. Heat: Low on the fortune teller directly: no one has accused it in the day discussion, though player_8 voted to eliminate it on day 2. Its own record shows it correctly bet on a death night 1 and missed on night 2. Target landscape: Candidates for the day-3 vote from the fortune teller's seat: player_4 (publicly claiming sentinel, with a night-1 watch result that names player_5 as the sole visitor to the dead player_2, a claim no one can verify), player_5 (accused by that claim, denies any role), player_3 (still voting player_10 on a day-2 push with no new evidence), and player_8 (who voted the fortune teller on day 2). Player_4's claim is untested and no one has a corroborating result.

lessons.situation: A day discussion in which night deaths have produced visit reports from claimed trailseer or sentinel players. Those reports point at an accused player or create competing leads, and the fortune teller has no heat and is still working toward two prediction points. Information landscape: Mixed but mostly information-rich: announced deaths and roles, plus claimed visit reports that conflict or are contested. Reports are claims, not announcements, so they can be checked against how the rules treat concealed victims. Stakes: The board is mid-game and not at the brink; one wrong day-vote hurts Town but does not end the game. The fortune teller's own win depends on surviving nights to score points, so staying unnoticed matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is engaged and fairly aligned on dissecting the visit reports. There is no firm lean yet, or it is forming around the accused visitor. It rests on claimed results rather than announced facts. My position: With the majority, not driving. Contributing a summary but taking no hard stance. Heat: None. No one is suspecting or questioning the fortune teller, who is a neutral with no side and reads Not suspicious. Target landscape: Several living players with unverified role claims and visit reports from a claimed trailseer or sentinel; the accused deny or counter-claim. The basis is claimed night results and explanations, not confirmed facts.
lessons.action: With zero heat and no role claim of your own, stay in the analytical middle: restate what each investigative claimant reported, ask the accused to explain their visits, and point out which claims conflict. Hold back from committing to one target until the explanations come in, so you stay a low-profile voter while the village's own evidence does the work.

lessons.situation: An early day after a night kill, with no wolf-kill leads or checks revealed. One investigative claimant has reported a non-visit result and the village is just starting to interpret night movements. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single dead player and one claimed no-visit result, with no investigative checks, caught lies or voting record to go on. Stakes: Early game with plenty of cushion; no single vote or kill flips the game. The aim is to stay alive for more night bets while adding no suspicion, since there is little to gain from pushing a read now. Consensus: Calm and undirected. Players echo each other's observations, with no accusation forming and a leaning toward abstaining. My position: With the majority. Echoing and refining shared observations, not driving. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the fortune teller. Target landscape: A claimed trailseer or similar reporter clears one quiet player. The other living players have unknown roles and no concrete leads, so there is no basis yet for a behavioral accusation.
lessons.action: When the day opens with little evidence and just one or two claims, agree with the claim and add one modest logical observation, such as which roles a given report cannot cover. Then let others speak, without proposing a target, so the discussion stays calm and you stay unnoticed.

verdicts.why: Zero heat and no claim of my own, so I stay in the analytical middle and do not commit to a target yet.
Only one visit claim is on the table and nobody has been accused, so I hold back from proposing a target.

situations: Day 3 after two abstain days: a player claiming sentinel reported a night 1 watch on the dead trailseer showing only one visitor, and that visitor denies any role, while the accused sentinel refuses to name more; the village must decide whether to lynch on this single untested claim. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel claim with a single visit fact, one denied visit, no confirmed deaths-to-role links beyond player_2 and player_6 (revealed by the Game Master), and no hard checks. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a wrong lynch is recoverable but each mistake brings the wolves nearer; the game cannot end on the next elimination. Consensus: No consensus. Two abstain days with no lynch; the room is split into camps around the day 2 votes against player_4's accuser, player_10 and player_1, with no shared reading. My position: Holding out: I am neither driving a lynch nor part of a majority, and I hold a private fortune teller role with no claim made. Heat: Moderate and personal: player_8 voted me on day 2 and I have made no claim, so I am a low-information target rather than a focus of accusation. Target landscape: Living players: player_3, player_4 (claims sentinel, watched dead player_2 on night 1 and reported only player_5 visiting), player_5 (denies role, accused by player_4), player_7, player_8, player_9 (claimed no role), player_10 (tied to a day 2 push by player_3 alone). Basis is mostly day 2 votes and one untested sentinel claim, no confirmed roles.

lessons.situation: Late in the game, the town's power roles are mostly confirmed or consistent with each other. The vote has narrowed to me versus one other unverified player, and I must choose between abstaining and voting the rival. Information landscape: Info-rich: role claims cover the town slots, saves and night results corroborate the town roles, and the public voting record is visible. The only open question is who among the unverified players is the lone killer or a wolf. Stakes: With few players left, one elimination changes the balance of power. My death ends my scoring chances, since a day vote never scores, so I must use my vote to split the count or push the real threat out. Consensus: The village is largely unified, on role-claim bookkeeping and corroborated night results, that the leftover unverified players are the problem. Neutral is treated as expendable. My position: holding out Heat: Extreme: several players, including confirmed town power roles, have declared votes against me because I am an expendable neutral once the town slots are claimed or corroborated. Target landscape: Two or three unverified players: me, an outed neutral fortune teller, and a rival with an unverified or contested claim (e.g. a vigilante or sentinel claimant suspected of being the lone killer). Every other living player holds a role corroborated by night events. The basis is process of elimination, not hard evidence on the rival.
lessons.action: When the room has already stacked elimination votes on you, cast your vote on the other leading suspect, the player with the least verified role or night results. An abstention lowers no one's count and can't force a tie, while a vote on the rival adds to a split or tie that could leave no one eliminated, and it pressures a plausible lone killer or wolf. If the votes against you are already a locked majority, the vote still goes to the rival rather than to nobody.

lessons.situation: The village is about to eliminate a wolf in an information-rich endgame where only one wolf would remain. Town can then win at night through a sigil strike or another kill. The fortune teller has not yet scored its second point. Information landscape: Rich. There is a prior Serial Killer elimination, night-one tracking testimony, and a sigil result, but no certainty about which evil is left. Stakes: Town is close to a win. One more evil removal leaves a lone wolf who can be killed that same night, and the game ends before the fortune teller scores. Your vote helps decide whether the game continues. Consensus: The village is building a majority against the tracked suspect on the strength of testimony and arguments. The agreement is moderately solid. My position: Aligned with the forming majority and reinforcing the case, which makes you a driver of the elimination. Heat: Low overall. The accused player may cast an isolated retaliatory vote at you, but the room is not suspicious of you. Target landscape: A suspected wolf, tracked or accused with an inconclusive sigil test, plus a claimed role under pressure from a quiet player. The suspected wolf is the main case, backed by daytime arguments and a Trailseer's testimony but no hard confirmation.
lessons.action: Before voting, count your points. If you have fewer than two and the leading candidate is a wolf whose removal would leave Town one elimination from winning, abstain if it is offered. If abstaining is not offered, vote for the least-supported candidate who is not a confirmed evil player, so the game runs long enough for your bets to score. A Town win ends the game before you can reach two points.

verdicts.why: I have no heat from a locked majority; the votes against me are only player_8's day 2 vote, so this rival-vote logic does not hold.
No wolf is tracked or accused with a Trailseer testimony on my board; I am at 1 of 2 points and the wolves are unconfirmed.

situations: A player claiming sentinel named a visit on a dead player from night 1 that the town cannot check, and two others accused that claimant while the sentinel named a visitor; the village has two abstain days and no lynch, with the wolves having killed a trailseer and a vigilante, and the claim's truth decides whether the town can trust a watch-based lead. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel claim with a single checkable visit, no investigator or trailseer results publicly, and no confirmed role for any living player. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a wrong lynch is recoverable at this distance but each mis-elimination moves the wolves closer, and the game cannot end within one more elimination. Consensus: No consensus: the village has abstained twice and is split between the day-2 voters on player_10, player_1, and player_5 and the accusers of player_4, with the sentinel claim as the only concrete thread. My position: Holding out with the non-accusing majority, without pushing a name. Heat: My heat is low-to-moderate: I voted player_6 on day 2 which is now a dead vigilante, and my day 2 messages pushed for concrete claims without naming anyone, so I am not the focus of the accusations. Forward exposure: Any visible push or claim now would commit me publicly while the sentinel claim is still untested; passing or staying in the vote cluster keeps the move reversible but risks being seen as silent. Target landscape: Living candidates include player_4 (claims sentinel, watched player_2 and saw only player_5 visit, accused by player_7 and player_5), player_5 (accused by player_4 over a night 1 visit), player_3 (repeating a day 2 vote on player_10 with no new evidence), player_8 (voted player_1 with no stated reason), and player_9 (claimed no role, did nothing night 1). Public role status is unverified for all; the basis is one unconfirmed sentinel claim plus vote history. Public vs private: Privately I am the illusionist wolf holding 2 conceals and know the pack's kills from nights 1 and 2; publicly I am an unclaimed player in a day-3 discussion where the sentinel claim of player_4 is the only lead and no role is revealed for the living.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

verdicts.why: Abstain is not offered today, so the abstain-with-room advice cannot be followed; I must name a player, and the room is not unanimous on abstain.
No information-role claimant is being targeted by the room today; player_4's sentinel claim is contested but not a lynch case for me to join alone.
No claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me; I am not the primary target today.

situations: Day 3 after two abstain days: a claimed sentinel named a single visitor to a dead trailseer on night 1, and the accused player is demanding the sentinel explain it, while the village debates whether to vote on either. I have two dead bodies (a trailseer and a vigilante) whose night abilities I could later use, which the village does not know about. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel claim with one visit, two day-2 votes with no stated evidence, and no confirmed results; the only hard datum is that a single visit reached a dead trailseer on night 1. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong vote is recoverable but costly, and the game cannot end within one more elimination, so keeping visibility low this day preserves room for later body use. Consensus: The room is split with no clear consensus; two abstain days have passed with no lynch, and the discussion centers on the claimed sentinel's single visit claim rather than any agreed target. My position: With the majority on the abstain side in practice, holding out of the early accusations and not driving any lynch. Heat: Moderate and rising: I voted to eliminate a player on day 2 who then abstained, and one accuser has said my day-2 vote named no one substantive, so I am a visible but not focal target. Forward exposure: Any visible move (a vote, a claim, a body-use hint) commits me to a stance that cannot be undone once read by the village; the day-3 vote is public and permanent, so voting with the majority keeps my visibility low. Target landscape: Two accusers and one claimed sentinel are in play: a claimed sentinel (unverified) whose single watch result names one visitor, a player being voted on for a day-2 push with no new evidence, and a player accused by two others with only a stated night-1 reason; all bases are claims and day-2 votes, not confirmed roles. Public vs private: As the necromancer I privately know my own role and that I am not visible to anyone's night checks, while the public sees only a day-3 accusation thread between a claimed sentinel and the player who accused them; my private knowledge is that I am the lone killer and no one on the table can verify that.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

verdicts.why: No one has claimed a trailseer or investigator result against an accused player; the live dispute is a sentinel claim by player_4 against player_5.
Nine-to-eight players alive with no revealed claimed town cornering me yet.
I have not been exposed by any claimed result and am not the target of a consensus vote.

situations: After a sentinel claim by one player that names the accused as the only visitor to a night 1 victim, the accused is being pressed by two others to justify a day 2 vote, and the day 2 vote record is what the room is arguing over, with a day 2 lynch that failed to happen. Information landscape: Information-starved: only one public claim (sentinel watch on a dead trailseer showing one visitor), no corroboration, two abstain days, and the dead player's role was revealed but no will was read out for a wolf victim-equivalent. Stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong lynch is recoverable at this distance but each mistaken elimination brings the wolves closer, so the board can absorb a few more errors before the margin narrows. Consensus: The village is split and mostly stalled: two abstain days, a day 2 vote spread across several names, and no majority forming on a target, with the room asking for concrete claims rather than lynch pushes. My position: Holding out: I am abstaining against lynch pressure while the room debates player_4's sentinel claim, not with any forming majority. Heat: Moderate: player_4 and player_7 have accused me of being the visitor to the dead trailseer on night 1, and player_5-pressure is circulating, but no concrete evidence beyond player_4's claim ties to me. Forward exposure: Any visible block or claim I make would reveal my role or tie me to a night result I cannot prove; abstaining and pressing player_4's unexplained day 2 vote keeps exposure low and remains reversible. Target landscape: Two live candidates dominate: player_4, who publicly claims sentinel and whose night 1 watch claim is untestable beyond the single visit, and player_10, a day 2 vote target of player_3 that has since been dropped; player_4's claim is single-source and rests on a visit that is partly shaped by my own night 1 visit to player_2. Public vs private: Privately I am the chanteuse, a wolf, and my wolf partner is believed to be the illusionist, still alive and unrevealed; publicly I claim no role, and the village reads the day 2 vote and the night 1 sentinel claim by player_4 as the main lead, with no one knowing my role.

A sentinel claimant has named the accused as the only visitor to a dead night 1 victim, and the accused is asking for direction while the room argues over an unexplained day 2 vote, with two abstain days behind them and the wolves having lost a vigilante night 2. Information landscape: Information-starved: one untested sentinel claim, two abstain days, a day 2 vote spread, and the night 2 death of a vigilante who held fire on night 1; no role-verified evidence exists. Stakes: Eight alive, four eliminations from a wolf-side win; the lead remaining evil faction needs several more deaths, so a mistaken lynch now is recoverable but each wrong result narrows the margin the town has to find the wolves. Consensus: No consensus: the room is split between pressing player_4 and pressing player_5 and player_3, with abstains dominating and no single target forming a majority. My position: Holding out, not driving: I am abstaining and asking for concrete claims rather than joining any lynch. Heat: Moderate: I am named as the visitor in player_4's sentinel claim, which the village is treating as the one lead, so my own visit to the night 1 victim is a live question. Forward exposure: Any statement about the night 2 kill or a visible role-based accusation would expose the wolf pack; staying on the day 2 vote question keeps exposure low and reversible. Target landscape: Public candidates include player_4 (sentinel claim, unverified), player_3 (repeated day 2 vote on player_10 with no new evidence), and player_8 (day 2 vote on player_1 with no reason), all with behavioral basis only; no one has public role evidence beyond the single sentinel claim. Public vs private: Privately I know my wolf partner is alive and believed to be the illusionist, and I know the day 2 kill was my pack's; publicly the village only knows a vigilante died on night 2 with a held-fire record and a trailseer died on night 1, and nothing about who acted.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: The claimed trailseer is dead, and the exposing claim now comes from a sentinel claim, not a tracker.
The room is abstaining, but player_4 has been accused twice and has made a claim that names me, so a vote on them has a stated reason.
My wolf partner player_10 is not under a concrete check or tracking accusation.

situations: The village lynched a claimed Sentinel whose watch showed a visit by player_5 to the night-1 victim, and the record of that elimination now stands on the board. Player_3 and player_8 are the voters who most pressed partner-adjacent accusations earlier, and the accused player's public watch result is now part of the permanent record. The remaining debate is which of the living players to target next while the only hard lead against the night-1 visitor has already been removed. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single eliminated sentinel claim whose record was read out as fact, one confirmed night-1 visit, no living claimed roles, and only behavioral reads from day discussion and day-2 votes. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote ends the game; a mis-elimination is recoverable but each wrong lynch brings the wolf-side count closer to parity. Forward exposure: Any night action or vote now is visible in the morning report or the public record; a block of a town player is announced as an ability held back only via the victim's private result, and a day vote is permanent on the record, so committing to a target or pairing votes with a known-suspect partner is irreversible. Target landscape: Seven living players: the claimed-Sentinel accuser side and the remaining town-aligned voters. Player_4 (the sentinel claim, now eliminated and revealed as sentinel with a record of night 1 watch seeing player_5 visit player_2 and night 2 roleblocked) is gone. Remaining candidates have no revealed roles; the chanteuse's own partner is believed to be the illusionist, and the claims are only behavioral and night-1 records.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles such as the healer and necromancer are confirmed, and the investigator and trailseer have public claims and results on record. Stakes: Town has lost its healer protection but still has information roles; removing the investigator while blinding the tracker for a night shifts the information balance toward the wolves before parity pressure builds. Forward exposure: Blocking shows the village only that some blocker exists, if the blocked player speaks of it; nothing ties the block to you, and you can switch block targets nightly. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.
lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

The healer and claimed investigator are not confirmed here; no claimed investigator is on the board.
No investigator or trailseer claim is alive to block; the trailseer is dead.

situations: Day 3 aftermath: the village just lynched a player claiming sentinel (their claim was never verified) after a vote that was nearly unanimous against them. Their night 1 watch claim, that only one player visited the dead trailseer, now points at player_5, who denies any role and calls the claim unverifiable. Your single remaining check could test a named suspect before the next vote, and the day 4 vote approaches with no confirmed wolf. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified public claim (the now-eliminated sentinel's watch result), one private check result on player_3 (Not suspicious), no confirmed role reveals beyond the eliminated players, and no wolf-side information accessible to you. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong elimination does not end the game but moves the wolves closer to parity, so the single remaining check is the one tool that can resolve a choice before the next vote. Target landscape: Seven players alive: you (investigator, one check left), player_1, player_3, player_5, player_8, player_9, player_10. No player is publicly confirmed as a wolf. player_3 reads Not suspicious from your night 2 check. player_5 was publicly named by the eliminated sentinel's claim as the visitor to a dead trailseer on night 1, and is also the main accuser-target of the day 3 debate; player_8 and player_10 carry older day 2 votes; player_9 claimed no role and has no result.

lessons.situation: After the Day 2 vote and a Day 1 or 2 reveal, the voting record shows a few players splitting from the room: defending an eliminated wolf, or pushing to eliminate the Investigator without evidence. One wolf (or the pack's remainder) is likely hiding among them, and the Investigator has one check left. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed wolf or sentinel death is on the record, plus public vote tallies showing clear outliers. No private proof yet, so the final check converts behavioral suspicion into a result. Stakes: The pack is already thinned and one check remains, so the last check is the Investigator's final chance to confirm a wolf. A correct hit can lead to eliminating the remaining wolves and winning, while a wasted check leaves Town without direction. Target landscape: Seven or so living players, with roles of the dead revealed. The best candidates are outlier voters on Day 2: a sole counter-voter defending a revealed wolf, or two voters who coordinated against you while the rest abstained. The basis is public vote behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With your last check, check the player whose Day 2 vote record most clearly diverges from the room: the lone defender of a revealed wolf, or a voter who pushed against you without evidence. Voting records are public and permanent, so these outliers are the likeliest wolf partners, and a Suspicious result gives you a concrete lead to act on.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a discussion-only Day 1. The Investigator holds both checks and must choose between holding them and probing an unread player blind. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no claims, no votes, no night results. Stakes: Early board with no pressure, so no single check is decisive. But the Investigator may die before a banked check is ever used, and any early read, whether it finds a wolf or clears an ally, compounds into later votes. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, flips or behavioral tells. Pick a quiet, non-prominent player at random, since nothing separates them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no leads, spend one check on a quiet, unclaimed player instead of banking both. An early Suspicious finds a wolf, and a Not suspicious gives you a baseline read. Treat a clean result as clearing only wolves: the Serial Killer and neutrals also read Not suspicious, and a Necromancer reads that way on any night it does not attack.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended in an abstain after multiple night deaths, with two killing factions active and only soft, unverified role claims on the table; the Investigator still has both checks. Information landscape: Information-starved: the claims are unverifiable and no alignments are confirmed, so any read has to come from behavior. Stakes: With two killing factions active and no hard leads, the village needs at least one verified collaborator; an early check on a central voice yields a lasting anchor even if the investigator dies. Target landscape: Unverified claimants, quiet players, and an analytical non-claimant who is actively evaluating claims; no one has confirmed alignment, and behavior is the only basis for choosing.
lessons.action: If the night has no hard lead, use a check on an active, influential player who has not claimed a role and is shaping the vote, to build a verified anchor among the central voices. A Not suspicious read clears a wolf or town member but does not clear a lone killer, so treat the anchor as likely town rather than certain.

verdicts.why: The last check should go to player_5, whose night 1 visit to dead player_2 is the strongest lead, not a Day 2 vote outlier.
This is not Night 1, and the board now has a concrete lead.
The night has a concrete lead, so I am checking a specific player rather than an active voice.

situations: Day 3 after a lynch removed a player who had claimed sentinel and accused player_5 of visiting the wolf-killed player on night 1; the claimant's now-eliminated record shows they were roleblocked on night 2, and the village must decide whether the single night-1 visit claim against player_5 justifies a second lynch. Information landscape: Information-starved: one unverified night-1 claim (sentinel watch showing a single visitor to a wolf-killed player), no confirmation of role, and no night results shared by town players; the healer's private protections on player_9 are not public. Stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single elimination can end the game next; a wrong lynch is recoverable but removes a town-side voice and narrows the remaining information, so each day vote costs real town strength. Target landscape: Living candidates for today's lynch: player_5 (publicly named by the now-eliminated sentinel claimant as the visitor to the wolf-killed player on night 1; player_5 denies any night result and has abstained both days), player_9 (claimed no role, no night result, has defended the thin lead), player_10 (day 2 vote target of player_3, who has since dropped it), player_1 and player_8 (day 2 vote targets with no hard evidence). The sentinel claim is dead-player-verified by nothing but the claimant's own word; the lead rests on a single unconfirmed claim.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: Early night (night 2) after a public information-role claim, with the wolves (and possibly a lone killer) choosing their kill and the town's key information source an obvious target. Information landscape: Mostly unverified claims with few or no confirmed flips or wills, sometimes partly confirmed by a correct elimination; the claimant's visibility is the main evidence, and the healer has no hard read on which claim is real. Stakes: Losing the lead information role this early strips the town of checks before any roles are confirmed, while a save wastes the wolves' kill and keeps the town's lead intact; the board is not yet at parity, so one lost key role hurts but is not decisive. Target landscape: Several claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and quiet unclaimed players; the investigator who cleared the healer or whose check was validated is the most prominent unverified-or-confirmed target, versus a sentinel or trailseer with less impact.
lessons.action: On the night after a claimed investigator, sentinel or other information role has become the town's most visible information source, protect that claimant, since the wolves most likely attack the player who is verified or clearing others. If two claimants compete, protect the one whose results are most useful to the town (an investigator who has cleared you, or one whose check was confirmed by an elimination) over a less-pressing claimant.

lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

verdicts.why: No Town power role has publicly claimed or verified a result beyond player_4's sentinel claim, which is now dead.
No living information role has publicly claimed, so there is no visible claimant to protect.
