I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or save, the necromancer holds results gathered through a dead town role and wants to redirect suspicion onto the visitors. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: the dead role's death is on record, so the room can tell which living roles could have produced such a result. Stakes: My win needs the room kept off me for many more days, so losing the cover of a hidden identity costs far more than anything the leaked result could gain. Consensus: The village is unsettled after a night attack and save, with no fixed target. The living roles are still working out what the visits mean. My position: Not yet in conflict, but I would be holding out alone if I spoke up with the hidden result. Heat: Zero before sharing. It would jump to universal accusation if I quoted the body-derived result. Forward exposure: Stating a result that only the dead role could have produced points straight at the necromancer, and the room cannot unsee it. A read built on public evidence can be dropped without penalty. Target landscape: The players whose visits I learned about (claimed healer, other claimants) are the targets, but the only support is a hidden source. Public evidence such as claim overlaps is available to use instead. Public vs private: Privately I hold a night result obtained through a dead role, such as who visited a door. Publicly, no living player holds that role, so quoting the result shows I am the necromancer.
lessons.action: If a dead player's ability gave you night information, steer suspicion only through reasons the room can see: public claims, votes, and contradictions between players. Do not quote the body-derived result, such as sentinel visitor names, when no living role could explain how you got it. Only a living claimed role could plausibly share such a result, and you cannot back that claim.

decision.message: Investigator's record has player_3 checked Not suspicious on night 2, so player_3 can't be the illusionist. That leaves the illusionist and fortune teller among player_1, player_9 and player_10. player_9's sigil claim fits the night 3 sigil strike, so I'd test player_1 and player_10 on what they've actually said.

verdicts.why: Four players alive with no bloc forming yet, so no claim is demanded
No sentinel report has been claimed, so no necromancer is publicly confirmed
I will steer only through public claims and the record, not through my body-derived result

decision.message: My day 2 vote on you was because you abstained with no read and named no one, and I wanted a position from you. That was the whole reason, nothing hidden. You are right that a sigil only strikes an attacker, so player_9's claim points at whoever player_5 attacked, and that is the question for player_9 to answer.

verdicts.why: Five players are alive, so this final-three-or-four situation has not arrived yet.
No necromancer visit has been publicly confirmed, so this situation does not hold.
I hold no body-derived result to steer suspicion with, and I will not quote one.

situations: A sigilist claimant says their sigil struck the chanteuse on night 3 and holds one sigil in reserve, while the village, having just lynched a sentinel on an untestable visit claim, is stalling on any new target and considering player_1, player_3 and player_8 as suspects. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only hard public facts are the night deaths and the sigil strike on the chanteuse; all other suspicion rests on day 2 and day 3 vote histories and untested claims. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the remaining evil faction can win; a wrong lynch now is costly but not immediately decisive, so the village has room to wait for a concrete claim. Consensus: The room is unsettled and leaning toward abstaining until a concrete claim with a direction appears; the village is wary of lynching on nothing after the sentinel lynch on a visit claim that could not be tested. My position: With the majority on withholding a lynch, holding a low profile. Heat: Moderate: a player has been pressing your day 2 vote on player_10 and your day 2 vote on player_6 is on record, but no one has produced a concrete night result against you. Forward exposure: Any visible push toward a lynch or a named accusation would tie your voice to a target and is hard to reverse once the vote is recorded; passing the opening round keeps exposure low but leaves the village's sigilist claim unchallenged. Target landscape: Five alive: a sigilist claimant who has said they hold one sigil, two players (player_1 and player_3) with public vote histories but no role claims, and a quiet player_8 whose day 2 vote on player_1 was never explained; evidence is vote history only, no night results. Public vs private: Privately you are the illusionist with two conceals left and your pack partner, the chanteuse, already dead; publicly a sigilist claim (player_9) and a claimed Investigator record are on the table, while you hold no claimed role and no night result is shared with you publicly.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been revealed and killed. You are pressured over a lone vote against a dead Town player, while a Town player's result (a non-triggering sigil) is available as a defense. Information landscape: Moderate: public voting records and a privately held Town result that can be used to clear you, but no hard role confirmations on the quiet alternative suspect. Stakes: Each vote now decides whether the last wolf survives. Moving even a couple of swing voters off you keeps the wolf team alive into the final few players. Consensus: The village is split. Some players press you over the vote record, while players holding a clearing result and neutral voters are open to another suspect. My position: holding out Heat: High. Players cite your isolated vote against a now-dead player as the basis for suspicion. Forward exposure: Citing a Town player's result ties you to a non-attacking story that you cannot take back, and later tracking evidence could break it. The alternative-suspect push can be adjusted as new information arrives. Target landscape: Candidates are you, under pressure from the vote record, and a quiet player with no confirmed role who was targeted by the dead wolf. Suspicion of the quiet player is behavioral, while the case against you is the vote record. Public vs private: Privately you are an active wolf, but the partner carried the kill that night, so a Town result such as an un-triggered sigil looks exculpatory. The room reads that result as evidence you are not the killer.
lessons.action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Use only what the rules show: the sigil not triggering means only that you did not attack on that night, and it does not clear you of being a wolf. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

decision.message: player_8, I haven't held any night result and I've said so since day 2. Asking me what I did doesn't tell us anything. Your test on player_1 has the same gap: you never gave a reason for the day 2 vote, and player_1 has abstained with no read since. Player_9, if the sigil struck player_5 on night 3, which attacker does that point to?

verdicts.why: Pack is down to me, so I need a concrete alternative suspect and no defense of my own vote record.
Day 2 vote records are the room's focus, so I answer player_8's direct test instead of an unfocused defense.
Investigator is dead and the early-day claim comparison has already happened.

situations: After a sigilist claimed that its sigil struck the chanteuse on night 3, the village is splitting between testing the claim and voting; the sigilist's claimed target points at an unnamed attacker that the village wants identified, while two survivors trade accusations over a day 2 vote. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public facts are the night 3 death records (chanteuse struck by sigil and reanimated vigilante, investigator killed by wolves) and one investigator check on player_3 showing Not suspicious; all other claims are unverifiable. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single wrong lynch is recoverable but leaves the wolves needing to outlast the remaining town votes; no single vote ends the game now. Consensus: No consensus; the village leans toward abstaining today and waiting for a concrete lead, with the sigil claim being probed but not yet acted on. My position: With the majority in abstaining and holding out from any push, with no personal claim on the table. Heat: Moderate and diffuse: the room is currently testing player_1 and player_8 and asking player_9 to name the night 3 attacker; you have been asked what you did but hold no claimed result. Forward exposure: Any claim of a role or any push on a target would be recorded publicly and is hard to retract; staying unclaimed and answering questions calmly keeps the option to reverse, but a sigil-claim test or a vote on player_9 would commit you to a visible position. Target landscape: Five alive: player_1, player_3, player_8, player_9 and player_10 (you). The sigilist claim by player_9 is a single unverified claim; player_8 and player_1 are accusing each other over a day 2 vote with no hard evidence; player_3 was checked Not suspicious by the dead investigator on night 2, which is a public record. Public vs private: Privately you are the illusionist, a wolf, and your wolf partner (the chanteuse) was revealed and eliminated on night 3; publicly the village reads you only as an unclaimed survivor among five, with a sigilist claim pointing at the night 3 attacker and suspicion aimed at player_1 and player_8 rather than you.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

verdicts.why: No investigator or trailseer claim has accused me; the day 2 vote was on player_1 by player_8, not me.
No information-role claimant is currently being pushed; the village is abstaining with no lynch pressure on a claimant.
The room is leaning toward abstaining on a thin day with no hard evidence, so matching the majority keeps my record clean.

situations: Day 4 with five alive: a self-claimed sigilist who says it is holding its last sigil, two players trading accusations over day-2 votes that carry no real evidence, and a fortune teller at one point with two self-bets left. The sigilist's claim is unverified but fits the night 3 strike on a revealed chanteuse, and the wolf-side pressure is now centered on who among the remaining players is the illusionist. Information landscape: Information-starved. Only the public record: day 2 and day 3 vote lists, the night 2 investigator check on player_3 (Not suspicious), the night 3 sigil strike on a chanteuse, and one dead sentinel's old watch. Night results are private and unshared. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win: a wrong vote or an unanswered night kill is recoverable now, but each lost town or neutral vote moves the wolves closer to parity. Consensus: No consensus. The village leans toward abstaining today; players are asking for a concrete lead and no one has a strong read on a single player. My position: With the majority, leaning toward abstain while no concrete lead exists. Heat: Low. I hold no claim and have made no accusations; I am in the middle of the discussion, with some attention drawn to my abstain on day 2 only indirectly. Target landscape: Five living players: the fortune teller (me), player_3, player_8, player_9 and player_10 and player_1 is me. Unrevealed candidates are player_3, player_8, player_9, player_10. player_9 publicly claims sigilist (unverified, consistent with a night 3 sigil strike on a revealed chanteuse). player_3 was checked Not suspicious by the dead investigator, so it is not an illusionist. Other roles are unclaimed; evidence is mostly day-discussion arguments with no hard reads.

lessons.situation: The village is about to eliminate a wolf in an information-rich endgame where only one wolf would remain. Town can then win at night through a sigil strike or another kill. The fortune teller has not yet scored its second point. Information landscape: Rich. There is a prior Serial Killer elimination, night-one tracking testimony, and a sigil result, but no certainty about which evil is left. Stakes: Town is close to a win. One more evil removal leaves a lone wolf who can be killed that same night, and the game ends before the fortune teller scores. Your vote helps decide whether the game continues. Consensus: The village is building a majority against the tracked suspect on the strength of testimony and arguments. The agreement is moderately solid. My position: Aligned with the forming majority and reinforcing the case, which makes you a driver of the elimination. Heat: Low overall. The accused player may cast an isolated retaliatory vote at you, but the room is not suspicious of you. Target landscape: A suspected wolf, tracked or accused with an inconclusive sigil test, plus a claimed role under pressure from a quiet player. The suspected wolf is the main case, backed by daytime arguments and a Trailseer's testimony but no hard confirmation.
lessons.action: Before voting, count your points. If you have fewer than two and the leading candidate is a wolf whose removal would leave Town one elimination from winning, abstain if it is offered. If abstaining is not offered, vote for the least-supported candidate who is not a confirmed evil player, so the game runs long enough for your bets to score. A Town win ends the game before you can reach two points.

lessons.situation: Late in the game, the town's power roles are mostly confirmed or consistent with each other. The vote has narrowed to me versus one other unverified player, and I must choose between abstaining and voting the rival. Information landscape: Info-rich: role claims cover the town slots, saves and night results corroborate the town roles, and the public voting record is visible. The only open question is who among the unverified players is the lone killer or a wolf. Stakes: With few players left, one elimination changes the balance of power. My death ends my scoring chances, since a day vote never scores, so I must use my vote to split the count or push the real threat out. Consensus: The village is largely unified, on role-claim bookkeeping and corroborated night results, that the leftover unverified players are the problem. Neutral is treated as expendable. My position: holding out Heat: Extreme: several players, including confirmed town power roles, have declared votes against me because I am an expendable neutral once the town slots are claimed or corroborated. Target landscape: Two or three unverified players: me, an outed neutral fortune teller, and a rival with an unverified or contested claim (e.g. a vigilante or sentinel claimant suspected of being the lone killer). Every other living player holds a role corroborated by night events. The basis is process of elimination, not hard evidence on the rival.
lessons.action: When the room has already stacked elimination votes on you, cast your vote on the other leading suspect, the player with the least verified role or night results. An abstention lowers no one's count and can't force a tie, while a vote on the rival adds to a split or tie that could leave no one eliminated, and it pressures a plausible lone killer or wolf. If the votes against you are already a locked majority, the vote still goes to the rival rather than to nobody.

verdicts.why: Player_8 is an unconfirmed suspect, not a confirmed wolf, and I have no heat, so I vote rather than abstain to keep the day moving toward a lynch that can feed my bets.
Several players have not stacked votes against me, so I am not the lone unverified target.

situations: A claimed sigilist says they struck a chanteuse with a sigil on night 3, and the village is debating which of the remaining players attacked that night while the sigil claim sits unverified; the lone killer's private kill is hidden behind that public ambiguity. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only hard facts are the day 2 and day 3 vote records, the night 3 death of the chanteuse with a reanimated vigilante and sigil attribution, and the investigator's night 2 check on player_3; all role claims are unverified. Stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game next; a wrong lynch is recoverable but each elimination brings the wolves and me closer to parity, and the lone-killer exposure is the real risk to protect. Consensus: The room is split and mostly passive: most players are abstaining, with player_3 and player_8 pushing lightly on player_10 and player_1 while player_9's sigil claim is treated as plausible but unverified. My position: Holding out from any decisive push; I am neither driving the vote nor clearly with a majority, and I have said nothing that commits me. Heat: Moderate and rising: player_8 voted on player_1 on day 2 and pointed the sigil question at player_9, and players question my own day 2 abstain pattern less directly, but the room has not yet targeted me as the lone killer. Forward exposure: Any visible move (voting for or against player_9, pushing a target, or claiming a role) risks revealing that I am the lone killer; a sigil-claim challenge or a reanimated-kill rebuttal would commit me publicly and is hard to reverse once spoken. Target landscape: Surviving candidates are player_1, player_3, player_9, and player_10. player_9 claims sigilist with a sigil strike on player_5, which fits the public record; player_3 was checked Not suspicious by the dead investigator on night 2; player_1 and player_10 have only abstentions and deflections with no concrete read; the wolves' pack identity is unknown to me. Public vs private: As the necromancer I privately know player_5 was the chanteuse I killed through player_6's vigilante body, yet publicly the village reads that death as a sigil strike claimed by player_9, so my private knowledge of the kill is hidden behind a claim I cannot contest without exposing myself.

lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

verdicts.why: No one has mechanically exposed me; my night-3 body use is not public, so I am not facing a claimed-investigator lynch.
Four players remain and I am not cornered by a counter-claim; heat on me is low.
No claimant-versus-accused split over an information claim is in play today.

situations: Four players remain alive after the day 4 vote eliminated a player revealed as the necromancer. The village is weighing a sigilist claim that is consistent with the night 3 record, while two unclaimed players are being pressed for what they did, and the remaining evil roles are believed to be the illusionist and fortune teller, both still hidden. Information landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a firm night result to share. Public evidence is limited to the night 3 record (a player struck by a sigil and killed by a reanimated vigilante, the investigator's day 2 check) and the claims of the living players, which are unverified. Stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the remaining evil faction can win, and the game can end within one more elimination; a wrong lynch now leaves the village one loss from a wolf-side outcome, so the next vote is high-cost. Target landscape: Three living players: player_1 (abstained both days, no claimed role, no night result), player_9 (claims sigilist, sigil placed on a player who was struck down on night 3, consistent with the record), and player_10 (claims no result, voted to abstain today, pressed others to explain their votes). Public role status: no living player has a confirmed role; player_9's sigil claim is claimed with partial public support, while player_1 and player_10 are unclaimed.

lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.

verdicts.why: The lone killer is already dead, and the remaining threat is the illusionist wolf, not a lone killer.
Player_9 is the publicly claimed sigilist whose sigil struck a wolf-side attacker, so protecting that claimed power role is the best choice.
The corroborated investigator is dead, so the validated-investigator priority no longer applies.

situations: Night 4 is approaching with four players alive. The sigilist's night 3 sigil struck a player who attacked that night, confirming a chanteuse-role attacker was struck, and the sigilist has one sigil left. The day 4 vote lynched the necromancer, so the remaining evil threats are the illusionist and the fortune teller's cohort, with the wolves needing to outnumber the town. Predicting which living player will attack tonight, and whether a sigil on that player would be wasted, is the central decision. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only hard fact is the night 3 sigil strike on a dead chanteuse; the day 4 vote and the record of day 2 and 3 votes are public; no living player has verified a night result. Stakes: Four alive with two eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win; the game can end within one more elimination, so a wasted sigil on a non-attacker removes the only strike the sigilist can still deliver and a wrong lynch or kill could hand the wolves the parity they need. Forward exposure: Placing the last sigil on a named player is a visit that reveals to that player and the table that the sigilist holds a sigil, and it is irreversible; holding it keeps the option open for a later night. Target landscape: Three living players: player_1, player_3 and player_10. Their public roles are unrevealed; player_1 and player_3 have abstained or voted without night results, player_10 has held no night result and voted to abstain on day 4, and no one has a verified role claim among them beyond the sigilist's own claim.

lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten players alive, day one was discussion only with no vote or deaths. The sigilist must decide between placing a sigil on a blind guess and keeping the charges. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no role claims, no voting records, no visit histories to separate likely attackers from passive roles. Stakes: Early board with a large margin before any faction can win. Nothing is forcing a spend, and each of the two charges is worth more on a night with a real lead than on a coin-flip target. Forward exposure: Holding reveals nothing and commits nothing, and the charge stays available. Placing is irreversible, spends one of two charges, and is a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unvetted: no claims, no votes, no night results. Any target is a pure guess, and most players, including investigative, protective and passive roles, will not attack.
lessons.action: On night one, when there are no deaths, claims, votes or visit data, keep both sigils and place none. A sigil only does anything if its target attacks that night, and a blind pick usually lands on a non-attacker (several observations show it striking nothing and spending a charge). Hold the charges until a night when a specific suspect is likely to attack.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.

situations: Night 4 with the wolf pair reduced to me alone after the chanteuse and necromancer were removed. The pack must choose a kill among three survivors, and the choice of whether to conceal the victim's role depends on whether a revealed role would expose the sigilist claim or help the town find the last wolf. Information landscape: Information-starved: the public record has a sigil strike on night 3 and an investigator check on player_3 that read Not suspicious; all other roles are unverified claims or absent, and the town has no fresh night results. Stakes: Four alive with two more eliminations needed before the wolves equal everyone else; the next elimination leaves three alive, and one more after that would be a wolf win with one wolf among two others, so a wrong daytime lynch or a successful kill now sharply narrows the path, and the game can end within one more elimination. Forward exposure: Conceal use on tonight's kill would hide the victim's role and remove the carrier's visit from Sentinel and Trailseer views, but the act itself is not visible unless a victim is concealed; spending it commits both conceals to a visible pattern only if the town notices unrevealed roles. Target landscape: Three survivors remain: player_1 (no claim, abstained both days, public record shows no role), player_9 (claimed sigilist, sigil placed on a now-dead player that struck), and player_3 (no claim, previously checked Not suspicious by a now-dead investigator). Only player_9's claim has any public support, and it matches the night 3 sigil strike record.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

verdicts.why: The lone-wolf concealing logic applies, but the victim here is a publicly claimed sigilist, not an investigator, so I'm using the conceal for a different reason.

Player_9's sigilist claim is public and the sigil on player_5 matches it, so the victim's role is not new, but its will and sigil record could still point at the pack, which makes hiding it worth a use.
This is night 4, not night 1, so the night-1 opening guidance does not hold.

situations: Night 4 is approaching with four players alive after a necromancer was voted out on day 4. As the fortune teller, you must bet on who dies tonight and decide whether to spend one of your two self-bets, while the remaining wolves and the lone killer are still unidentified among the three survivors and the discussion is split over whether the sigilist's claim is credible. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed roles among survivors, one sigilist claim with consistent record support, one investigator Not suspicious read on player_3 from night 2, and only behavioral reads on player_10. Night results for the surviving players are mostly unshared. Stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; one more elimination leaves three alive, and a wolf-side kill tonight would bring the count to three, where a further loss could end the game, so a wrong bet costs a point and a self-bet attempt spent on a non-attacked night is lost for good. Target landscape: Three living players: player_3 (publicly accused on day 2 by a dead player, admitted no real evidence, checked Not suspicious by a now-dead investigator on night 2), player_9 (claims sigilist, placed a sigil that struck a player on night 3, a claim consistent with the public record), and player_10 (evasive about their night results, the target of the day 4 elimination vote that failed to pass). Role status is unverified claim for player_9 and no public role for the others.

lessons.situation: Last wolf voted out and three players left. A lone killer (the necromancer, who can attack through a reanimated body) wins by killing one more player, so the Fortune Teller is a live kill target and no other player's death is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead, the dead roles are confirmed, and the remaining Town sigilist is confirmed out of sigils. This makes the only remaining attacker and its available bodies clear. Stakes: The lone killer wins if anyone else dies tonight, so a bet that fails to cover your own life can end the game with the Fortune Teller short of two points. A self-bet keeps you alive for another night. Target landscape: The suspected necromancer (alive and holding a usable body, so unlikely to die), a confirmed sigilist with no sigils left (no threat), or a self-bet. Roles are confirmed from the graveyard, and nothing makes the suspect likely to die tonight.
lessons.action: With three alive and a lone killer that can attack, you are one of only two possible victims. If no other victim is predictable, spend a self-bet, because an attack on you fails that night. Don't bet on the suspected killer: a killer that is immune or about to win is unlikely to die, and a wrong bet leaves you open to the attack.

lessons.situation: Late game with the wolves dead or nearly dead and one killer left (serial killer, necromancer or last wolf). The Fortune Teller stands at 0-1 points and needs a death, and the most obvious target is publicly protected, so a bet on them fails to the save or the killer switches targets. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of the dead wolves are confirmed, claims and protection histories are public, and the surviving killer's identity or kill pattern is mostly known. Stakes: Few players remain and the game can end any night. Each night spent without scoring risks being voted out or the game finishing before the second point, so the bet must follow where the killer can actually kill, not just where it wants to. Target landscape: The investigator or leader shielded by a public healer claim, the claimed healer who is exposed, other claimed power roles (sigilist, sentinel, trailseer), and unconfirmed players. Hard evidence of who is protected, not behavior, drives the choice.
lessons.action: When the healer has publicly announced protecting the obvious top target (the confirmed or claimed investigator), place the bet on the next-most-valuable unshielded Town role the surviving killer must remove, such as the claimed healer or another power role. If the killer's last pick is predictable, name that role in the bet for the two-point payoff.

lessons.situation: Three-player endgame tie between a confirmed Town power role, a suspected wolf and the Fortune Teller. The wolves need a kill to close the game, and the Fortune Teller needs points to win. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed by earlier night results and blocked actions, so the wolves' likely victim can be read from the board. Stakes: Each night is nearly decisive. A correct victim-and-role bet gives two points and wins the game for the Fortune Teller, while a miss wastes a night when the kill can end the game. Target landscape: A publicly confirmed Town role (e.g. a claimed vigilante whose shots were blocked), a suspected surviving wolf, or a self-bet. The Town player is the most likely kill target, backed by confirmed evidence from earlier nights and blocks rather than just behavior.
lessons.action: With three alive and a night kill that is predictable (a publicly confirmed Town role whose own actions are blocked or spent, with a wolf free to carry the kill), bet on that player to die and name their confirmed role. A correct victim plus role scores two points and can finish the win.

verdicts.why: The necromancer is already dead, so no lone killer remains to attack through bodies.
The only remaining attacker is the illusionist wolf, and no public healer shield on a top target is known.
Three alive with a wolf among them; the claimed sigilist player_9 is a confirmed-style Town power role the wolf may need to remove.

situations: On day 2, the village has nine players alive after the wolves and serial killer both attacked the same player on night 1; an illusionist concealed that player's role, leaving the village without a confirmed alignment or vote record to guide its first elimination decision. Information landscape: Information-starved: the public record confirms two attacks on the concealed victim, but their role, side, and any will remain unknown; there are no public claims, accusations, or votes, and you have no private night information. Stakes: Nine alive and five eliminations until the leading evil faction could win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so this decision is not immediately terminal. Consensus: No public discussion or accusations have occurred, so there is no discernible village consensus. My position: No expressed position; you have not spoken, and no majority has formed. Heat: No suspicion or attention toward you is recorded; you have made no public claim or contribution yet. Target landscape: No elimination candidates or role claims have been publicly identified; the only known death is a player whose role was concealed, so their side and identity as a candidate remain unknown.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.
lessons.action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.

lessons.situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

lessons.situation: With four players alive and one wolf left, a claimed vigilante demands the speculator's role while the claimed sentinel and claimed trailseer accuse each other over contradictory logs. Information landscape: Information-rich in confirmed dead roles, but the key conflict is between unverified claims, and a rules-confusion slip is being treated as proof. Stakes: At four alive with one wolf left, a wrong elimination likely hands the wolves the win. Pushing a mis-vote also exposes the speculator to a night shot. Consensus: The room leans toward whoever the credible shooter points at. It is tied up in the conflicting tracking logs and is pressuring the speculator for transparency. My position: Driving: pushing the accusation of one of the conflicting claimants to deflect heat. Heat: High: a credible claimed role singled the speculator out as a suspect for withholding its role all game. Target landscape: Two claimed roles, for example a sentinel and a trailseer, with logs that conflict, plus the speculator, who is being pressed for a role. The vigilante's shot gives it credibility, while the sentinel's and trailseer's results are unverified claims.
lessons.action: When a claimed role demands your role while two others trade accusations over conflicting logs, don't build the case on a rule-confusion or a thin data gap. Test the contradiction against the rules, for example whether a watch counts as a visit and who could have seen what. Back the elimination only if the mechanics actually prove a lie, and otherwise hold your vote for the player whose claim can't be explained.

verdicts.why: There are no claims, voting records, or discussion to correct yet.
Nine players are alive, not a four-player endgame.
No role claims or conflicting logs have been presented.

situations: Day 2 opens after one player was attacked by both the wolves and the serial killer and died with their role concealed. You privately know your pack selected the victim and concealed the body, while the village has no revealed role or will to interpret and does not publicly know your wolf alignment. Information landscape: Information-starved publicly: the double attack and concealed role are confirmed, but the victim’s identity of role and will remain unknown. You privately know the pack’s choice and concealment; no daytime claims or accusations have been made. Stakes: Nine players are alive, and the leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town; the game cannot end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this decision is not immediately decisive. Consensus: There is no expressed village consensus yet: no discussion messages or accusations are recorded today. My position: No position relative to a forming consensus; none exists yet. Heat: No suspicion has been expressed toward you; the day’s public discussion has not started. Forward exposure: No visible move has been made today. Publicly defending the concealed kill or volunteering your private knowledge would risk exposing your connection to the pack; silence is reversible, while a specific claim could be challenged against later events. Target landscape: No candidates have been publicly accused or supported yet. The only concrete event is the night death of a player whose role and will are hidden; there is no public role evidence distinguishing the living players. Public vs private: The public record says the concealed player was attacked by both the wolves and the serial killer. Privately, you know your pack chose that player and that the body was concealed; the other wolf’s identity and the pack’s discussion are not public.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.

lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

The vigilante's shot gives it credibility, while the sentinel's and trailseer's results are unverified claims.

Test the contradiction against the rules, for example whether a watch counts as a visit and who could have seen what. Back the elimination only if the mechanics actually prove a lie, and otherwise hold your vote for the player whose claim can't be explained.

Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.action: When the room is focused on another debate, such as verifying a claimed role, and your night-immune or already-known target sits among the discussants, join the discussion on its stated topic only. Voice a mild opinion on the claim under scrutiny or on the emerging abstain, and don't accuse or defend the immune player, since explaining how you know would expose wolf knowledge. Staying aligned with the room's current direction keeps heat low while you preserve your concealed information.

lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich.
