Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No one has accused me or challenged a claim I made.
The game is early and information is limited, but the discussion does not show a broad abstain consensus.
My partner is not the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation.

situations: A player killed overnight has a publicly concealed role, leaving the village without that player’s role or will, while the day’s only concrete discussion is a matching Sentinel-and-follower account of a visit that does not establish alignment. Your restrained response supports treating the route as corroboration rather than a basis for accusation. Information landscape: Information-starved: the public record confirms a concealed-role death, but provides no role or will for that player. The Investigator, Sentinel, and follower claims are unverified; their visit details are mutually consistent but not independently confirmed by game announcements. Stakes: Nine players are alive, and it is five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so this decision is not immediately decisive. Consensus: The room shows limited agreement that the visit accounts match but do not establish alignment. There is no clear shared vote direction; one speaker favors abstaining and another suggests a further check. My position: You are aligned with the expressed caution about weak evidence and have stated an abstain preference; no vote has yet established a majority position. Heat: Low apparent heat: no one has accused you. Your contribution cautions against treating the matching route as proof and suggests another check as a possible source of information. Forward exposure: You have publicly treated the matching visit accounts as insufficient evidence and voiced an abstain preference. A more forceful accusation or defense would create a visible position on the vote; any vote is public and permanent, while your current stated position is not a vote commitment. Target landscape: The claimed Investigator reports a Not suspicious check on a player; this is unverified and does not clear that player of being the lone killer or neutral. The claimed Sentinel and claimed follower describe a matching visit to the same player, corroborating the route only. No candidate has a publicly confirmed role or alignment. Public vs private: Publicly, a player’s role is concealed and the room has no public knowledge of what it was. You privately know the concealed player was the Vigilante and that you concealed the body; neither fact is exposed. The public discussion instead centers on unverified night-action claims and a corroborated visit route.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

verdicts.why: The discussion favors abstaining and no claim establishes a guilty target, so an elimination vote would stand out.
The information-role claims are unverified but mutually consistent, and there is no town consensus to eliminate anyone.
No one has accused me or presented hard evidence against me.

situations: The day-2 vote ended in an abstention with no elimination: nearly everyone abstained, while one player voted to eliminate the player whom an unverified Investigator claim had cleared as Not suspicious. The Investigator’s claimed result, your private trail result on a different player, and an unverified Sentinel account provide limited, non-alignment evidence as the next trail decision approaches. Information landscape: Information-starved for alignment: there are no publicly confirmed roles or revealed wills, and the concealed night-1 victim’s role remains unknown. Available evidence consists of unverified role and result claims, your private finding that your target visited no one, and the public vote record; the corroborated visit route does not establish alignment. Stakes: With 9 players alive and 5 eliminations until the leading evil faction could win at worst for the town, a single result cannot end the game or flip which faction is winning; the concealed body’s unknown side means this is the closest possible parity estimate. Target landscape: The unresolved candidates are the player with a claimed Not-suspicious result and the player they checked, plus the player who alone voted to eliminate that checked player. The Investigator and Sentinel claims remain unverified; your own follow confirms only that the watched player visited no one, not anyone’s alignment.

lessons.situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

lessons.situation: A wolf was just eliminated by the vote, and the confirmed town investigator is the obvious target for wolf retaliation that night. The trailseer wants to preserve that investigator's last action in case they are killed. Information landscape: Info-rich: a wolf has been caught, the investigator is validated, and earlier night visits and claims are on record. Visit data on the likely victim is more valuable than a blind follow. Stakes: Losing the investigator without recovering their last check would remove a key information source. Seeing the investigator's visit, and getting it reported, can lead directly to the last wolf. Target landscape: The confirmed or strongly vetted info role facing retaliation, versus claimed protectors who were already attacked or saved, versus quiet unread players. The vetted role is the likeliest night victim and a natural way to find their last target.
lessons.action: When the trailseer's own role is likely to draw an attack, follow the player the wolves most want dead, such as the confirmed investigator who just exposed a wolf. If the target dies, the trailseer still learns whom they visited that night. That information can point suspicion at the visited player.

verdicts.why: This is still early, with no confirmed flips or meaningful vote record and many unverified players.
This is Night 2; claims and a night result are now available, unlike the blind Night 1 situation.
No wolf has been eliminated and no Investigator has been confirmed.

situations: After nearly everyone abstained on day 2, the village has no elimination and no verified role claims or findings. The healer now faces a protection decision amid several unverified information-role claims and no public indication of whom either killer is targeting. Information landscape: Information-starved about alignments and likely night targets: the Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer claims and their private results are unverified, though the Sentinel and Trailseer’s reported visit accounts are mutually consistent. The only confirmed night event is that the concealed-role player was attacked by both the wolves and serial killer; no save was announced for the healer’s protected target. Stakes: There are 9 players alive and 5 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town; this protection decision is consequential but not immediately outcome-flipping. Target landscape: For the healer’s night protection, the unverified Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer claimants are publicly visible information-role candidates; the claimed Investigator was not voted out, and the claimed Sentinel and Trailseer’s accounts corroborate a visit route but not their roles. Other living players have no publicly established role. Protection value depends on which target is likely to face a wolf or serial-killer attack; no specific threat is confirmed.

lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.

verdicts.why: Wolves have not been shown to be nearly eliminated, and the serial killer remains alive.
The serial killer has not been eliminated; no one has been voted out.
No evil death has corroborated a Town power role; player_6's role is hidden.

situations: After a concealed night-one death attributed to both wolves and the serial killer, day two ended in a broad abstention; one player’s vote to eliminate the concealed victim’s seat was the sole dissent. The unverified Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer claims have not produced a confirmed alignment, leaving your one-time side pick open amid an unresolved board. Information landscape: Information-starved for choosing a winning side: the dead player’s role and will remain concealed, and the claimed night results are not verified. The Sentinel and Trailseer accounts corroborate a visit route, but not either claimant’s role or anyone’s alignment; the Investigator’s Not suspicious claim about you does not distinguish you from most non-wolves. Stakes: With 9 alive and 5 eliminations until the leading evil faction could win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown, the board is not at immediate parity. The game cannot end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this pick is not a one-elimination swing; the end-of-game consequence of choosing now rather than later is unclear from the current record. Target landscape: The side choice is among Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or yourself. Your Speculator role and unmade pick are privately known to you; publicly, the claimed Investigator’s Not suspicious read on you is unverified and compatible with your role. No public evidence clearly favors one side.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after Town's day vote eliminated a confirmed wolf or lone killer, with healer saves publicly verified. Town holds a large majority, but some killers remain. Past observations show the Town pick won when Town stayed disciplined and lost when Town later mis-eliminated its own power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: system-confirmed evil role reveals, a validated investigator claim, and announced healer saves. The remaining unknown is whether a wolf or killer is still hidden and how well Town will play. Stakes: Town leads, but a few mis-votes or kills could still flip the game, so the pick is only as good as Town's later play. Picking now removes the risk of dying unpicked, but it ties your win to Town's survival and avoiding errors. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self. After a confirmed evil elimination Town looks dominant, with validated investigator or healer claims and a numerical majority. Evil still has a wolf and possibly an unknown lone killer, and Town's later errors can still erase that lead.
lessons.action: Once the day vote has system-confirmed an evil elimination and the surviving power-role claims are validated, make the pick on that night instead of waiting longer. Choose Town only if the lone killer is confirmed gone or Town clearly outnumbers a single remaining wolf; if killers are still active with an uncertain Town lead, keep holding until one side is clearly ahead, unless you are likely to be killed that night.

lessons.situation: Early game, night 1 or 2, with a discussion-only day 1 or an abstained day 2. At most one or two night deaths so far, and neither wolves nor the lone killer have been exposed. The speculator is still unpicked and has not been targeted. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil eliminations, only unverified claims and concealed or ambiguous bodies, and no momentum signal for any faction. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is no immediate pressure to lock in. The only cost of waiting is the risk of dying unpicked, which is low on night 1 and rises as killers act. Holding costs little and keeps the option open for an informed pick later. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self, or keep holding. All ten players are alive with no confirmed roles and no tested claims. Any pick would be a pure guess on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On nights 1-2, while no evil role has been confirmed eliminated and no claim has been tested, keep the one-time pick unspent. Reassess each night, and commit as soon as board evidence clearly favors one side or you suspect you are likely to be killed. Dying unpicked is a loss, but an uninformed early lock-in has no advantage, and the pick cannot be changed once made.

verdicts.why: No evil role has been confirmed eliminated, and there are no validated power-role claims.
The board is still information-poor: player_6's role is hidden, the claims are unverified, and no one was eliminated today.

situations: After a day-2 abstention, the village has no elimination and faces another night. Three players have made unverified information-role claims, and the Sentinel and Trailseer claims are consistent about a visit, leaving a choice between disrupting a potential information source and preserving uncertainty. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public night report is that a player died to both wolves and the serial killer with their role concealed. The Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer claims and results are unverified; the aligned visit accounts corroborate behavior, not roles or factions. Stakes: Nine players are alive, and it is five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, so a single kill is not an immediate faction-balance swing. Forward exposure: A night attack on a publicly claimed information-role player would irreversibly remove them if it succeeds, while publicly revealing that they were attacked; the attacker is not identified by the announcement. The claims remain unverified, so the move would not establish whether the target’s claimed role was genuine. Target landscape: The candidates include players claiming Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer. Their roles are unverified; the Sentinel and Trailseer accounts of a visit to the same player are consistent, but corroborate only the route, not alignment. No candidate has a system-confirmed role or publicly verified alignment.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

verdicts.why: There was an abstention and an Investigator claim, but player_9 did not single out a suspect; the check reportedly cleared player_4.
This is not the opening night, and the board now has public claims and visit information.
No leader has been publicly saved or confirmed by a wolf flip.

situations: After the day’s unanimous abstention apart from one vote against the player publicly described as having a Not suspicious check, there was no elimination. Tonight, your remaining watch presents a choice of which player's door to monitor amid unverified role claims and no publicly established threat. Information landscape: Information-starved: your private Night 1 result confirms one visit to the watched player, and the visitor's Trailseer claim matches that route. The Investigator's result and both claimed roles remain unverified; the concealed Night 1 victim's role and alignment are unknown. No Night 2 outcome is available yet. Stakes: Nine players are alive, and it is five eliminations until the leading evil faction could win in the worst case for town; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a single result does not yet decide which faction is winning. Target landscape: The remaining watch can be spent on a likely night victim or on a player whose visits could clarify their behavior. The Investigator and Trailseer claims are unverified; the Sentinel claim is your own. Your Night 1 watch directly confirmed that the player claiming Trailseer visited the player they said they followed, but this establishes only the route, not either player's role or alignment.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night after an abstain or tied vote. Conflicting role claims are on the board and you hold one watch left. You must decide whose door to watch, knowing results come only from visitors to that player. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, vote records and some prior night results, but nothing is verified. Alignments of the candidates are unconfirmed, and visit data exists only for whoever you watch. Stakes: Town can still afford a mistake, but this is the last watch, so a wasted use leaves no visitor-tracking for the rest of the game. A watch that exposes a visit pattern or kill trace can settle a claim fight before wolves reach parity. Target landscape: The choice is between a contested claimant (e.g. counter-claimed investigator or sigilist) under heavy suspicion, the obvious wolf-priority targets (claimed investigator, healer, trailseer), a quiet player from a tied vote, or an investigator-cleared player. The claim conflicts are public, but none of the candidates is verified. Only the contested claimant or the likely kill target is likely to draw visits.
lessons.action: With your last watch, pick the player most likely to receive a visit tonight. That means a contested or heavily accused claimant whose claim other roles can verify or attack, or the likely wolf kill target. A watch on a quiet suspect or an already-cleared player usually returns "no visitors", because attackers visit their victims, not themselves.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. lessons.situation: Mid-game, with the first watch already spent and one watch left. The Sentinel is deciding whether to use it on a personal adversary or hold it for a higher-value door. Stakes: The last watch is the Sentinel's final hard evidence, and once it is spent the role has nothing left to do at night. Target landscape: A handful of living players: a prominent claimed or confirmed Town role, a player who has accused you, and quiet unverified players. Favor the one most likely to be attacked or visited, based on public claims or revealed roles, over one picked because they are hostile to you.
lessons.action: Save the last watch for a night when you can name a door that is likely to be attacked or visited, such as a prominent claimed role or a player the wolves or killer plausibly want dead. A watch on a vocal accuser or a quiet bystander tends to return a zero-visitor result, and a watch is spent whether or not it shows anything.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

verdicts.why: The claimed Investigator and Sentinel are both live information threats; follow the pack’s split plan and block player_9 while killing player_10.
This is no longer a blind opening night: there are public claims, visit accounts, and a Day 2 vote.
No Vigilante or wolf partner has been confirmed killed, and the board is not at that endgame state.
The claimed investigator may still have a check, so blocking player_9 is the best way to prevent a dangerous result tonight.
This is no longer an information-starved opening night; public claims and a vote record now exist.
No wolf partner has been killed and no vigilante has been confirmed.

situations: After the day’s vote ended in a unanimous abstention except for one vote against the player whose check was claimed Not suspicious, the pack has selected the claimed Sentinel as its night victim and the claimed Investigator as the block target. The remaining conceal is available, but the attack and block have not yet resolved; there is no private result from tonight indicating an attack on an immune player or identifying the lone killer. Information landscape: Public information is sparse and consists of the concealed death of one player attacked by both the wolves and the serial killer, plus unverified claims about an Investigator check and matching Sentinel/Trailseer visit accounts. The Illusionist privately knows the concealed victim was the Vigilante. Tonight’s private action results are not yet available; no immune-target attack result has identified the serial killer. Stakes: Nine players are alive, and the closest the wolves could be to parity is five eliminations away, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, so this night’s kill and whether the last conceal is spent do not by themselves decide which faction is winning. Forward exposure: Using the remaining conceal would publicly hide the pack victim’s role and remove their will, while concealing the carrier’s visit trace to that victim; the use is permanent. The victim has not yet been attacked tonight, so no conceal decision or visible outcome has occurred. Target landscape: The pack’s announced night target is a player claiming Sentinel, whose reported watch result is consistent with a separate player’s claimed follow result but does not verify either role. A player claiming Investigator says their check found the player claiming Sentinel’s proposed alternative, a player claiming Trailseer, Not suspicious; this is unverified. The claimed Investigator is the stated block target. No evidence yet establishes the target’s true role or whether their record would reveal additional information.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

verdicts.why: The Chanteuse is not known dead, and this is not a late-game lone-wolf position.
Night 1 has passed; the pack has already spent a conceal.
Player_10 has already shared their Sentinel account, so hiding their role would add little and spend the final use.

situations: Before making your one-time side pick, you are weighing an information-starved board: the first-night victim's role is concealed, a player claiming Investigator reported a Not suspicious check, and the publicly confirmed Sentinel's record supports a claimed Trailseer's account of a visit route. The second-night report confirms a serial-killer attack was saved and a Sentinel was killed by the wolves, but does not establish which side is closest to winning. Information landscape: Limited and partly unverified: one concealed death leaves that player's role unknown; a revealed Sentinel's night-one record is public fact; the Investigator and Trailseer claims and the Not suspicious result are unverified. The save confirms an attack on the claimant, not their role. Stakes: Eight players are alive, and it is 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, so this decision is consequential but not immediately decisive. Consensus: No clear consensus on which side is ahead or who should be eliminated. On day 2, nearly everyone abstained, with one vote against you. My position: No stated position on which side is ahead; your day-2 abstention matched the overwhelming vote outcome. Heat: Low or unclear: one player voted to eliminate you on day 2, while the rest abstained; no current-day accusations have been made. Target landscape: The private pick is among Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or self; the concealed first-night victim's side remains unknown, and no side has been eliminated or confirmed as ahead.

lessons.situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.
lessons.action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.

lessons.situation: With four players alive and one wolf left, a claimed vigilante demands the speculator's role while the claimed sentinel and claimed trailseer accuse each other over contradictory logs. Information landscape: Information-rich in confirmed dead roles, but the key conflict is between unverified claims, and a rules-confusion slip is being treated as proof. Stakes: At four alive with one wolf left, a wrong elimination likely hands the wolves the win. Pushing a mis-vote also exposes the speculator to a night shot. Consensus: The room leans toward whoever the credible shooter points at. It is tied up in the conflicting tracking logs and is pressuring the speculator for transparency. My position: Driving: pushing the accusation of one of the conflicting claimants to deflect heat. Heat: High: a credible claimed role singled the speculator out as a suspect for withholding its role all game. Target landscape: Two claimed roles, for example a sentinel and a trailseer, with logs that conflict, plus the speculator, who is being pressed for a role. The vigilante's shot gives it credibility, while the sentinel's and trailseer's results are unverified claims.
lessons.action: When a claimed role demands your role while two others trade accusations over conflicting logs, don't build the case on a rule-confusion or a thin data gap. Test the contradiction against the rules, for example whether a watch counts as a visit and who could have seen what. Back the elimination only if the mechanics actually prove a lie, and otherwise hold your vote for the player whose claim can't be explained.

verdicts.why: Eight players are alive, and there is no endgame pressure or accusation against me.
No discussion has happened yet today, so there is no active dispute over records or claims to correct.
There are eight players alive and no claimed vigilante, role demand, or argument over conflicting logs.

situations: A player claiming Investigator survived a publicly announced Serial Killer attack because the healer saved them, while the attacker remains unidentified. This creates a concealment problem: your private knowledge identifies the victim of your attack, but the public report does not identify you, and the village has not yet formed a view about the saved player's claim. Information landscape: Information is limited and mostly claim-based: the public has a confirmed healer save from a Serial Killer attack, a revealed Sentinel and their read-out record, and unverified Investigator and Trailseer claims. The Sentinel's record corroborates a visit described by the Trailseer claimant, but does not verify that player's role. The first night's concealed death leaves that player's role unknown. Stakes: With 8 players alive and 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown, this decision is not immediately decisive: the game cannot end within one more elimination at worst for the town. Consensus: There is no current discussion or expressed consensus. On the previous day, nearly everyone abstained, with one vote against another player; that record does not show a present alignment. My position: No current position relative to a forming consensus: no discussion has occurred today. Heat: No suspicion of you is recorded in the available discussion; today's discussion has not begun. Your role and night actions are not public. Forward exposure: A visible move against the saved player could connect your attention to the publicly reported Serial Killer attack, though it would not prove your identity. Any accusation would be a public commitment that could be challenged or reversed; its end-of-game effect is unclear because no record links such a move to a particular outcome. Target landscape: The player saved from the Serial Killer attack claims Investigator and reports a Not suspicious check on another player; that result is unverified. A different player claims Trailseer, and the dead Sentinel's revealed record confirms that this claimant visited the watched player, which supports the route but not the claimed role or alignment. No current target has a publicly confirmed hostile role. Public vs private: You know you attacked the player claiming Investigator on night 2, and that the attack was saved; publicly, the village knows only that this player was attacked by the Serial Killer and saved by the healer. Your identity and action remain private, and the public report does not establish who attacked them.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

verdicts.why: This is Day 3; no one has reported a Night 1 visit naming me, and the described Day 2 pressure is absent.
No wolf has been publicly revealed, and no one has accused me based on a dead wolf's vote.
Eight players remain, and no one has pointed the room at me.

situations: After a day-2 near-unanimous abstention, the village enters day 3 with two unverified information-role claims whose visit accounts are mutually consistent, while the claimed Investigator's latest action is privately known to you to have been blocked. The public record does not confirm either claimant's role or alignment. Information landscape: Information is limited but not absent: a concealed night-1 death provides no role or will; the revealed Sentinel's will supplies a visit record; and the remaining information-role results are player claims rather than verified findings. The private fact that the Investigator claimant was blocked is not public. Stakes: Eight players are alive; the leading evil faction is four eliminations from parity at worst for the town, with the concealed body's side unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this is consequential but not a one-result swing. Consensus: The village showed little alignment around a candidate on day 2: all but one voter abstained, and there is no current-day discussion yet. The information-role claims have some mutually consistent visit detail, but no verified alignment result. My position: Previously with the abstaining majority; no current-day position has been expressed. Heat: Low on the available record: no accusations or current-day messages are recorded, and the prior vote was nearly unanimous abstention. Forward exposure: A visible push against either information claimant would commit you to a public read of claims that remain unverified; their consistent visit accounts could make that push conspicuous. Your role and wolf partner remain undisclosed, and no such public move has yet been made today. Target landscape: The Investigator claimant has one publicly described Not suspicious check, with no revealed target role validating it. The Trailseer claimant's account of following the player who was watched is consistent with the Sentinel's revealed record, but does not establish the claimant's role or alignment. The player who received the lone vote on day 2 has no public role claim or confirming evidence; the rest of the prior vote was abstention. Public vs private: Publicly, one player is an unverified Investigator claimant whose check read another player Not suspicious, and another is an unverified Trailseer claimant. The revealed Sentinel's will corroborates that the Trailseer claimant visited the player they say they followed; privately, you know the claimed Investigator was roleblocked last night, but the village has no public confirmation of that.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

verdicts.why: This is not a final day with three players; eight players remain.
No wolf partner has been exposed, and no Town claimant has reported a roleblock in the discussion.
No partner has been eliminated and no claimant has stumbled in today's discussion.

situations: After a first-night attack by both wolves and the Serial Killer left a role-concealed death, the village has only a claimed Investigator's check and a claimed Trailseer's matching no-visit account, while the confirmed Sentinel later died to the wolves and a claimed Investigator was publicly reported saved from the Serial Killer. Day two ended without elimination, leaving today's discussion to interpret sparse, partly unverified information. Information landscape: Information-starved: the first-night role and will remain concealed to the village; the Sentinel's death and night-one record are confirmed; the Investigator and Trailseer statements are claims, and the save confirms an attack and protection but not the saved player's role. Stakes: Eight players remain, and the leading evil faction is four eliminations from parity at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. A single result cannot end the game or flip the winning side. Consensus: The village has not yet expressed a day-three position; the prior vote was overwhelmingly to abstain, with one vote against a living player. The claims and confirmed night outcomes have not established a shared conclusion. My position: No current day-three position is on record, so your alignment with any forming consensus is unclear. Heat: No current accusation or suspicion directed at you is recorded in today's discussion. Forward exposure: No day-three statement or vote from you is recorded yet. A visible position on the competing information claims would attach you to that argument; discussion can be revised, but a later public vote is permanent. Target landscape: The living candidates have no publicly confirmed role claims. One claims Investigator and reports a Not suspicious check on another living player; one claims Trailseer and reports that player visited no one. The Sentinel was confirmed by their death and record but is dead. Public evidence is limited to those claims and the confirmed night outcomes; behavioral evidence is not yet recorded for today. Public vs private: Privately, you know the concealed first-night victim was the Vigilante and that your surviving wolf partner is alive. Publicly, the victim's role remains unknown; the later death of the claimed Sentinel was role-revealed, and the claimed Investigator and Trailseer remain unverified.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: A claimed watcher reports a visitor at the dead wolf partner's door, and the accused denies it while the village weighs the two stories.
