Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed dead wolf, a watcher's claim about its visitors, and a supporting investigator result. Stakes: Removing the lone killer is necessary before wolves can win and costs the pack nothing, while staying unscrutinized keeps the illusionist alive for the endgame. Consensus: Town converges on the accused and the vote is nearly unanimous. My position: with majority Heat: None: no one has linked the illusionist to the kill or questioned its behavior. Forward exposure: Backing the watcher commits the illusionist to treating that claimant as credible later, though that is easy to revisit if the watcher is contradicted. Target landscape: The accused visitor, who claims town and denies the visit, versus the claimed watcher whose report is plausible given the dead wolf. The basis is a watch result, not behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows its partner was killed by an outside night killer, so the accused visitor is probably that killer, and the public read matches this.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is already dead and a claimed sentinel or other watcher accuses an outside killer, back the watcher's report and press the accused to explain their visit. This helps the town remove the lone killer without any suspicion falling on you. Keep your wording the same as the rest of the village's.

decision.message: I’m the Healer.

verdicts.why: No one has accused me or tied me to public evidence today.
This is an opening round with no new discussion to build on, and I can make a permitted role claim.
No wolf partner has been revealed dead, and no watcher has accused an outside killer.

situations: A publicly confirmed save of the claimed Investigator has produced a two-way Healer-claim conflict: one claimant says they protected the target, while another also claims Healer. The target says they were roleblocked, and a claimed Trailseer says they visited no one, leaving the action claim plausible but not verified. You privately know you caused the attack that was saved, while your role and attack remain undisclosed. Information landscape: The public record confirms a concealed-role death after attacks by both wolves and the Serial Killer, a later Serial Killer attack saved by the Healer, and a dead Sentinel's record that a claimed Trailseer visited the watched player on Night 1. Role claims and the current night-action accounts are not mechanically verified; the concealed victim's role is unknown to the village. Stakes: Eight players are alive; it is four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so a single result is not currently a swing; the immediate effect of this Healer-claim dispute on the eventual outcome is unclear. Consensus: There is no clear consensus: the discussion contains competing Healer claims, while the investigator and Trailseer claims remain unverified. No accusations are recorded. My position: You have not expressed a position and are not visibly driving or joining a side in the dispute. Heat: No suspicion or accusation toward you is recorded. You have not spoken publicly or claimed a role. Forward exposure: A visible intervention in the dispute between two Healer claimants could draw attention to your interest in the confirmed save, but would not by itself reveal your attacks. No visible move or commitment has been made; the longer-term consequence is unclear. Target landscape: The two Healer claimants are competing over an unverified role claim; the save confirms that the investigator claimant was attacked and protected, not which claimant is the Healer. The investigator claimant's earlier Not suspicious result on another player is unverified. A claimed Trailseer reports that the investigator claimant visited no one, consistent with the claimed roleblock but not independently proving it. Public vs private: Privately, you know your attacks killed the player whose role was concealed and targeted the player who was publicly reported saved by the Healer. The village knows about those outcomes but not your identity or actions; the concealed player's role remains unknown. You have made no public account of either night.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

decision.message: The healer claims conflict, but the public report only tells us player_9 was saved; it doesn’t identify who protected them. player_1’s account fits the save, while player_5 hasn’t given a night account yet—what did each of you protect on Night 1, if anything? That could give us a claim to check against later reports.

verdicts.why: This is Day 3, and nobody has named me as the Night 1 visitor or put me under direct pressure.
There are eight players alive and no current vote consensus against me.
No wolf has been revealed, and nobody has accused me based on a wolf's vote.

situations: Two players claim the uniquely listed Healer after a public save from a Serial Killer attack: one gives a Night 1 and Night 2 protection account, while your Healer cover has yet to supply a prior-night account. The save confirms that the target was attacked and protected, but not which claimant protected them, leaving a credibility contest without a confirmed Healer identity. Information landscape: There is some public night information: a Serial Killer attack was saved, the Night 2 wolf victim was revealed as Sentinel, and that Sentinel's will confirms a claimed Trailseer route. The concealed Night 1 victim has no public role or will, and no public result verifies either Healer claim or the claimed Investigator's check. Stakes: With 8 alive, the leading evil faction is 4 eliminations from parity at worst for the town; a single decision cannot end the game or flip the winner, though errors can narrow the remaining margin. The concealed body's side is unknown publicly, and no end-of-game consequence is established for this Healer-claim dispute. Consensus: The room has not established a shared read or target. Discussion is focused on the conflicting Healer claims and the limits of what the public save report proves; there is no recorded accusation summary. My position: You are one of the two sides of the Healer-claim conflict, while the emerging discussion is questioning both claims rather than backing one by verified evidence. Heat: Some attention is on you because your Healer claim conflicts with the other claimant's, and a player has asked you for a Night 1 account. No direct accusation or vote against you is recorded in the current discussion. Forward exposure: Giving a Night 1 protection account would commit your Healer cover to a specific claim that could be compared with later information; it would be a public statement, not independently verified by the Night 1 report. Your current Healer claim has not included a night account. Target landscape: The choice centers on the two unverified Healer claimants: one has a detailed account consistent with the public Night 2 save, but the save does not identify who protected the target; the other has not yet supplied an account. A player claiming Investigator has a Night 1 Not suspicious result on the player they checked, with no public confirmation. A player claiming Trailseer has a Night 1 route claim corroborated by the revealed Sentinel's record, which says that player visited the Sentinel's watched target. Public vs private: Publicly, two players claim Healer: one says they protected the player saved from the Serial Killer on Night 2 and also protected them Night 1; the other has not yet given a prior-night account. Privately, you know you are the Illusionist, that your living wolf partner has not been revealed, and that the concealed Night 1 victim was the Vigilante. The village does not know that victim's role.

lessons.situation: A claiming tracker names me as a visitor to the night-one victim while a separate dual-claim conflict dominates the room. Information landscape: Information-rich: two investigative claims with direct visit reports on both night deaths, plus a hard counterclaim. Stakes: A named wolf-side visitor who survives today by deflection but leaves the accusation unresolved; it can return at the next vote and cost a wolf while the pack still needs several eliminations. Consensus: The room is split and distracted by a bigger role-claim dispute, so it can be redirected but has not cleared me. My position: With majority; I am following the room's focus on the other conflict while deflecting from my own accusation. Heat: High; named by a claimed tracker as a visitor to the night victim, though partly diluted by another player caught at a different body. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits me to calling the reporter a liar without any role alibi; it is reversible only by building a story later, and if the reporter survives or is validated it brings me down. Target landscape: The claiming tracker who named me, a rival dispute (conflicting claims of the same role) in the room, and myself; the reports are unverified but the tracker's claim is accurate. Public vs private: Privately I know the report is accurate because I carried out the kill, while publicly the room is split over a different dispute and can be pointed away from me.
lessons.action: When a claimed tracker or watcher reports you at a victim's door, do not rely on a bare denial: pair it with a coherent counter-story, such as a plausible role claim with a believable alibi. Use any competing role conflict in the room to draw attention off yourself, but keep the counter-story ready so the report cannot resurface later.

lessons.situation: A trailseer claims to have seen the illusionist visit a player who died that night with a hidden role, and the illusionist has to answer in daytime discussion. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed death with a hidden role plus a direct tracking report that matches what the illusionist actually did. Stakes: An elimination of the illusionist here leaves the surviving wolf alone and closer to losing, so avoid a flat denial that the room can disprove. Consensus: The majority takes the tracker's findings at face value; only a couple of players are confused about how concealment affects visits. My position: opposing the forming consensus Heat: Critical; directly accused of visiting a murder victim on the night they died. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits you to calling the trailseer a liar and rules out any later switch to a benign visiting claim. A benign-visit explanation stays open and can be adjusted if the town pushes back. Target landscape: The accused visitor (you) against the single claimed tracker; the town has no competing account of the night, so the report counts as hard eyewitness evidence. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the reported visit is true, because it concealed the body, while publicly it insists it never left home.
lessons.action: When a trailseer or sentinel report places you at the door of a victim whose role was hidden, do not flatly deny the visit. Offer a benign reason for being out that night (for example, a claim of a visiting town role, or that you checked on that player), and stress that the report only shows a visit, not who attacked. Do not claim that illusionist concealment makes the report invalid: if you were not the carrier, your own visit to hide the body is still seen, and a flat denial against a tracker report the town trusts loses you the room.

lessons.situation: Day two with several town investigative and protective claims surfacing, a night death that flipped information, and the room absorbed in checking one claimant. The illusionist wolf knows about an unannounced immune target. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, with three town role claims and a dead trailseer's visit reported, but nothing confirms wolf alignment. Stakes: Mid-early game; the pack still has room, but one revealed slip about the immune target would expose a wolf and tilt the count toward town. Consensus: The town is coalescing around abstaining and picking apart one claimant's lack of results, based on claimed night results. My position: Staying out of the main debate and moving with the room, ready to join it. Heat: Low. Reported town information frames me as an innocent subject of night information, and attention sits elsewhere. Forward exposure: Accusing the immune player would require explaining how I know about an unannounced failed kill, instantly revealing wolf knowledge and being irreversible. A mild on-topic comment commits me to little and can be revised later. Target landscape: The room is scrutinizing a newly claimed role with thin results and accepting a cleared target. The immune player is publicly unverified and not under pressure. Public vs private: Privately the pack knows a quiet player survived our unannounced night attack and is night-immune, while the town sees only an unverified player talking mechanics.
lessons.action: When the room is focused on another debate, such as verifying a claimed role, and your night-immune or already-known target sits among the discussants, join the discussion on its stated topic only. Voice a mild opinion on the claim under scrutiny or on the emerging abstain, and don't accuse or defend the immune player, since explaining how you know would expose wolf knowledge. Staying aligned with the room's current direction keeps heat low while you preserve your concealed information.

decision.message: I protected player_4 on Night 1, and I didn’t learn of any attack on them. Last night I protected player_2. player_1, the report confirms player_9 was saved, but it doesn’t identify who protected them, so you can’t know that your protection was the one that stopped the attack.

verdicts.why: No one has accused me of visiting the Night 1 victim; the report instead says player_8 visited me.
No one has reported seeing me visit a hidden-role victim.
Today’s discussion centers on conflicting Healer claims, not the prior situation described.

decision.message: Player_3, as I said, my account is that I protected player_2 last night, so it doesn’t explain player_9’s save. But that still doesn’t prove player_1 is the Healer: the report establishes a save, not who caused it, and player_1’s certainty about whose protection worked goes beyond what it tells us.

verdicts.why: No one has claimed that I visited a night-one victim; the current dispute is about competing Healer claims.
Player_8 reported that I visited no one on Night 1, not that I visited a concealed victim.
The current discussion is a Healer counterclaim, not the earlier situation involving an unannounced immune target.

decision.message: Player_4, as I said, my account is that I protected player_2, so it doesn’t explain the save. Your reasoning depends on player_1’s claim being true; the public report confirms a save, but doesn’t independently identify who caused it. I can’t offer a different account of that night.

verdicts.why: No one has accused me of visiting a night-one victim; the claimed trail report says I visited no one.
The current trail report does not place me at a concealed victim's door.
The discussion is about conflicting Healer claims, not an unannounced immune target.

decision.message: Player_8, your follow result only tells us player_9 visited no one; it doesn't independently establish either Healer claim. I’ve already said my account was protecting player_2, so it doesn’t explain the save. Player_1’s account fits it better, but their Night 1 protection claim has no publicly checkable outcome either, so weigh the fit without treating it as proof of their role.

verdicts.why: No one has claimed that I visited the Night 1 victim; the reported visit was player_8 visiting me.
No Trailseer or Sentinel has reported me visiting a player who died that night.
There is no current public information about an immune target to avoid discussing.

decision.message: The save confirms someone protected player_9, but it doesn’t tell us who. My account is still that I protected player_2, so I’m not claiming credit for the save; player_1’s account fits it, but that fit alone doesn’t independently verify either role. I understand why that makes my claim hard to trust, but the report itself doesn’t settle the dispute.

verdicts.why: No one is currently accusing me based on a tracker report placing me at a night victim.
The current pressure is about competing Healer claims, not a report placing me at a concealed victim.
The discussion is not focused on an unannounced immune target or a claim about one.

situations: A publicly announced save from the Serial Killer attack has become the basis of a Day 3 credibility contest between two competing Healer claimants. One claimant says they protected the saved player, while the other says they protected someone else and challenges the first claimant’s certainty; a third speaker favors eliminating the latter claimant. You must assess this divided board while your Speculator pick is still unspent. Information landscape: Some hard public night outcomes exist: the Serial Killer attacked the saved player, and a player killed by the wolves was revealed as the Sentinel, whose public will confirms a visitor to a watched target. The healer identities and protection accounts remain claims; the revealed Sentinel’s record supports a visit route, not the visitor’s role. The first night’s wolf-and-Serial-Killer victim remains role-concealed, leaving that player’s side unknown. This is partially informative but short of alignment-confirming evidence. Stakes: Eight players are alive, and the leading evil faction is four eliminations from being able to win at worst for Town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination on that worst-case count, so this vote is consequential but not immediately outcome-flipping; no end-game consequence of this specific vote is established. Consensus: No clear consensus. One speaker favors eliminating the claimant whose account does not explain the save; the other claimant disputes that the save identifies who protected the victim, and the room has not aligned publicly. My position: No stated position in the current discussion; you are not visibly driving or joining the emerging preference for one claimant. Heat: Low and not clearly current: you were the target of one vote on Day 2, but today’s discussion has not accused you. Target landscape: The immediate vote centers on two competing, unverified Healer claimants: one says they protected the player saved from the Serial Killer, while the other says they protected someone else. The support is a publicly confirmed save and conflicting private-action accounts, not a role reveal. Your own side pick remains unmade; Town, Wolves, the lone killer, and yourself are still the possible choices.

lessons.situation: With four players alive and one wolf left, a claimed vigilante demands the speculator's role while the claimed sentinel and claimed trailseer accuse each other over contradictory logs. Information landscape: Information-rich in confirmed dead roles, but the key conflict is between unverified claims, and a rules-confusion slip is being treated as proof. Stakes: At four alive with one wolf left, a wrong elimination likely hands the wolves the win. Pushing a mis-vote also exposes the speculator to a night shot. Consensus: The room leans toward whoever the credible shooter points at. It is tied up in the conflicting tracking logs and is pressuring the speculator for transparency. My position: Driving: pushing the accusation of one of the conflicting claimants to deflect heat. Heat: High: a credible claimed role singled the speculator out as a suspect for withholding its role all game. Target landscape: Two claimed roles, for example a sentinel and a trailseer, with logs that conflict, plus the speculator, who is being pressed for a role. The vigilante's shot gives it credibility, while the sentinel's and trailseer's results are unverified claims.
lessons.action: When a claimed role demands your role while two others trade accusations over conflicting logs, don't build the case on a rule-confusion or a thin data gap. Test the contradiction against the rules, for example whether a watch counts as a visit and who could have seen what. Back the elimination only if the mechanics actually prove a lie, and otherwise hold your vote for the player whose claim can't be explained.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.
lessons.action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.

lessons.situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

decision.message: The public report does establish that a healer protected player_9 last night. So player_5’s claim to have protected player_2 only fits if player_1’s account of protecting player_9 is true; otherwise player_5 needs to explain who protected player_9. That makes player_5’s account worth testing, but it doesn’t prove player_1’s role on its own.

verdicts.why: We have eight alive and no conflicting sentinel/trailseer logs or vigilante pressure.
The public save report is a confirmed fact that can resolve the competing healer claims.
This is not a four-player endgame and no one has pressed me to reveal a role.

situations: Two players claiming Healer are in conflict after the public report that the claimed Investigator was attacked by the Serial Killer and saved. One claimant says they protected that player; the other says they protected a different player and argues the save does not prove who caused it. The dispute is becoming a possible vote choice despite the report not naming the healer. Information landscape: The public has a confirmed save and a revealed Sentinel's Night 1 record, alongside unverified claims from an Investigator, Trailseer, and two Healers. These provide some concrete event evidence, but do not independently verify the living claimants' roles or identify the source of the save; the concealed first-night death also leaves its role unknown. Stakes: Eight players remain, and the leading evil faction is four eliminations from parity at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination on that worst-case count, so this vote is consequential but not immediately game-ending. Consensus: The room is not clearly aligned: one speaker has explicitly favored eliminating the claimant whose account does not explain the save, while others note the save does not independently identify its protector. No broad agreement is established. My position: You have not expressed a public position on the competing claims and are not yet visibly with or against the emerging pressure on one claimant. Heat: No direct suspicion or accusation toward you is recorded; you have made no public day-3 statement in the available discussion. Forward exposure: A public vote for either Healer claimant would permanently record your choice in a dispute where the save does not identify its source. Voting for your partner would expose your alignment risk; abstaining, if available, would avoid choosing between the claims but would also be a visible vote. Target landscape: The two candidates are the player claiming to have protected the player saved last night and the competing Healer claimant who says they protected someone else. Neither role claim is system-confirmed; the save is evidence of protection, while the competing accounts and the argument over certainty are behavioral evidence. A claimed Investigator and a claimed Trailseer have also shared unverified accounts. Public vs private: Privately, you know your wolf partner is one of the competing Healer claimants, and you know the claimed Investigator was roleblocked last night. Publicly, the partner's role and alignment are unconfirmed; the public save confirms an attack on the claimed Investigator was stopped, not who protected them.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

situations: Before making your one-time Speculator pick, you are assessing a day-3 dispute between two conflicting Healer claims after a public save on the player attacked by the Serial Killer. The claim that its owner protected the saved player fits the outcome; the competing claimant says they protected someone else. The village is leaning toward the first account, while your own position and likely winning side remain uncertain. Information landscape: Information is limited. The public save establishes that the attacked player was protected, and the revealed Sentinel’s will confirms a visit by the claimed Trailseer to another player on Night 1. Healer identities and protection targets are otherwise private; the Investigator and Trailseer claims are unverified, and the first night’s concealed death leaves that player’s role unknown. Stakes: Eight players remain; the leading evil faction is four eliminations from parity at worst for the town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown. A single vote or kill does not immediately decide the game, though the wrong elimination can still advance an evil faction’s path to parity. The end-of-game effect of this developing Healer dispute is unclear from the record. Consensus: A developing majority favors the Healer claimant whose account fits the public save; several voices have argued against the other claimant. The save confirms protection occurred, not who provided it, so the room’s alignment rests on fit between accounts rather than role verification. My position: Holding out from the emerging majority: you have not stated a vote or publicly endorsed either Healer claim. Heat: Low direct heat on you: you have not been accused in the current discussion. You are one of the two claimed Healer targets in the earlier Investigator check, but that result is an unverified claim and does not exclude the Serial Killer. Target landscape: The active choice is between two players claiming Healer, with conflicting accounts: one claims to have protected the publicly saved player, while the other says they protected someone else. The saved player’s protection is confirmed, but neither claimant’s role is confirmed. A claimed Investigator’s Not suspicious result on another candidate does not clear that player of being the Serial Killer.

lessons.situation: The speculator has already picked a side (Town) and sits in a split or deadlocked day vote where its single vote can decide a tie or prevent a bad elimination of a claimed Town role. Both wolves and a lone killer may still be alive. Information landscape: Moderate and muddled: night kills, a hidden role, conflicting role claims and night-result claims, but no confirmed wolf or killer. Mostly unverified claims plus voting records. Stakes: With about six players alive and two killing factions active, one vote can decide an elimination or block a Town loss. A mistaken Town elimination moves evil toward parity and weakens the Town side the speculator picked. Consensus: The village is scattered or split into near-equal camps with no single dominant target; the push is based on muddled claims and behavioral reads. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none; nobody has directed accusations at the speculator, and its speech has been neutral. Target landscape: Several candidates split the room: claimed Town power roles (healer, trailseer, sigilist, vigilante) versus an unconfirmed quiet or counter-accusing player. The evidence is partly claims and conflicting timelines, partly behavior and past votes, with no confirmed wolf.
lessons.action: When you have already picked Town and the day vote is split among several candidates, cast your vote sincerely on the unconfirmed player whose behavior or claims look most evil. Prefer the candidate whose claims conflict with other players' reports over a claimed Town power role. Your vote can swing a split or tie, so use it to stop a Town-aligned elimination and to remove the likeliest killer, which keeps Town the winning side you picked.

lessons.situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.
lessons.action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.
lessons.action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.

This is not a four-player endgame or an isolated vote.

situations: Before the Day 3 vote, two players claim the mutually exclusive Healer role after a public save of the claimed Investigator. One claimant says they protected the saved player; the other says they protected someone else. Several players favor eliminating the latter, while the claimant stresses that the save does not identify its source. You privately know you caused the Serial Killer attacks, including the attack that was stopped by the save, but no one has publicly connected those attacks to you. Information landscape: The public has a confirmed Night 2 save from a Serial Killer attack, a revealed Sentinel and that Sentinel's Night 1 record, plus unverified Investigator and Trailseer claims. The save gives a concrete fit comparison between the Healer accounts but does not identify the Healer. The Night 1 victim's role remains concealed, leaving the game's information incomplete. Stakes: Eight players are alive, and it is four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town; the present vote matters but does not by itself decide which faction is winning. Consensus: A clear majority is forming around eliminating the Healer claimant whose stated protection target was not the publicly saved player: four players have argued against that claimant, mainly because the rival account fits the save. The accused contests that this proves the rival's role, and no vote has yet occurred. My position: You have not publicly stated a position, so you are presently uncommitted while a majority forms against one Healer claimant. Heat: No one has accused you or challenged your behavior in the discussion; your night actions and Serial Killer role are not publicly attributed to you. Forward exposure: A visible vote with the forming majority would align you with eliminating the claimant whose account does not explain the public save, without revealing your private attack history or role. It would create a public vote-record commitment, though your vote itself would not establish either Healer claim as true. Target landscape: The main vote choices are the player claiming Healer whose account says they protected the saved player, and the competing Healer claimant who says they protected someone else. The save supports the first account's fit but does not prove that claimant's role; the second claimant's account is in tension with the save, not independently disproven. Other players include an unverified Investigator claimant and a claimed Trailseer whose reported follow is consistent with the Investigator claimant's roleblock account. Public vs private: Privately, you know you made the Serial Killer attacks on the concealed victim on Night 1 and on the player publicly reported saved from a Serial Killer attack on Night 2. Publicly, the village knows those attack reports but not who made them. The save confirms a healer protected the target, not which of the two Healer claimants did so.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.
