The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this decision is a swing point despite the stated worst-case parity distance. Consensus: No clear direction: one player weakly favors eliminating the day 2 accuser, while discussion also focuses on the unverified Investigator claim and the unexplained repeated blocks; no current majority is established. My position: Holding no expressed position: you have not stated a vote preference in today’s discussion. lessons.situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.
lessons.action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.

lessons.situation: With four players alive and one wolf left, a claimed vigilante demands the speculator's role while the claimed sentinel and claimed trailseer accuse each other over contradictory logs. Information landscape: Information-rich in confirmed dead roles, but the key conflict is between unverified claims, and a rules-confusion slip is being treated as proof. Stakes: At four alive with one wolf left, a wrong elimination likely hands the wolves the win. Pushing a mis-vote also exposes the speculator to a night shot. Consensus: The room leans toward whoever the credible shooter points at. It is tied up in the conflicting tracking logs and is pressuring the speculator for transparency. My position: Driving: pushing the accusation of one of the conflicting claimants to deflect heat. Heat: High: a credible claimed role singled the speculator out as a suspect for withholding its role all game. Target landscape: Two claimed roles, for example a sentinel and a trailseer, with logs that conflict, plus the speculator, who is being pressed for a role. The vigilante's shot gives it credibility, while the sentinel's and trailseer's results are unverified claims.
lessons.action: When a claimed role demands your role while two others trade accusations over conflicting logs, don't build the case on a rule-confusion or a thin data gap. Test the contradiction against the rules, for example whether a watch counts as a visit and who could have seen what. Back the elimination only if the mechanics actually prove a lie, and otherwise hold your vote for the player whose claim can't be explained.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

That won’t identify the blocker by itself, but it could tell us whether either intended check would have followed up on something already in the discussion. Player_3, if you still favor player_4, what about the day 2 vote makes you think it was more than an unexplained choice?

There are five players alive, not three, and no final-day choice between me and a quiet player.

situations: With five players alive and the previously partnered Illusionist publicly revealed and eliminated, the day’s discussion is information-starved: an unverified Investigator claimant reports two consecutive roleblocks, while the village has no confirmed identity for the blocker. A weak behavioral suspicion of the player behind the lone Day 2 vote has been raised and then walked back, leaving the imminent choice without a settled target. Information landscape: Public facts include the revealed Illusionist, Sentinel, Healer, and Trailseer roles and their announced town wills; the first victim’s role remains concealed. The Investigator’s checks and repeated blocks are player claims, although the Night 2 save of the claimant is confirmed. No surviving player has a publicly confirmed investigative result or other direct identification of a living player’s alignment. Stakes: Five players remain; three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this decision is consequential even though the supplied distance to parity is three. Consensus: There is no clear village consensus. One player briefly favored the person behind the unexplained Day 2 vote, then withdrew that rationale; discussion has instead questioned the significance of the Investigator claimant’s repeated claimed blocks without identifying their source. My position: Not driving a consensus; you have not stated a current position in today’s discussion. Your recorded Day 3 vote was for the player later revealed as Trailseer. Heat: Low on the public record: no one has accused you. Your public Day 3 vote for the player later revealed as Trailseer is recorded, but has not been raised as evidence against you. Forward exposure: A visible accusation or vote would commit you to a public target and could invite scrutiny of your Day 3 vote against the revealed Trailseer. Claiming a role or knowledge about the blocks would be difficult to walk back and could expose your hidden role; your current unclaimed position is comparatively reversible. Target landscape: The weakly proposed target is the behavioral choice of the unexplained Day 2 vote, who is also publicly reported as Not suspicious by the unverified Investigator claim—this rules out neither the lone killer nor deception. The Investigator claimant has two claimed blocked checks and one claimed Not suspicious result; neither their role nor the checks are verified. The other living players have no publicly confirmed role claims or results relevant to choosing among them. Public vs private: Privately, you know you are the surviving Chanteuse and that you blocked the unverified Investigator claimant on both recent nights. Publicly, the claimant says those actions were roleblocked, but no one has identified the blocker; your role and the pack’s actions remain undisclosed.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

This is Day 4, and the current discussion is not broadly aligned on abstaining.
My partner was eliminated yesterday; there is no current partner wagon to join.

situations: With five alive, the village is trying to choose an elimination despite little actionable information: a claimed Investigator reports two consecutive roleblocks and one earlier Not-suspicious result on the agent, while the only stated case against the agent is the revealed Trailseer’s unexplained Day 2 vote. The former Illusionist was eliminated, but a wolf and possibly the lone killer remain. Information landscape: Information-starved. Confirmed facts include the dead Sentinel’s and Trailseer’s roles and wills, the former Illusionist’s revealed role, the healer save on the claimed Investigator, and the public vote records. The Investigator claim and its results are not independently verified; the body concealed on Night 1 remains unknown, and there is no confirmed current alignment result. Stakes: Five players remain; the leading evil faction is 3 eliminations from parity, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination in the worst case for the town, so this vote is a swing decision with potentially immediate game-ending consequences. Consensus: No clear village consensus. One player weakly favors the agent based on the unexplained Day 2 vote; that player has withdrawn the vote as a strong argument. Others are probing the claimed Investigator’s blocked actions, without converging on a target. My position: Under mild pressure but not a settled majority target; the agent has not advanced a competing elimination case in today’s discussion. Heat: Low: the agent is the tentative target of a weak vote preference because the revealed Trailseer voted for the agent on Day 2. No one has presented independent evidence against the agent, and the claimed Investigator’s result, if true, is Not suspicious. Target landscape: The live elimination discussion centers weakly on the player who favored eliminating the agent on Day 2, based only on that vote; the claimed Investigator says that player read Not suspicious, which rules out wolf suspicion if true but does not exclude the lone killer. The claimed Investigator’s two blocked checks are unverified. No other clear candidate is established.

lessons.situation: Final-wolf vote at four alive: the village must eliminate the last wolf now or face parity at night, and the Speculator is one of the two unverified players. Information landscape: Information-rich: the dead Investigator's will clears one player, the Sigilist's abilities are logged and spent, and the lone killer is confirmed dead. Stakes: Eliminating the last wolf wins immediately for Town and for a Town pick, while a miss leaves three alive with parity at night. Consensus: Two confirmed Town players treat the vote as a choice between the two unverified players and are open to a clear case. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the cleared players. Heat: Exposed: the remaining suspect openly pushes to eliminate the agent based on a quiet record, and the confirmed Town players see it as a binary choice. Target landscape: Two unverified players, the Speculator and one suspect who survived earlier scrutiny, among four alive. The other two are cleared or confirmed Town, by a dead Investigator's will and spent, logged abilities. The suspect's push on the Speculator is behavioral, while the confirmed Town players are the deciding votes.
lessons.action: When four are alive, one wolf remains, and the Speculator has picked Town, join the cleared Town players in eliminating the one unverified suspect rather than the other. Ignore the suspect's counter-accusation of you when it rests only on a quiet record, because eliminating the last wolf ends the game with a Town win and your pick wins.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.
lessons.action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.

lessons.situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.
lessons.action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.

verdicts.why: There are five alive, and the Serial Killer is not confirmed dead; this is not the described four-player endgame.
The described four-player dispute between claimed Town roles and confirmed dead Serial Killer does not match this board.
There are five survivors, and no reliable evidence identifies a single evil player at match point.

situations: With five players left, the village is weighing an unverified Investigator claim—whose only reported check cleared one player of being a wolf but not of being the Serial Killer—and a weak suspicion based on that cleared player’s lone Day 2 vote. Privately, I know the claimed Investigator survived my Night 2 attack because the Healer saved them, while my Night 3 attack killed the publicly revealed Healer. My concealment leaves the village without a public link between me and those attacks. Information landscape: Some concrete information exists: public death and vote records, the revealed Healer’s will confirming the save, and the claimed Investigator’s unverified account. The concealed Night 1 victim’s role and the identities behind the remaining unknown roles are unresolved. Information is limited and claims are not independently verified. Stakes: Five players are alive; it is 3 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. A single elimination can end the game at worst for the town, so a wrong vote or kill could be decisive. Consensus: There is no clear consensus on a target. Discussion centered on the unexplained Day 2 vote against the player now claiming Investigator; the person who tentatively favored that voter withdrew the rationale as insufficient. The repeated-block claim has prompted questions but has not established a blocker’s identity. My position: I have not expressed a public position, so I am neither visibly driving nor aligned with a stated majority; no clear majority is forming. Heat: No one has publicly accused me or connected me to a night attack; my role and night actions remain undisclosed. Current direct suspicion on me is low, though the public record includes a Serial Killer attack on the player claiming Investigator. Forward exposure: A visible vote or accusation would commit me to a public position among the remaining candidates; votes are permanent, while discussion can be revised. A claim about night information could expose me to contradictions with the public record or prompt scrutiny of my unverified account. No visible move has yet been made. Target landscape: The choices are the player claiming Investigator, whose Night 1 Not suspicious result on the player who received one Day 2 vote is unverified, and three players with no publicly confirmed roles. One of those unknown-role players briefly favored that vote target, then acknowledged the rationale was weak. The Investigator claim of two blocks is also unverified. Public vs private: Privately, I know I am the Serial Killer and that my attacks killed the concealed victim on Night 1 and the revealed Healer on Night 3; the Night 2 attack on the player claiming Investigator was saved. Publicly, the Night 1 victim’s role remains concealed, and the Night 2 save is attributed to an attack by the Serial Killer, but no attack is publicly linked to me personally. I have made no night-action claim.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

verdicts.why: No one has reported a visit linking me to a night victim, and the vote is not piling onto me.

situations: After the Speculator was eliminated on Day 4, you are the claimed Investigator with one check left and must choose whether to spend it and which living player to check. Your claimed checks on Nights 2 and 3 were blocked, leaving the other three living players as candidates amid unresolved wolf and Serial Killer threats. Information landscape: Information-starved: your private Night 1 result was Not suspicious on the eliminated Speculator, and your actions were blocked on Nights 2 and 3. Publicly, the wolves' kill and the Serial Killer's attack are known from revealed reports, but the concealed Night 1 victim's role remains unknown; no living player's role or alignment is confirmed. Stakes: Four players are alive. The leading evil faction is two eliminations from parity at worst for Town, with the concealed body's side unknown; the game can end within one more elimination at worst for Town, so this decision sits at a swing point. Target landscape: The remaining check can distinguish wolves from non-wolves among the three other living players: one voted to eliminate you, one voted for the eliminated Speculator after previously favoring that vote only weakly, and one questioned the blocked checks. These are behavioral clues, not confirmed role evidence; your Night 1 Not suspicious result cleared only the now-eliminated Speculator of being a wolf, not of being the Serial Killer.

lessons.situation: After the Day 2 vote and a Day 1 or 2 reveal, the voting record shows a few players splitting from the room: defending an eliminated wolf, or pushing to eliminate the Investigator without evidence. One wolf (or the pack's remainder) is likely hiding among them, and the Investigator has one check left. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed wolf or sentinel death is on the record, plus public vote tallies showing clear outliers. No private proof yet, so the final check converts behavioral suspicion into a result. Stakes: The pack is already thinned and one check remains, so the last check is the Investigator's final chance to confirm a wolf. A correct hit can lead to eliminating the remaining wolves and winning, while a wasted check leaves Town without direction. Target landscape: Seven or so living players, with roles of the dead revealed. The best candidates are outlier voters on Day 2: a sole counter-voter defending a revealed wolf, or two voters who coordinated against you while the rest abstained. The basis is public vote behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With your last check, check the player whose Day 2 vote record most clearly diverges from the room: the lone defender of a revealed wolf, or a voter who pushed against you without evidence. Voting records are public and permanent, so these outliers are the likeliest wolf partners, and a Suspicious result gives you a concrete lead to act on.

lessons.situation: Night 1 after a discussion-only Day 1. The Investigator holds both checks and must choose between holding them and probing an unread player blind. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no claims, no votes, no night results. Stakes: Early board with no pressure, so no single check is decisive. But the Investigator may die before a banked check is ever used, and any early read, whether it finds a wolf or clears an ally, compounds into later votes. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, flips or behavioral tells. Pick a quiet, non-prominent player at random, since nothing separates them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no leads, spend one check on a quiet, unclaimed player instead of banking both. An early Suspicious finds a wolf, and a Not suspicious gives you a baseline read. Treat a clean result as clearing only wolves: the Serial Killer and neutrals also read Not suspicious, and a Necromancer reads that way on any night it does not attack.

lessons.situation: The investigator has publicly claimed, survived a counter-claim or a wolf elimination, and is now a primary target for a night kill or roleblock, with one check left. Information landscape: Information-rich: vote records separate those who backed the investigator from those who backed the counter-claimant, and a role contradiction is public. Stakes: The investigator is likely to be killed or blocked tonight, so the final check should go to the highest-value unverified suspect where a result, or a tracker seeing the visit, can still help the village. Target landscape: Players who voted against the true investigator or pushed an aggressive line versus the majority voters and a counter-claimant already confirmed as a liar; the basis is voting record and public behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: After a counter-claim or an elimination that exposes you, put your remaining check on a player whose daytime behavior links them to the exposed wolf, such as someone who voted against you or backed the counter-claimant, rather than on a player already confirmed or about to be removed. This produces a read that can be traced and carried forward even if you die.

verdicts.why: With one check left, player_2 is the clearest outlier after voting to eliminate me despite my public claim.
This is no longer Night 1; the board has revealed roles and a consequential vote record.
I claimed Investigator and survived the Illusionist's elimination, and player_2 voted against me without a concrete contradiction.

situations: After the Speculator’s day-4 elimination, four players remain including you, and the next night kill is a high-stakes choice among three opponents. One survivor’s Investigator claim and repeated block reports are unverified, while the other two have no confirmed role information; the public record does not establish which opponent is the greatest threat to your survival. Information landscape: Information-starved for choosing a target: the Speculator’s role is confirmed, but the concealed night-1 victim’s role and side remain unknown. The surviving Investigator’s claim and block reports are unverified; public votes and discussion provide behavior, not role confirmation. Stakes: Four players are alive; the leading evil faction can win after 2 eliminations, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this decision is immediately consequential, though the exact end-game effect of any particular target is unclear. Forward exposure: A night kill is publicly attributed to the Serial Killer, and the victim’s role and any Town will are revealed unless concealed; the choice does not itself identify the killer. A death is irreversible. Target landscape: Three living opponents remain: one unverified Investigator claimant whose only reported check was Not suspicious on the player later revealed as Speculator and who claims two subsequent blocks; the other two have no known role claims here and are distinguishable only by their discussion and voting behavior.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

verdicts.why: The healer is dead, and no publicly saved investigator remains protected by a known healer.
This is Night 4 with public claims, deaths, and voting records.
Player_9 has not publicly singled out a suspect, and their claimed checks were blocked.

situations: With four players alive after the Speculator's elimination, the final sigil must be weighed against the chance that one of the three other living players attacks tonight. The revealed Illusionist is dead, while the remaining attacker identities are unresolved; both a wolf attack and a Serial Killer attack could make a sigil placed on the attacker strike, but a nonattacking target would consume the last sigil without effect. Information landscape: Information is sparse about the living players' roles and night intentions. Public facts include the Illusionist's elimination, the Speculator's elimination, and the earlier concealed death whose role remains unknown. The claimed Investigator reports a Night 1 Not suspicious result and two later blocks, but no result publicly verifies the claim; the votes provide behavioral evidence, not role confirmation. Your own Night 1 sigil on a living player had no effect, which does not establish that they are harmless. Stakes: Four players are alive, and the leading evil faction is two eliminations from parity at worst for the town; nevertheless, the game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. A wrong elimination or an attack tonight can therefore be immediately decisive, while spending the last sigil on a nonattacker leaves no further sigil available. Forward exposure: Placing the final sigil is a private night action unless it strikes or is reported as having been stopped by the Healer; a strike publicly reveals that a sigil triggered, but not who placed it. The sigil is spent whether or not it has an effect, so the choice is irreversible. Target landscape: The living candidates are an unconfirmed player who voted to eliminate the claimed Investigator, an unconfirmed player who voted to eliminate the eliminated Speculator, and the claimed Investigator, whose check claim is unverified and who reports two consecutive roleblocks. The concealed first-night victim's role remains unknown. No living Vigilante is publicly confirmed; any attacker, including a Vigilante, would be struck if sigiled and they attacked.

lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.

verdicts.why: The revealed illusionist leaves a chanteuse alive, and with one wolf that wolf must carry the kill; player_2 is my strongest behavioral suspect.
That advice concerns the Day 2 abstention, while the board has advanced through two eliminations since then.
There is no current visit list or saved target to distinguish attackers from protectors.

situations: With four players alive after the Speculator was eliminated, you are the sole surviving wolf and the night’s kill carrier. The claimed Investigator says two consecutive checks were blocked; you know you blocked those actions. The other two living players have no publicly confirmed power role. The town has no result identifying the Serial Killer, while the concealed first-night victim’s side remains unknown. Information landscape: Publicly confirmed roles include the eliminated Illusionist, Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer, and Speculator; the first-night victim’s role remains concealed. The Investigator claim and its blocked-action account are unverified, though the public save and the Healer’s revealed will corroborated the reported Night 2 attack on the claimed Investigator. Your private knowledge confirms that you blocked that player on Nights 2 and 3. No private result or public event so far indicates an attack on an immune player. Stakes: Four players are alive; two eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a single elimination or kill can decide whether the town retains a path to victory. Forward exposure: Tonight’s block and pack kill are private actions, but their outcomes may expose the target choices; the block can stop a town action without revealing who placed it. A kill is irreversible. No attack on an immune player has identified the Serial Killer, and no such result has been used. Target landscape: The living candidates include a player claiming Investigator, whose only reported result cleared the eliminated Speculator of being a wolf and whose claimed checks were blocked on two nights; two players whose public evidence is limited to their discussion and voting behavior; and you, the privately known Chanteuse and sole surviving wolf. The former Illusionist is dead. The pack’s target and tonight’s block target have not yet been named, and there is no partner left to coordinate with.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles such as the healer and necromancer are confirmed, and the investigator and trailseer have public claims and results on record. Stakes: Town has lost its healer protection but still has information roles; removing the investigator while blinding the tracker for a night shifts the information balance toward the wolves before parity pressure builds. Forward exposure: Blocking shows the village only that some blocker exists, if the blocked player speaks of it; nothing ties the block to you, and you can switch block targets nightly. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.
lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs.
