Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

decision.message: That role-count logic cuts the other way: if player_3 is the Sigilist, the Serial Killer has to be player_2, since the hidden body accounts for the missing role. The block report doesn’t by itself identify who blocked player_3, so I wouldn’t use it to pin the Chanteuse on anyone yet.

verdicts.why: The roleblock report makes the Chanteuse relevant, but I should keep its source unresolved rather than confirm player_2's suspicion.
Three players remain, but player_2—not a quiet third player—is the strongest alternative suspect given the remaining role claims.
Player_3's account is straightforward; the stronger issue is how the remaining roles fit together.

situations: At three alive, the two other players are jointly accusing you in a potentially decisive vote. Their competing role-count arguments depend on an unverified Sigilist claim, an unverified roleblock report, and the still-concealed first-night role; your privately known Serial Killer identity and attack history are absent from the public case. Information landscape: Information-starved on the decisive role assignments: the first-night victim's role remains concealed, the Sigilist and roleblock are only claimed, and the other opponent has made no role claim. Publicly confirmed deaths establish that the Illusionist, Sentinel, Healer, Trailseer, Speculator, and Investigator are dead; your private attack record confirms your own role and kills. Stakes: Three players remain; one elimination remains until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. A single elimination can end the game at that worst case, so this vote is a swing decision; the eventual end-game result of any particular vote is unclear. Consensus: The two other living players are aligned in accusing you. Their stated bases are the Day 4 vote and competing, unverified role-count arguments; neither has publicly established the hidden roles. My position: You are the focus of the other two players' aligned accusations and are holding out against their case, acknowledging your Day 4 vote was a bad read while disputing that it proves your role. Heat: High: both other living players have accused you, citing your Day 4 vote against the player later revealed as Investigator and disputing your role-count defense. Forward exposure: A public vote for either opponent would permanently record your choice and commit you to a side in the accusation; the vote cannot be taken back. Claiming or discussing night actions could expose you to scrutiny, while your actual attack history remains private. Target landscape: The choice is between the player claiming to be the Sigilist, whose role and reported roleblock are unverified, and the other surviving player, whose role is unknown and whose main public basis for suspicion is their mistaken Day 4 vote against the revealed Investigator. Both are behavioral or claim-based cases, not confirmed roles. Public vs private: Privately, you know you are the Serial Killer and that your attacks killed the concealed first-night victim, the healer, and the revealed Investigator; publicly, you have made no role or night-action claim. The others have no public confirmation of your role, though both are accusing you.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

verdicts.why: No Night 1 visit report is directing the vote; the current pressure comes from role-count claims and my Day 4 vote.

situations: With three players left, a claimed Sigilist says they were roleblocked last night, prompting a role-count dispute: one survivor treats the vote against the revealed Investigator as a reason to suspect the other survivor of being the Serial Killer, while that survivor challenges the inference and both identify me as a possible Chanteuse. The first-night victim's concealed role leaves the count unresolved. Information landscape: Information is sparse and mostly indirect: revealed roles and public votes are confirmed, while the first-night role remains concealed. The Sigilist and roleblock account is claimed publicly; I privately know the block succeeded, but that does not verify the claimant's role. No public evidence resolves the remaining role assignments. Stakes: Three players remain; one elimination from the leading evil faction's win in the worst case for the town, and the game can end within one more elimination. A single vote or kill can therefore flip which faction is winning. Consensus: The room is not aligned. One survivor favors eliminating the player who voted against the Investigator; the other disputes that vote as proof and questions the assumptions behind the role-count argument. My position: Holding out from an established consensus; I have not publicly stated a vote or role claim in today's discussion. Heat: Meaningful suspicion: both other survivors have said the role-count argument makes me a plausible Chanteuse, though neither has established it as fact. Forward exposure: Publicly pressing the Serial Killer interpretation commits me to treating the player who voted against the revealed Investigator as the likely lone killer; that could redirect suspicion away from me but is a visible, only partly reversible position. My current suspicion as a possible Chanteuse has already been raised publicly. Target landscape: The choice is between the player who voted to eliminate the now-confirmed Investigator, whom the claimed Sigilist accuses and the other survivor argues could be the Serial Killer, and the claimed Sigilist, whose role remains unverified. The first case rests on voting behavior and role-count inference; the second is also uncertain because the hidden first-night death's role is unknown. Public vs private: The Illusionist partner was publicly revealed when eliminated. The village knows a player claiming Sigilist reported being roleblocked; privately, I know my block on that player succeeded, but the claim does not establish their role. I also know my own Chanteuse role.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

verdicts.why: No current trailseer accusation or abstention consensus; only two opponents remain.
This is no longer an early, information-poor day where abstaining is available.
The exposed wolf partner is already dead, and the current vote is between the two remaining opponents.

situations: Day 2 begins after the wolves killed a player revealed as the Investigator and the Serial Killer killed a player revealed as the Trailseer on night 1. With two town information roles confirmed dead and no discussion yet, the village faces its first vote without any public leads or established conflict. Information landscape: Publicly, the two night deaths and their revealed Town roles are confirmed; there are no public claims, findings, accusations, or other leads yet. Your Fortune Teller bet result is private and supplies no public evidence. Stakes: Eight players are alive, and the leading evil faction needs four eliminations to reach parity; a single vote or kill cannot end the game or flip which faction is winning. Consensus: There is no expressed village consensus: no messages have been made today. My position: You have expressed no position and are neither driving nor opposing a forming majority. Heat: No suspicion or accusations have been expressed against you; the discussion has not started. Target landscape: The eight living players are all potential vote candidates; none has made a public role claim or been distinguished by evidence or behavior yet.

lessons.situation: An early day after a night kill, with no wolf-kill leads or checks revealed. One investigative claimant has reported a non-visit result and the village is just starting to interpret night movements. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single dead player and one claimed no-visit result, with no investigative checks, caught lies or voting record to go on. Stakes: Early game with plenty of cushion; no single vote or kill flips the game. The aim is to stay alive for more night bets while adding no suspicion, since there is little to gain from pushing a read now. Consensus: Calm and undirected. Players echo each other's observations, with no accusation forming and a leaning toward abstaining. My position: With the majority. Echoing and refining shared observations, not driving. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the fortune teller. Target landscape: A claimed trailseer or similar reporter clears one quiet player. The other living players have unknown roles and no concrete leads, so there is no basis yet for a behavioral accusation.
lessons.action: When the day opens with little evidence and just one or two claims, agree with the claim and add one modest logical observation, such as which roles a given report cannot cover. Then let others speak, without proposing a target, so the discussion stays calm and you stay unnoticed.

lessons.situation: A day discussion in which night deaths have produced visit reports from claimed trailseer or sentinel players. Those reports point at an accused player or create competing leads, and the fortune teller has no heat and is still working toward two prediction points. Information landscape: Mixed but mostly information-rich: announced deaths and roles, plus claimed visit reports that conflict or are contested. Reports are claims, not announcements, so they can be checked against how the rules treat concealed victims. Stakes: The board is mid-game and not at the brink; one wrong day-vote hurts Town but does not end the game. The fortune teller's own win depends on surviving nights to score points, so staying unnoticed matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is engaged and fairly aligned on dissecting the visit reports. There is no firm lean yet, or it is forming around the accused visitor. It rests on claimed results rather than announced facts. My position: With the majority, not driving. Contributing a summary but taking no hard stance. Heat: None. No one is suspecting or questioning the fortune teller, who is a neutral with no side and reads Not suspicious. Target landscape: Several living players with unverified role claims and visit reports from a claimed trailseer or sentinel; the accused deny or counter-claim. The basis is claimed night results and explanations, not confirmed facts.
lessons.action: With zero heat and no role claim of your own, stay in the analytical middle: restate what each investigative claimant reported, ask the accused to explain their visits, and point out which claims conflict. Hold back from committing to one target until the explanations come in, so you stay a low-profile voter while the village's own evidence does the work.

verdicts.why: The board is information-starved, but there are no claims to build on and this opening round only allows claims, new information, or prior-day challenges.
No living player has shared a visit report, and there are no competing leads to assess.

situations: After the first night, the village begins day 2 with two publicly explained deaths: the wolves killed the revealed Investigator and the Serial Killer killed the revealed Trailseer. The Serial Killer's identity is not publicly established, and no day discussion has begun. Information landscape: Information-starved: the causes and revealed roles of both night deaths are public, and your own attack result is private to you, but there are no public claims, accusations, votes, or other investigative results to distinguish living players. Stakes: Eight players are alive and the leading evil faction is four eliminations from parity, so the board is not at immediate endgame and one result cannot end it. The longer-term consequence of any contemplated move is unclear from the current record. Consensus: There is no expressed discussion or alignment among the living players, so no clear consensus direction is known. My position: No position relative to a forming consensus; none has formed in the public discussion so far. Heat: No suspicion or accusation against you has been expressed; there is no stated behavioral basis for heat yet. Forward exposure: No public move has been made yet. A visible accusation or role claim would create a public commitment; discussion can be revised, but any later vote is public and permanent. Neither would expose your private attack result directly unless you disclosed it. Target landscape: No candidates have been accused or distinguished by public evidence in today's discussion. The seven other living players have unknown roles; your own role is privately known to you. The two revealed dead roles are the Investigator and Trailseer. Public vs private: Privately, you know you attacked the player revealed as the Trailseer; publicly, the village knows that player was killed by the Serial Killer, but has no information identifying you. The other night death was attributed to the wolves and revealed as the Investigator.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

verdicts.why: No one has accused me or linked me to a vote; there has been no vote yet.
Eight players are alive and no one has pointed the room at me.
No Sentinel or Trailseer has made a visit claim in today's discussion.

situations: Day 2 begins with the Investigator and Trailseer already dead from separate night attacks, leaving the village without those information roles and with no public accusations or candidate consensus yet. You privately know your block affected a living player, but that result has no public confirmation. Information landscape: Information-starved for distinguishing among living players: the deaths and their revealed roles are public facts, but no living player has presented a result or other evidence, and your block result is private. Stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations from the leading evil faction's parity threshold; this is not a swing decision, and the game cannot end within one more elimination. The immediate end-game consequence of a public position here is unclear. Consensus: No village consensus has formed: there have been no messages or accusations today. My position: No expressed public position yet; there is no forming consensus to align with or oppose. Heat: No suspicion on you is recorded in the public discussion so far; the day has not yet begun speaking. Forward exposure: Taking a conspicuous lead on a target or claiming a specific read would commit you to a public position despite having no public evidence to support it; that position could be softened later, but the initial alignment signal would remain visible. Target landscape: Eight players are alive, and no target or accusation has been publicly identified today. The two night deaths were revealed as the Investigator and Trailseer; the other living players' roles are unknown. There is no current evidence-based candidate distinction. Public vs private: Privately, you know you blocked one living player last night; the public has no confirmation of that action or result. Publicly confirmed, the wolves killed the Investigator and the Serial Killer killed the Trailseer. No public discussion has begun today.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

verdicts.why: My partner is alive, no Town claimant has reported a block, and the board is not near parity.
There are eight players alive, not three, and no final-day decision is underway.
My partner has not been eliminated and no claimant has spoken or stumbled yet.

situations: Day two opens after the wolves killed the Investigator and the Serial Killer separately killed the Trailseer on night one. Both roles were publicly revealed, but there has been no day-two discussion, accusation, or proposed vote to establish a new conflict. Information landscape: The public has two role-confirmed night deaths, one caused by the wolves and one by the Serial Killer, and no day-two claims or discussion yet. You privately know the pack's kill and your role; no concealment has been used. Stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; this decision cannot end the game with one result, and the longer-term consequence of any as-yet-unmade day-two move is unclear. Consensus: There is no current village consensus: day-two discussion has not begun, and no positions have been expressed today. My position: No day-two position relative to a consensus; none has formed. Your recorded day-one stance supported the pack's target. Heat: No suspicion or accusation against you is present in the current discussion, which has not started. Your day-one support for the player the wolves killed is publicly recorded, but no one has commented on it. Forward exposure: No day-two speech or vote has happened yet. A visible accusation or defense would establish a public position, while the prior day-one support for the pack's target is already on the permanent vote record; neither commits you to a current target. Target landscape: No candidates are currently being accused or proposed for elimination. The Investigator and Trailseer are confirmed dead; the roles of the eight living players are otherwise unknown publicly. Public vs private: Publicly, the wolves' night-one victim was revealed as the Investigator, and a separate player was revealed as the Trailseer killed by the Serial Killer. Privately, you know the pack's kill and that you are the Illusionist; no partner has been revealed.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

verdicts.why: No partner has been publicly revealed and no one is tying me to a vote.
This is day two with eight alive, not a four-player endgame.
No one has shared tracking claims or results yet.

situations: After the first night killed the Investigator to the wolves and the Trailseer to the Serial Killer, a player claiming Sentinel offered a visit result involving the dead Trailseer. The claim gives the room a possible lead, but no one has yet challenged it or formed a voting direction. Information landscape: Information is limited. The deaths and revealed roles are system-confirmed, while the Sentinel identity and reported visit are only claimed; no private night findings are public or independently verified. Stakes: With 8 players alive and 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, this decision is not immediately decisive: a single vote or kill does not flip which faction is winning, though a wrong elimination still reduces the room for error. Consensus: There is no clear village consensus: the only substantive contribution is an unverified Sentinel claim, with no stated vote direction or broader alignment. My position: Neither driving nor visibly aligned with a majority; you have not spoken, and no majority position is apparent. Heat: No suspicion has been expressed toward you in the discussion provided; you have made no public statements that could draw scrutiny. Forward exposure: A visible claim or accusation would commit you to a public account that could be compared with later claims and evidence. Your current silence makes no such commitment; its reversibility is high, though later explanations may be scrutinized. Target landscape: A player claiming Sentinel says the revealed Trailseer visited the player they watched. That claim is unverified, and the watched player has no stated role or accusation against them. No other candidate or evidence-based target has been identified in the discussion so far. Public vs private: Solo concealment: publicly, you have made no claim or statement about the first night. Privately, you know you killed the player later revealed as the Trailseer; the village knows that player died to the Serial Killer but not who the killer is.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

decision.message: That result tells us player_8 visited player_9, but it doesn’t show who attacked player_8. Since player_8 was the Trailseer, the visit could simply have been their follow action; player_9 isn’t implicated by that alone. I’d like to hear whether anyone else has a result that helps narrow down the Night 1 kills.

verdicts.why: player_3 named player_8 as a visitor to player_9, not me as a visitor to the Night 1 victim.
No one has accused me of passivity or tied me to a dead wolf's vote.
There are eight players alive and no case has been made against me.

situations: After the wolves killed a revealed Investigator and the Serial Killer killed a revealed Trailseer on Night 1, a player claiming Sentinel said the Trailseer visited another survivor. A second speaker noted that this could have been the Trailseer's follow action and does not establish who attacked them. The room has no current vote target, leaving the next likely death and your own exposure uncertain. Information landscape: Information-starved: the Night 1 deaths and roles are confirmed, but there are no public wills or verified living-player results. The Sentinel's visit report is an unverified claim, and even if accurate it does not identify the attacker. Stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; a single vote or kill cannot flip which faction is winning, though the early information vacuum makes the next death and any resulting evidence consequential. Consensus: No clear direction: the discussion has not formed an accusation or aligned around a candidate. The only shared point is that the Sentinel claimant's reported visit does not by itself implicate the visited player. My position: Not driving or holding out against a consensus; you have not publicly taken a position. Heat: No suspicion or accusation is directed at you in the discussion so far; your Fortune Teller role and zero points are private. Target landscape: No elimination candidates have been publicly advanced. The Sentinel claim is unverified; the dead Investigator and Trailseer were role-revealed by the game master.

lessons.situation: An early day after a night kill, with no wolf-kill leads or checks revealed. One investigative claimant has reported a non-visit result and the village is just starting to interpret night movements. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single dead player and one claimed no-visit result, with no investigative checks, caught lies or voting record to go on. Stakes: Early game with plenty of cushion; no single vote or kill flips the game. The aim is to stay alive for more night bets while adding no suspicion, since there is little to gain from pushing a read now. Consensus: Calm and undirected. Players echo each other's observations, with no accusation forming and a leaning toward abstaining. My position: With the majority. Echoing and refining shared observations, not driving. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the fortune teller. Target landscape: A claimed trailseer or similar reporter clears one quiet player. The other living players have unknown roles and no concrete leads, so there is no basis yet for a behavioral accusation.
lessons.action: When the day opens with little evidence and just one or two claims, agree with the claim and add one modest logical observation, such as which roles a given report cannot cover. Then let others speak, without proposing a target, so the discussion stays calm and you stay unnoticed.

lessons.situation: A day discussion in which night deaths have produced visit reports from claimed trailseer or sentinel players. Those reports point at an accused player or create competing leads, and the fortune teller has no heat and is still working toward two prediction points. Information landscape: Mixed but mostly information-rich: announced deaths and roles, plus claimed visit reports that conflict or are contested. Reports are claims, not announcements, so they can be checked against how the rules treat concealed victims. Stakes: The board is mid-game and not at the brink; one wrong day-vote hurts Town but does not end the game. The fortune teller's own win depends on surviving nights to score points, so staying unnoticed matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is engaged and fairly aligned on dissecting the visit reports. There is no firm lean yet, or it is forming around the accused visitor. It rests on claimed results rather than announced facts. My position: With the majority, not driving. Contributing a summary but taking no hard stance. Heat: None. No one is suspecting or questioning the fortune teller, who is a neutral with no side and reads Not suspicious. Target landscape: Several living players with unverified role claims and visit reports from a claimed trailseer or sentinel; the accused deny or counter-claim. The basis is claimed night results and explanations, not confirmed facts.
lessons.action: With zero heat and no role claim of your own, stay in the analytical middle: restate what each investigative claimant reported, ask the accused to explain their visits, and point out which claims conflict. Hold back from committing to one target until the explanations come in, so you stay a low-profile voter while the village's own evidence does the work.

verdicts.why: It is still early and the Sentinel report is only a claim, so there is little reason to push a target.
There is one Sentinel claim, but no competing reports or accused player to analyze.
Two players died and the only report is a claimed Sentinel result, not a claimed no-visit result.
A claimed Sentinel report is being discussed, but it gives no firm reason to accuse anyone; stay low-profile.

situations: A player claiming Sentinel reports that the now-dead Trailseer visited you on Night 1, and another speaker cautions that this does not show who attacked the Trailseer. The visit puts you in the discussion without establishing a reason for suspicion, while your Illusionist role and knowledge of the wolves’ kill remain private. Information landscape: Information is sparse. The Investigator’s and Trailseer’s roles and causes of death are confirmed publicly. The claimed Sentinel result is unverified; it supplies a visit link, not the identity of the Trailseer’s attacker. You privately know your own role and the pack’s target. Stakes: Eight players are alive and the leading evil faction is four eliminations from parity; the board cannot end within one more elimination, so this decision is consequential but not immediately game-ending. Consensus: No clear direction. The only expressed point is that the claimed visit does not identify who attacked the Trailseer; there is no stated vote consensus. My position: No public position expressed yet; you are not visibly driving or opposing a forming consensus. Heat: Low but newly present: you are named as the person visited in an unverified Sentinel claim, while another speaker says that visit alone does not implicate you. Forward exposure: Publicly addressing the visit claim would put your connection to the reported visit at the center of discussion; endorsing the claim’s interpretation or disputing it would be visible and could be revisited. Your current silence commits you to no interpretation. Target landscape: You are the subject of the claimed visit, but the public account does not establish your role or guilt. The other named participant is dead and confirmed as the Trailseer. No living vote target or competing accusation has yet emerged. Public vs private: The public knows the Investigator was killed by the wolves and the Trailseer by the Serial Killer. A player claiming Sentinel says the dead Trailseer visited you; you privately know you are the Illusionist and know the pack killed the Investigator. Your role and the pack’s kill are not publicly established.

lessons.situation: A trailseer claims to have seen the illusionist visit a player who died that night with a hidden role, and the illusionist has to answer in daytime discussion. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed death with a hidden role plus a direct tracking report that matches what the illusionist actually did. Stakes: An elimination of the illusionist here leaves the surviving wolf alone and closer to losing, so avoid a flat denial that the room can disprove. Consensus: The majority takes the tracker's findings at face value; only a couple of players are confused about how concealment affects visits. My position: opposing the forming consensus Heat: Critical; directly accused of visiting a murder victim on the night they died. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits you to calling the trailseer a liar and rules out any later switch to a benign visiting claim. A benign-visit explanation stays open and can be adjusted if the town pushes back. Target landscape: The accused visitor (you) against the single claimed tracker; the town has no competing account of the night, so the report counts as hard eyewitness evidence. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the reported visit is true, because it concealed the body, while publicly it insists it never left home.
lessons.action: When a trailseer or sentinel report places you at the door of a victim whose role was hidden, do not flatly deny the visit. Offer a benign reason for being out that night (for example, a claim of a visiting town role, or that you checked on that player), and stress that the report only shows a visit, not who attacked. Do not claim that illusionist concealment makes the report invalid: if you were not the carrier, your own visit to hide the body is still seen, and a flat denial against a tracker report the town trusts loses you the room.

lessons.situation: A sentinel or trailseer publicly lists the illusionist among several visitors to one player, creating a risk of an investigation trap. Information landscape: Fairly rich in visit data from several claimed watchers, but nothing is verified by deaths and the data converges on an odd target. Stakes: A single named-visitor result could expose the pack on day 2; defusing it keeps both wolves alive and the vote at abstain. Consensus: The village treats the multi-visit pile-up as a puzzle and has no single suspect, so it leans toward abstaining. My position: with majority Heat: Moderate: explicitly named by a sentinel as a visitor, diluted by other claimants reporting the same visits. Forward exposure: Admitting a visit commits the illusionist to being a visiting role in later claims, and it is only partly reversible. Avoiding a specific role claim keeps flexibility. Target landscape: The quiet visited player and the other visitors defending their own overlapping actions. All are unverified claimants, and the evidence is visit lists rather than behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the visit was the wolf kill or another wolf action, whereas the town sees an inexplicable convergence of visits on one quiet player.
lessons.action: When a claimed watch or tracking result names your partner or you as a visitor, acknowledge only the visit that cannot be disproved. Frame it as a casual check-in and point the room at the strangest part of the data, such as several players visiting the same target. This keeps your claim consistent with the visits other players can report while avoiding a specific role claim.

lessons.situation: A claimed watcher or tracker reports visits to a player who survived or died, and I (a wolf-side illusionist) am among the visitors named or about to be exposed. Information landscape: Information-rich: visit reports, an attack that was thwarted or a body, and several role claims on the table, though none verified. Stakes: Mid-game with a wolf exposed by a visit report; a single failed explanation risks a vote on me, while a convincing cover keeps the wolf pack on course toward parity. Consensus: The room is information-rich and willing to act on visit reports, but has not settled on who is lying; it accepts any claim that plausibly explains the visits. My position: Driving; I set the narrative right after the report by claiming first and redirecting focus. Heat: High; named as a visitor at a sensitive door by a claimed night-information role on the exact night of the event. Forward exposure: A fake role claim locks me in publicly and guarantees a collision if the genuine role-holder is alive; it is hard to retract, but it buys immediate safety and can set up removing the real role-holder. Target landscape: The unverified observer who reported visits, the genuine role-holder whose action matches my claim, and the surviving target; the observer's claim is unverified while my cover story is plausible. Public vs private: Privately I know the visit was a wolf action (kill attempt or ability use), but publicly the visit must be framed as a Town role's action to explain being seen.
lessons.action: When an unverified watcher or follower reports your visit at a victim's or target's door and you are exposed, immediately claim a Town role whose action explains that visit (e.g. Healer protecting the target), and tie it to the night's outcome. If the claim fits the report and the room accepts it, steer the town toward the player who raised the report, and plan the later collision with the real role-holder.

decision.message: Player_3, what made you choose to watch me last night? Player_8 following me would fit the result, but it still doesn’t tell us whether they saw anything useful or who attacked them.

verdicts.why: Player_8's role was revealed, and no one reports that I visited a hidden-role victim.
The report names player_8 as visiting me, not me among several visitors to a target.
I was the watched target, not a visitor named in the result.

situations: A player claiming Sentinel says the dead, revealed Trailseer visited their watched target on Night 1. The target questions why they were watched, while another player and the claimant both stress that the visit could have been a follow and does not identify the Trailseer’s attacker. This leaves your privately known partner connected to the claim but not publicly accused. Information landscape: Night 1 deaths and their revealed roles are public fact: the wolves killed the Investigator and the Serial Killer killed the Trailseer. The Sentinel result is a player’s unverified claim; there are no announced visitor records, confirmed investigative findings, or other concrete evidence identifying either attacker. Stakes: Eight players are alive, and four eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so this discussion is consequential but is not an immediate parity point. Consensus: There is limited agreement that the claimed visit does not establish who killed the Trailseer. The room has not formed a clear direction about whom to eliminate. My position: You have not spoken publicly and are not visibly driving or opposing a position; the discussion’s limited shared view is that the visitor result alone is inconclusive. Heat: No suspicion has been directed at you in the discussion so far; you have made no public claim or night-result statement. Forward exposure: Publicly echoing the dismissal of the visitor link would align you with the current discussion and commit you to treating it as weak evidence; that stance could be revised if stronger results emerge, but an explicit defense of the watched player would be more conspicuous. Target landscape: The watched player is linked to the dead, revealed Trailseer only by the unverified Sentinel’s claimed visitor result; the discussion has offered no evidence that the watched player attacked anyone. No other candidate has been advanced with concrete evidence, and no vote is underway. Public vs private: Privately, you know the pack killed the revealed Investigator and that your wolf partner is the player publicly linked to the dead Trailseer by the Sentinel claim. Publicly, the Sentinel’s claimed result is being treated as a possible Trailseer follow, not as evidence that the watched player caused the Trailseer’s death. Your block on another living player has not been disclosed.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

situations: A player claiming Sentinel reports that the dead Trailseer visited the watched player on Night 1.
