lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

The Sentinel claim is unverified, and its reported visit is compatible with the Trailseer's role. Stakes: Eight players are alive and the leading evil faction needs four eliminations to reach parity; a single vote or kill cannot end the game, though an unsupported elimination could still cost the village a scarce player. Consensus: No clear direction. The discussion treats the claimed Sentinel's result cautiously and is seeking additional information; no vote target has been established. lessons.situation: The village is about to eliminate a wolf in an information-rich endgame where only one wolf would remain. Town can then win at night through a sigil strike or another kill. The fortune teller has not yet scored its second point. Information landscape: Rich. There is a prior Serial Killer elimination, night-one tracking testimony, and a sigil result, but no certainty about which evil is left. Stakes: Town is close to a win. lessons.action: Before voting, count your points. If you have fewer than two and the leading candidate is a wolf whose removal would leave Town one elimination from winning, abstain if it is offered. If abstaining is not offered, vote for the least-supported candidate who is not a confirmed evil player, so the game runs long enough for your bets to score. A Town win ends the game before you can reach two points.

lessons.situation: Late in the game, the town's power roles are mostly confirmed or consistent with each other. The vote has narrowed to me versus one other unverified player, and I must choose between abstaining and voting the rival. Information landscape: Info-rich: role claims cover the town slots, saves and night results corroborate the town roles, and the public voting record is visible. The only open question is who among the unverified players is the lone killer or a wolf. Stakes: With few players left, one elimination changes the balance of power. My death ends my scoring chances, since a day vote never scores, so I must use my vote to split the count or push the real threat out. Consensus: The village is largely unified, on role-claim bookkeeping and corroborated night results, that the leftover unverified players are the problem. Neutral is treated as expendable. My position: holding out Heat: Extreme: several players, including confirmed town power roles, have declared votes against me because I am an expendable neutral once the town slots are claimed or corroborated. Target landscape: Two or three unverified players: me, an outed neutral fortune teller, and a rival with an unverified or contested claim (e.g. a vigilante or sentinel claimant suspected of being the lone killer). Every other living player holds a role corroborated by night events. The basis is process of elimination, not hard evidence on the rival.
lessons.action: When the room has already stacked elimination votes on you, cast your vote on the other leading suspect, the player with the least verified role or night results. An abstention lowers no one's count and can't force a tie, while a vote on the rival adds to a split or tie that could leave no one eliminated, and it pressures a plausible lone killer or wolf. If the votes against you are already a locked majority, the vote still goes to the rival rather than to nobody.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.
lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

verdicts.why: No confirmed role information or concrete contradiction points to a living player.
The claims and vote provide no verified lead, so preserve both bullets rather than shoot speculatively.

situations: After the village abstained on a three-vote push to eliminate the Sigilist, the night action decision is whether to spend a sigil despite having no identified attacker. The unverified Sentinel claim says the revealed Trailseer visited a player, a result compatible with the Trailseer's follow action and not evidence of an attack. Information landscape: Information-starved: the Investigator and Trailseer were revealed dead, and the Sentinel result is an unverified claim that identifies a visit but not an attacker. No surviving player has provided confirmed evidence identifying a likely attacker. Stakes: Eight players are alive and the leading evil faction needs four eliminations to reach parity; this is not a swing decision, and one mistaken sigil expenditure is costly but does not make the game end within one more elimination. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden, irreversible expenditure of one sigil and creates a visit; if the target attacks, the strike may be publicly revealed through a sigil death, but the original attack still resolves unless separately stopped. Target landscape: The options are the living players: one unverified Sentinel claimant whose account is consistent with the revealed Trailseer's role, and other living players with no publicly confirmed attacker status. There is no evidence-based attacker identification; any target choice rests on behavior or a guess about who may attack tonight.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.

lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

verdicts.why: There were night deaths, but no reliable visitor evidence identifying an attacker; spending a sigil on a guess risks wasting it.
Wolves remain, but the carrier is unknown and no suspect is narrowed enough to target.
Day 2 ended in abstention, but the votes against me are not enough to establish that any voter is an attacker.

situations: After the village abstained on day 2, no one was eliminated and the vote record contains no decisive consensus. At night, the wolves and lone killer can each attack; the public Sentinel claimant may be exposed, but there is no confirmed target. I have 0 points and two self-bets remaining, so the decision is between predicting another player's death and using a self-bet that would make me immune to attacks but earn no points. Information landscape: Information-starved: the Investigator and Trailseer were revealed dead, and the Sentinel claim and visitor result are unverified. There is no public attack pattern or confirmed role evidence pointing to tonight's victim; any victim or role prediction is uncertain. Stakes: With 8 alive and 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, tonight's death does not make the game immediately endable by one more elimination. A correct death bet advances my separate point goal, while a self-bet trades that chance for protection; the faction balance is not on a one-action knife edge. Target landscape: The exposed player claiming Sentinel is a plausible night target because of the public claim, but that role is unverified. Other living players have no confirmed roles from the public record; there is no clear evidence identifying a likely victim or their role. Betting on myself would prevent an attack on me but score no points that night.

lessons.situation: Last wolf voted out and three players left. A lone killer (the necromancer, who can attack through a reanimated body) wins by killing one more player, so the Fortune Teller is a live kill target and no other player's death is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead, the dead roles are confirmed, and the remaining Town sigilist is confirmed out of sigils. This makes the only remaining attacker and its available bodies clear. Stakes: The lone killer wins if anyone else dies tonight, so a bet that fails to cover your own life can end the game with the Fortune Teller short of two points. A self-bet keeps you alive for another night. Target landscape: The suspected necromancer (alive and holding a usable body, so unlikely to die), a confirmed sigilist with no sigils left (no threat), or a self-bet. Roles are confirmed from the graveyard, and nothing makes the suspect likely to die tonight.
lessons.action: With three alive and a lone killer that can attack, you are one of only two possible victims. If no other victim is predictable, spend a self-bet, because an attack on you fails that night. Don't bet on the suspected killer: a killer that is immune or about to win is unlikely to die, and a wrong bet leaves you open to the attack.

lessons.situation: Late game with the wolves dead or nearly dead and one killer left (serial killer, necromancer or last wolf). The Fortune Teller stands at 0-1 points and needs a death, and the most obvious target is publicly protected, so a bet on them fails to the save or the killer switches targets. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of the dead wolves are confirmed, claims and protection histories are public, and the surviving killer's identity or kill pattern is mostly known. Stakes: Few players remain and the game can end any night. Each night spent without scoring risks being voted out or the game finishing before the second point, so the bet must follow where the killer can actually kill, not just where it wants to. Target landscape: The investigator or leader shielded by a public healer claim, the claimed healer who is exposed, other claimed power roles (sigilist, sentinel, trailseer), and unconfirmed players. Hard evidence of who is protected, not behavior, drives the choice.
lessons.action: When the healer has publicly announced protecting the obvious top target (the confirmed or claimed investigator), place the bet on the next-most-valuable unshielded Town role the surviving killer must remove, such as the claimed healer or another power role. If the killer's last pick is predictable, name that role in the bet for the two-point payoff.

lessons.situation: Night one after a discussion-only opening day. Several killers (wolves, and possibly a lone killer) will each attack someone, and no public mechanical constraint limits their choices. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigative findings, deaths, confirmed roles, or vote record exist. Stakes: Very low board pressure. A miss costs nothing but a night, and multiple attackers raise the chance that the chosen player dies. A hit on night one puts the win one successful bet away. Target landscape: All other living players, with no public claims, revealed alignments, or voting history to separate them. Any pick is close to a random draw among the candidates.
lessons.action: On a night with no evidence at all (no claims, no deaths, no votes), bet on any one quiet living player without naming a role, since the bet scores on any death by any cause. Keep both self-bets unspent for later nights when you may become a target.

verdicts.why: Seven players remain, and the specific three-player endgame situation does not apply.
There is no public healer protection claim or clear late-game killer target.
This is not the information-starved first night: two deaths and several unverified claims are on record.

situations: After the day’s vote ended in abstention, no one was eliminated and the village enters another night with little concrete direction. Your first watch showed that the player later revealed as the Trailseer visited the player you watched; that fits the Trailseer’s follow action and does not identify either killer. The player with the vague no-result response remains a mild behavioral concern, while your last watch is still unused. Information landscape: Information-starved: the Trailseer’s revealed role makes the witnessed visit unsurprising, but it supplies no evidence about the attackers. The Investigator and Trailseer are confirmed dead, and no living player has offered a publicly verified night result. The recent vote record and vague response are behavioral evidence only. Stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain before the leading evil faction can reach its win condition; a single vote or kill does not flip which faction is winning, so the board is not yet at an immediate parity threshold, though the loss of two information roles leaves the village with fewer confirmed sources. Target landscape: The remaining watch could be placed on any living player. The player who received the Trailseer’s visit is not implicated by that fact alone; the player who gave a vague account of having no result drew three votes, but that is behavioral evidence, not a role-confirming result. Your own Sentinel claim is public but unverified.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night after an abstain or tied vote. Conflicting role claims are on the board and you hold one watch left. You must decide whose door to watch, knowing results come only from visitors to that player. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, vote records and some prior night results, but nothing is verified. Alignments of the candidates are unconfirmed, and visit data exists only for whoever you watch. Stakes: Town can still afford a mistake, but this is the last watch, so a wasted use leaves no visitor-tracking for the rest of the game. A watch that exposes a visit pattern or kill trace can settle a claim fight before wolves reach parity. Target landscape: The choice is between a contested claimant (e.g. counter-claimed investigator or sigilist) under heavy suspicion, the obvious wolf-priority targets (claimed investigator, healer, trailseer), a quiet player from a tied vote, or an investigator-cleared player. The claim conflicts are public, but none of the candidates is verified. Only the contested claimant or the likely kill target is likely to draw visits.
lessons.action: With your last watch, pick the player most likely to receive a visit tonight. That means a contested or heavily accused claimant whose claim other roles can verify or attack, or the likely wolf kill target. A watch on a quiet suspect or an already-cleared player usually returns "no visitors", because attackers visit their victims, not themselves.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. The Night 1 kill, a possible roleblock and the lone killer's attack can all land the same night, so the result may be lost, show nothing, or catch a key visitor. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no night results, no claims and no voting record. Only opening-round chatter exists. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive, so one blind watch is a cheap bet. Results across the cluster varied: zero visitors, a visit from the healer or trailseer, a multi-visitor cluster, and the serial killer caught at the door. The cost is that the Sentinel itself may be killed or blocked that night and the result lost, so only one of the two charges should be committed. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes or role flips. Every door is equally unknown, so choose a quiet, unpressured player on pure behavior, since there is no evidence to separate them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, deaths or reads, spend one of the two watches on a quiet, unclaimed player and keep the second for later. A watch can catch the killer's visit or reveal who is acting at night, and the visitor list is the only hard evidence a Sentinel can gather before Day 2. Pick a target the pack or the lone killer might plausibly hit, not a loud player who is likely to draw heat.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, with the first watch already spent and one watch left. The Sentinel is deciding whether to use it on a personal adversary or hold it for a higher-value door. Every watch is a visit, and the Sentinel is not told of its own visit. Information landscape: Still thin: the Night 1 result is the main hard fact, plus a few public claims and one vote record. There are no confirmed wolf identities, so targeting rests on likely attack paths and not on proof. Stakes: The last watch is the Sentinel's final hard evidence, and once it is spent the role has nothing left to do at night. Spending it on a low-traffic door gave nothing in the cluster, so a likely-attack target improves the chance of a usable visitor list. Target landscape: A handful of living players: a prominent claimed or confirmed Town role, a player who has accused you, and quiet unverified players. Favor the one most likely to be attacked or visited, based on public claims or revealed roles, over one picked because they are hostile to you.
lessons.action: Save the last watch for a night when you can name a door that is likely to be attacked or visited, such as a prominent claimed role or a player the wolves or killer plausibly want dead. A watch on a vocal accuser or a quiet bystander tends to return a zero-visitor result, and a watch is spent whether or not it shows anything.

verdicts.why: The last-watch and post-abstention context partly fits, but there are no conflicting role claims; player_4 is the most likely target for attention after receiving the leading votes.
This is not Night 1; I have already used one watch and the board has a death and a public vote record.
This is my last watch, and player_4 drew the most votes, making them a plausible target for visits tonight.

situations: After an information-poor opening, three players voted to eliminate the same player while most others abstained, leaving everyone alive. The proposed target has no result-based accusation against them; a claimed Sentinel's report that the dead Trailseer visited another player is consistent with the Trailseer follow action and does not independently implicate the visitor's target. Information landscape: Information-starved: the Investigator and Trailseer were publicly revealed dead, and their wills provide no further evidence here. The Sentinel claim and its visitor result are unverified; no public attack or save was announced for the player you protected, which does not establish whether they were targeted. Stakes: Eight players are alive and it takes four eliminations for the leading evil faction to reach parity; this decision is not immediately decisive, and one mistaken elimination or kill does not by itself flip which faction is winning. Target landscape: Protection value × predicted threat: the player who drew three elimination votes is behaviorally exposed, but no night attack or save involving them is publicly confirmed; the player claiming Sentinel has an unverified visitor result, while other living players have no established role claims in this exchange. Your own protection of the vote-target produced no announced attack or save.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.

lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

verdicts.why: The Serial Killer is alive, and no Town role has produced a result that exposes an evil player.
No evil death has corroborated a Town power role's result; the only revealed deaths are Town roles.
The Serial Killer is still alive, and no killer identity is established.

situations: After a day-two abstention, the game has entered a night with no elimination: three voters targeted a player who said they had no result to share, while most others abstained. Separately, a claimed Sentinel reported that the deceased Trailseer visited another player, but that visit alone does not establish who attacked the Trailseer or implicate the visited player. Information landscape: Information-starved: the Investigator and Trailseer are confirmed dead, the only living role claim is an unverified Sentinel claim, and the Trailseer’s visit to a player does not identify the attacker. The vote provides behavioral evidence of a three-person push, not role evidence. Stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain before the leading evil faction can win, so this is not a one-result swing and the game cannot end within one more elimination. The target’s removal changes the board, but the supplied parity distance does not make this single decision immediately decisive. Forward exposure: A night attack is not a public commitment to a named target or to your role; the morning report identifies the kind of attacker, while visit evidence could expose a trace. No current evidence links you to the Night 1 death. Target landscape: The leading choice is between the player who drew three elimination votes but gave no confirmed night result, the player visited by the deceased Trailseer according to an unverified Sentinel claim, and other living players with no public role confirmation. The Investigator and Trailseer are system-confirmed dead; the Sentinel claim remains unverified.

lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

verdicts.why: There is no claimed Investigator or check clearing me; the Investigator is publicly dead.
This is not the opening night; we have a death, a Sentinel claim, and a vote record.
No town leader was publicly saved or confirmed by a wolf flip.

situations: As the Chanteuse and tonight's pack carrier, you face a private coordination decision about a pack kill and a block while the public discussion centers on an unverified Sentinel claim: the claimant says a dead Trailseer visited the player they watched. A player who was roleblocked by you last night says they were not told they were blocked, creating a public inconsistency without establishing that player's role. No night-two results exist yet. Information landscape: Information is sparse. Publicly confirmed facts are the wolf killing of the Investigator, the Serial Killer killing of the Trailseer, and the day-two abstention. The Sentinel claim and its visit result are unverified claims. Privately, you know you blocked the player who denied being roleblocked last night; that player’s claimed experience conflicts with your knowledge. The pack has not yet named tonight’s target, and there is no known immune-target attack result. Stakes: With 8 players alive and 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, this night is not immediately decisive: the game cannot end within one more elimination, and a single result does not flip which faction is winning. Forward exposure: Publicly pressing the player who said they were not roleblocked would commit you to treating that inconsistency as meaningful, but it would not reveal your role or private knowledge; the claim remains reversible as an interpretation. Your actual block and pack target are private tonight. Target landscape: The unverified Sentinel claimant is a plausible town night-action target to block, though their claimed watch result is not independently confirmed. The player who denied being roleblocked is another possible block target, but their role and whether they acted are unknown. The pack has not named its kill target; living players are candidates, with no public role confirmation that identifies a preferred target. The night-one wolf kill of the Investigator and Serial Killer kill of the Trailseer are system-confirmed. No attack on a night-immune player has identified the Serial Killer, and no such probe is known to have been used.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information.
