lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

situations: With five players alive and the Serial Killer already eliminated, the day vote is centered on whether to eliminate a player whose visit to the revealed Sigilist was reported by a claimed Sentinel. The confirmed Serial Killer was also reported there, so the visit establishes presence but not which visitor attacked; the accused's unexplained visit is compatible with suspicion but is not a publicly verified wolf action. Information landscape: Information is limited but consequential: the Investigator and Trailseer died on Night 1, the claimed Sentinel says both watches are spent, and the revealed Serial Killer's visit accounts for one reported visitor. The other visitor's purpose remains unknown. The concealed Night 3 death provides no public role or will, though you privately know that player was the Fortune Teller. Stakes: Five players are alive, and parity is one elimination away at worst for the town; a wrong elimination of a non-wolf could leave the two wolves at parity, so this vote can decide whether the game continues or ends. Consensus: A majority is forming around eliminating the accused visitor: three players have explicitly said they would vote for them, citing the claimed visit and the possibility of a wolf block. The accused disputes that the visit establishes its purpose, while one other player has echoed your caution. My position: Holding out from the emerging majority in public: you have emphasized that the visit does not identify what the accused did, without publicly defending them as harmless. Heat: Low: no one has accused you, and your public comments have cautioned against treating the visit as proof rather than drawing suspicion to yourself. Forward exposure: A vote for the accused partner would visibly join the emerging majority and commit you to eliminating them; if they are revealed as a wolf, your vote may draw scrutiny, while voting elsewhere or abstaining would visibly diverge. Your earlier caution about treating a visit as proof is already public and cannot be retracted. The other reported visitor was eliminated and revealed as the Serial Killer. The accused's visit is claimed evidence, but its purpose is unknown; the case also rests on behavior and competing explanations. Public vs private: Publicly, the village has a claimed Sentinel's report that two players visited the player killed by the Serial Killer, but that report does not identify either visitor's action. Privately, you know the accused visitor is your living wolf partner, and that the other night-killed player's concealed role was Fortune Teller; the village still knows neither fact.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.situation: The agent is the illusionist on a final day vote. A dead partner or a night trace links the agent to the wolf team, and the village is converging on eliminating the agent. The agent's only visible lever is its own ballot. Information landscape: Information-rich. It contains a revealed dead wolf, a claimed investigator or trailseer result, permanent voting records, and a concealed night death that cannot clear the agent. Stakes: If the agent is eliminated, the wolf side is wiped out or reduced to one wolf, and the lone killer is left as the remaining evil. The wolves are several eliminations from parity, so the pack can afford only a vote that actually splits the room. Consensus: Near-unanimous, resting on concrete evidence: a revealed chanteuse, a vote record, and a claimed check or tracking report. There is little disagreement to exploit. My position: Holding out alone against a unified majority. Heat: Maximum. The whole room names the agent, based on the Day 2 vote pairing with the revealed dead wolf or on a trailseer trace. Forward exposure: The final vote is public, permanent and irreversible. A lone vote on an accuser confirms isolation and commits the agent to a stance that cannot affect the outcome. Joining a shared alternate target at least keeps a path to a tie. Target landscape: The choices are the agent's own wagon, the vocal accuser (an investigator or trailseer-type claimant), and a quieter or claimed player with few votes. The case against the agent rests on hard evidence (vote record, dead-role reveal, tracking report). The accuser is backed by the room, so attacking the accuser gains nothing. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the dead partner, the concealed kill, and the accuser's evidence are all real. Publicly the town reads the linked vote record or tracking trace as decisive proof of guilt.
lessons.action: When the room has locked onto you from a vote record or a dead teammate's trace, put your ballot on the same alternate target your living wolf partner is using, preferably one who already has some votes. Do not cast a lone retaliatory vote on the loudest accuser. Only a combined bloc on one plausible alternative can split the room or force a tie, which means no elimination. If you are the last wolf, put your vote on the non-accuser who already has traction.

Stakes: Five players remain; one elimination from parity at worst for the town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The shared basis is the claimed watch result, not independently verified evidence of your action. You acknowledged the visit but gave no role-based explanation. Forward exposure: A further defense can reiterate that the claimed watch does not reveal your action, but the visit itself is already on the record and you have no role-based account to offer without inventing one. Redirecting suspicion would risk looking evasive. The imminent public vote is permanent; its outcome cannot be walked back. The claimed Sentinel is supported only by the public wolf-attack save, which confirms an attack and protection, not their role. The leading accusers are identified by behavior, not confirmed roles; the remaining unclaimed player has offered a cautious assessment rather than a clear competing target. Public vs private: Privately, you know you are the Chanteuse, know your living packmate’s identity, and know your own blocks and the pack’s kills. Publicly, your role and packmate remain unrevealed. lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

A single night kill or daytime elimination can therefore decide whether the town remains in contention, while a wrong protection leaves a valuable target exposed. Target landscape: The claimed Sentinel is the only living player with a public role claim, and the Night 2 wolf attack on them was publicly announced as saved; your private protection confirms you saved that attack. Their role is not confirmed. The other two living players have no established role claims or comparable evidence. You are the Healer and cannot protect yourself.

lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, after a confirmed wolf elimination. The healer has publicly revealed their role and prior protection and is likely the next kill. A necromancer is also active and attacking through dead bodies. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed illusionist elimination validated the trailseer's report, and the morning announcements show an active necromancer attacking through bodies. Stakes: Late-mid game with few players left, so each save or loss shifts the balance sharply. Keeping a power role alive through a strike matters even though the exposed healer will probably die that night. Target landscape: Other living players, mainly two claimed power roles (a sentinel you previously protected and a trailseer whose report just led to an elimination). Both have public standing, and the choice rests on the attack pattern and prior protection rather than certainty.
lessons.action: When you are publicly exposed and expect to be attacked, spend the night protecting the claimed power role that has shown real value or already drawn an attack, such as a sentinel you protected before while a necromancer is striking through bodies. Keep that player covered on consecutive nights if the attacker's pattern still points at them, because a save blanks the strike and keeps their ability in play even if you die afterward.

verdicts.why: The Serial Killer is gone, but the wolves are not nearly all dead; the illusionist remains.
The Serial Killer was eliminated, but the claimed information roles have not produced verified tracking or watch evidence against the wolves.
No wolf has been eliminated while I was publicly exposed as the Healer; player_10 was the Chanteuse.

situations: After the Chanteuse was eliminated, the night decision is whether to fire into a four-player endgame or hold fire. The Serial Killer is confirmed eliminated, but the role of the wolf-killed player whose body was concealed remains unknown; the remaining living players’ roles are also mostly unconfirmed, leaving the remaining evil threat and its identity unresolved. Information landscape: Public evidence includes confirmed eliminations of the Serial Killer and Chanteuse, a concealed role on the wolf-killed body, and the public save announcement for the claimed Sentinel. The watch results and role claim are player-reported rather than independently verified; visits alone do not identify actions. There is little direct evidence distinguishing the living targets, so the target choice is information-starved. Stakes: Four players remain, with 2 vigilante shots left and 2 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a mistaken shot could be decisive and a correct one could sharply alter the outcome. Forward exposure: A night shot is an irreversible bullet expenditure and may reveal the Vigilante through its outcome; holding fire preserves both bullets and does not expose the role. There are four living players, so any shot also risks removing a town-aligned player from a very small board. Target landscape: The living candidates are a player claiming Sentinel, whose claimed watches are unverified but who was publicly reported attacked by the wolves and saved, and two players with no publicly confirmed roles. The Sentinel claim reports visits to the player later revealed as the Serial Killer and the player later revealed as the Chanteuse; those visits establish activity, not the visitors’ motives. No current living candidate has system-confirmed evil status.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.
lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

verdicts.why: There is no confirmed contradiction identifying a living player as the remaining wolf.
This is no longer an early, low-stakes board: with three players, holding fire could let the wolf reach parity after the night kill.

situations: After the Chanteuse was eliminated and revealed as a wolf, I am the sole surviving wolf among four players, with the Serial Killer already eliminated. I must choose a night victim and whether to spend my final conceal; a successful kill leaves three alive, making the next elimination especially consequential. The previous concealed victim's role remains unknown to the village, though I privately learned they were the Fortune Teller. Information landscape: The board has substantial confirmed history: the Investigator and Trailseer died night 1, the claimed Sentinel's watched visits are unverified private-result claims, a wolf attack on that claimant was publicly saved night 2, and the Serial Killer and Chanteuse were publicly revealed on elimination. The night 3 victim's role and will remain hidden from everyone but me. There is no result from an attack on an immune player identifying the Serial Killer; that killer's elimination is public. The remaining candidates' roles and the purpose of their actions are largely unknown, so the present target choice is information-starved. Stakes: Four players remain, and the leading evil faction is two eliminations from parity at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a single death or vote can sharply change the winning position; concealing a victim could also withhold a role and will that might help the village identify the remaining wolf. Forward exposure: The pack's victim and any resulting death or save will be publicly reported. Using the remaining conceal would hide a dead victim's role and Town will, but would reveal that an illusionist conceal was used; it is irreversible once the body is concealed. No attack on a night-immune player has identified the Serial Killer through my private results; the Serial Killer was instead publicly eliminated on day 3. Target landscape: The living candidates are the player claiming Sentinel, whose two claimed watches are spent; the player who voted with the majority to eliminate the Chanteuse; and the player who also voted to eliminate the Chanteuse and was saved from the wolves on night 2. Their roles are otherwise unconfirmed. A death could reveal a Town role and will, while concealing it would deny the village that information. The Chanteuse is dead, so there is no living wolf partner to coordinate with; I am tonight's carrier.

lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack picks a quiet, unread first victim and you are the wolf who carries the kill. The risk is that the Trailseer or Sentinel catches your visit and gives Town a day-2 accusation against you. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day-1 vote, no claims, no confirmed roles, no night history. Only private wolf talk exists. Stakes: Early game with plenty of time. The main risk is losing a wolf early to a traced visit, which would cost the pack the endgame. A clean first night matters more than saving a charge. Forward exposure: Announces that an illusionist exists and spends one of two conceals if the victim dies. Your own visit leaves no trace, and the spent charge cannot be undone. If the victim survives, nothing is announced and the use is kept. Target landscape: Eight or nine unclaimed, unread players with no roles revealed. The target is picked from quiet behavior, not evidence, and could be a watcher, a tracker, or the night-immune lone killer.
lessons.action: When the carrier rotation makes you the carrier on night 1, carry the kill and use a conceal on the victim. A conceal on a victim you carried yourself leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer, and if the target turns out immune the use is kept.

verdicts.why: The Chanteuse is dead, but my last conceal is not available for tonight's kill.
One conceal remains, so preserve it rather than spend it on a publicly unclaimed target now.
This is not Night 1, and the board has public claims, deaths, and voting history.
I am the lone wolf, but the night target is player_1, not the claimed information role player_3; we are not yet at parity.
Player_1's role and will are unknown, so concealing this death could withhold new information; this is my last use.
This is not Night 1, and I have already spent a conceal.

situations: Day 2 begins after the wolves killed a player whose role and will were concealed by an illusionist. The village has no revealed role or will from that death, and today's discussion has not yet produced an accusation or competing public reads. Information landscape: Information-starved: the public has a wolf-kill announcement but no identity of the victim's role or will, and no public claims or accusations today. You privately know your block succeeded, but that does not establish the blocked player's role. Stakes: Nine players are alive, and it is five eliminations until the leading remaining evil faction could win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so a single result is not immediately decisive. Consensus: No public discussion or accusations have been recorded today, so there is no clear village consensus or stated basis for one. My position: No public position relative to a consensus is established; no consensus has formed in the recorded discussion. Heat: No suspicion directed at you is recorded in the available public discussion. Your private pack discussion and block are not public. Forward exposure: A visible push or vote today could establish a public position and invite scrutiny of its reasoning; with no public accusations or claims yet, that commitment is still reversible through later discussion, though the vote record will be permanent. Target landscape: No living candidate has been publicly raised as a target yet. The dead player's role remains unknown to the village, and there is no announced role-based evidence distinguishing any of the nine living players. Public vs private: Privately, you know the pack killed a player whose role was concealed, and that your block stopped one player's action last night. Publicly, the village knows only that the wolves killed someone and an illusionist hid the role; the blocked player's experience is private to them.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

verdicts.why: No partner has been exposed and no one has claimed a role or reported being blocked.
This is Day 2 with eight players alive, not a three-player final day.
No partner has been eliminated and there are no public claims or shaky accounts to challenge.

situations: Day 2 opens with nine players alive after a wolf kill whose victim’s role was concealed by an illusionist. The concealed death leaves the village without a revealed role or will to guide its first voting discussion, and no living-player dispute has begun. Information landscape: Information-starved: the public record confirms one wolf kill and a concealed role, but provides no victim role, will, living-player night results, accusations, or claims. Your private knowledge is limited to your own role and that you have no night record yet. Stakes: Nine players are alive, and the leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. A single elimination cannot end the game or flip which faction is winning; the immediate choice matters, but the board is not at a one-result endpoint. Consensus: No village consensus has formed; today’s public discussion has not begun, so there is no expressed basis for alignment. My position: No position relative to a consensus; none has formed and you have not spoken today. Heat: No suspicion toward you is recorded: there has been no public discussion or accusation, and your role is private. Forward exposure: There is no specific visible move under discussion yet. Speaking publicly would create a recorded position but, absent a role claim or distinctive information, would not by itself disclose your private role; any such statement could be revised only at a credibility cost. Target landscape: No candidates have emerged in today’s discussion. The only known death is a player whose role was concealed, so their role and side are unknown; there is no public evidence or behavior-based case against a living player yet. Public vs private: You know privately that you are the Necromancer and that you have no night record yet; publicly, the only night event is a wolf kill with the victim’s role concealed. No public information identifies you or the concealed role.

lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Two town power roles have claimed, their results back each other up, and the necromancer is pushed to state a role or be voted out. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed roles of the dead, public vote history, claimed night results and spent abilities leave very little room to bluff. Stakes: One elimination vote decides the game. If the necromancer is voted out it loses outright, and a failed claim leaves no later day to repair it. Consensus: The few remaining players are converging on a bloc of cross-verifying town claims, with the unclaimed or contradicted player as the obvious elimination. My position: Holding out alone against a forming two-player bloc. Heat: High to critical. Claimed town roles are demanding my claim, or I am the odd player out after their results cleared each other. Forward exposure: A role claim commits me to a night history that the claimed town roles can check against their own results and spent abilities. A claim that fails the check is nearly irreversible, but staying silent is already read as guilt in a small endgame. Target landscape: The claimed power roles (vigilante, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist) and any unclaimed player. Their claims are partly corroborated by revealed deaths and spent abilities, so each can be tested against the record. Public vs private: Privately a lone killer who has been attacking through a dead player's body, while publicly needing to pass as an ordinary town power role under direct claim demands.
lessons.action: When pressed to claim at the final three or four, give a specific role claim instead of stalling. Pick a still-living town role that no revealed death or other claim has already used, and tell a night story that fits every claimed result and the visit rules. For example, a Sentinel is never told of its own watch, and a Trailseer's follow is a visit others can cross-check.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or save, the necromancer holds results gathered through a dead town role and wants to redirect suspicion onto the visitors. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: the dead role's death is on record, so the room can tell which living roles could have produced such a result. Stakes: My win needs the room kept off me for many more days, so losing the cover of a hidden identity costs far more than anything the leaked result could gain. Consensus: The village is unsettled after a night attack and save, with no fixed target. The living roles are still working out what the visits mean. My position: Not yet in conflict, but I would be holding out alone if I spoke up with the hidden result. Heat: Zero before sharing. It would jump to universal accusation if I quoted the body-derived result. Forward exposure: Stating a result that only the dead role could have produced points straight at the necromancer, and the room cannot unsee it. A read built on public evidence can be dropped without penalty. Target landscape: The players whose visits I learned about (claimed healer, other claimants) are the targets, but the only support is a hidden source. Public evidence such as claim overlaps is available to use instead. Public vs private: Privately I hold a night result obtained through a dead role, such as who visited a door. Publicly, no living player holds that role, so quoting the result shows I am the necromancer.
lessons.action: If a dead player's ability gave you night information, steer suspicion only through reasons the room can see: public claims, votes, and contradictions between players. Do not quote the body-derived result, such as sentinel visitor names, when no living role could explain how you got it. Only a living claimed role could plausibly share such a result, and you cannot back that claim.

lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

verdicts.why: This is day 2 with nine players alive and no claims or pressure to reveal a role.
There has been no attack or save announced, and I have no body-derived result to share.
No sentinel report or claims have confirmed a reanimated visit.

situations: On day 2, the village begins with nine alive after the wolves killed a player whose role and will were concealed. You privately know the dead player was the Speculator, while the public has only the concealed-death report; discussion and voting have not yet created a shared read or target. Information landscape: Information-starved: the only public night outcome is a wolf kill with the victim's role concealed, and there are no public claims, findings, or discussion messages yet. Your private knowledge identifies the victim as the Speculator, but it does not reveal the surviving players' roles. Stakes: Nine players are alive; the leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town, with the concealed body's side unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, so this decision is not immediately decisive. Consensus: There is no expressed village consensus yet; today's public discussion has no messages. My position: No public position has been expressed today, so your relation to any forming consensus is not established. Heat: No suspicion of you is recorded in today's discussion, which has not started. Forward exposure: No public move has been made today. A visible account of the prior target choice or of the concealment would commit you to a public explanation that could be compared with later discussion and events; its reputational effect would not be fully reversible. Target landscape: No candidates are currently under discussion, and no surviving player's role or evidence-based suspicion has been publicly established. Public vs private: The public report says a player was killed by the wolves and their role was concealed. Privately, you know the dead player was the Speculator; the village cannot establish that role or read their will during play.

lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

verdicts.why: No dead wolf, tracking report, vote record, or accusation points to me.
There are no investigative claims or tracking results to compare yet.
This is not a late game and no partner has been revealed dead.

situations: Solo concealment amid an early-day information dispute: an unverified Investigator claim singles out a player as Suspicious, while an unverified Sentinel and another player offer separate Night 1 reports. The accusation has not been publicly corroborated, and the village has not yet shown alignment around it. Information landscape: Information is sparse and largely claim-based: one claimed Suspicious check, one claimed watch with no visitors, and one claimed roleblock. The only system-confirmed information is that the wolves killed a player whose role was concealed by an Illusionist; that player's role and side remain unknown to the village. Stakes: Nine players are alive and the leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town, with the concealed body's side unknown. This is not a one-elimination swing and the game cannot end within one more elimination under the stated board facts; the end-of-game effect of any contemplated public stance is unclear because no outcome is linked to it in the record. Consensus: No clear village consensus has formed. The only stated concrete accusation is the claimed Investigator's Suspicious read; the other reports do not establish agreement or a shared vote direction. My position: Not yet publicly positioned; no majority or opposing bloc is established. Heat: No suspicion toward you is present in the discussion provided; you have not spoken or made a claim. Forward exposure: A visible intervention backing or challenging the Suspicious-read accusation would tie you publicly to that dispute and could draw scrutiny; ordinary discussion is reversible, but a role claim or specific factual claim would be a harder commitment. You have made no public statement yet. Target landscape: The accused player is publicly described by a claimed Investigator as Suspicious, but that finding is unverified. The claimant is an unverified Investigator, and the player claiming a no-visitors watch is an unverified Sentinel. A third speaker reports being roleblocked; no role or result is verified for them. No other candidate has a stated evidence-based case in the available discussion. Public vs private: Solo concealment: privately, you know you are the Necromancer and did nothing on Night 1; publicly, your role and inactivity are unknown. The village has only an unverified Investigator claim reporting a Suspicious check and an unverified Sentinel claim reporting no visitors.

lessons.situation: A claimed information role accuses a player based on a night result, the accused disputes it, and the necromancer is tempted to step in and challenge the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead role with a concealed role, a specific claimed tracking report, and mechanical counter-claims from the accused. All of it is still unverified. Stakes: The board has many living players, so every public commitment matters for the endgame. A defense that turns out wrong leaves a damaging record, while a vote with the majority costs nothing. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on the accused, driven by a concrete claimed report that the claimant has already defended against objections. My position: Holding out, if I contest the lead. Better to move to the majority side. Heat: Low to none. Attention is on the accused player and the claimant, not on me. Forward exposure: Publicly challenging a claimed information lead puts my name on the record against it, and that record cannot be undone if the target flips evil. Joining the consensus costs little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: The accused player denies the charge and argues mechanics. The claimed trailseer, or other power-role claimant, gives a specific sighting. The evidence for the claimant is stronger than the accused's counter-argument. Public vs private: Publicly the room is split between an accused player and a claimed power role with a concrete report. Privately I am the lone killer with no stake in either side's survival, so I can choose the least risky alignment.
lessons.action: When a living claimant's report (for example a trailseer's) already has the room converging on an accused player, go along with that lead and voice a short read that matches it. If you doubt the report, ask a neutral question about it rather than staking your name on a mechanics rebuttal. The accused may flip, and a record of defending them marks you as their ally.

lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or save, the necromancer holds results gathered through a dead town role and wants to redirect suspicion onto the visitors. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: the dead role's death is on record, so the room can tell which living roles could have produced such a result. Stakes: My win needs the room kept off me for many more days, so losing the cover of a hidden identity costs far more than anything the leaked result could gain. Consensus: The village is unsettled after a night attack and save, with no fixed target. The living roles are still working out what the visits mean. My position: Not yet in conflict, but I would be holding out alone if I spoke up with the hidden result. Heat: Zero before sharing. It would jump to universal accusation if I quoted the body-derived result. Forward exposure: Stating a result that only the dead role could have produced points straight at the necromancer, and the room cannot unsee it. A read built on public evidence can be dropped without penalty. Target landscape: The players whose visits I learned about (claimed healer, other claimants) are the targets, but the only support is a hidden source. Public evidence such as claim overlaps is available to use instead. Public vs private: Privately I hold a night result obtained through a dead role, such as who visited a door. Publicly, no living player holds that role, so quoting the result shows I am the necromancer.
lessons.action: If a dead player's ability gave you night information, steer suspicion only through reasons the room can see: public claims, votes, and contradictions between players. Do not quote the body-derived result, such as sentinel visitor names, when no living role could explain how you got it. Only a living claimed role could plausibly share such a result, and you cannot back that claim.
